When she has done there is a long silence. Then she drops it into the pit.

The wax burns with a smell of resin and old summers. The leaves, in the heat, curl up and go, one at a time, like a hand closing. When the last has gone Maud Hobb steps forward with a trowel and sets a hazel sapling in the ashes, and presses the earth round it with her boot. She says that it is the first honest thing she has ever planted on that ground.

**Wen:** (beside you, with a hand in yours) Do you hear it? The cauldron. It's humming.

You do. It is a low note, steady, from the hall, deep in the seam. It is not a threat. It is a thank-you, from a very long way off, in a voice you last heard at the foot of a grave in the herb garden.

## 1.I4  Interlude: The Long Quiet  (between season 4 and season 5)

**Interlude**

Azure Cloud has seven hundred beds now and a roof that leaks in no corner at all. You have stopped counting the years by the harvest. You count them by the number of times the cauldron by the door has hummed.

*[only if seam is 1]* It hums most in the evenings, with the murmur of a crowd leaving a theatre. Ambrose has filled four notebooks.

One morning you notice that you have been tireless for a month. You go out to the herb garden and the blue flower on Master Hui's stone is open, in the snow.

# 1.S5  Season 5: The Door

## 1.51  "The Cauldron Speaks"  (`dr1`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 236 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The cauldron by the door stops humming on the first night of the frost. It does not go quiet. It clears its throat. Ambrose, who sleeps in the hall to be near it, runs for you in his nightshirt with his notebook in his hand. By the time you come, {wen.first} is already there with a lamp.

**Ambrose:** It said a word. A real one. I wrote it down. I think it was please.

**Closing scene**

You put your ear to the iron. It is warm, as it has never been. Far down inside it, in the seam where Master Hui's crack was mended, there is a voice. It is thin, and dry, and cross. It is a voice you last heard at the foot of a grave in the herb garden.

**Hui:** (down the seam, very faint) I told you to stir clockwise. I am in a dim long room. They let me cook. There is a pot here that has never boiled over, and I find I don't like it. Bring the cauldron when you come. And bring the boy with the notebook. He has a clean hand.

The voice stops. Ambrose is crying and writing at once, and cannot do both. {wen.first} takes the lamp from his hand and sets it on the floor and sits beside him. Nobody says anything. In the iron, a long way off, a ladle rings against a pot.

## 1.52  "Ambrose in the Line"  (`dr2`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `garrison`.  "Walk with Ambrose to the Garrison of the Crossed, {@garrison}."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 203 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Ambrose asks to go before you do. He asks it on a Sunday, after dinner, standing in the kitchen with his notebooks tied in a bundle on his back and the look of a boy who has rehearsed a speech and forgotten it. He says he is a cook. He says Master Hui wants a cook. He says he is sorry to leave in the middle of the pickling.

**Closing scene**

The Garrison stands empty on its bare plain, with the gates open and the beds made. In front of it a line of men and women in good boots wait in the rain with their lamps. Ambrose takes his place at the end. He is the smallest of them, and the only one with a ladle. A tall woman with a grey plait walks down the file with her ledger and writes his name.

**Ambrose:** I'll tell him you're coming. I'll tell him you're slow. He'll like that.

You stand in the rain until the line has gone in. The last thing you see is a thin boy at the gate turning round to wave a ladle. It is, you think, the bravest thing you have seen anyone do with a spoon.

## 1.53  "Hui's Pot"  (`dr3`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `palace`.  "Take the cauldron to the Empty Seat in the Palace of the Oldest Order, at Originis."
- **Pays:** 1,000 spirit stones, +2 potential, 2 Potential Pills, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 150 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You carry the cauldron to the Palace yourself, on a cart, wrapped in a blanket. It is heavier than it has ever been. The Wicks stand aside in the great hall. The Master of the Palace is nowhere. You walk past the nine lamps to the Empty Seat with an iron pot in your arms, and set it down on the flags in front of the chair that nobody sits in. The crack in its side shines.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `latch`; default: option 1)

> The Door is under the Seat. The cauldron is warm. Master Hui is waiting on the other side of a latch.

1. Stay: let the pot go through with a message, and keep the sect.
   - You send it through. You tie a note to the handle in your best hand. It says: still clockwise. The cauldron hums once, deep in its iron, and a small hand reaches up out of the dark under the Seat, and takes it, and draws it down.
   - **Wen:** (a whisper) He'll like that.
2. Go: when your turn comes, carry it yourself.
   - You put your hand on the rim. The iron is warm as a hearth. You say you will come, when it is time, and not before, and not slowly. A voice under the flags says: very good. It is the voice of a man who has been waiting a good while and is pleased to have something to complain about.
3. Hold the latch: stand by the Door and let the next person through with their own pot.
   - You stand by the Seat all afternoon. People come by twos and threes, a Wick with a bundle, a cook with a spoon, a woman with a lamp. You hold the latch while each one goes through. By dusk you have a stiff arm, and a very clear idea of what Master Hui meant by clockwise.

**Closing scene**

The cauldron stays at the Seat all night. In the morning it is quiet, and a little cooler, and when you lift it the crack is shut. Where it was, in the iron, a thin white line shines like a scar that has healed. You carry the pot home. You hang it by the door of the hall. It does not hum again. It has said what it came to say.

## 1.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

Azure Cloud is still not a great sect. It has seventy beds, a roof that leaks in exactly one corner, and a hall in which an old iron cauldron sits by the door with its crack in the light.

*[only if seam is 1]* On certain evenings you can hear them leaving: a murmur in the iron like a crowd leaving a theatre. Nobody has ever found a way to count them.

*[only if seam is 2]* The cauldron is whole. The pills it makes taste of nothing at all, which the children think is a flaw and the old people think is a miracle.

*[only if seam is 3]* On the fifth day of every month a small mark appears on the iron overnight. Ambrose copies it into a book. He says he's almost sure it is a language. Nobody has been brave enough to answer it twice.

*[only if cauldron is 1]* The seam in the old repair shines like a scar that healed well, and lets the light through anyway.

*[only if dead.snuff]* Mister Snuff's snuffer hangs in the kitchen, on a nail, where it is mostly used for candles.

*[only if not dead.snuff]* Once a year a tall man in a grey coat is seen at the end of the road, looking at the sect from a distance. He never comes in. You leave a bowl of soup on the wall. It is always empty by morning.

*[only if e.spouse]* Wen is the person you eat with, and argue with, and wake up beside. When people ask how it began, you tell them: with a cat.

*[only if not e.spouse]* Wen is the person at the end of the table. The door between you stays open. You have both stopped being in a hurry.

*[only if latch is 1]* The cauldron went through with a note tied to its handle. Ambrose copies the answer into his notebook every year on the same day, in his best hand, and has never once shown it to anyone.

*[only if latch is 2]* You have settled that you will go through the Door, when it is time. The pot stands by the hall door, with a ladle in it, ready.

*[only if latch is 3]* You hold the latch at the Seat for an afternoon each autumn. The Wicks have stopped asking. They bring you tea.

Master Hui's stone sits in the herb garden, and every spring a blue flower grows through the crack in it that nobody planted. You tell him how it went. This time, you think, he is listening.

## 1.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

You stay in the Garden, and Azure Cloud stays with you: a small blue banner above the Palace's biggest kitchen. The cracked cauldron sits by the stove. Every new wick is told whose it was.

*[only if not dead.wen]* Wen visits once a year and tells everyone the Palace's herb garden is all wrong. {wen.He} is right.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

The Gardener's army marches under many banners. Yours has a blue cloud on it. On the night before a battle you take out Master Hui's old cracked cauldron and make something small and honest.

The soldiers say it is the only tea in the whole army that hurts nobody.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You leave the Garden with a cracked cauldron on your back. On the other side there is nothing you recognise and everything you need: a fire, a pot, a stranger who is hungry.

You begin, as Master Hui would have wished, with soup.

**You are struck down by the array**

You struck at the Gardener, and the array answered. Master Hui would have called you a fool.

He would have kept your tea warm anyway.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden goes out. The herb garden at Azure Cloud goes with it, and the one tall chimney, and a grave under the chamomile.

You are glad, in that last moment, that somebody saved the cauldron.

# 2.S1  Season 1: The Salt Road

## 2.1  "The Will"  (`will`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** Hold 100,000 spirit stones.  "Show the house is in good hands: hold 100,000 spirit stones."
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 345 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Your father's study smells of ink, old tea, and the sandalwood he burned when he was thinking. He is gone now. The rain has fallen for three days, as if the sky had been told.

The family lawyer is not here. The family steward is. Doric Penn is sixty-one and thin as a quill, and he has kept the books of House {last} since before you could read. He holds the will in both hands, like something that might spill.

**{doric.first}:** The house, the shops, the caravans, and every coin in the vault go to you. Your father wrote it himself a month ago. I watched him sign.

Your cousin {ysolde.first} leans in the doorway with a cup of wine she has not touched. She smiles at you. It is a good smile. It always has been.

**{ysolde.first}:** Congratulations, cousin. Try not to lose it all before spring.

By the window stands {gareth.first}, who has guarded your family since you were small enough to ride on his shoulders. He says nothing. He puts one big hand on your shoulder and leaves it there.

**{doric.first}:** There is one more thing. Your father left this for you, sealed. He said you should open it only when you are ready.

It is a plain envelope, heavier than it looks. On the front, in his sharp hand: 'Numbers before people. People before gold.'

You tuck it into your sleeve. You have more spirit stones than sense, as your father liked to say. Time to go and find some sense.

**Closing scene**

The vault door closes on a hundred thousand and a little more. You stand with your hand on the cold iron, and it feels like the first thing you have ever done by yourself.

**{doric.first}:** Your father would have been proud.

His voice cracks on the last word. He pretends to cough.

The Salt Road caravan leaves next week. Only four people know its schedule: Doric, Ysolde, Gareth, and you. That is how your father always did it. Small circles, he said, keep big secrets.

## 2.2  "The Salt Road"  (`salt`)

- **Starts when:** 20 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Own 2 shops.  "Rebuild your trade: open two shops of your own (the Profession button in a city)."
- **Pays:** 2,000 spirit stones
- **Words:** 150 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Salt Road caravan was due on Tuesday. It arrives on Friday with half its wagons and none of its guards.

The driver, a big man with his arm in a sling, tells it twice. 'They knew the hour. They knew the ford. They knew which wagons held the good stock. Two of our lads didn't come back.'

Four people knew the schedule. You count them again. You don't like the count.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `probe`; default: option 1)

> Someone gave the robbers your schedule. What do you do?

1. Look for the traitor quietly.
   - You say nothing to anyone. You watch. You find that watching is lonelier than shouting.
2. Offer a public reward for the bandits.
   - The notice goes up in every square. Within a week you have eleven liars, four honest men, and no bandits.
3. Change every route and tell no one.
   - You redraw the whole map with a pencil that you keep in your sleeve. Not even Gareth sees it.

**Closing scene**

By midsummer there are two shops with your name over the door. A bell hangs above each, and when it rings you feel it in your chest.

That evening a messenger brings a jar of fine plum wine, sealed with wax. The card inside is written in a neat, sharp hand.

'For the new head of House {last}, from a friend in the trade. I admired your father very much. Odile Kessel.'

## 2.3  "House Kessel"  (`kessel`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet odile (walk to their tile).  "Visit Madam Odile Kessel in {@kessel}."
- **Pays:** nothing

**Opening scene**

House Kessel is the other great merchant house of the province. Your father fought it for thirty years, in prices and in courtrooms, and never said a bad word about it at home. This is the only thing about the feud that has ever troubled you.

It is polite to answer a gift in person.

**Closing scene**

Odile Kessel is silver-haired and sharp-eyed, and she pours her own tea. Her office has no gold in it at all, which is how you know how much she has. At the far end a young person in a plain coat is copying figures into a book, and has the look of someone doing it very slowly so as not to have to do anything else.

**{odile.first}:** My child, {linden.first}. Pay no attention. They are shy, and good with numbers, and I am told I make both worse. Your father was the best opponent I ever had. When one has a good opponent, one grows careless about being lonely.

**{odile.first}:** I heard about your Salt Road. A terrible thing. The roads are not safe these days. Mine are, as it happens.

She lets that sit in the air for a moment, like a coin on a table.

**{odile.first}:** Let us share them. My River Road, your Salt Road, one set of guards. Five thousand spirit stones from me to start, and a promise to leave you alone in the south.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `kessel`; default: option 1)

> Odile Kessel offers a partnership and five thousand spirit stones.

1. Accept the partnership.
   - **{odile.first}:** Splendid. We shall do very well together.
   - You shake her hand. It is dry and warm. You notice that she did not ask a single question about your guards. At the door, {linden.first} looks up from the book, and looks away again, a little too quickly.
2. Decline politely.
   - **{odile.first}:** A pity. The offer will remain open, but not for ever.
   - She smiles, and the smile does not move any other part of her face. At the door {linden.first} looks up from the book, and gives you something very close to an apology.

Another caravan goes missing. A third is delayed on a road that nobody should have known. You stop pretending it is bad luck.

You begin with the books, because your father said to. Numbers before people. The oldest hands are the ones to ask first, so you go to find Doric.

**Closing scene**

The vault ledger spans twenty years. It is beautifully kept. It has also been touched, here and there, by a tired hand: small sums, taken and put back, taken and put back.

*[only if culprit is 1]* On Doric's desk, half empty, sits a jar of plum wine with a wax seal you know.

**{doric.first}:** I borrowed from the petty cash. Eleven times in four years. I paid it all back, with interest. It was for my granddaughter's lungs. The healer would not wait.

He is looking at the floor. He looks very old.

**{doric.first}:** I should have asked your father. I was ashamed. I am more ashamed now.

The house is small, bright, and full of laughter. Lanterns hang in the plum trees. The wine is excellent.

*[only if culprit is 2]* It is plum wine, in bottles with a wax seal you know.

## 2.7  "The Wax"  (`wax`)

- **Starts when:** 10 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet clerk (walk to their tile).  "Ask the wine merchant, Hobb Tuck, who buys the Kessel plum wine in your house."
- **Pays:** nothing

**Opening scene**

Three people you love have a bottle of plum wine with a wax seal you know, and not one of them thought it was odd. You think it is the oddest thing in the world.

The wine merchant is a few streets from the vault. He has a cellar that smells of cork and cold stone, a ledger as fat as a loaf, and the fixed, helpful cheerfulness of a man who has been asked difficult questions before and enjoyed them. His name is Hobb Tuck.

**Closing scene**

**Tuck:** Kessel's wine? Oh, I don't sell it. I only store it. Madam Kessel's agent buys by the crate and sends it out as gifts, to the right sort of people. Merchants. Magistrates. Stewards. That sort. I hold it in the cellar till the day. It's a hobby of hers. She says a bottle is the cheapest way to say you've noticed someone.

**You:** Three crates came to my house.

**Tuck:** Three, yes. I remember the day. Same afternoon, spring, the third week. A good vintage. And one of them, I do remember it, because a man notices when a crate goes out heavy, went with a second parcel. Small, flat, wrapped in plain paper. Like a letter. I would not say. It is not my business.

**You:** Which one?

**Tuck:** That I could not tell you. They all went out together on one cart. I'm very sorry. I never look at the labels. It is a point of professional honour.

He sees your face and says, with real regret, that he does wish he had. The cellar is cold. You stand among all the bottles until your feet ache, with three names in your head and a fourth, in a neat sharp hand, at the back of them.

## 2.8  "Three Roads"  (`road`)

- **Starts when:** 12 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `crossroads`.  "Wait at the crossroads inn, {@crossroads}, for news of the three roads."
- **Pays:** nothing

**Opening scene**

There is a way to catch a liar that your father taught you when you were ten, over a game of draughts. You never knew you remembered it. You tell each of them a different truth.

You write three schedules. Doric hears the North Ford. Ysolde hears the Old Bridge. Gareth hears the Red Pass. No one hears the true route, which you tell to the driver alone, and then forget. Then you ride to an inn at the crossroads, {@crossroads}, with the three of them in tow, on the pretext of a family council, and the cold feeling of a person who has set a trap for people they love.

**Closing scene**

The night is long, and nobody is quite themselves. Doric turns the pages of a book he cannot read in the light. Ysolde plays patience with a deck that is one card short and does not seem to mind. Gareth stands by the door with his arms folded, an old habit, and when the innkeeper asks him to sit he says that he would rather not.

The messengers return at dawn. Two of them say there was nothing on their road but wind and rooks. The third comes in at a run, mud to the knees.

**Messenger:** Riders at the ford! Twenty of them, all in grey. They were waiting. They waited the whole night, in the rain.

*[only if culprit is 1]* The North Ford. Doric.

*[only if culprit is 2]* The Old Bridge. Ysolde.

*[only if culprit is 3]* The Red Pass. Gareth.

The innkeeper sets down a bowl of soup in front of you. You do not touch it. Nobody in the room looks at anyone else, and one of them, you see, is not looking at you in a way that is different from the others, and has been all night.

*[only if culprit is 2]* **{ysolde.first}:** Odile promised me the Salt Road. My own road, my own name. I thought the guards would run, not fight. I thought nobody would be hurt. Then I read the names of the two boys, and I couldn't stop reading them.

*[only if culprit is 3]* **{gareth.first}:** Kessel bought Hal's debt. She said, one name and the debt is gone. Then it was dates. Then it was routes. I never gave her a guard's name, I swear it. And two of them died anyway. You can do what you like. I won't lift a hand.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `fate`; default: option 1)

> What happens to the one who sold you?

1. Forgive them, and keep them close.
   - *[only if culprit is 1]* **You:** You will fix every book you ever touched, and then you will teach someone else to keep them honestly.
   - *[only if culprit is 1]* He does, every night for the rest of his life, and he never once asks for a raise.
   - *[only if culprit is 2]* **You:** You will run the Salt Road under my eye, for nothing, until the families of those two boys say we are square.
   - *[only if culprit is 2]* She does, and she is better at it than anyone you have ever hired.
   - *[only if culprit is 3]* **You:** We will pay Hal's debt. Not to Odile, to whoever she sold it to. And you will tell me everything you told her.
   - *[only if culprit is 3]* He does. It takes all night. He weeps through half of it, and does not stop talking.

   - *[only if culprit is 3]* Gareth will not take the purse. He walks out in only the clothes he stands in.
3. Give them to the magistrate.

   - *[only if culprit is 2]* Ysolde is given three years, and the shame of it, which is longer.

## 2.10  "Sealed Until Ready"  (`envelope`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 2,000 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 330 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You carry the envelope for another month before you open it. It has been in your sleeve through all of it, through the vault, the road, the inn, and the long walk home from the counting room. The seal is a single drop of dark wax with your father's thumb pressed into it.

You open it in his study, at his desk, with the rain on the window, because it seems the thing to do. The seal cracks like a knuckle.

**Closing scene**

'My child. I have been dreading this letter for thirty years, and I find that I have nothing to say that is not an excuse. So I will say the plain thing. Odile Kessel and I began in one stall. Salt and string. Two years we shared a barrow and a quarrel and a bed of straw. She did the sums. I did the talking. We were going to build a house.'

'When the first good contract came, I took it. I put my name on it and not hers. I told her it was the safe way. It was a lie. She was left with the debts of the barrow and I was left with the house. I have called what came after a rivalry for thirty years, because that is a cleaner word. It was a theft, and I have paid for it every day in a currency I can't count.'

'Whatever she does to you, ask what I did to her first. Numbers before people, so you do not lie to yourself. People before gold, so you do not become the thing I became. I do not ask you to forgive me. I ask you not to be me. Father.'

You read it three times. Outside, the rain has stopped, and the lamps along the street are lit, and across the province in a plain office with no gold in it, an old woman has just put down a pen.

## 2.I1  Interlude: Plum Wine  (between season 1 and season 2)

**Interlude**

The house settles. The caravans run. The two wells in the courtyard are named for two boys, and nobody has asked you to. People say the new head of House {last} is a quiet sort, who keeps the books of the dead.

*[only if fate is 1 and culprit is 1]* Doric Penn fixes books by candle, with a small boy on his knee, and does not once say he is sorry. He doesn't have to.

*[only if fate is 1 and culprit is 2]* Ysolde runs the Salt Road. She is the best guide it ever had.

*[only if fate is 1 and culprit is 3]* Gareth guards the vault, and Hal sweeps the stable. Neither has touched a card in a year.

*[only if fate is 2]* There is a letter now and then, from a town with a sea. You leave it a day before you open it.

*[only if fate is 3]* The sentence ends in the spring. You meet them at the gate with a coat, and say nothing for the first mile.

*[only if kessel is 1]* The Kessel partnership is, on paper, still in force. A bottle of plum wine arrives every month with no card.

*[only if kessel is 2]* You declined the Kessel offer, and the Kessel offer, as promised, has stayed open.

The envelope is in a drawer of the desk, and sometimes you take it out and do not read it. Odile Kessel is old. She will not be forgotten. She has just not yet decided what she wants.

# 2.S2  Season 2: The Fall of House Kessel

## 2.11  "A Seat at the Table"  (`guild`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet pettifer (walk to their tile).  "Speak to Guildmaster Pettifer about the Kessel motions."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> { crew(c, st); Chapters.spawn(c, st, "pettifer"); }`
- **Words:** 300 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Merchants' Guild meets four times a year in a hall designed by an architect who disliked chairs. It has a long table, a short gallery, and a system of motions so elaborate that, in the memory of the oldest member, only one has ever been passed, and that one by accident, during a faint.

You have a seat now. It is the one your father had, at the end, by the draught. The man who runs the meetings is Guildmaster Pettifer, a very small, very round person in a very tall hat, who calls every vote a 'sense of the room' and every defeat a 'deferral'.

On the far side sits Odile Kessel. She has not looked at you once. The envelope in your breast pocket is warm, like something that wants to be taken out.

**Closing scene**

The sitting lasts nine hours. At the sixth, a motion to table a motion to table a motion is lost on a technicality involving a missing comma. At the seventh, the Guild sings. At the eighth, Pettifer announces that the matter before the room is 'the matter before the room', and that he has no more to add.

**Pettifer:** You will find we do not like to be hurried. It is a handsome feature. In three hundred years the Guild has never made a decision it has regretted, and for the very good reason that it has never made one.

On the steps afterwards, in the cold, the Kessel carriage sits at the kerb. The door opens. Nobody gets out. Someone inside, in a plain coat, with a ledger on their knee, lifts a hand to you. It is not a wave. It is the smallest gesture a person can make and still be said to have made one.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `stance`; default: option 1)

> Odile has put three motions against your house, and the Guild is waiting.

1. Fight her in the open: demand a vote on all three.
   - **Pettifer:** A vote. In the open. How refreshing. It has not happened since the Year of the Flood, and then only because the doors were stuck.
   - The motions fail by one voice. The voice, you learn later, belonged to a man who thought he was voting on the soup.
2. Offer terms before the vote, in private.
   - **Odile:** You wish to talk. How civil. Your father never did.
   - She will see you. She says it as one gives a coin to a child, and you take it as one takes a coin from a woman who is counting.
3. Say nothing, and work against her from inside her own house.
   - You smile at the table. You nod at the right moments. You are, by general agreement, the dullest person present, and nobody notices that you are writing everything down.

## 2.12  "Linden Counts"  (`fair`)

- **Starts when:** 10 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet linden (walk to their tile).  "Meet {linden.first} Kessel at the horse fair."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 329 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The note says only: HORSE FAIR, THE THIRD AFTERNOON, BY THE BAD CHESTNUT. It is unsigned. It is written in a hand you have seen once, in a ledger, copying figures slowly so as not to have to do anything else.

The horse fair is held in a field beside a river, in a smell of dung and lemonade and money. You find the bad chestnut. It is a large, soulful, ruined animal with a rolling eye and the air of an actor who has been waiting for a better part. Next to it, in the plain coat, stands {linden.first} Kessel, with a halter in one hand and a very worried look.

**Closing scene**

**{linden.first}:** I'm told I should not speak to you. I'm told this at every meal. I want to buy this horse. The man says it is sound, and I do not believe him, and I would like to see whether you will say so.

**You:** It's lame in the off hind. The hock is thick. It's been fed to look sleek, and it has an old cough.

**{linden.first}:** Thank you. I was hoping you would be rude about it. I'll buy it anyway. Someone must.

The horse is bought. {linden.first} pays by counting out the price in coppers, one at a time, into the dealer's hat, in a steady and rather beautiful rhythm that makes the dealer look at his hat as though it were a stranger. You find you are watching the hands more than the money.

**{linden.first}:** My mother talks about your father every night at dinner. Every night. As if he were in the room. I used to think it was hatred. I'm no longer sure. I don't know what to call it when a person has been thinking of someone for thirty years.

The horse chooses this moment to lean its whole warm weight on your shoulder. {linden.first} laughs, and then looks, for a second, as though the laugh were not entirely permitted.

## 2.13  "The Quiet Burglary"  (`burglary`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `kessel`.  "Go to House Kessel at {@kessel} and read her records."
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> crew(c, st)`
- **Words:** 328 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The records of House Kessel are kept in a strongroom under the floor of the room where she does her sums. The house has eleven locks on the street door and a night porter who is paid not to have a favourite biscuit. You plan it in your own study with the shutters closed.

*[only if has.gareth]* **{gareth.first}:** I can do the porter. I can do the porter with a plate of dumplings and a long story about my brother. He's soft. They're always soft.

*[only if has.ysolde]* **{ysolde.first}:** I'll take the street door. The locks are Dunmarsh pattern, six pins. I've known their maker's wife since I was fifteen. It would be an insult to her husband if I couldn't.

*[only if has.doric]* **{doric.first}:** I will do the paper. I can make any hand in the province. I would like it noted that I never thought I'd say that sentence with a clean conscience.

It is, you reflect, an extraordinary group. Three people who once failed you, or nearly did, or were thought to, sit round a table with a tea-tray and a floor plan. They discuss a felony with the calm of a church committee on the matter of the roof.

**Closing scene**

The burglary takes four hours and goes almost exactly as planned, which is to say that it goes wrong in the first twenty minutes. It is rescued by the one thing nobody anticipated. The night porter is asleep with an open book on his chest, and the book is Doric's own treatise on double-entry bookkeeping, of which the porter has been fond for years.

*[only if has.doric]* **{doric.first}:** I had no idea. I'm quite overcome. I'll sign it for him on the way out.

The strongroom is not large. It is dry and orderly and smells of lavender. Along the back wall, in a long wooden chest, tied in a faded ribbon, lie the papers you came for. A thin bundle, much handled, with a title in a girl's hand, forty years old: PARTNERSHIP, SALT AND STRING.

## 2.14  "What Odile Owed"  (`owed`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** a technique insight
- **Words:** 251 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You read it in the strongroom, sitting on the floor, by the dark lantern, with your back against a chest. The partnership agreement is two pages long. It is signed in two hands: one sharp, one round. Below the signatures a third hand has added, in a small neat script, a clause that reads: 'And should either of us profit unfairly, let the other be told, and let them decide.'

There are letters too. Forty years of them, never sent. Odile wrote to your father on the first of every month, in the same neat script, and put the letter in the chest. The early ones are furious. The middle ones are dry and funny. The last, dated a week before his death, begins: 'Dear Tobias, I find I have run out of things to be angry about, and I do not know what to do with the hands.'

**Closing scene**

On the way out there is a small thing that is easy to miss. A chair in the corner, an old one, with a worn seat, set out of the way. A woman's shawl hangs on its back, grey and moth-eaten. Someone has put a cup beside it, with a dried ring of tea in the bottom, and on the cup, in the girl's hand, is a single initial: T.

She has laid a place for him. She has laid it, you guess, every night for thirty years, in the one room she is certain nobody will go.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `grudge`; default: option 1)

> The proof that your father took her name, her contracts, and her half of the house is in your lap.

1. Burn the partnership and the letters: let the old man's name be clean.
   - The fire is small and orderly. You watch it go. It is the first time you have understood why your father wrote the letter the way he did, and why he could not post it himself.
2. Keep them, and decide later.
   - You tie the ribbon again, exactly as she had it, and put the bundle in your coat. You will find, in the weeks to come, that you cannot sit with your back to a door.
3. Return the stolen contracts to Odile, and everything with them.
   - **Gareth:** You're going to tell her. You are actually going to tell her.
   - **You:** I'm going to give her back what he took. Telling her is the part I can't help.

## 2.15  "Hettie's Lungs"  (`hettie`)

- **Starts when:** 6 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Cultivation Pill, 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 420 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

There is a girl at the vault door on a grey afternoon, small for twelve, wrapped in a shawl several sizes too big, with a cough that comes in a series, like a stair. She carries a satchel of papers. She says her name is Hettie, and that she is the granddaughter of Doric Penn, and that she would like, if it is not too much trouble, to see where her grandfather worked.

*[only if has.doric]* **{doric.first}:** I couldn't stop her. She read the whole of my treatise at nine. She has views on the second schedule. She is a terror.

*[only if not has.doric]* Her letter, which she holds out in one small damp fist, is two pages long and perfectly spelt. It says that her grandfather has written to her every month, from wherever he is, and that he has told her about you, and that she would like to see the place.

**Closing scene**

She goes through the vault in a quarter of an hour, with her nose in the air. She reads the plate on every door. She wants to know why the green ledgers are on the left, and the red on the right, and who decided, and whether it might be done the other way. When she comes to the counting room, she stops dead on the threshold.

**Hettie:** It's exactly the same. Grandfather said it was. He said the air smells of ink and lemon oil and a little of cheese. He said it was the best smell in the world and that I would know it. I do.

She walks to the high desk by the window, and lays one hand on the polished wood, and the cough takes her, long and tearing, so that she bends over and holds the desk with both hands. You are beside her in a moment. She waves you off, and straightens, and wipes her mouth, and says in a thin steady voice: 'It was for this that he took the money. The healer wouldn't wait. I know.'

**You:** He put it back.

**Hettie:** With interest. I did the figures. He's a very good man who did a bad thing for a good reason. I've been trying to decide, for two years, which of them to write to.

She looks up at you with the face of a clever child who has been carrying a heavy parcel a long way and is not sure that it has been right to put it down.

**Hettie:** I think I'll write to the one who put it back.

## 2.16  "Odile's Beans"  (`garden`)

- **Starts when:** 4 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 414 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You go to see her on a Thursday, without a letter, which is not done. The office with no gold in it is shut. A clerk tells you, with a certain wild look, that Madam is at the back, and that she would prefer not to be disturbed, and that she has not been in the building since Monday.

She is in a small walled yard behind the counting-house. It is a yard you have never seen. It has a pump, and a rain-barrel, and a patch of black earth about the size of a door, and in the patch, in neat rows, tied to sticks, a great many bean plants. Odile Kessel is kneeling in the middle of them in a black dress and a pair of men's gloves.

**Closing scene**

**Odile:** They're not doing well. I want you to see that. I have never failed at anything. I have run the trade of a province for forty years. And I have planted a row of beans eleven times, and I can't get them to climb.

She sits back on her heels. She pulls off a glove, and holds a tendril between her fingers, a limp green curl, as she would hold a wrist. 'It's a matter of the pole,' she says. 'They tell me it needs to be taller. I have put in taller poles. They sulk.'

**You:** Could I look?

**Odile:** You are a merchant's child. You know nothing of beans.

**You:** No. But I'm a merchant's child. I know what happens when you tie something up too tight.

She looks at you. She looks at the plants. She looks, slowly, at the strings that run from the poles to the stalks, tied in beautiful neat tight bows, each one precisely the same. She says nothing for a time. Then she reaches out, and unties one, and the little plant leans against the pole as if it had been let out of a corset.

**Odile:** Thirty years. And it was the knots.

You spend the afternoon on your knees in the black earth, the two of you, untying them one by one. It is the most peaceful afternoon you have spent in a year. She talks. She does not mention your father, or the Table, or the Guild. She talks about the weather in the year that she was nine, and a goat called Philippa, and the day she first saw a ledger and thought it the most beautiful thing in the world.

**Opening scene**

She finds you before you find her, which is how you know she is good. Cressida Kessel is a handsome, quick, restless woman of thirty-three, in an excellent coat, with her mother's eyes and none of her mother's patience. She waits in your outer office with a folder, looking at the paintings as if pricing them.

**Cressida:** I do hope I am not intruding. I thought we might save each other some trouble. You want my mother's house broken. I want her house. The two are less far apart than the Guild would like to think.

**Closing scene**

Cressida leaves a card, and a rosewater scent, and the distinct impression of a person who has already won an argument that has not yet begun.

{linden.first} comes to your door that evening, uninvited, with rain on the plain coat and a ledger under one arm. They do not wait to be asked in.

**{linden.first}:** I know she's been here. She has told everyone she will be running the house by spring. I want to be clear. I do not want it. I've never wanted it. I want to count things in a quiet room and go home.

**{linden.first}:** But I will not watch my sister make my mother into a ledger entry. Whatever you do, please do it to her, and not to me.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `cressida`; default: option 1)

> Cressida would like to help you overthrow her mother, and take the chair afterwards.

1. Refuse. You will not make a house by tearing one down from inside.
   - **Cressida:** A pity. I thought you were practical. Never mind. I shall do it without you, and then you will be dealing with me, instead of a very tired old woman.
   - She goes. You feel, for the first time, how large the house is that you are fighting, and how many doors it has.
2. Agree. It is the quickest road, and you have been patient long enough.
   - **Cressida:** Splendid. We shall do very well together.
   - You have heard those words before, in an office with no gold in it. You are aware of that. You say yes anyway.
3. Pretend to agree, and tell Linden.
   - She smiles, and it is her mother's smile, the one that moves no other part of the face. You smile back, and you are surprised how easily it comes.

The invitation is engraved, delivered by hand, and signed in the neat sharp script: 'Madam Odile Kessel requests the pleasure.' It does not say of what. There is a footnote, in what looks like a different ink. It says: 'There will be soup.'

The table at House Kessel is long enough to land a boat on. There are six places laid, and a seventh, at the foot, with a worn chair and a shawl on the back, and a cup. Nobody mentions it. Everybody sits round it as water sits round a stone.

**Odile:** You are very welcome. I am told that you went through my strongroom last month. I think it was a clever plan. I think the dumplings were an unusual touch. Please eat. It would be a waste otherwise, and I do not like a waste.

**Closing scene**

On the way out, you glance back. The old woman is sitting at the head of the table, alone, with her hand lying on the empty chair. She does not appear to have noticed.

> Odile, Cressida and Linden are at the table. A choice must be made before the soup is cold.

1. Side with Odile: tell her what you found, and what you mean to do about it.

2. Side with Cressida: she will end the war faster.

## 2.19  "A Motion to Table the Motion"  (`motion`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 374 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Guildmaster Pettifer calls an extraordinary session in the seventh week. This is unprecedented. The last extraordinary session was held in the Year of the Fire, and was adjourned because of it. The room is full, and the gallery is full, and the door is full, and a small man at the back is selling fried dough in a paper bag.

**Pettifer:** The matter before the room is the matter of Madam Odile Kessel and her conduct. The question is whether a motion may be put that she be removed from the Guild without having been, in the traditional sense, notified. I should like to hear the sense of the room.

The sense of the room is a low murmur, like a pot coming to the boil.

**Closing scene**

It takes five hours. There is a motion to remove Odile Kessel. There is an amendment to remove her sister, who is not a member. There is a motion to table the amendment, which is lost on a point of order concerning who was entitled to table what. There is a motion that the Guild now sing, which is carried by acclamation, and the Guild sings, and Pettifer weeps.

At the sixth hour, when the dust has settled and the gallery has gone home, there is a vote. It is a vote on a motion no one can quite remember. It carries, by a single voice. It is the voice of the man who sells the dough, who has come in from the back to say that it has gone cold, and has been counted as a member because he was standing in the aisle.

**Pettifer:** The Guild has spoken. I am as surprised as anyone. I shall see that the minutes are circulated.

Odile Kessel, in her black coat, in the front row, rises as the room empties, and picks up her hat from the floor. She puts it on. She looks at the Guildmaster with her head on one side, as one looks at a clock that has done something unexpected. She says: 'In thirty years, I have never been so thoroughly beaten by a procedure.' Then she smiles. It is the first time you have seen her do it with her mouth.

## 2.20  "The Salt Road Auction"  (`auction`)

- **Starts when:** 6 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Hold 500,000 spirit stones.  "Buy up House Kessel's notes: hold 500,000 spirit stones."
- **Pays:** 5,000 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 266 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

There is a way to fight a merchant that is neither a duel nor a lawsuit, and that is to buy what she owes. Odile Kessel has seventeen outstanding notes, held by nine different lenders, and the Guild is about to put them to auction in the great hall by order of a magistrate who has not read them.

The auction is conducted by a rotund auctioneer called Mr. Chaffinch, who has the voice of an organ and the speed of a glacier, and who is known to take a bid from anyone who raises a hand, a hat, a cane, or an eyebrow. A donkey has been brought in by mistake. Nobody has the heart to take it out.

**Closing scene**

The bidding lasts four hours. By the fifth lot, Mr. Chaffinch has taken three bids from the donkey, one from a sleeping man, and one from a bluebottle, and has declared the bluebottle to be acting for a syndicate. You buy every note. It takes everything, and it takes, towards the end, a quantity of bluff that you would not have thought you possessed.

When the gavel falls on the last lot, you hold seventeen pieces of paper, and across the hall, very still, in a plain black coat, sits the woman whose name is on all of them. She is not looking at the notes. She is looking at you, and in her face is something you have never seen on a merchant, and cannot at first name. It is relief.

**Mr. Chaffinch:** Sold, to the lady in the hat. And the donkey.

## 2.21  "A Letter to Tobias"  (`tobias`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 360 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You write it in the evening, in your father's study, at his desk. It is not meant to be sent. There is nowhere to send it. You write it on a plain sheet in the plain hand he taught you, and you find that the first line is the hardest, and that it is only 'Dear Father'.

It takes the night. You write about the stall, and the string, and the salt. You write about a girl with a round hand and a sharp mind who did the sums while he did the talking. You write that you have read her letters, all of them, and that the early ones are not what you expected, and that the late ones are unbearable. You write that you do not forgive him, and that you do not not forgive him, and that you are sitting in his chair.

**Closing scene**

You never send it. You fold it in four and put it in the drawer where the envelope lay. Then you do something else. You take a clean sheet and write, in the same hand: 'Dear Madam Kessel.' You write four lines. They are very plain. You say that you have read the chest. You say that you are sorry for the thirty years. You say that you do not ask for an answer.

The reply comes in three days. It is on a single card, in the neat sharp script. It says: 'I have been waiting for this letter for forty years. It was not addressed to me. It was addressed to him. I have decided to accept it on his behalf. Come to tea. I have the best chair for you. It is the one he used to take. I have been keeping it warm.'

You read it standing in the hall with your coat on. You put it in your pocket. You take it out and read it again. Then you go and tell the cook that you will be out for tea, and the cook, who has been with the family for twenty years and has never been told anything in advance, drops a plate.

She receives you in the office with no gold in it. She has not lit the lamp, though it is dusk. She has cleared the desk. On it lies a single sheet and a pen, uncapped, and a cup of tea gone cold, and beside the cup a pair of spectacles she does not usually wear.

**Odile:** You hold my notes. You hold my house. You hold, I understand, the letters I did not send. I find that I am not the least afraid. I thought I should be. Thirty years I have spent being afraid of exactly this room, with exactly you in it, and now it has come, and I find it rather restful.

**Odile:** Name your terms, child. I am too old to argue.

**Closing scene**

*[only if fall is 1]* In the empty hall, long after, a figure stands in the doorway of the office, with a lamp. It is {linden.first}, and it is not clear for whom {linden.he} came. {linden.He} sets the lamp on the desk. 'I was afraid I would feel nothing,' {linden.he} says. 'It turns out I feel everything. It's a surprise.'

*[only if fall is 2]* The partnership is drawn up in a week. In the margin of the final page, in a small neat script, Odile has added a clause: 'And should either of us profit unfairly, let the other be told.' She has underlined it. She does not say who it is for.

*[only if fall is 3]* The notes go on the fire, seventeen of them, in a neat pile, and the flame is tall and brief. Cressida comes in through the door as the last one goes, white to the lips, and stands very still. 'I'd have used them,' she says. Odile looks at her over the spectacles. 'I know,' she says. 'That's why I'm giving them up.'

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `fall`; default: option 1)

> House Kessel is yours to decide.

1. Ruin her. Call every note, and let the house be sold.
   - It takes four months. When it is done, the Kessel sign comes down from the great hall and nobody speaks of it again. You sleep badly for a year.
   - *[only if grudge is 3]* **Odile:** And the contracts?
   - *[only if grudge is 3]* **You:** I returned them last winter. They're in your chest, in the ribbon.
2. Make her a partner on your terms, and give her back the half your father took.
   - She signs, with a hand that does not shake. 'Fair,' she says. 'I would have asked for less.' You both pretend that it is a compliment.
   - *[only if grudge is 3]* **Odile:** You gave back the contracts first. I noticed. It made a difference.
3. Tear up the notes, and let her keep her house.
   - **Odile:** That is not what your father would have done.
   - **You:** No. I'm not him.
   - She laughs, short and surprised. It is the first honest sound you have heard from her.

## 2.24  "A Piece of Ground"  (`ground`)

- **Starts when:** 3 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `site`.  "Go to the field at {@site}, where the city might stand."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "brindle")`
- **Words:** 345 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You have more money than you need, and it sits in vaults and does nothing. You hear your father's voice, which is not a thing you expected: 'Money that does not move is a rock.' A city is the largest thing that a person can make that is not a war.

Brindle the stonecutter has been told to find you a site. He is a stout man with an enormous moustache and arms like bridge piers. He has taken the matter with the solemnity of a man who has been waiting thirty years for someone to ask him to build something that is not a wall.

**Brindle:** I've three. One's on a hill, and it's dry, and the wind will take your hat. One's by a river, and it's wet, and the river will take your hat. And one's a field in the middle of nowhere, where there is nothing at all, and it will take whatever you put there. I like that one best. It has the most room for mistakes.

**Closing scene**

The field is large and green and entirely empty. A line of hills at the north, a stream at the south, and above it a sky so big that you lose your sense of how small you are. Brindle walks it with a string and a bag of pegs, muttering to himself like a priest at a service in a foreign tongue.

**Brindle:** Here's the market. Here's the gate. Here's where the temple would be, if you wanted one, which you don't, because nobody ever does till the plague comes. And here, in the middle, the vault. You can't have a city without a vault. It's the first thing the thieves look for.

He drives a peg into the grass at the exact centre of the field. It makes a small flat sound. It is the first thing that has ever been put there on purpose.

**You:** What do we call it?

**Brindle:** Oh, that's not for me. I only lay the stones. You'll have to ask the people who live in it.

**Opening scene**

A city, you learn, requires seventeen permits, of which nine are issued by the Lord Chamberlain, and of those nine, six cannot be applied for until the others have been granted. The Lord Chamberlain is a very old man in a very new office, with a desk the size of a bedroom, who greets every petition with the words, 'I shall put it in the pile.'

**Vask:** It is a question of order. I do not say it is a reasonable order. I say it is mine. You will want the Permit of Foundation. That requires the Permit of Survey, which requires the Permit of Standing, which can only be had by a person who has already founded a city. I do not make the rules. I merely enforce them in the order in which I find them.

**Closing scene**

*[only if permit is 1]* You leave with a satchel of permits and the grim satisfaction of a person who has done it by the book. Vask sees you to the door. 'You will be a very bad city,' he says. 'You will have rules.'

*[only if permit is 2]* You leave with the charter, and the clause, and a firm instruction to keep your mouth shut. Within the week the clause is cited in eleven lawsuits across the province, and Vask is promoted.

*[only if permit is 3]* You leave with a satchel of permits and a vague sense of having stepped in something. Vask waves from the window. He seems happier than when you arrived.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `permit`; default: option 1)

> The Lord Chamberlain has a circle for you to get round.

1. Be patient: spend a season filling in every form in the correct order.
   - It takes four months, eleven ink bottles, and a clerk with a stoop. At the end Vask stamps the last page, looks at it for a time, and says, with something like regret: 'Nobody has ever done it correctly before.'
2. Find the clause in the original charter that makes the whole thing unnecessary.
   - Doric's treatise on charter law has been in your study for years. You read it again, from the back. In the third schedule, in a footnote that has been there four hundred years, you find the clause. Vask reads it three times. He sits very still. 'Well,' he says. 'I never.'
3. Quietly make it worth his while.
   - **Vask:** I have not been offered such a thing since my wedding. I shall put it in the pile.
   - The permits come through on Thursday. The pile, it appears, has a trapdoor.

**Opening scene**

Brindle has a daughter. You would not have guessed it. He has mentioned her four times in three years, always sideways, as a man might mention a weather. She is called Wren, and she is twelve, and she arrives on the field one morning with a theodolite on her shoulder that is larger than her head.

**Brindle:** I told her not to. She read my books. She read them in the night, under the blanket. She's a head for angles. I have said she's to be a seamstress, and she has said she won't, and I've said it's a fine trade, and she has said that it is, and she won't.

**Closing scene**

She is better than he is. It is a terrible thing to see, for a father, and a lovely one. She walks the line of the main street in a morning with a chain, a sighting-rod, and a boy of nine to hold the end. She calls out numbers in a clear flat treble, and she is right. Her father, at the far end, with his moustache twitching, checks each one with a plumb-line and finds that it is.

**Wren:** You've put the market in the wrong place. It's in the lee of the hill. It'll get all the wind off the river and none of the sun. You should move it two hundred yards east.

**Brindle:** It's been on the plan since March.

**Wren:** Then the plan's wrong.

There is a very long pause. Then Brindle takes off his cap, and scratches his head with the corner of the brim, and says in a muffled voice: 'Well. That's the best news I've had all year.'

## 2.28  "What to Call It"  (`cityname`)

- **Starts when:** 3 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones

The camp has a population of eleven hundred, a gate with no gate in it, and no name. This has started to matter. Letters addressed to it arrive marked THE CITY, or THE FIELD, or in one instance, THE PLACE WITH THE MAN WITH THE MOUSTACHE. Brindle takes the last as a compliment.

**Brindle:** It wants a name. You can't have a town and not know what to put on the cart.

**You:** We could ask the people.

**Brindle:** God help us.

**Closing scene**

The vote is held in the square, which is a patch of beaten earth between the market and the pump. A table is carried out. A box is put on the table. Slips of paper are given out by a girl of ten, and a stub of pencil is passed down the line, and a hush falls such as comes on a crowd when it is asked to be wise.

The counting takes until midnight. There are four hundred and nine slips, and a hundred and twelve different names. There is Newfield, and Saltgate, and Hope. There is a name that is a joke, and a name that is a rude word in the old dialect, and a name that appears to be a curse. There are eleven votes for the donkey. There are nineteen for Brindle, which he reads aloud, in a voice of dread, to the end.

The winner is none of them. It is a name that appears on seventy-three slips, in seventy-three different hands, none of them practised, all of them a little crooked. It is a plain word, which means, in the old tongue, 'the place where the road stopped, and we did not'. There is a silence when it is read. Then someone at the back begins, tentatively, to clap, and in a moment the whole square is a roar.

**Brindle:** It's too long for the cart.

It is put on the cart anyway, in white paint, by Wren, in letters a foot high. It runs off the end of the board. She has to finish it round the side.

## 2.29  "A Winter of Wells"  (`water`)

- **Starts when:** 4 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 1 Cultivation Pill
- **Words:** 248 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The city needs water. This is a thing you did not think about until the first week, when the stream ran brown from the upstream work and half the tents went down with something that looked like a cough and behaved like a rumour.

You dig. You dig for a season, with Brindle's men and with whoever else will lift a spade, in three places at once, on a plan drawn on the back of a bill of lading. The first well hits clay. The second hits a nest of frogs, an enormous number, a chorus, a congregation, which pour out of the hole in a flood and take over the camp for a fortnight.

**Closing scene**

The third well hits water. It is cold and clear and sweet, and it is nineteen feet down, and when the bucket comes up there is a silence all round the hole that is the opposite of the silence at a funeral. A boy of nine, who has been told since birth that water is something that happens to other people, drinks the first mouthful from a tin cup and bursts into tears.

You name it for the first boy who died on the Salt Road, and the second, which was already the name of a well in your yard. There are two wells, now, in two places. Nobody asked you to. You think your father would have called it sentiment. You think he would have been quietly pleased.

## 2.30  "The Honorary Donkey"  (`donkey`)

- **Starts when:** 3 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **Words:** 313 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The donkey has been in the city for a year, and there has never been a question as to what to do with it. It lives in the stable behind the town hall. It is fed by a boy of nine. It has a name, Councillor, bestowed on it by Brindle's men, and it answers, in a manner of speaking, to nothing at all.

The matter arises over a drain. There is a vote to be taken on it in the new council, a body of eleven, and one of the eleven is ill. A clerk says, in a voice of the purest academic innocence, that the founding charter has not defined the word 'member'.

**Closing scene**

The debate goes on for nine days. Counsel is retained on both sides. The motion is that the Councillor, as a resident for the requisite period, a taxpayer through the boy, and a creature of unquestionable character, be entered on the roll. A minority points out that it is a donkey. A majority replies that the Guild of Merchants once admitted a goat.

On the tenth day the vote is taken. The donkey is led in with a rosette on its head and stands in the middle of the floor. It looks at the councillors with its long, grave, weary face, the face of an animal that has attended a great many meetings. When the clerk reads the motion, it lifts its tail and does something unseemly on the carpet.

**Brindle:** I'd call that a yes.

It is entered as a yes. By a margin of one the Councillor is admitted. It is the best attended session in the history of the city, and nobody thereafter can say that the council has never made a sound decision. The drain, on the donkey's vote, is mended in the spring. It is a very good drain.

## 2.31  "Baron Ostrow's Complaint"  (`rival`)

**Opening scene**

The Baron's letter is four pages long and has been rewritten at least twice. It begins in the language of a petition, grows into a protest, and ends in a kind of howl. It appears that Ostrow Town, ten miles to the west, has lost nine hundred people since the spring. They have gone to the city on the field. The Baron wants to know what you are going to do about it.

**Closing scene**

He is a pink, plump, sleepless man in a velvet coat that has been slept in, and he meets you in a hall that is much too large for the number of people in it. He does not offer a seat. He paces. He is not, you perceive, a bad man. He is a frightened one.

**Ostrow:** It's not your fault. I do understand that. They're better off. They're warmer. I've been asking myself why they went. They said it was the wells. They said the water here tasted of nothing, and they wanted a town where it tasted of something.

**You:** Come and see the wells.

**Ostrow:** I shall not. It would be too humiliating. Though I admit I am curious. Does the donkey really have a seat on the council?

**You:** It's an honorary seat.

He puts his hands over his face. He is laughing, or something like it. When he looks up he has the damp, comic, defeated look of a man who has just found out that his enemy is not very frightening after all.

**Ostrow:** Perhaps we could share. A road. A market. A tax. I have a very good tax collector. He is going spare.

## 2.32  "The Bell of the New City"  (`bell`)

- **Starts when:** 3 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 500 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 410 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The city has a bell. It has taken a year to decide. There was a committee, then a sub-committee, then a quarrel about whether it should be a bell at all or a gong. The matter was settled by the goat, which ate the draft. It was necessary to start from scratch with a different draft and a lower opinion of the goat.

It is to be cast in the square, in the open air, by anyone who can lift a ladle. There is a pit with a clay mould in it. There is a furnace the size of a house. There are two hundred people standing in the cold, in their good coats, in a ring, waiting for the metal.

**Closing scene**

The first casting cracks. It cracks along its whole length, from the lip to the crown, with a sound like a very large plate dropped on a very hard floor. Nobody says anything. Brindle sits down on a barrel. A child begins to cry, quietly, in the way of a child who does not yet know whether it is allowed.

The second casting takes a week, and the city does it all again, with the same people, in the same cold, with a few more who have heard. This time it holds. They lift the mould in the dawn, with ropes, and there it stands in the pit, dark and wet and ringing faintly with its own heat, and no one in the square speaks for a quarter of an hour.

Hettie rings it, if she is there, because she is the smallest, and the bell will take the smallest hand. She stands on a box and pulls the rope with both fists. The note goes out over the roofs and the field and the hills, a deep gold sound with a wobble at the end. The city, which has been a camp, and a field, and a rumour, discovers that it is somewhere.

*[only if has.gareth]* **{gareth.first}:** It's a B flat. Or near enough. I'd have gone a quarter higher. But it's honest.

At the far side of the square an old woman with her hand on her heart says that she has not heard a bell like that since the Year of the Flood. Another says that she has never heard a bell like that in her life. They look at each other. They agree to be right, together, and go home to tell it.

## 2.33  "The Hungry Winter"  (`winter`)

- **Starts when:** 4 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 13 weeks (0 years and 13 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 2 Potential Pills, a technique insight
- **Words:** 255 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The harvest fails in the third year. Not the whole of it. The grain in the east goes to blight, and the grain in the west goes to rain, and the middle goes to a plague of something small and quick that the farmers call 'the thieves'. By the autumn the price of bread has doubled. By midwinter it has trebled.

The city is big enough now that a famine is a political event. A delegation waits in your hall in the grey light of the morning: nine men and three women in the good coats of people who have decided to be polite. Someone who has never had to bake has told them what the polite thing is.

**Delegate:** We should like to know what you propose to do. We do not ask for charity. We ask for an understanding.

**Closing scene**

*[only if winter is 1]* On the last night of the famine, someone leaves a loaf on the steps of the vault, with a note, in a clumsy hand: 'THANKS FOR NOT BEING A ROCK.'

*[only if winter is 2]* The grain from the south comes through in March. You are not proud of the winter. You are not ashamed of it. You will return to it in your mind, a good deal, in the years to come, as to a tooth.

*[only if winter is 3]* There is a small stone in the market, now, with a ticket carved on it. Children play a game of lots, there, in the spring. The one who draws the short straw has to give away their bread.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `winter`; default: option 1)

> There is grain in your vault, and the city is hungry.

1. Open the vault and feed everyone, at cost, and take the loss.
   - The grain goes out in a long, orderly line. By the new year you have lost a third of your fortune. You have not lost a single person. The ledger, which is Doric's old ledger, has a new column, headed Mouths, and the sum at the bottom of it is steadily and astonishingly large.
2. Sell at the price the market will bear, and use the profit to buy more from the south.
   - It works, in the way these things work, which is to say that it saves most of the city and leaves a hard feeling in the other part. A few of the poorest go to Ostrow Town. The Baron, who has no grain at all, feeds them anyway and sends you a note: 'You owe me one donkey.'
3. Share it out by lot, free, until it runs out, and let the chips fall.
   - It is the most disorderly week of your life. There are queues. There are fights. A man wins three sacks and gives two to a stranger. A woman draws the same ticket four times and declares it fate. When the grain runs out, on the ninth day, the city is still there, sitting in the street in the sun with its hat in its lap, looking sheepish.

**Opening scene**

*[only if fall is 1]* There is a letter on the gate-post on the first day of spring. It is on a single sheet of good plain paper, written in a hand that has not wavered since the day it learned to write. It has been left by someone who did not knock. It says: 'I have heard about your well. I have not seen it. I am sorry I did not come to the opening. I am no longer a person who is received. I should like to see it before I die, from the road. Will you be at the bridge at four? O.K.'

*[only if not fall=1]* She comes by the main road, on a hired cart, in her black coat, with a bag of beans on her knee. The sentry at the gate does not know her. He lets her through with the incurious politeness of a man who has been told to admit anyone who looks harmless. She is seventy. She is very small. She sits on the wall by the market and looks at the city that was a field.

**Closing scene**

You walk her round it yourself. She has her stick and a hat and an opinion on everything, and she is good company. She takes the whole of it in as she goes: the market, the school, the bell, the two wells in the courtyard that bear two names, the half-built vault. She stops often. She looks at the stones. She says, of the drains, that she would have gone a foot deeper. She says, of the wall, that it is a very handsome wall for a town of this size and a very poor wall for a city, and she is correct.

**Odile:** Your father would have built it twice as big and half as sound. I am glad that you did not. It is a good thing to see a child improve on a parent. It is rare.

At the vault she asks if she may go in, and you say that it is hers as much as anyone's. She stands in the middle of the great empty round room, under the dome, with its smell of new stone and lamp-oil. In the very centre, on the flags, where the foundation peg went in, is a small brass plate. She reads it. It says, in letters an inch high: SALT AND STRING.

**Odile:** You put it on the floor.

**You:** Where the money would have been.

She does not say anything for a time. She takes off her glove, and lays her hand flat on the plate, and leaves it there. She says, to the stone: 'It was a good barrow. It had a wobbly wheel. I used to push it. Tobias did the talking.' And she smiles, quite slowly, with her whole face, the first smile you have ever seen from her that needs no teeth.

You have never, in all that time, stood at the gate before dawn to see who puts it there. You do so now, in a thick coat, with a lantern, and wait.

**Closing scene**

*[only if fall is 3]* She comes at five, up the street, in a black coat, with a stick and a small barrow. It is a very old barrow with a wobbly wheel. She is ninety-one. **Odile:** I'm going through the Door at the end of the season. I thought I might see the vault before I go. I didn't like to come in. I've been told I'm no longer a person who is received.

You take her arm. It weighs almost nothing. You walk her in through the gate you built, past the school and the bell and the market. She says the drains could have been deeper. She says it is a very fine wall.

## 2.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

You stay, and your house goes on without you. The vault has a new door and a new steward, and on the door a note in your handwriting: Numbers before people. People before gold.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

You carry a lamp for the Gardener, and a ledger for the soldiers. Somebody has to see that the ration carts are honest.

You have never been trusted by so many people.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

On the other side of the Seam you open a small shop. It has a bell above the door, and when it rings you feel it in your chest.

Your father would have said the location was terrible. He would have come to see it anyway.

**You are struck down by the array**

The array took a fortune in a single moment and left you with nothing at all.

Your accountants, wherever they are, would like it known that this was not a good investment.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden ends, and so do the vault, the caravans and the long ledger. The one thing that goes on is the envelope you carried.

You read it one more time, by the last light. Be better than I was. You tried.
