There is a woman standing in the ford with water up to her shins and a sword across her shoulders like a yoke.

**{kasumi.first}:** I am {kasumi.first}. I have crossed this river forty times, and on every crossing I have fought whoever was on the other bank. It is a stupid habit. I do not wish to stop.

**You:** I am only passing through.

**{kasumi.first}:** Everyone is only passing through. That is why I like the ford.

She does not draw. She waits. If you want to cross, you will have to take up her challenge: type 'attack' while you stand beside her.

**Closing scene**

*[only if dead.kasumi]* She is on the bank. The river goes on. It is not a good victory, and you know it.

*[only if not dead.kasumi]* She sits on a rock, wringing out her sleeve, grinning like a child.

*[only if not dead.kasumi]* **{kasumi.first}:** Forty-one. Now that was a fight. You stand like someone who learned on a wagon.

*[only if not dead.kasumi]* **You:** I learned on a road.

*[only if not dead.kasumi]* **{kasumi.first}:** Same thing. Here. Take this. It's the one thing I own that's worth more than my sword.

*[only if not dead.kasumi]* She hands you a rolled slip of paper. It is a diagram, drawn in a quick hand, of how she holds her wrists when she cuts. You will use it for years.

### "The Last Cargo"  (`caravan`)

- **Comes up when:** a road tale: drawn at random (about 1 in 30 turns once it may come), only one in every few years; and this condition holds: `(c, st) -> after(st, 2) && wild(c)`
- **Task:** Go to the place `deliver`.  "Deliver the blue chest to a woman in {@deliver}."

- **When it closes, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.set(st, "delivered", 1)`

**Opening scene**

A caravan master sits propped against a wagon wheel by the roadside, alone, with a blanket over his knees and a clay pipe gone out in his hand. His wagons stand empty. His men have gone to town for help, and will not be back in time.

**Caravan master:** You're a road-kid. I can tell by your walk. Come here. I haven't much breath.

**Caravan master:** I've one cargo left, in that blue chest. A tea set. It's for a woman in {@deliver}. Thirty years I've promised it to her. I never did. Will you?

He presses the chest into your arms. It is heavier than it looks. He is lighter than he should be.

**Caravan master:** Tell her I'm sorry about the delay.

He is gone before his men are back.

**Closing scene**

The woman is old, and small, and sharp-tongued. She opens the chest and sees the tea set. She is quiet for a very long time.

**Old woman:** He said he'd bring it the spring after we parted. He had a good reason, I'm sure. A war. A flood. A fool who couldn't read a map. Thirty years.

She lifts one cup to the light. It is thin as an eggshell and as white as milk.

**Old woman:** Stay and have tea with me. I have a good reason to use the cups, finally.

You stay for the afternoon. She tells you everything about him, and you listen. It is a fine tea.

**Opening scene**

The well in the village square has a long queue, and somebody at the front is arguing with the bucket.

The somebody is a traveler about your age, with a patched coat and a laugh that carries. {sol.He} has dropped {sol.his} rope. {sol.He} has also dropped {sol.his} bucket. {sol.He} is now negotiating with the well.

**Sol:** I know you can hear me. I only want a drink of water. I'm not asking for your hand in marriage.

You lend them your rope. It is not a grand gesture. You will think about it for years.

**Sol:** Sol. And you are?

You tell them. They nod, solemnly, as if you had told them the name of a minor god.

**Sol:** Well, {first}. We seem to be going the same direction. Shall we be going the same direction together, as far as the next village?

Four autumns have gone by since the well. You have seen Sol three times. Once in a flooded town, once at a funeral, once in a market where you both reached for the last peach.

This time you meet on a hill above a river, at sunset, without having planned to. Sol is thinner. There is a scar on {sol.his} chin you do not remember.

**Sol:** I thought about you. I won't pretend I didn't. I told myself it was silly. Two people who can't stay in one place, trying to stay near each other.

**You:** It is a bit silly.

**Sol:** It is very silly. I'd do it again.

**Question** (kept as the flag `solk`; default: option 1)

> Sol is standing very close, and is not joking now.

1. Kiss them.
   - It is a short kiss, clumsy and warm. When it is over, Sol laughs, and then you do, and the whole river seems to laugh with you.

   - **Sol:** That's all right. I can wait. I'm very good at waiting. I've been practising on you.
   - {sol.He} squeezes your hand, once, and lets go. The hill smells of woodsmoke and dry grass.

The ferry across the Grey River is a flat boat with a creaky rope. The ferryman is a short, broad man who talks to the river more than to his passengers.

You pay your coin. He glances at your wrist, where the cord with the token has slipped out of your sleeve, and stops with the rope in his hands.

**Ferryman:** That mark. Where did you get that mark?

**You:** It's been with me all my life.

**Ferryman:** Twenty years ago, in a winter storm, I carried a woman across this river at midnight. Nobody else would. She had that mark on a cord at her neck. She had a cut on her arm, and she was running from something.

**Ferryman:** I asked her name. She wouldn't give it. She gave me a coin as big as my palm, and said that if anyone ever came asking, I should say nothing. I said nothing. But you're not asking, are you? You're just a traveler with a token. I think it's all right.

You thank him. Your hands are not steady on the rope.

His coat is torn, and underneath it, on a cord, is a mark you know.

**Soldier:** Where did you...? Never mind. Sit. Please. I'd like to talk to someone before I stop.

**Soldier:** I was a guard at the House of the Seventh Star. We were told it was a peaceful winter. It wasn't. There was a coup in the dark of the night. Torches in every window. My lord was dead before the second bell.

There is a very old woman selling pickled plums from a basket on the roadside. She has no teeth and a great deal to say.

**Old maid:** Now, a plum like this takes eleven days in the jar...

She stops. She is looking at your token.

**Old maid:** I was a maid in that house. I was twelve years old. I carried the lady's slippers.

**Old maid:** She isn't dead, you know. People say so, but she's alive. I see her light, some nights, the shrine at the crossroads on the Ash Road, a day's walk from here. She sits at the window and she watches the road.

She gives you a handful of plums, and a look you will remember for the rest of your life.

### "Paper Boats"  (`boats`)

- **Comes up when:** a road tale: drawn at random (about 1 in 30 turns once it may come), only one in every few years; and this condition holds: `(c, st) -> after(st, 2) && town(c)`
- **Task:** No task: the closing scene follows at once.
- **Pays:** nothing

**Opening scene**

On the last night of autumn the whole town goes down to the river with paper boats, and a candle in each boat, and a name in each candle.

A child hands you a boat. It is a poor one, folded crooked. There is a stub of candle in it.

**Child:** You have to think of someone you lost. It doesn't matter who. They'll find it.

**Question** (kept as the flag `boats`; default: option 1)

> You hold the little boat, and the river is dark.

1. Think of Old Brannoch.
   - You say his name under your breath. The boat tips, rights itself, and goes bobbing away, ridiculous and brave.
2. Think of the woman who gave you away.
   - You have neither her name nor her face. You think of a storm, and a cut arm, and a coat. The boat floats a long way before it goes out.
3. Think of nobody, and just watch the lights.
   - You watch two hundred small lights drift away down the river, and for a little while you are part of something.

### "The Thief Who Wasn't"  (`thief`)

- **Comes up when:** a road tale: drawn at random (about 1 in 30 turns once it may come), only one in every few years; and this condition holds: `(c, st) -> after(st, 2) && town(c)`
- **Task:** No task: the closing scene follows at once.
- **Pays:** nothing

**Opening scene**

You feel the tug at your belt. You have had your pocket picked by professionals. This is not one.

The hand is thick and slow, and belongs to a bald man of seventy with a medal pinned to his coat. You catch his wrist. He looks mortified.

**Old man:** I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. I haven't done this since the war. It's only that my pension was late, and I haven't eaten since Tuesday.

**You:** You were a soldier?

**Old man:** General, actually. Third Army. I'm not ashamed. Well. I'm a little ashamed.

You buy him a bowl of noodles. Two. He tells you about the Battle of the Reed Pass for the whole of both bowls.

### "Three Days of Rain"  (`rain`)

- **Comes up when:** a road tale: drawn at random (about 1 in 30 turns once it may come), only one in every few years; and this condition holds: `(c, st) -> after(st, 2) && town(c)`
- **Task:** No task: the closing scene follows at once.
- **Pays:** nothing

**Opening scene**

It rains for three days, and you are stuck in an inn with eleven strangers, a leaking roof, and a fire.

On the second night, a thin woman with a ladle for a walking stick offers to tell a story. Nobody argues.

**Storyteller:** Once there was a road that wanted to be a river...

It is a long story, with a talking carp in it, and a king who has lost his left sandal, and a girl who walks to the end of the world to find out whether it has an edge.

When it ends, nobody speaks. Then somebody says it was too short. The storyteller smiles, and begins again.

## 3.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

The Ash Road is still the Ash Road. You still walk it. Now there is a shrine on it where a lantern burns, and a house beside the shrine, and in the house a woman who knows your step. She has opinions about your coat.

*[only if home is 1]* The House of the Seventh Star has a roof now. It has a school, and a stable, and a table that does not wobble. It is not what it was. It is not meant to be.

*[only if home is 2]* The hall is a field with an apple tree in it. On the eve of the first frost, strangers come from three counties to light a candle under the branches. Nobody tells them to.

*[only if home is 3]* The Lamp Road runs to the end of the world. Children on it sing a song of seven verses. They think it was always the same song. It has a fifth verse now. Nobody remembers who found it.

*[only if stone is 1]* Perpetua's sugar bridge is a tradition at Pellmoor weddings. They collapse it on purpose.

*[only if lovet is 1]* {teodor.first} keeps the road's last light, on a coast where the world ends, and tells visitors that the other lanterns are in the way.

*[only if lantern is 2]* A paper lantern hangs in the shrine's window with one word on it. KID. Ilan lights it every night, after her own.

*[only if not dead.hush]* A thin grey person sometimes stands at the edge of the road, at dusk, with a small cup of tea, looking at the lamps. He never comes closer. Perpetua leaves him a slice of cake on the wall. It is always gone by morning.

*[only if latch is 1]* The lantern at the foot of the Empty Seat has never gone out. The Wicks light their own from it on their first night.

*[only if latch is 2]* You have left the door of the house on the Ash Road unlatched. There is a kettle on the stove.

*[only if latch is 3]* A lamp is lit at the Seat every evening, at dusk. A Wick has been given the job of keeping it. He says he is told it was a person once.

You are from the road. You are also, you find, from somewhere. It is a house on a hill, with a leaking roof. Somebody has put the kettle on.

## 3.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

The Palace's long corridors are not your road, but you walk them as you walked the Ash Road, in no particular hurry, with a lantern.

*[only if stay is 1]* Ilan lives a day's walk away. You see her every week, and the students think it very strange that you never stay anywhere long and always come back.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

You carry the lamp the way you carried a tinker's kettle: gently, with both hands.

In the evenings, around the army's fires, you tell of a road that ran past a thousand cooking fires. The soldiers listen. For a moment, they are home.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You step through the Seam the way you stepped through every town on the Ash Road, lightly and without looking back.

This time there is somewhere to come back to. The idea is so new that you stop, mid-step, to look at it.

**You are struck down by the array**

You never stayed anywhere long enough to be hurt. The array fixed that.

Somewhere on the Ash Road, in a small shrine, a lantern is lit tonight, as it is every night.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden goes out. The Ash Road goes out. The last thing to go is the lantern in the shrine window.

You watch it for as long as you can.

# 4. The Disgraced Disciple  (`disgraced`)

*Expelled for reading what you should not have. You still carry half a forbidden scripture and a grudge the size of a sect.*

Starts as: any, trait Scribe, Evil, potential 78, 100 spirit stones.

**What the plan says is the truth of this story:** The Disgraced Disciple (10 chapters). Half of the Scroll of Unbroken Breath was in your desk; the other half is in four seals hidden by Elder Zhao (a drowned library, a silent monk, a rival's vault, and Mei, your friend). Why your desk is rolled at the start: Zhao put it there to silence a question about the Pillar Fund, or a dying friend, Lan, hid it there, or the scroll found you. The technique grows (its name changes) with each seal. The scroll is good; Zhao feared it because a student who can mend and stand alone needs no master. [Mei Lingfeng, Brother Tse, Elder Zhao].

**People of the story** (real characters in the world; "fated" means only you can kill them):

# 4.S1  Season 1: The Desk by the Door

## 4.1  "The Gate of Stillwater"  (`gate`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** AGE 21.  "Stay alive until your 21st birthday."
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **Words:** 335 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The reading hall of the Stillwater Pavilion has a rule that is older than the building. Nobody enters the Closed Stacks. Not students, not teachers, not the cat.

You never entered the Closed Stacks. You woke one morning, and half of a scroll was in the bottom of your desk, wrapped in black silk, with its title written in a hand you did not know. The Scroll of Unbroken Breath.

You read the first line. That was the mistake. You read the second. That was the crime.

They found you at noon. The whole school stood in the courtyard in lines. Elder Zhao read the sentence in a calm voice, like a man reading a menu.

**Zhao:** Expelled, for owning a forbidden text. The text is to be burned.

You were not meant to keep the scroll. But there is something people forget about reading. Once a thing is in your head, burning the paper does not take it out.

The guards walked you to the gate. Mei Lingfeng, who sat beside you in every lesson, was waiting there with a bundle of rice cakes and a face that did not move.

**Mei:** I know you didn't take it. I don't know who put it there, but I'll find out. Stay alive.

You are eighteen. You are hated by the only home you have. And you know, with perfect clarity, half of a technique that nobody else alive can use.

The guards were told to make sure you left the province. They were not told what to do if you came back.

**Closing scene**

On your twenty-first birthday you eat a bowl of noodles in a roadside inn with no name. You pay with the last of your coins.

It is not much of a celebration. But you are alive, and nobody has found you, and a rice cake is still wrapped in a cloth at the bottom of your bag.

It is stale. You eat it anyway.

## 4.2  "The One Who Did Not Turn"  (`mei`)

- **Starts when:** 1 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet mei (walk to their tile).  "Meet Mei Lingfeng at the teahouse in {@mei}."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "mei")`
- **Words:** 338 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

A letter reaches you through three hands and a goat. It has no name on it, only a drawing of a small cat.

'The teahouse by the wall in {@mei}. Third table. Come alone. M.'

You cannot tell whether to trust it. You go anyway. You are tired of being a person who doesn't.

**Closing scene**

{mei.He} has grown taller. {mei.His} sleeves are the grey of an outer disciple who has not been promoted, which is a sign of someone who asked too many questions.

**Mei:** I looked into it. I wasn't supposed to. The Closed Stacks key is kept in three places, and the lock log says nobody opened it that night.

*[only if how is 1]* **Mei:** But there is one more entry. Elder Zhao's hand, under the date. Just a number. Eleven. It is the number of his private study. I think he took it out himself.

*[only if how is 2]* **Mei:** But there is one more name in the infirmary book, the same night. Lan. You remember Lan, who coughed so much. He died four days later. I don't know what he did. I know he asked for your desk to be moved to the warm end of the room.

*[only if how is 3]* **Mei:** But nothing else. Not a key, not a candle, not a footstep. The scroll was not taken out. It simply was in your desk. I've looked at that book a hundred times. I don't understand it.

**Mei:** There is something else. Elder Zhao cut the other half of the scroll into four pieces. He has hidden them. I copied the list from the study when he was sleeping. I wrote it in lemon juice on a bread wrapper. It's the only thing I've ever stolen.

{mei.He} slides the wrapper across the table. It smells like a breakfast.

**Mei:** Four seals, four keepers. You hold the first half of the breath. If you gather the second, the technique is whole. And if you're whole, he can't call you nothing again.

{mei.His} hand is shaking. You put yours over it, and neither of you says anything.

## 4.3  "The Drowned Library"  (`seal1`)

- **Starts when:** 40 weeks after the previous chapter ended; Major Lvl 1 or more (given up after 6 more years of waiting)
- **Task:** Go to the place `library`.  "Find the Drowned Library at {@library}."
- **Pays:** a technique insight
- **When it closes, the code:** `(c, st) -> technique(c, "Unbroken Breath, Third Part")`
- **Words:** 214 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The first seal is held by a place, not a person. On Mei's list it is called the Drowned Library: an old scholars' retreat that a river took long ago.

People say the water went down one year and left the library standing, with the books inside, dry as bone. Nobody goes there. The stacks are said to move.

You will have to go and see.

**Closing scene**

It is not a ruin. It is a hall of grey stone with mud halfway up the walls and a roof of green moss. Inside, the air is cold, and every sound you make comes back a moment late.

The stacks do not move. But the books are sorted by a system you do not understand, and each shelf has a small brass plate with a number. It takes you three days to see that the numbers spell something.

The seal is a flat clay tablet at the end of the last aisle, set into the wall. When you lift it out, the whole room exhales, like a held breath let go.

The first line reads: Breathing in, you hold the world. Breathing out, you set it down.

You sit on the cold floor and read until the light changes.

## 4.4  "The Monk Who Does Not Speak"  (`seal2`)

- **Starts when:** 40 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Defeat tse (only you can kill them).  "Face Brother Tse, the silent keeper of the second seal."
- **Pays:** a technique insight
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "tse")`
- **When it closes, the code:** `(c, st) -> technique(c, "Unbroken Breath, Half")`
- **Words:** 297 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The second seal is carried by a man. Brother Tse took a vow of silence before you were born, and has lived by it since. He has a mountain hut, an iron staff, and a very long list of people he has politely thrown off his path.

Mei's note says: He will not speak to you. He will fight you, and when it is over he will either let you pass or he won't.

You are not looking forward to this.

**Closing scene**

*[only if dead.tse]* It is quick. He does not cry out. He puts his hand on his chest, where the seal hangs, and gives it to you with a nod, as if to say: I knew somebody would come.

*[only if dead.tse]* You bury him with his staff. You say a few words over the grave, though you do not know what he believed.

*[only if not dead.tse]* He is on one knee, and you are standing over him with your blade, and you do not use it. He looks at you for a long moment.

*[only if not dead.tse]* **Tse:** Elder Zhao told me it was an evil text. That it would hollow out anyone who read it. That is why I took the vow. To be quiet when I wanted to ask him what he was afraid of.

*[only if not dead.tse]* He breaks his silence for the first time in thirty years. His voice is rusty, as if from disuse. He sounds, you think, relieved.

*[only if not dead.tse]* **Tse:** Take it. It was never mine to keep.

The second seal is a wooden bead on a cord. Inside it, rolled very small, is a scrap of paper in tiny writing. You need a glass to read it. You read it three times.

The second line reads: Breathing in, you are small. Breathing out, you are the world.

## 4.5  "A Cat on the Wrapper"  (`cat`)

- **Starts when:** 10 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet mei (walk to their tile).  "Meet Mei Lingfeng at the inn in {@mei}, who has left the Pavilion for one night."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **Words:** 417 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The letters have always come with a small drawing of a cat. It is a bad cat. It has the proportions of a loaf of bread with ears. It sits at the foot of each page, and sometimes it is asleep, and sometimes it holds a very small sword, and once it was upside down.

This time the letter is only four words long. It says: I AM IN {@mei}. DRAW BACK. Under it, the cat is waving.

**Closing scene**

{mei.He} has walked two days. {mei.He} has brought a satchel of food, three pairs of dry socks, and a bag of the plum sweets from the Pavilion kitchen that you used to steal. {mei.He} has not told anyone where {mei.he} was going. If {mei.he} is missed, it will be called an illness.

**Mei:** Don't look at me like that. I wanted to see that you were eating. You always forgot. In the second year you fainted in the Bamboo Hall and the master said you'd been meditating too hard.

You eat. You eat everything, in a corner of a common room, under a lamp, with the dice players shouting at the far end. {mei.He} sits across from you and watches, and does not say a word until the sweets are gone.

**Mei:** I'm frightened of the dark, you know. I've never told anyone. I sleep with a lamp. I've done it since I was seven. It's why I never ran. I couldn't have gone out of the gate at night.

**You:** You came out of it tonight.

**Mei:** I did. I counted. It's two hundred and eleven steps from the gate to the first lamp on the road. I did every one with my eyes shut.

{mei.He} says it lightly. {mei.His} hands are in {mei.his} lap, and they are not light at all. You turn yours over on the table, palm up, and say nothing, and after a moment {mei.he} puts one of {mei.his} into it, and the dice players roar, and neither of you looks round.

**Mei:** Teach me the first breath. The one you can do. Just the in. I'd like to have something of my own that nobody gave me.

You teach it at the table, under your breath, with your fingers on the back of {mei.his} wrist, until the lamp burns low. {mei.He} falls asleep in the chair before the end, in the middle of a sentence, with the lamp still lit beside {mei.him} and the cat drawn on the back of {mei.his} hand.

## 4.6  "The Rival's Vault"  (`seal3`)

- **Starts when:** 40 weeks after the previous chapter ended; Major Lvl 2 or more (given up after 6 more years of waiting)
- **Task:** Go to the place `vault`.  "Reach the Ironleaf Hall in {@vault}."
- **Pays:** a technique insight
- **When it closes, the code:** `(c, st) -> { technique(c, "Unbroken Breath, Three Parts of Four"); if (Chapters.flag(st, "vault") == 2) { c.ss = Math.max(0, c.ss - 3000); c.convertCurrency(); } }`
- **Words:** 174 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The third seal sits in the vault of the Ironleaf Hall, the Pavilion's oldest rival, in {@vault}. How Elder Zhao got it in there is a question you would like to ask him.

The Ironleaf Hall is famous for two things: its iron gate and its master, who is said to be a reasonable man if you catch him before lunch.

**Closing scene**

The vault is a plain steel room at the end of a plain corridor. The master of the hall, a stout man with ink on his cuffs, meets you at the door with a cup of tea.

**Master Hu:** I know why you're here. Zhao asked me to keep it safe, ten years ago. He said it was a family heirloom. I never believed him. I read the label.

**Master Hu:** I'm not a thief and I'm not a saint. What I am is a man who dislikes being used. Take it, buy it, ask me nicely, or sneak in. I'll make it easy either way. Zhao has hurt my hall more than once.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `vault`; default: option 1)

> Master Hu will let you have the third seal, one way or another.

1. Slip in at night and take it quietly.
   - You go at night, and it is easy, and that is the worst part. You take the seal. The master is awake in the corridor when you leave, and he does not say a word.
   - On the road, you feel faintly sick. It was an easy theft. You did not need to do it.
2. Pay him a fair price, in coin.
   - **Master Hu:** Three thousand.
   - You pay. He weighs the coins with great care and slides them into a drawer. 'Pleasure,' he says. It may even have been.
3. Ask him, honestly, for it.
   - **Master Hu:** Well, now. That's rare. Most people who come here are either rich or sneaky.
   - He gives you the seal and a second cup of tea. You talk for an hour about scrolls, and he tells you three things about Zhao you will use later.

## 4.7  "The Last Seal"  (`seal4`)

- **Starts when:** 30 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet mei (walk to their tile).  "Go to Mei Lingfeng, who has kept the last seal."
- **Pays:** a technique insight
- **When it closes, the code:** `(c, st) -> technique(c, "Unbroken Breath")`
- **Words:** 167 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The last seal is not on Mei's list. {mei.He} knew it, though. {mei.He} wrote it on the back of the wrapper in smaller letters, where you did not look until now.

'The fourth keeper is me. I am sorry. He gave it to me when I was thirteen and told me it was a prize. I only worked out what it was last year. I did not want to give it up until I knew you were ready. Come and ask me. M.'

**Closing scene**

{mei.He} is waiting at the same teahouse, third table. {mei.He} looks like {mei.he} hasn't slept.

**Mei:** I'm sorry. I should have said. I thought if I did, you would stop trusting me, and I couldn't stand it. I wanted you to have the whole thing, but I wanted you to need me a little first. That's an awful thing to say.

{mei.He} pulls a small iron key from {mei.his} sleeve. The seal is a lock-box about the size of a snuffbox.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `meiend`; default: option 1)

> Mei has kept the last seal for years, and not told you.

1. Tell {mei.him} you understand, and you are still {mei.his} friend.
   - **Mei:** You're a better person than I am.
   - **You:** Everybody is. It's how we know we're in the same school.
   - {mei.He} laughs, and then {mei.he} is crying a little, and then you are both laughing again.
2. Take the seal in silence, and leave it unsaid.
   - {mei.He} does not argue. {mei.He} watches you go. You do not look back, because you know you would stay, and you cannot stay. Not yet.

## 4.8  "Unbroken Breath"  (`breath`)

- **Starts when:** 1 year(s) after the previous chapter ended; Major Lvl 2 or more (given up after 6 more years of waiting)
- **Task:** Reach Major Lvl 2.  "Become strong enough to hold the whole technique: reach Major Lvl 2."
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 199 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You lay the four seals side by side on a table. Together with the half that has lived in your head for years, they make a whole.

It takes you eleven nights to read it through. You cannot sleep, so you sit by the lamp, and you read.

At the end there is a line you have been waiting for. It explains why Elder Zhao hid it.

**Closing scene**

The Scroll of Unbroken Breath is not evil. That is what is so unbearable. It is a plain, good, patient technique, which lets a cultivator mend themselves from nearly any wound, and teaches them to stand alone.

'A person who can mend themselves,' says the last line, 'has no need of a healer. A person who can stand alone has no need of a master. Teach it widely.'

So that is what he was afraid of. Not that it would hurt you, but that it would free you. Elder Zhao's power over his students was the fact that they needed him.

You close the scroll. You are still in the room, but it feels different, as if the walls have moved a little further back.

## 4.9  "Why Your Desk"  (`how`)

- **Starts when:** 1 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `grave`.  "Follow the last clue to {@grave}."
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 363 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

There is one question left. Why your desk? Why you?

The answer, you find, was in the scroll all along, if you knew where to look.

**Closing scene**

*[only if how is 1]* It is a stone hut outside a village the Pavilion once owned. Inside is a clerk who used to work for Zhao, now old and drunk and glad to talk. He sets a ledger in front of you.

*[only if how is 1]* **Old clerk:** The Pillar Fund. Ten thousand spirit stones a year, for the Pavilion's poor students. He took four of every ten. You were the only student who asked where it went. In the third year, you asked it out loud, in class.

*[only if how is 1]* So that was all it was. A question in a lesson. He needed a thing to ruin you with, and he had the thing in his private study. The Closed Stacks key was just a prop.

*[only if how is 2]* It is a little grave under a pear tree behind the infirmary, with a plain wooden marker. Lan. He coughed so much in class, and he was always a bit pale, and you never talked to him as much as you should have.

*[only if how is 2]* Under the marker is a note, folded small, in a jar. It reads: 'I took this from the Closed Stacks because I was dying and wanted to read one forbidden thing. I got scared and put it in the warmest desk. I am sorry. I think you will do something good with it.'

*[only if how is 2]* You sit under the pear tree for a very long time. You wish you had asked how he was.

*[only if how is 3]* It is a hill with one dead tree and a view of nothing. You have followed the scroll's own margin note here, in handwriting that is not Zhao's, not Lan's, and not any hand you know.

*[only if how is 3]* On the last page, in pale ink, the note reads: 'The reader found this because the reader needed it. Do not ask who left it. Ask what you will do with it. - a guest.'

*[only if how is 3]* You read it five times. You find you are not frightened at all. Someone, somewhere, wanted you to have this. You will try to deserve it.

## 4.10  "Elder Zhao"  (`zhao`)

- **Starts when:** 1 year(s) after the previous chapter ended; Major Lvl 3 or more (given up after 6 more years of waiting)
- **Task:** Defeat zhao (only you can kill them).  "Face Elder Zhao, and win."
- **Pays:** 3,000 spirit stones, gear a Major above you
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "zhao")`
- **Words:** 208 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Everything leads back to one man. He is sixty-three, strong as an oak, and he sits in the Elder's chair of the Stillwater Pavilion in {@pavilion}, where he has sat for thirty years.

You write one letter before you go. It is short.

'I know about the Pillar Fund, the scroll, and the seals. I am coming. - your old student.'

You have thought about this for years, and now you are afraid. It is a very small kind of fear, like the kind you felt in the courtyard that noon.

**Closing scene**

*[only if dead.zhao]* He falls on the courtyard stones, and the students stand in their lines, silent, as they stood on your day.

*[only if dead.zhao]* The silence goes on until the dust settles. Then someone at the back begins, quietly, to clap. Then somebody else. It is not a happy sound. It is relief.

*[only if not dead.zhao]* He is on his knees. The students are watching. You hold up the Pillar Fund ledger so that every one of them can see it.

*[only if not dead.zhao]* **You:** I could kill you. I won't. I want them to see what you were, and I want you to live and watch them learn.

*[only if not dead.zhao]* The courtyard is utterly silent. Zhao does not raise his head.

## 4.11  "The Pavilion's Door"  (`door`)

- **Starts when:** 1 year(s) after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 2 Potential Pills
- **Words:** 66 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Stillwater Pavilion has no master now. The Elders look at you, and the students look at you, and the great front door stands open.

You are not the child who was walked out of it. You are a different person.

You find yourself wondering what Lan would have wanted. What Mei would want. What Master Hu, the paper-stained man, would have said.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `door`; default: option 1)

> The Pavilion is in your hands.

1. Teach the Scroll of Unbroken Breath to everyone, and leave.
   - You spend a year copying it, line by line, in ten thousand hands. When you leave, the scroll is on every desk.
2. Take the Elder's chair, and rebuild the Pavilion as a school for those who are turned away.
   - The chair is hard. You hate it for a year. Then Mei comes and sits beside you, and then it is merely uncomfortable.
3. Burn the Closed Stacks, and let the Pavilion die.
   - It burns all night. The students stand and watch it, in no particular order. When the sun comes up, nobody says anything. Then someone passes round a bag of rice cakes.

## 4.I1  Interlude: Rice Cakes  (between season 1 and season 2)

**Interlude**

You were expelled at eighteen for owning half a scroll. You are the only person alive who knows the whole of it.

*[only if door is 1]* The Scroll of Unbroken Breath is taught in a thousand villages now. People who have never seen the Pavilion can mend their own cuts. Nobody remembers who first wrote it down. You like that best.

*[only if door is 2]* The Stillwater Pavilion has a new motto over its door: Nobody is turned away who asks a good question. It has a very large number of students and a very loud library.

*[only if door is 3]* The Closed Stacks are ash. The students who lived through that night became the most curious people in the province. They ask questions about everything. They are tremendous nuisances. You are proud of them.

*[only if dead.zhao]* Elder Zhao has a stone in the Pavilion's yard. It says only his name and the years. You decided not to add a verdict.

*[only if not dead.zhao]* Elder Zhao lives in a small hut at the edge of the school grounds. The students bring him soup. He never says thank you. He never stops watching them learn.

*[only if meiend is 1]* Mei teaches the youngest class. {mei.He} still keeps a drawing of a small cat on {mei.his} desk.

*[only if meiend is 2]* Mei sends a short letter once a year. It says: I am well. I think of you. You never answer, and you never throw one out.

*[only if how is 2]* Every spring you visit a pear tree behind the infirmary, and ask how he is.

There is a line in the scroll you did not quite understand at first. 'Breathing in, you hold the world. Breathing out, you set it down.' You understand the first half now.

A package comes to the Pavilion in the spring, addressed to you in a thin grey-green hand. Inside is a single leaf of paper, folded in four, and on it the words: THANK YOU FOR READING. The rest of the page is blank.

# 4.S2  Season 2: The Pillar Fund

## 4.12  "A Letter About Money"  (`invite`)

- **Starts when:** 3 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `pavilion`.  "Go to the Stillwater Pavilion, at {@pavilion}, and audit the Pillar Fund."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> { if (Chapters.flag(st, "hand") == 0) Chapters.set(st, "hand", 1 + GameDriver.rand.nextInt(3)); Chapters.spawn(c, st, "ibbot"); Chapters.spawn(c, st, "renn"); Chapters.spawn(c, st, "sunny"); }`
- **Words:** 488 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

*[only if door is 1]* The Pavilion goes on without you, as you meant it to. For three years it is a comfort to know that scrolls are being copied in a hundred villages, and that people who have never met you are mending their own wrists. Then a letter arrives, in the cramped hand of the Registrar, and it is about money.

*[only if door is 2]* The Elder's chair is as hard as ever. You have learned to sit in it with your feet tucked up like a child on a bench. You are passing the third winter in the Stillwater Pavilion when the Registrar brings you the quarterly figures, and puts them down carefully, as if they were a dish of something that might spill.

*[only if door is 3]* The Closed Stacks are ash and the school that grew from the ash is housed in a barn. It has a great many students, a terrible roof, and a library of eleven books, of which three are cookery. The Registrar finds you there in the autumn with a ledger under his arm and a face like a man who has been up all night with a headache.

**Ibbot:** It is the Pillar Fund. I do apologise. I had hoped the matter was closed. For forty years the Fund has paid ten thousand spirit stones a year to the school's poor students, and for twenty of those years Elder Zhao took four tenths of it, as you know. When he was gone, the Fund went on. The money went on arriving. And it went on going.

**Ibbot:** I have checked it six times. I am not a person who makes mistakes with figures. Somebody is still taking it. I should be grateful if you would come and look. You are the only person I could think of who is good at being angry in a useful direction.

**Closing scene**

The Pavilion is smaller than you remember. The courtyard where you were expelled is a vegetable garden. The reading hall has a new roof, and a cat on it. The gate where Mei once stood with a bundle of rice cakes is the same gate, with the same worn flagstone, and you stop on the flagstone for a moment before you go through.

{mei.first} is in the corridor. {mei.He} is carrying a stack of scrolls up to {mei.his} chin. You know the walk before you see the face: the long stride that is trying to be a short one, the habit of looking at the floor three paces ahead. {mei.He} puts the whole stack down on the floor.

**Mei:** You took your time.

**You:** So did you. There were sweets in the satchel. I never thanked you.

**Mei:** You thanked me for eleven minutes at the inn. I counted. Come here.

The embrace is clumsy and somewhat damaged by the scrolls. Somewhere behind you, in the corridor, the Registrar clears his throat in a way that is almost, but not quite, a cough.

## 4.13  "The Ledger of Poor Students"  (`ledger`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** a technique insight
- **Words:** 327 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Fund's books are kept in a room behind the Registrar's office, in a cabinet of dark wood that smells of camphor and lemon oil. They are very good books. They are written in a fine, even, upright hand, in black ink, with every entry ruled off, and every column carried forward.

You spend three days with them. You eat there, on a tray, with a pencil behind your ear. You find that you are happy, in the way of a person who has been given a good puzzle and a quiet room, and you feel faintly guilty about it, and carry on.

**Closing scene**

On the fourth day you find the first thing. Student number forty-one. A boy called Pell Winterbourne, admitted on the Fund at the age of nine, who has received a stipend every quarter for fourteen years. His name is in the ledger, and his signature, in a careful child's hand, and his receipt for every quarter's money.

**Mei:** I'll fetch the roll.

{mei.He} is back in ten minutes with the school roll. Pell Winterbourne appears on it for one year only, aged nine. Beside the entry, in red, is a note: Died of fever, third winter. The stipend goes on. The signature goes on. Somebody has been signing it as the boy grew up, in a hand that gets steadily firmer, and rounder, and more adult, like a child learning to grow.

**Mei:** He'd be twenty-three.

**You:** Yes.

**Mei:** Somebody has been giving him birthdays.

You find three more before the week is out. A girl who left to marry. A boy who ran off to sea. A third who has never, as far as the roll is concerned, existed at all. A small, quiet fraud, tended with great skill and love, like the garden of a person who has more time than they know what to do with. You cannot tell whom to hate. You want to find out before you decide.

## 4.14  "Three Desks"  (`desks`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet ibbot (walk to their tile).  "Take tea with Registrar Ibbot, Captain Renn, and the Librarian Sunny, one after another."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 483 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

There are three people in the Pavilion who could have kept those books. You have been through the numbers, and the numbers are clear. The hand is a clerk's, which means Ibbot, or a librarian's, which means Sunny. Or it is a very good forger's, which could be anyone who has spent twenty years reading the Registrar's accounts, including a captain of the gate with time on her hands and a neat way with a brush.

You accuse no one. You ask for tea. It turns out that people will tell a good deal to someone who has asked politely for tea.

**Closing scene**

The Registrar's office is the cleanest room in the Pavilion. He pours with the care of a man handling a live animal. He tells you he has not taken a coin from the Fund in his life. This is, so far as you can tell, true. After a very long pause he tells you that he has a sister in the east who is ill. For six years he has sent her sixty crowns a quarter, from a source he declines to name, and which he does not believe to be the Fund.

**Ibbot:** I do not like the look on your face. I wish to say that I know exactly how it sounds.

Captain Renn gives you tea on the wall above the gate, because she does not care for rooms. She is lean and brown and scarred along the jaw, and she talks about the guard rotas for twenty minutes with such pleasure that you almost forget the question. Then she says, flatly, that she took a bribe last year to look the other way for a night. She does not know what was carried through the gate. She does not want to know. She would like to be sacked.

Sunny Aldous gives you tea in the library, among the stacks, on a stool. He is a round-faced young man with an engaging smile and a habit of sitting on his own hands. He says he has never been so happy anywhere. He says the Pavilion is the first place that ever let him read what he wanted. Then, when you ask about the ledgers, he says without any change in his tone that he does not understand why anyone should object to a gift, and that he is sorry if that is a stupid thing to say.

Three cups, three stories, three kinds of honest. You go back to the Fund room and sit with the ledger open on your knee until the lamp wants trimming, trying to decide which of them is lying with their whole face. The answer has been in front of you the whole time, in something all three of them said, in almost the same words, as you were leaving. 'It's not for me. It's for someone else.'

## 4.15  "A Gilt-Edged Card"  (`gilt`)

- **Starts when:** 6 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `concord`.  "Go to the Concord of Healers' hall at {@concord}."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 263 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The card comes on the sixth day, hand-delivered by a footman in a green coat, on a salver. It is heavy and cream-coloured, with a gold edge and an engraved crest of a hand holding a flask. 'The Matron of the Concord of Healers requests the pleasure.' Under this, in a small neat hand: 'We have been wondering when you would come.'

**Mei:** The Concord. The apothecaries' cartel. They sell every cure in the province, at a price. They own half the physicians and most of the magistrates.

**You:** And they fund the Pillar Fund?

**Mei:** Under another name. The Lantern Trust. I've seen it in the donors' book, in the margin. I didn't know whose it was till now. It all begins to look like a very polite war.

**Closing scene**

The hall of the Concord is a handsome building of white stone and green glass, set in a garden of medicinal herbs, with a clinic on one side and a counting-house on the other. There are two queues at the clinic door: a short one for those who can pay, and a long one for those who cannot. The second has no one in charge of it, and moves by itself.

The footman takes you through the garden. He is a pleasant, indifferent man with a bad knee. He tells you, without being asked, that the roses at the south wall are for coughs, the lavender for sleep, and the valerian for anxiety. The Matron likes to have each of the three on her table, in a small glass, every day, 'for balance'.

## 4.16  "Dinner at the Concord"  (`dinner`)

- **Starts when:** 1 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet venn (walk to their tile).  "Dine with Matron Venn of the Concord of Healers."
- **Pays:** 2,000 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> { Chapters.spawn(c, st, "venn"); Chapters.spawn(c, st, "calder"); }`
- **Words:** 366 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Matron sits at the head of a table laid for six, in a room that has a ceiling like the inside of a seashell. She is sixty-two, silver-haired, in a plain grey gown with a high collar, and she gets up when you come in, which is a courtesy she does not extend to everyone. Her hands, you notice, are the hands of a woman who has done a great deal of work with them, and has chosen not to stop.

**Venn:** You are the Disgraced Disciple. I have wanted to meet you for twelve years. I had a very great deal of money riding on you not learning to read. I am, I confess, rather delighted that you did.

On her right is a tall, stiff man in a black coat, with a face like a closed door, who is introduced as the Lord Auditor Calder. He does not speak. He cuts his meat into nine equal pieces, and eats them in order.

**Closing scene**

**Venn:** I'll tell you what I believe, since you have come all this way. I believe in medicine. I believe that the sick are better off with a good cure at a fair price than with a miracle and a tragedy. I also believe that a person who can mend themselves is a person who has no use for me. You understand that. You are not a stupid man. The scroll you read is going to put my apothecaries out of work.

**You:** It's going to put them out of work, and it's going to save a great many people.

**Venn:** Yes. That is the trouble. I have never yet been able to decide which I mind more. I only know that I have employed a great many people, and that they have children.

You find, to your own discomfort, that you like her. She is not a villain. She is an economy in a gown. On your way out, in the corridor, the Lord Auditor Calder falls into step beside you and says, without turning his head, in a voice like a dry hinge: 'When she says it is accounts, it is accounts. When I say it, it is something else.'

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `venn`; default: option 1)

> Matron Venn has put her hands flat on the table. Dessert is on its way.

1. Refuse everything: the Fund is a theft, and you will say so in public.
   - **Venn:** Quite right. I should have thought less of you if you had not. But I'd like you to know that this is not personal. It is accounts.
   - She says it with a gentle sort of regret, like a woman closing a book she is fond of.
2. Hear her out, and bargain: you will keep quiet if the Fund pays the right people.
   - **Venn:** Now we are being sensible. You will find that I am very good at being bargained with.
   - She slides a paper across the cloth. It is a draft, in clean ink, and it has sixty-three clauses, and you read them all, slowly, while the cheese gets warm.
3. Accept: take the Concord's money for the school, and teach the scroll in your own time.
   - **Venn:** I did hope you would be realistic.
   - She smiles, showing very good teeth, and it makes you feel as if you have walked into a room where the temperature has been carefully arranged.

## 4.17  "Mei Teaches the First Breath"  (`mclass`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **Words:** 410 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The junior class meets in the old gymnasium behind the reading hall. It has a floor of sprung boards and a roof with a hole in it, through which the sun comes down in a hard bright pillar and the pigeons come in for lunch. There are thirty children. They are lined up in four rows, according to height, in grey shirts, with their hands behind their backs and their eyes on the ceiling.

Mei stands in front of them. {mei.He} has been a teacher for six months and looks, you think, a good deal more nervous than the pupils. {mei.He} has a bell in one hand and a wooden tablet in the other, and {mei.his} hair is tied back with what appears to be a piece of string. You stand at the back, behind a pillar, and do not breathe.

**Closing scene**

**Mei:** The first breath is the easiest thing you will ever learn and the hardest to do. I want you to breathe in. Not as much as you can. As much as you need. Now let it out. That's it. That is the first breath. The rest of your life is a kind of commentary.

A small boy in the second row puts up his hand. He wants to know what happens if you get it wrong. {mei.He} considers this seriously, for a moment, and says: 'You try again.' The boy thinks about it, and says that it doesn't seem very much of a lesson. Mei says, evenly, that it is the entire lesson, and that the rest of it is only practice.

They breathe. For ten minutes thirty children stand with their eyes shut and their stomachs going out and in, in a hall full of pigeons and light. The ones at the back start to giggle. The ones at the front hold their faces tight, like people trying to remember something. A girl in the third row, who has been crying since she came in, stops.

Afterwards, in the empty hall, {mei.he} comes to you with the string in {mei.his} hand and the look of someone who has just got off a ship. 'I thought I'd die,' {mei.he} says. 'I counted. It was two hundred and eleven times I nearly ran for the door.' And you say that you counted too, from behind the pillar, and that it was only a hundred and seven. 'Show-off,' says {mei.he}, and throws the string at you.

You come back to the Pavilion with the taste of the Concord's cheese in your mouth and a draft contract in your sleeve. The Fund room is as you left it. The light slants through the high window. Mei is sitting on the floor with her back to the cabinet and a bowl of rice on her knee.

**Mei:** I found it. Behind the camphor drawer. There's a false back. I didn't want to open it without you. I'm learning to be careful.

It is a plain notebook, grey, with a cloth cover. There are no entries in it for the Fund. There is only a list of names, each with a sum and a date, and beside each name, in a small tidy hand, a single word: faithful, or wavering, or doubtful, or new. At the top of the first page is a title: THOSE WHO ARE KIND.

**Closing scene**

*[only if hand is 1]* Registrar Ibbot is on the list. Beside his name is 'faithful', and a sum, and the words 'for the sister'. He had not known the money came from the Concord. He had thought it was a pension from his old school.

*[only if hand is 2]* Captain Renn is on the list. Beside her name is 'wavering', and a small sum, and the words 'one night'. Beside it, in another hand, is a note: she may be made useful. She does not know she has been written down.

*[only if hand is 3]* Sunny Aldous is on the list. Beside his name is 'new', and a large sum, and the words 'for the library'. He has been paid, regularly and generously, for three years, to be happy. He had thought it was a gift.

You close the notebook. Three names, and two others you do not know. One of the three is the hand that has been keeping the books honest, and the other two are only the hands that have been used. It takes you most of the night to be sure which, and the answer, when it comes, is the one that you were afraid it would be.

**Mei:** It's the one who writes the cats, isn't it? The small neat hand.

**You:** Mei draws the cats.

**Mei:** I know. I wanted to see your face.

## 4.19  "A Letter from Zhao"  (`zhaoletter`)

- **Starts when:** 1 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 490 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

*[only if dead.zhao]* It is found in the sealed drawer of the Elder's chair, by the boy who sweeps the study. It has been there for three years. It is written on a sheet of plain paper in a firm, narrow, upright hand, and it has no name on the outside. It is for you. You know it by the way it is folded, in four, with the fold pressed twice.

*[only if not dead.zhao]* It comes by the hand of a boy from the school, who brings it from the hut at the edge of the grounds where the old Elder lives. It is written on a sheet of plain paper in a firm, narrow, upright hand. It has your name on the outside. The boy says that the Elder wrote it with the shutters closed and the lamp lit at noon.

**Closing scene**

'I have been trying for some weeks to write a letter and have written eleven, and burned them. This is the twelfth. I will not apologise. It would be a lie of a new kind. I will tell you only what I know. I did not take the money for myself. I took it because the Pavilion was failing, and the Concord offered, and when I asked what the price was, they said: only that the school teach no one to mend themselves. It sounded small.'

'I want you to understand that I did believe it. I thought: a school that cannot heal is a school that needs its masters. I had been a poor boy once, and needed a master, and I thought what I was doing was keeping a door open. I did not know that a door which is kept open by a lack is a trap. You taught me that. You, with your question in the third year, in front of the whole class, in that terrible calm voice.'

'When you came to me in the courtyard I was relieved. I want you to know. It was the first time in thirty years that someone had looked at me and seen the whole of it. I could not say so. I was too proud. But I remember I thought: at last.'

'I have one request, and it is not for me. There is a boy in the third form whose name is Pell, and he cannot read. He is a bright child. Nobody has bothered. I should be obliged if you would see to it. That is all. Zhao.'

You fold it in four. You press the fold twice, with your thumbnail, the way he did. You find Pell in the kitchen, on a stool, peeling an onion. He is nine. He has the stubborn silent face of a child who has been told he is slow. You sit down beside him and say, 'Would you like to learn something?' And he looks at you, and the onion, and says: 'Is it hard?'

> The Concord's hand is standing in front of you, and has told you everything.

The Lord Auditor Calder comes to the Pavilion on a clear morning, alone, on foot, in the black coat. He walks in at the gate without being announced. He stops in the middle of the courtyard, which is a vegetable garden, and looks at the cabbages as though they had offended him personally.

**Calder:** The Matron has withdrawn her kindness. She asked me to inform you. I do not wish to be a bad guest, but I have also been asked to collect, on behalf of the Concord, a number of things that are not yours. The books. The Fund. The name. Your friend with the cat on her wrist.

One of them, a small boy, crosses the garden with a watering can and sets it down beside the body, for no reason that he can explain.

*[only if not dead.calder]* He goes down on one knee in the cabbages and stays there. 'That was extremely irregular,' he says, in his dry hinge voice. Then he gets up, and brushes his coat, and bows to the whole of the courtyard in turn. He leaves by the gate, and does not look back. A cabbage has attached itself to his sleeve. Nobody tells him.

On the gate, a few minutes later, you find a sealed note. It is from the Matron. It says: 'I withdraw the matter of the Fund. I would be glad to dine again. I am sorry about the cheese.'

She is standing at the Pavilion gate when you come back from market, in a gown the colour of the underside of a leaf. She is tall, and thin, and pale, with the long still hands of a woman who has never in her life been in a hurry, and her hair is the grey-green of a pond in autumn. She has a tea set on the wall beside her, on a tray, with two cups. She has been, you realise, there a little while.

**Gloam:** Madam Gloam. I do hope this is not an intrusion. I was passing, and it occurred to me that I had been rather rude. One should thank the people one has been writing to. Will you have a cup?

**Closing scene**

The tea is excellent. It is, you think, the best tea you have tasted, though you cannot recall drinking it. You have the odd sense of having been given back something that was always yours.

**Gloam:** I left you the scroll. I wanted to say so in person. I left it in a number of hands, you see, over a number of years. I did hope it would find someone patient. Nobody else got further than the third line. You got to the end.

She says it with a kind of pride, like a woman who has set a hard puzzle and watched someone solve it. You do not like how much it pleases you.

**Gloam:** I should like to tell you the story. It is not a long one. May I?

**Closing scene**

*[only if how is 1]* The first is the Elder's study, in the corridor off the great hall, which has been shut since the Elder was removed. It is clean. Someone has dusted it. A window is open. On the desk there is a little brass key, and a sheet of paper with a single line in his upright hand: IT SEEMED A SMALL THING. You sit in his chair. It fits you better than you would like.

*[only if how is 2]* The first is the pear tree behind the infirmary, where there is a small grave with a plain wooden marker. Lan. Someone has kept it weeded. The second is your own desk, in the old reading hall, which the school has kept exactly as it was. The lid still has your initials cut into the corner. You lift it. Inside, at the bottom, on the old ink-stain, there is nothing at all. But the wood is warm, the way a seat is warm where somebody has just got up, and you stand with your hand on the lid and feel, very clearly, the shape of an absence that is also a gift.

The third is the gate, where Mei stood, on the worn flagstone, on the day of the expulsion. You stand on it and look down the road. It is a grey road, going round a hill. A boy of eleven comes along it with a bundle. He is expelled, or leaving, or on an errand. He stops before you and looks up with enormous grave eyes and asks if this is the Stillwater Pavilion. You say that it is. He asks if they have a library. You say they have a very good one.

**Boy:** Is there a part you're not allowed in?

**You:** There used to be.

**Boy:** Good. I'll start with that.

It is Mei who thinks of it. {mei.He} comes into the reading hall at dawn with a map under {mei.his} arm and the fixed pale look of someone who has been counting. 'You are not the only one,' {mei.he} says. 'She said so herself. She left it in a number of hands. Where are the others?'

It takes a month, and it is more pleasant than it should be. You find them in ones and twos, in villages the map has no names for, by asking in inns about a grey-green gown, and a cup of tea that one is not sure one drank.

**Closing scene**

A baker, in a river town, who found a leaf in a loaf. A road-mender who found one in the lining of his coat. A girl of fifteen who found it pinned to her pillow. None of them kept the leaf. None of them could say what it said. All of them, when you ask, smile at once, a wide slow smile that arrives before the question has finished.

They are, without exception, the happiest people you have met. They are quiet and kind and extremely easy company. The baker's bread is the best you have eaten. The road-mender's road has no ruts in it. The girl has been, her mother says, a joy since the day it came: never cross, never sad, never frightened.

**Mei:** Look at them. Look at where they're standing.

You look. The baker is standing a hand's breadth to one side of his own shadow. The road-mender, who has not stopped smiling, has not moved his eyes from a point somewhere beyond your shoulder for the whole of the conversation. The girl is half a pace to the left of herself.

**Mei:** She's not harming them. That's what I can't get past. They're better than they were. They're all better. And they're all just a little not here.

You walk home in the dusk, side by side, without speaking. About a mile from the Pavilion, {mei.he} takes your hand and holds it, quite hard, and does not seem to notice that {mei.he} has.

## 4.28  "A Gourd by the Road"  (`inn3`)

**Opening scene**

You walk to the inn at {@inn} because you need to walk. The road is dry. The trees are green. You have nothing particular in mind except a bowl of something warm and a corner away from the question.

The old man is already in the corner. He is a small, shabby, cheerful person in a coat with too many patches, and a battered straw hat pushed back on his head. He sits on the floor with his back against the wall, a red gourd on his knee and a cup beside it. He raises the cup to you gravely. He has been drinking since morning. It does not seem to have slowed him down.

**Closing scene**

**Old man:** Ah. You've met the Guest. It's the tea. She does a very fine tea. I would stay away from it. I'm told it's the best in the Garden, and I say that as a man who has made a study of the field.

**You:** Who are you?

**Old man:** Oh, nobody. A man who walks about. I sing a bit. I have a gourd with a hole in it, which is a great problem for a gourd.

He pours you a cup out of the gourd, and it is plain water, cold from a well, and tastes of nothing and everything. You drink it. The room settles. The question, which has been pressing on the back of your head for a week, lightens, a little, like a coat taken off.

**Old man:** She isn't wrong, you know. That's the trouble. Everything she says is true. It's an awful thing to be set down. It's also, I'm told, restful. I've known some who went that road and were grateful. I only don't care for the way she does the asking.

He lets his head fall back against the wall. His hat tips over his eyes.

**Old man:** If you can't think of a thing, find someone who'll tell you what they were like when they didn't know. That's a very good question to ask a person. Go and ask your friend with the cat.

## 4.29  "Mei's Question"  (`meiq`)

- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones

**Opening scene**

She asks it in the kitchen, at night, over a bowl of cold noodles, with a candle burning between you and the whole school asleep. She has her feet up on the rungs of your chair. She is eating with her fingers. It is the kind of hour at which the Pavilion is a house like any other, and the two of you are only the people who are awake.

**Closing scene**

**Mei:** What is it like? Setting it down. I want you to tell me properly. Not the way you do in the lectures. What does it feel like?

**You:** It's like standing at the top of a flight of stairs with a heavy pot, and being told you can put it on the step. And you put it on the step. And you can see the whole of the hall, suddenly. You didn't know there was so much hall.

**Mei:** And then?

**You:** And then you don't want to pick it up. That's the thing. It's not that you can't. It's that the hall's so big.

She is quiet. The candle gutters. She turns her chopsticks over, and over, and looks at them. Then, in a smaller voice than she has ever used with you, a voice you remember from a roadside inn, she says: 'I don't have a lot to put down. Did you know? I thought about it. I thought, I'm happy. I really am. It's just a house and a cat and you. It's very small.'

**You:** It's a good size.

**Mei:** It's a good size. That's what I'm saying. I don't need the hall.

She picks up her bowl and goes round the table and sits down beside you on the bench. She leans her whole weight against your shoulder. After a minute she says, into your sleeve: 'I'd like to be the thing you pick up.' And you say that you were thinking exactly that, and neither of you moves until the candle is out.

## 4.30  "The Cat's Opinion"  (`catop`)

The Pavilion cat has formed a view. It is a large, stout, torn-eared tabby called, for no reason anyone can discover, Magistrate, and it has lived on the roof of the reading hall for nine years. It has a reputation. It does not like anyone. It tolerates Mei. It has, on occasion, been seen to stand on a desk and look at a student in the way that judges look at people who have been late with a fine.

On the afternoon that Madam Gloam takes tea at the gate, it comes down from the roof.

You have never seen it move so fast. It comes across the courtyard like a thrown hat, flat out, tail like a bottle brush, and stops six feet from the wall where the tea tray stands. It sits. It raises its ragged head. It looks at the guest with an expression of perfect, serene, concentrated hatred, and begins very slowly to growl: a long, low, rising note, like a kettle thinking about it.

**Gloam:** What a handsome animal.

She puts out a gloved hand, palm up, in the manner of one used to the approval of beasts. The cat stares at the glove. Then it turns its back on her, with the most extreme deliberateness, lifts its tail, and sprays the leg of the tea table.

There is a silence. Madam Gloam looks at the stream of cat running down the leg. She smiles, very slightly, with one corner of her mouth, and takes her hand back, and folds it with the other in her lap. 'I see,' she says. 'It is always the small ones who are best informed.'

She does not take the tea. She leaves it where it is, steaming, on the wall, and rises, and bows to the cat. The cat does not bow back. It is washing its face.

The technique, when it comes, is very simple. It takes one breath. You draw it in, as the first line says, and you hold the world. You let it out, as the last line says, and you set it down. For the space of the breath there is nothing. Not darkness, not silence, not peace. Simply no weight. You have not known how much you carry until it is gone.

## 4.33  "The Students' Questions"  (`questions`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended

**Opening scene**

The school has been asking questions, because that is what it does. They arrive at the door of your study in a trickle, then a stream, then a flood, in the evenings, in ones and twos, carrying their slates. They have heard that there is a guest. They have heard that there is an offer. The Pavilion has no secrets, and a school with no secrets runs on conversation like a mill on water.

The youngest is a boy of nine. He comes last, after the rest have gone, and stands in the doorway with his hands behind his back and an expression of fierce, practical, horrified concentration.

**Closing scene**

**Boy:** Does someone who puts the world down still love people?

It is the best question you have been asked. You look at him for as long as you decently can. Then you admit that you don't know. You have met people who put it down and were gentle, you tell him, and you cannot tell if they were also kind. The difference might be that kindness costs you something and gentleness doesn't.

**Boy:** So you have to pick it up again. To love.

**You:** I think so. I think you have to hold it. You can't love a thing you've put on the floor.

He thinks about this. He turns it over, visibly, like a coin. Then he says, with a judicial air, that it seems an awful lot of trouble, and that he will probably do it anyway, and goes away to the kitchen to see about his supper.

You sit in the empty room until the lamp wants oil. The page is on the desk, and not a word of it is written. You dip the brush, and put it down, and pick it up. Then you go out for a walk, and come back at dawn with the answer, which is shorter than you thought.
