**Opening scene**

She takes you down in the evening, by herself, without being asked. Not to the forge. To the Garrison of the Crossed: a plain, flat and grey, in a country you do not know, with an empty fortress at the far edge and its gates standing open. The Door is a long day's walk from here, under the Palace. This is where the called wait for their turn. A line of men and women stands outside the gate, in good boots, with their blades at their sides, quietly in the rain.

**Iron:** This is where they wait before they go through. It is not a grand place. The Gardener does not care for grandeur. It is only a gate in a wall. I have stood here for every company. I have given each one a word. I could not give them anything else.

**Closing scene**

She walks along the line. She knows them by name. She stops in front of each, and says something short, and moves on. A boy of sixteen gets a pinch on the cheek. A woman of seventy gets a bow. A big man in a leather jerkin, who is crying without noise, gets a hand put flat on his chest, over the heart, and held there while he breathes.

When the last has gone in at the gate, she lowers herself on to a block of stone beside it, slowly, as if every joint were a separate effort. Her hands, in her lap, are scarred in a way you have seen only on the very best smiths, and on soldiers. There are the flat white tracks of old burns and old cuts, and something older that looks like the print of a hot chain.

**Iron:** I forged the first nine blades myself, you know. The first nine, for the first nine of us. I gave every one a weight it had to carry. I have not touched a hammer since. I thought that was a kind of wisdom.

**Iron:** Then I met a smith who would not make a thing for a person he had not met. I thought: oh. It is not wisdom. It is just not looking. I have been not looking for a very long time.

She lifts her face to the rain. It is the face of someone who has been very tired for a very long time and has decided, for the length of a breath, not to be.

## 5.32  "The Hundred and First"  (`needle`)

- **Starts when:** 3 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill

**Opening scene**

The hundred and first soldier is not a soldier. She comes in out of the rain on a Wednesday at dusk with a satchel and a lantern, a small brown woman in a grey coat, with her sleeves pushed up and a smell of vinegar and boiled linen. Her name is Dr. Perin. She is forty. She is a field surgeon, attached to the third company, and she has been told by Elder Iron that she may have a blade, and she has come to say that she doesn't want one.

**Perin:** I'm sorry. I know it's an honour. I know you've been up since four. I'd be a liar if I said I could carry a sword. I'd drop it. I'd cut my own foot off. But I'd like to ask for something, and I've been rehearsing the words for a week, and they sound ridiculous.

**Closing scene**

**Perin:** I want a needle. A good one. Curved. With a long eye, strong enough to go through a leg. The needles I've got keep breaking. They're thin, and cheap, and made by people who've never had to put a man's arm back on in the dark.

You make it. It takes a whole night. It is the smallest thing you have ever forged, no longer than your finger, curved like a new moon, with an eye the width of a hair. You do it by lantern and by feel, with Pia holding the work in the tongs and Tam holding his breath. It is the hardest piece of work you have done since the sword. You do not know why.

She tests it on a scrap of belt leather. It goes through like water through a sieve. She runs her thumb along the curve, and holds it up to the lantern, and the light comes through the eye.

**Perin:** That's it. That's the one. Oh, you beauty.

She puts it in a small tin box. She shuts the lid. She does not say thank you. She says that she will count how many it saves, and send you the number. She says it is a thing she does. She says she has a book.

She goes out into the rain with the lantern. At the door, Pia murmurs, 'Number one hundred and one,' and writes it on the wall. Beside it, in the space where the thing asked for goes, she chalks one word: NEEDLE.

She comes back. It is the second month of spring and the road is soft. The Dame comes up the hill on her own two feet, her bad wrist strapped to her chest and the heavy blade slung on her back. She has been through the gate. She has been, she says, a long way. She has come, in her own words, to complain.

**Orsolya:** It is too heavy.

**You:** You asked for it heavy.

**Orsolya:** I did. I was a fool. I asked for what I wanted to be, and not for what I was. Sit down. I shall have to say something I do not enjoy.

**Closing scene**

She lays the blade on the bench. It is notched. There is a gap in the edge the width of a thumb, and a long scratch across the flat where it turned a spear. She turns it over. There is a dent in the pommel the shape of a skull, and she runs her thumb across it with the tenderness of someone touching a sleeping dog.

**Orsolya:** I used the other hand. Just as I said. For three weeks. And then in the fourth, on a hill, in the rain, with my bad one on my chest, I could not lift it, and I put it down, and I took up a stick off the ground. And I fought with the stick. I want you to know that it was an excellent stick.

She tells it plainly. She is a soldier of the old kind: she has no wish to be admired. She says that the stick was ash, and the length of her arm, and had a knot at the top, and that she broke a man's wrist with it, and that she would like another. She says she would like a stick.

**Pia:** We don't make sticks.

**Orsolya:** You make what's asked for. It's your rule. Don't tell me you've no pride in the principle.

You make it. It takes an afternoon. It is the strangest thing that has come out of the forge: a plain rod of steel, hand-length and a half, with a knot of folded iron at the top, and a leather grip. It looks like a walking stick for a mule. She takes it in her good hand, and hefts it, and her whole face changes.

**Orsolya:** That is the first thing anyone has made for me, in sixty-five years, that was the right size.

The Gardener comes himself after all, on a morning of first frost, in the shape of an old man in a patched coat with a bag of apples. He does not announce himself. He walks in at the door, nods to Pia, nods to Marl, and sits down on the bench by the hearth and starts peeling an apple with a small, blunt knife. He does it very slowly. He does not seem to be in any hurry.

**Old Man:** I wanted to see the place that made them. I have the numbers, of course. I have all the numbers. It is not the same.

He has the kind of face that you think you could describe, and that is gone from your mind when he turns away. His hands are the hands of a man who has held a great many things for a very long time.

**Old Man:** They tell me you wouldn't make one for a person you hadn't met. I want to say that I would not have asked. I would have asked someone else, and the someone else would have said yes, and the blades would have been made, and nobody would have known the names. I want you to know that I know the names.

**Closing scene**

He lays the last apple on the bench. He looks at Evenfall on the wall. He looks at the hook by the door, and the blade that hangs on it, the one you made for yourself.

**Old Man:** I am a long way from fair. I have asked a great deal of a great many people, and I have not always known what I was asking. I would like to repay a part of it. I cannot do much. I can do something small.

He puts out a hand and touches the blade, and it rings, very softly, like a cup struck with a spoon. Something goes through the forge: a feeling, more than a sound, like the first warm day after a long winter. The fire flares up of its own accord and settles. The ticking, which has not been heard since the Marshal, begins again, and this time it does not stop.

**Pia:** What did you do?

**Old Man:** I gave it a little of what I have. I'm told that is how it is meant to be done.

When you look round, he is gone. There is a half-peeled apple on the bench, with a single curl of skin hanging from it, exactly as if he had stepped out for a moment. You eat it, because it seems rude not to.

## 5.I3  Interlude: The Mending Post  (between season 3 and season 4)

The forge runs on. The sign has four names on it and a fifth, in a child's hand, that nobody will paint over. Pia has her own hammer now, with her own mark on the head. The blades go out into the Outside, a hundred of them, and a hundred and one.

A parcel arrives on a Tuesday in brown paper, tied with a bit of green cord. There is no stamp. There is no carrier. It is on the doorstep when you open up. It smells of smoke and rain and somewhere far off.

I tell them what you told me: you don't make a thing for a person you haven't met. They look at me as if I were mad. Then, a week later, they bring me a nail and ask for a blade.

## 5.45  "Who Holds the Hammer"  (`hammer`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 500 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 136 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You are tired. You have been tired for a spell. You notice it first in the morning, at the quench, when your wrist does not answer as it used to. You notice it again in the evening when the hammer feels a pound too heavy. Pia sees. She says nothing. She brings a stool and sets it by the anvil and, without comment, stands in your place.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `forge`; default: option 1)

> The forge is yours, and Pia stands at the anvil.

1. Give it to her: the sign, the hammer, the name, and keep a stool by the bellows.
   - You hand her the hammer. You do it in the yard at sunset in front of the whole forge, Marl and Voss and the boys and the girl with the freckles. You give her the sign, the keys and the account books. She takes the hammer in both hands and says nothing at all. Then she goes into the shop, and strikes. It is the first stroke of a different smith.
   - **Voss:** (to himself, wiping his eye) Number Three.
2. Share it: both names on the sign, and the work divided as it falls.
   - You share it. The sign is repainted, in black, in a new hand. It says: PIA AND YOU, SMITHS. The work divides itself. She takes the long blades and you take the small. She takes the loud days and you take the quiet. It is the happiest arrangement either of you has ever had, and it lasts for the rest of your working life.
   - **Marl:** (counting) It adds up. I'm so surprised.
3. Keep it, and let her build her own beside it.
   - You keep it, and you help her build her own. It takes a year. She has the old stable, across the yard, with a new chimney and a new bellows and an anvil from the scrapyard. It is called PIA'S. For a season there are two forges in one yard and a good deal of friendly noise. Then the blades start to come in addressed to either, and then to neither, and one winter morning you wake to find the two have a single door.
   - **Pia:** I did not mean to do that.

**Closing scene**

The hammer rings in the shop. You listen from the bench by the window with a mug of tea. It is not your stroke. It is a little quicker, a little lighter, a little more sure. It is the sound of the forge getting on with its work. You find you are smiling. You find you have not wished, for a moment, to be at the anvil.

## 5.46  "Quiet Fires"  (`quiet`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 2,000 spirit stones, +3 potential, 4 Potential Pills, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 249 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The forge is quiet at night. The fire is banked and the bellows are still, and the air in the shop smells of hot iron and linseed and tea. The mending parcels come twice a week now, and Pia and Voss and Marl and the boys work through them in a long unhurried line. You sit on the stool by the anvil, in the glow, with a blanket round your knees. You have taken to watching.

**Closing scene**

Tonight a parcel has come that no one has opened. It is brown, and tied with the green cord, and has your name on it in a strange careful hand. You undo the knot. Inside, wrapped in a soft grey cloth, there is a small iron nail. It is bent, and rusted, and has been through a fire. There is a card with it. It says: Do you remember? You made it for a boy called Tam. He kept it.

You turn it in your fingers. It is the first thing you ever forged, at the age of eleven, in your father's shop, with your father's hand on your wrist. It was a nail. It was the worst nail in the world. You gave it away, for luck. You had not thought of it in forty years.

**Pia:** (from the bellows, quietly, after a while) What is it?

**You:** It's a nail.

**Pia:** (coming to look, with a face grown suddenly young) It's a good nail. It's the best one I ever saw.

## 5.I4  Interlude: The Long Quiet  (between season 4 and season 5)

**Interlude**

The forge has three names on the sign now, and a fourth, in a child's hand, that nobody will paint over. The blades go out, and the stories come back. You keep the hammer by the door.

*[only if tamgo is 1]* Tam keeps the bellows. He says he is only keeping them warm.

A blade arrives by the Seam in a plain sack. It is notched. It has a drawing of a bird on the tang.

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended

**Opening scene**

It comes in a sack, left on the step in the night, with no note. It is a plain short sword, dull-edged and heavy in the hand, notched in eleven places. You turn it over in the light of the forge. You know the work. It is yours. You made it, a long time ago, for a boy who asked for a thing he could carry.

**Closing scene**

The tang has a small drawing scratched into it, a bird, in a nervous careful hand. Under it, in the same hand, a line: I kept it sharp. I'm sorry about the notches. They were all for something. The grip is wrapped in a strip of green cloth that you do not remember. It smells of apples.

*[only if tamgo is 2]* **Pia:** (looking over your shoulder, with soot on her nose) He's alive. It's from him. It's his handwriting.

*[only if not tamgo=2]* **Pia:** (looking over your shoulder, with soot on her nose) That's a blade from the Outside. I'd know the quench anywhere. Somebody has been looking after it.

You hang it on the wall above the anvil. It does not look out of place. After a time you notice the other blades on the wall have turned a very little, all of them, toward it, as plants lean toward a window.

## 5.48  "The Thousand and One"  (`dr2`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight

**Opening scene**

Elder Iron sends for you. She is at the gate of the Garrison with a lamp, in her leather apron, standing in the rain with her hands behind her back. She asks whether you would like to see where the blades go. She says she has never asked anyone to watch twice.

**Closing scene**

The line is long. Each of them has a blade at their side. You know most of them by the grip. There is the long one with the walnut handle, for the sergeant. There is the little curved knife for the girl from the salt flats. There is the plain blade you made for a man who would not lift it, and he is lifting it, and he has a smile on his face you have never seen on a soldier.

**Iron:** I forged the first nine. I forged them for the nine of us. I gave each one a weight to carry. I have never been sure that was right. I am watching your hundred and first walk in at the gate, and I think it was.

She puts a hand on your arm. It is hard and warm, and has a long white scar. She says nothing more. You stand beside her until the last of them has gone, and then she hands you the lamp, and walks into the dusk, and you do not follow.

## 5.49  "Evenfall"  (`dr3`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `palace`.  "Go to the Palace of the Oldest Order, at Originis, to the Empty Seat."
- **Pays:** 1,000 spirit stones, +2 potential, 2 Potential Pills, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 121 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Evenfall hangs in a sheath that thinks twice. You take it down on the first morning of winter and carry it, as you would carry a child that was a bit too old, to the Palace. The Wicks make way. The Seat is cold. The nine lamps burn without a flicker. Under your arm the blade makes a sound like a held breath.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `latch`; default: option 1)

> Evenfall is in your arms. The Door is under the Seat.

1. Stay: hang Evenfall on the wall of the Palace forge, for Elder Iron's successors.
   - You hang it in the forge under the Palace, on a hook that Elder Iron's hands have worn. It settles. The whole room seems to breathe out. A young smith with a burned apron stands by the door, very pale, and asks if she may touch it. You say she may. She does. Nothing happens, and she bursts into tears.
   - **Iron:** (from the doorway, gruff) That is exactly what is supposed to happen.
2. Go: carry it through, and leave it where it can be borrowed.
   - You stand with it in the doorway of the Seat. You stay on the threshold and say that you will go in when the forge is quiet. You find that you have said it in the voice you use for customers, and that it is a promise, and for once you do not mind that it is a long one.
3. Hold the latch: stand by the Door and hand a blade to each one who has none.
   - You spend the winter at the Seat with a bag of knives and a whetstone. You hand a blade to each one who comes without. They look at it, and at you, and go through. It is the humblest work you have ever done. Elder Iron stands at your back some nights with her arms folded, and does not say a word.

**Closing scene**

The forge at home has a new sign. It is hand-lettered, in black paint, in a hand that is yours and Pia's and Tam's and a child's. It says: WE MAKE THINGS. THEY GO WHERE THEY ARE NEEDED. It hangs under the old sign. The wind does not swing it. Nobody has asked who hung it.

## 5.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

The sign over the forge still says {last} and Child. You repainted it again in the spring, and this time you added a small line underneath, in Pia's hand, which says AND PIA, AND TAM, AND EVERYONE ELSE WHO KNOCKED.

*[only if tamgo is 1]* Tam stayed. He took over the bellows, then the forge, then the sign, and he has the decency to pretend that he is only keeping it warm.

*[only if tamgo is 2]* Tam went. He sends word through the Seam, now and again: a note, a drawing of a bird. The blade you made him is on the wall of his room in the Outside, and it has never once been drawn.

*[only if tamgo is 3]* Tam went through the gate, and came back through it after a year, and does not talk about it. He keeps a notched blade by the bed and a box of apples at the foot of it, and he is, Pia says, a better smith than the two of you together.

*[only if edge is 1]* The blade by the door dulls itself on a stone whenever you leave it near anyone who is angry. Visitors say it is the strangest thing in the forge.

*[only if edge is 2]* The blade by the door is the best you ever made, and you do not take it down. It is a good thing to know that you could.

*[only if edge is 3]* The blade by the door has no name, and no mark, and it makes you feel as though the forge itself were listening. Children are allowed to look at it. They never ask what it is for.

*[only if e.spouse]* Marl keeps the accounts and the chickens, and tells people at dinner that the forge was a bad bet but the smith was a good one. You have never been sure which of you is meant to be the joke.

*[only if not e.spouse]* Marl still brings the eggs. The gate still does not squeak. You have both decided that this is a kind of answer.

*[only if dead.ketter]* The salt flats are green now. Somebody planted barley.

*[only if latch is 1]* Evenfall hangs in the Palace forge, on a worn hook. The young smiths touch it before their first quench. Nothing happens. They say it helps.

*[only if latch is 2]* There is a blade by the door of the forge, with no scabbard, and a promise attached to it that is not yet due.

*[only if latch is 3]* A man with a bag of knives stands at the Empty Seat on winter evenings. The Wicks say he gives them away.

Evenfall hangs on the wall over the forge, in a sheath that thinks twice. Children are allowed to look. When they ask what it is for, somebody says: nothing. They look let down. Then somebody else always adds that this is the best thing about it.

## 5.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

The Palace's forge is the best you have ever seen. You do not make a single weapon in it. You make hinges and kettles, and a sign for the kitchen door that says Welcome.

Pia would have approved.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

The army needs spears, and you spent a lifetime deciding which ones you can carry. You make them honestly and well.

Every night you set your father's sword on the armoury table, to remind the others what a blade is for.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You leave the Garden with a hammer on your shoulder. Evenfall is finished, but there is room in the Outside for a second blade, you decide.

You find a forge. It is cold. You light it.

**You are struck down by the array**

Evenfall does not cut anyone who has not raised a hand. You had, that day. It is the one time its maker would have been ashamed.

He would have forgiven you before the end of the sentence.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden dims. The forge cools. The last thing to go is the sound of a small hammer on a small anvil, tick, tick, tick, like a clock in a very small house.

# 6.S1  Season 1: The Fox

## 6.1  "The Tune in the Throat"  (`voice`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** Go to the place `meadow`.  "Go to the meadow at {@meadow} and wait for whatever has been watching the house."
- **Pays:** 1 Cultivation Pill
- **When it closes, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.companion(c, st, "fox", FOX_NAMES[Math.max(0, Chapters.flag(st, "fox") - 1)], "Grey Fox", Math.max(6, c.lvl), true)`
- **Words:** 456 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You were seven when your mother walked into the mountains. Your father told you she had gone to look for something, and he said it the way you tell a child the sun will come up, as though it were a matter that did not need his help.

He raised you on a farm at the edge of the wild: forty goats, a pond, a kitchen that smelled permanently of onions. The animals were calm around you. The geese did not hiss. Once a wolf stood at the treeline for an hour watching you hang the washing, and then left without doing anything about it, which the neighbours, when you told them, found more upsetting than if he had.

Your father gave you nothing of your mother's except a tune. He hummed it when he cooked: three slow notes, and then the same three, higher. You asked him once where it came from, and he said he couldn't remember. He was lying. You could tell, because he stopped humming, and a man who has forgotten a tune does not stop in the middle of it.

You are eighteen now. The farm runs itself, more or less, the goats having formed views. You have decided to find out what the wild wants with you. You will begin with the meadow past the north fence, where the grass is tall enough to hide in, and where for a week something has been watching the house.

**Closing scene**

It is a young thing, grey, fox-shaped, with ears too big for its head, as if somebody had cut them for a larger animal and used the offcuts. It stands in front of you in the long grass with its weight on its back legs and one paw lifted, ready to bolt.

You don't move. You do the only thing you can think of, which is to hum. Three slow notes. The same three, higher. It feels absurd, like singing to a locked door.

The fox sits down. She tilts her head one way and then the other, with the expression of someone who has had a word on the tip of her tongue for years. Then, from deep in her throat, scratchy and a little flat, she answers: three slow notes, and the same three, higher.

Nobody has taught her the tune. As far as you know, nobody has taught anyone the tune but you.

She comes forward through the grass in a series of small hops and pushes her forehead into your palm, hard, the way a cat does. You find you are crying, that she does not mind, and that she is also, with great seriousness, trying to eat your sleeve.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `fox`; default: option 1)

> She will need a name.

1. Burdock, because she sticks to you.
   - Burdock. She looks at you with the polite incomprehension of someone being called after a weed, and decides to allow it.
2. Hum.
   - Hum. She makes the sound at once, and with obvious approval, and then does it again, louder, in case you missed it.
3. Tuppence, which is what she is worth and what you would pay to keep her.
   - Tuppence. She sneezes, which you take as a yes.

## 6.2  "What the Fox Ate"  (`crimes`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 3 weeks (0 years and 3 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **Words:** 345 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

In three weeks, {fox.first} eats a boot, most of a cheese, the church's harvest offering of turnips, one of your father's reading glasses, and a bar of soap, which she regrets at once and for some hours. She does not eat the goats. She appears to regard them as a committee.

She also follows you. Not in the way a dog follows, which is a form of worship, but in the way a very small, very vain landlord follows a tenant: always a little behind, keeping an eye on the premises. When you stop, she sits. When you laugh, she checks the faces of everyone near you to see if the joke was on her.

**Father:** She's the colour of the one your mother had. Not the same one. Her mother's mother's, maybe. They keep to the same hill.

You turn round. He is standing in the kitchen door with a tea towel, looking at the fox in a way that you have never seen him look at an animal. She looks back at him, and does not eat anything.

**Closing scene**

That night he cooks. You are sitting on the step, with {fox.first} asleep across your boots, when the humming starts. It is the tune. He does not stop in the middle of it this time. He hums the six notes, and hums them again, and when he gets to the end he stops, and holds the wooden spoon in the air as if it might add something.

**Father:** She always stopped there. Your mother. Six notes, and then she'd look at the ceiling and say there was another one, a seventh, somewhere in the tune, and she couldn't find it. It drove her half mad. She said all the great beasts had a piece of it, if she could only get them to sing at the same time.

**You:** You told me you couldn't remember it.

**Father:** I remembered it perfectly. That was the trouble.

{fox.first} wakes at the spoon, looks at the two of you, and begins very softly to snore the tune.

## 6.3  "Goats in Committee"  (`goats`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **Words:** 398 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The goats have a government. It took you eighteen years to see it, and it took {fox.first} nine days. There is a nanny called Dowager who sits at the top of the hill and decides, by means of a long yellow look, where everyone will graze. There is a billy who is thought to be in charge and is not. There are three kids who go everywhere together and are, as far as anyone can tell, the opposition.

{fox.first} has not been accepted. She has made this her project. For a week she has crept up the hill every morning to sit as near the Dowager as she dares, ears flat, her whole body saying that she is only here to look. Every morning the Dowager looks at her for a moment and then deliberately turns her back.

**Father:** She'll be there till Midsummer. Dowager held out against your mother for a year. Isha went up that hill with a bucket of oats and a lot of nerve, and she came down with a goat who wouldn't go anywhere else. I never saw a woman lose an argument so politely.

**Closing scene**

It is a fox that settles it, though not the one you expected. A real one, a stranger, a rangy red dog fox, comes down off the moor one night to look at the kids. The Dowager is on her feet before he has cleared the wall. She puts down her head and goes at him like a falling cart. {fox.first}, who has been asleep on the roof of the shed, drops on his back from above with a noise like a kettle boiling over.

It is over in about ten seconds. The red fox goes back over the wall and does not stop until the moor. {fox.first} stands in the yard, quite out of breath, with a mouthful of somebody's tail and a faint look of surprise.

The Dowager comes and stands in front of her. Nobody breathes. She puts out her long yellow face and examines {fox.first} from nose to tail, and then, with great deliberation, as if conferring a title, turns round and lets her pass.

**Father:** Well. That's you in, then.

From the next morning {fox.first} grazes on the hill, which is to say that she lies on it. Nobody has ever seen a fox look so pleased with herself.

## 6.4  "The First Quarrel"  (`quarrel`)

- **Starts when:** 6 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 374 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It is the first time you have shouted at her. She has been into the dresser. She has found, behind the cups, in a biscuit tin, a bundle of old letters in a blue ribbon. She has eaten the ribbon and a corner of three of the letters. Now she has settled on the hearth rug with the remains of a fourth and an expression of deep, bright, sticky satisfaction.

They are not yours. They are your father's. He has kept them in a tin, in a dresser, for twenty years, and has never once taken them out. You see the writing and you stop. It is a woman's hand, quick and slanted, with the tails of the letters going off the line like birds. It is a hand you have seen on the back of a flour sack, once, under a drawing.

**Closing scene**

You say a number of things. They are loud and not fair. {fox.first} listens to all of them with her ears flat and her whole body gone small. When you stop to draw air she gets up and goes away, very slowly, out of the door and into the yard, and does not come back that night.

You find her in the morning in the loft over the barn, in a nest of hay, with the scrap of letter between her paws. It has a word on it. She has been guarding it. It says: ...and tell the child that the wild is not a thing you go into. It is a thing you let come to you.

You sit down in the hay beside her. You say no sorry, because she would not know the word. You put out your hand, flat, on the hay, and after a long while she puts her chin on it. She is trembling a little. You say: 'You can have the ribbon.' She sneezes. It is, you gather, forgiveness.

**Father:** (from the foot of the ladder) I heard. I'll tell you something. I read those letters every night for the first year. Then I put them in the tin. I couldn't bear to look at them, and I couldn't bear to burn them. I think she did you a favour.

## 6.5  "Isha Wildmere"  (`legacy`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended; Major Lvl 1 or more (given up after 6 more years of waiting)
- **Task:** Reach Major Lvl 1.  "Reach Major Lvl 1, and learn what your mother was."
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **Words:** 285 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The letter comes by a boy on a mule, and it is in your father's careful hand, because he is not a man who writes letters, and so he writes them as if each one were the only one.

'My child. I have been a coward, and I would like to stop. Your mother was Isha Wildmere. In her day they called her the Voice of the Wild. She spoke to the great beasts and they listened. She had three: Moss, who sleeps in a lake in the north; Quill, who nests where the storms break; and Old Ember, who was her oldest friend and the most dangerous.'

'When you were seven she went into the mountains to find Ember, who had gone missing. She did not come back. I did not follow her. I had you. I made that choice and I do not regret it, but I regret everything round it. Enclosed is her bone whistle. She told me to give it to you when you were old enough to be afraid of nothing. You were never afraid of anything. I should have sent it years ago.'

{fox.first} has found the folded paper before you have finished it and is trying to take it away to somewhere private. You let her.

**Closing scene**

The whistle is yellow with age, no longer than your finger, with a tiny hole at each end. You put it to your lips and stop short of blowing. You are not ready, and you suspect it knows.

You say the three names aloud, to see what it is like. Moss. Quill. Ember. {fox.first} stops what she is doing, and turns, and looks at the north.

## 6.6  "What the Father Kept"  (`trunk`)

- **Starts when:** 6 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 404 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You are packing for the road north when your father comes into the room with a trunk. It is a small one, black, with brass corners and a broken lock. He sets it on the bed and stands looking at it the way he looks at a pot he is not sure is done.

**Father:** I have been keeping this for eleven years. It is not a secret. I did not know how to hand it to you. You have to hand a thing like this over at the right time, or it turns into a speech.

**Closing scene**

There is not much in it. A hairbrush, with a long grey feather caught in the bristles. A bone comb. A pair of men's gloves, much too small for a man. A page of music, ruled by hand, with a tune on it that you know, six notes in two lines, and below the sixth, in a big impatient scrawl, a seventh bar, empty, with a question mark.

And under the music, folded small, a child's drawing. It is done in charcoal on the back of a flour bag. It shows three animals in a field. One is big and round, with a head like a stone. One is long and white, with her neck up. The third is black and enormous, with tusks, drawn so large that he goes off the edge of the paper. Under them, in the unsteady capitals of a five-year-old, is written: MOSS. QUILL. EMBER.

**You:** I drew this.

**Father:** You did. The summer you were five. They came to the farm.

He sits on the edge of the bed. His hands, on his knees, are not steady. He tells it without looking at you.

**Father:** She brought them, all three, for three nights. In the north field. She said you ought to know them while you were small enough not to be frightened. The tortoise ate the cabbages. The crane perched on the barn and told the weathercock what it was doing wrong. And the big one, the black one, wouldn't come in the gate. He lay down outside it with his chin on the road. You went out in your nightgown and sat on his head.

**Father:** You don't remember. I know you don't. I think she made you forget, a little, for your own sake. She said you'd remember in your own time. I think this is your own time.

**Opening scene**

The inn at {@town} is called the Cracked Egg, for reasons the landlord will tell you at length. {fox.first} has been refused entry three times and has succeeded on the fourth by way of the kitchen. You find her under a table in the back room, in the lap of a stranger, who is looking down at her with the tense, shifting expression of a man holding a bomb.

He is forty-odd, big in the shoulder, with a scar through one eyebrow, a clean shirt, and a table of other men who have the fixed, cheerful look of people who are being bought drinks. He is talking, and you catch only the tail of it: twenty spears, and a price, and the Cinder Boar.

**Brodin:** Forgive me. I seem to have been adopted. Is she yours? She's very forward. I don't mind. I'd just like to know if I'm about to be bitten.

**Closing scene**

**You:** You're the one who's going after Ember.

**Brodin:** Captain Brodin. And yes. You've the look of someone who has opinions. Say them. I'd rather have them over a table than hear them later from behind a tree.

**You:** He's one of three. He belonged to someone. You can't collect a price on a creature that belonged to somebody.

**Brodin:** He killed eleven people. I counted them. I went and counted. The last of them was nineteen years old and he was told to stay at the edge of the wood with the water. He didn't. They never do. I've his belt buckle here. I'm not saying that to be unpleasant. I'm saying it because you asked what the price was for.

He puts it on the table between you. It is a plain iron buckle, worn bright on one side. {fox.first} puts her nose to it, and then, in the manner of a creature who has understood something she was not meant to, leans against the man's arm and leaves it there.

**Brodin:** I'll be in the Burned Wood by autumn. I would ask you not to come. I would be surprised if you listened.

## 6.8  "A Stone on the Path"  (`stones`)

- **Starts when:** 10 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 281 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The first stone is on the doorstep in the morning, and you think nothing of it. It is round and smooth and the green-black of deep water, and it is wet. It has not rained. {fox.first} sniffs it for most of a minute, sneezes, and goes to sit as far from it as the step will allow.

The second is on the path to the well. The third is in your boot. Each one is a different shape, and each is wet, and each, if you put your ear to it, has the faintest sound in it, very low and very slow, like a heartbeat heard through a wall. By the fourth, you understand that someone is being polite.

On the fifth morning there are tracks. They are in the dust of the lane, wide and shallow and slightly wet at the edges, and each one is the size of a table. They come from the north. They stop at your gate, and they turn round.

**Closing scene**

The last stone is the biggest, and it is warm. You hold it in both hands. It hums: one note, enormously low, so far down that you feel it first in your knees. It is the tune. It is not the tune. It is six notes sung by a creature that has all the time there is, and it ends where your mother always stopped.

{fox.first} has got up. She stands in the lane with her ears forward, looking north, with her whole small body pointed like a compass. She looks back at you once, to check you are coming. Then she sets off, and you pick up your pack.

## 6.9  "The Night the Fox Went Out"  (`night`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 369 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You wake in the small hours with the sense of a draught, and find the door ajar and the place by the hearth empty. {fox.first} has gone out. She has gone out before, for a mouse, or a moon, but never with the door left open behind her. That is a message. You pull on your boots and go after her, across the yard and the fence and over the pasture, in the dark.

You find her at the edge of the north field, sitting very upright in the frost, with her tail round her feet, looking at the wood. She does not turn her head. In front of her, a few yards off, sits the great grey wolf with the torn ear.

**Closing scene**

They are not fighting. They are not doing anything. They are sitting on opposite sides of a patch of silver grass, a fox and a wolf, in the dead of a winter night, and between them is a feather. It is long and grey, with a white tip. It is not a goose's. It is not a hawk's. It is lying on the frost where one of them put it down.

You do not move. After a time the wolf stands, slowly, and turns, and goes away along the edge of the wood, without a sound. {fox.first} gets up. She walks to the feather, and picks it up in her teeth, very carefully, by the quill. She carries it back across the field to you, and puts it down on your boot, and sits.

It is the feather from your mother's hairbrush. You are sure of it, though you have no reason. It is the same grey, the same white tip. Either someone brought it here, or it has been brought, over a great many years, by a series of creatures who each took it a little further and put it down for the next.

{fox.first} licks your hand once, gravely, as one signs a receipt. Then she walks back to the house in front of you, with her head up, and does not look round, and when you come in she is asleep before you have the bolt across.

## 6.10  "The Road North"  (`north`)

- **Starts when:** 3 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 375 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You walk, because that is how it is done. You have never been farther than the market town. The road goes north past a quarry, a chapel, and a farm with a loud dog. By the second day you have learned a number of things about travelling with a fox, the chief of which is that everyone is her friend and she is nobody's.

She knows the inns by their smell. She knows which kitchens have a door that sticks. She spends the evenings in the hearth of whatever place has one, chin on the warm stone and one eye on the room. She spends the mornings in the rafters, where she has collected a number of items she cannot account for: a candle, a glove, the landlord's spectacles.

**Closing scene**

On the fifth morning you are crossing a long open moor when {fox.first} stops. Her ears go up. She stands in the heather with one forepaw lifted, looking at the edge of a wood a quarter of a mile away, where something grey is standing at the treeline.

It is a wolf. It is large, old, and rangy, with a torn ear and a stripe of white across the muzzle, and it is watching you. You know it. You have known it for years. It stood at the edge of the north pasture for an hour once, watching you hang washing, and went away without doing anything about it, and the neighbours were never the same.

It does not come closer. It turns, slowly, and starts to trot ahead of you, along the edge of the trees, northward, at exactly the pace you walk. When you stop, it stops. When you sit to eat, it lies down in the heather a long stone's throw off and licks a paw. {fox.first} regards it with an expression of the most complete disapproval, and at the second day's end, gives it half her sausage.

It sees you to the foot of the hills. At the last ridge it sits, and watches, and lifts its muzzle to the sky, and howls: one long, low, steady note, held a very long time. You have heard it before. It is the first tone of the tune.

## 6.11  "Nobody's Lake"  (`moss`)

- **Starts when:** 4 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `lake`.  "Find the sleeping lake at {@lake}."
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill
- **When it closes, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.companion(c, st, "moss", "Moss", "Lake Tortoise", Math.max(10, c.lvl + 3), false)`
- **Words:** 441 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The north is cold and full of water. The lake is called Still Water on the maps and Nobody's Lake by the people who live beside it. A hunter once tried to wade across and came back an hour later with a mild, confused expression and no memory of the middle.

People say the lake is asleep. People say that if you listen carefully you can hear it breathe. {fox.first} has stolen an apple from a market stall at the last village, and carries it all the way in her mouth, which has not made her any more popular.

**Closing scene**

The lake is flat and wide and green as bottle glass. There is a small island in the middle, and it is only when you are standing on the shore that you notice the island has a head. You sit on a flat stone. You wait all day. The light moves. A heron lands, thinks better of it, and goes. At dusk a great slow voice speaks in your mind, in no language you know, and you understand every word.

**Moss:** You smell of her. You have her way of sitting. She came here when she was younger than you, and said she would be back, and I have been patient. I am good at it. You waited a whole day without being asked. That is the answer. She never hurried either.

The island rises. Water pours off a shell the size of a house, and a vast, soft, ancient face turns towards you and blinks once. {fox.first} walks to the edge of the water with the apple, and puts it down at his chin, and sits back with the air of someone who has delivered a package.

**Moss:** What is that?

**You:** It's an apple.

**Moss:** I have heard of them. I have never tasted one. It is very small.

He eats it. It takes a long time, and nobody speaks. When it is over he says it was sweet, and sour. It was, he says, the first new thing to happen to him in two hundred years, and he would like to come with you, if it is no trouble. He says he will be slow.

**Moss:** Sing it for me. The one she sang. I want to hear if you stop in the same place.

You hum the six notes, and he answers them, low as the floor of the lake. You stop. He waits for you to go on, and you cannot.

**Moss:** Yes. That is where she stopped, too. There is one more, you know. I have been waiting a hundred years to hear what it is.

## 6.12  "Slow, and Then Slower"  (`slow`)

**Opening scene**

There turns out to be a great deal to learn about travelling with a tortoise the size of a barn. He cannot go by the road, which would damage it. He cannot go by the river, which would damage him. He goes, therefore, through the fields, at about the speed that a man might walk if he were thinking about something else.

{fox.first} rides on his shell with her chin on her paws, and regards the world from there with the cool, proprietary look of a ship's captain. The children of the first village follow for a mile. The old men of the second take off their hats. In the third, a farmer comes out and says, with enormous dignity, that someone ought to have asked before putting a lake in his turnips.

**Closing scene**

On the last evening of the trip he falls asleep in the middle of the road, between one step and the next, with one foot raised, and does not wake up until morning. A cart is stopped behind him. The carter climbs down, looks, climbs back up, and unharnesses his horse, and the two of them sit by the side of the road with a flask until daylight.

**Moss:** I'm so sorry. I do that.

**Carter:** Don't mention it. My wife says I do the same in the pew.

You make your camp beside a tortoise, in the dust, at the top of a hill, with a fox asleep in a hole in his shell. Above you, in the north-west, there is weather coming, a long bruised line of it, with lightning walking inside like someone going from room to room.

**Moss:** That would be Quill. She has a nest where the storms break. She is fond of drama.

## 6.I1  Interlude: Three Slow Notes  (between season 1 and season 2)

**Interlude**

You have a fox, who sleeps across your boots, and a tortoise, who sleeps across the road. You have a whistle that has never been blown and a tune that will not finish. You have, at last, a mother, in the form of other people's accounts of her: she hummed, she stopped, she looked at the ceiling.

*[only if dead.fox]* There is a small hole in the grass beside the farm, under the apple tree, and you go there on the days when the weather turns.

*[only if not dead.fox]* {fox.first} has stopped, by general agreement, being a stranger. She has opinions on the goats, the church, the cheese. She sings in her sleep. It is a whole six notes, and when she stops she looks at the ceiling.

*[only if not dead.brodin]* Captain Brodin sits in an inn somewhere with a belt buckle on the table, counting.

In the north-west, the weather is getting closer.

## 6.13  "Weather"  (`weather`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended; Major Lvl 1 or more (given up after 6 more years of waiting)
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **Words:** 309 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The sea has been unkind to the coast this year. In the harbour towns they say it began with the autumn gales. Four ships went down inside a month between the headland and the Reef of Teeth, and by midwinter nobody would speak a ship's name aloud in a tavern.

The stories vary in the details and agree on the culprit. A great white bird, they say, taller than a horse, that circles the Last Step in bad weather and is seen where the ships go down. She brings the storms. She eats the sailors. She is, depending on the pub, a witch, a god, an omen, or a clerical error on the part of the weather.

**Moss:** Ah.

He says it as he says most things, after a pause long enough to have a small weather of its own. {fox.first} has gone very still on his shell.

**Moss:** She is fond of drama. I did say. I am afraid she is also very fond of sailors.

**Closing scene**

The road north runs along the coast for three days, and every harbour has the same smell: tar, salt, and a particular kind of fear that has been mended with rope. Women in black stand at the end of piers with their hands in their sleeves. In one village a boy of ten leads you to the beach and shows you what the tide brought in that week: a barrel, a cap, a boot, a small wooden horse.

**Boy:** Mother says the bird eats them. I don't think so. I think she'd have kept the horse.

It is a child's argument and you can find nothing wrong with it. Ahead of you the cliff comes up out of the sea haze, black and straight and ridiculous, like a door that somebody has left open on the end of the world.

## 6.14  "The Last Step"  (`cliff`)

- **Starts when:** 1 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Words:** 291 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Sailors call it the Last Step, because it is the last thing they see before the clouds close over, and there is a sort of hush in the harbour when someone says it. Nobody climbs it. A great white shape circles over it in bad weather. Some say it is a bird. Some say it is a bird's ghost. All of them have the same wary look when they say it, as if the thing might be listening.

You stand at the foot of the cliff with a whistle round your neck that you have not yet blown. The wind has already tried to take your hat twice.

**Closing scene**

It takes six hours, and for much of it you cling to the rock by your fingertips and a great deal of stubbornness. The wind tries to remove you twice. {fox.first} is tied to your back in a sling of sailcloth, with her head out, regarding the drop with the interested disgust of an animal who has not been consulted.

At the top is a nest the size of a barn. It is built of driftwood, rope, spars, old netting and what looks like several hundred hats. In the centre stands a crane taller than a horse, white as paper, with a bill like a long sword, and one cold gold eye turned on you with a look you would call disappointed if you knew her better.

**Quill:** You are slower than your mother. But you have her feet.

**Quill:** I do not take anyone up unless they trust me. The wind is wild, the cliff is high, and I am proud of how I catch things. Step off the edge, and I will tell you what the weather is for.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `quill`; default: option 1)

> The edge is very near, and very far down.

1. Step off the cliff.
   - The wind takes you. For one sweet endless instant you fall, and then something enormous and white closes underneath you like a cup. You are laughing before you know it. She is laughing too, in her crane way, with a sound like a rusty gate.
   - **Quill:** Well. That was easier than your mother. She screamed.
2. Climb back down, and ask her to meet you at the bottom.
   - You climb down. It takes seven hours. At the bottom she is waiting, perched on a rock at the tideline with one leg tucked up, looking smug.
   - **Quill:** Sensible. Your mother would have jumped. I shall have to teach you to jump.

## 6.15  "Hats"  (`hats`)

- **Starts when:** 3 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "dray")`
- **Words:** 385 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The nest is, you discover, a museum. There are hats on every ledge. Oilskin hats, knitted caps, a magistrate's wig, one top hat, a green felt thing with a feather, a hundred and twelve sou'westers. They hang in rows on the spars with a care that would shame a hat shop. Each of them has a label tied to it in Quill's crooked beak-writing: a name, a date, the name of a ship.

**Quill:** I keep what they leave. When a ship is lost the sea brings back the hats. It brings back very little else. Somebody should say their names.

{fox.first} has found a bowler hat and is sitting in it with the air of someone about to be photographed.

**Quill:** Some of them are alive. That is the part that nobody wants to believe. I take them off the rocks and carry them to the beach below the village of Salt Landing and put them down where they will be found. They never look up. They do not think of birds. They think of rescue.

**Closing scene**

He is sitting on an upturned crate by the quay: a thin man in his fifties with a face like a mended sail. He drinks tea from a tin cup in the careful manner of someone who has swallowed a great deal of salt water. He is looking at the ground. There is a stripe of paler skin on his forehead where a hat used to be.

**Dray:** I was on the Marigold when she went. Twelve years. I woke on the shingle with a broken arm and a headache, and a white shape going away over the cliff. I thought it was the Lord. I told people. They gave me a cap with a chin strap and said it was shock.

**You:** She's got your hat.

He looks up. Then he looks at {fox.first}, who is wearing a sou'wester in a fashion that does not suggest a good conscience. He starts to laugh, helplessly, the way a person laughs who has been told something very large in a very small voice.

**Dray:** I knew it. I knew it. Oh, she's a lovely thing. Eleven of us walked off that beach. The company said it was a miracle. It was a bird with a very fine sense of timing.

## 6.16  "Flying Lessons"  (`lessons`)

{fox.first} wants to fly. She has made this clear by climbing to the highest ledge of the nest every morning and standing on it, looking at the sky, with the rapt, stupid hope of an animal who has been told that anything is possible.

**Quill:** It is not possible. She has no wings. She is a fox. I have said so several times.

**Moss:** You said so with one eye on the ledge.

**Quill:** I have a reputation.

It becomes the work of the month. Quill instructs. Moss supervises from below with the weary patience of a headmaster. And {fox.first} leaps from the ledge into a sling of netting that the crane has spread across two spars, falls, bounces, and climbs back up, with fresh enthusiasm and a sharply declining dignity.

Then {fox.first} is lying across the crane's back with her paws out and her fur on end, her eyes wide as a pair of plates. She is making a thin sound that you identify, after a moment, as joy.

**Quill:** I have never caught one of them before. My mother used to say it was the thing to do. I did not understand. I had thought it was a duty. It is rather lovely.

## 6.17  "Salt Landing"  (`fair`)

- **Starts when:** 4 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **Words:** 420 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Salt Landing holds its autumn fair on the shingle below the village, when the tide is out and the boats are drawn up in rows with their keels in the air like a congregation at prayer. There is a man selling herring in paper cones and a man selling the paper cones. There is a stall of hats, because the hats are why you have come.

Captain Dray has brought his family to meet the crane. It is a larger family than you expected. There is a wife with a face like a plate of warm buns, and a mother-in-law who has views. There are seven children, from a boy of fifteen to a baby on the hip of a girl of nine. They stand in a row on the shingle with their hats off, and Quill, on the headland above, lowers her great head and regards them with her one cold gold eye.

**Dray:** She doesn't like crowds. I'm sorry. I did tell them. They wanted to see her.

**Quill:** I do not mind being seen. I mind being regarded. There is a difference, and it lies in the quantity of children.

**Closing scene**

It is the baby who settles it. Nobody could say how it happens. A girl of nine, who is holding it, trips on a net-float and sits down hard on the shingle. The baby rolls out of her arms and comes to rest, unharmed and extremely pleased, against the very toes of the crane.

Quill goes rigid. Seven children and a mother-in-law hold their breath. The baby looks up the whole fifteen feet of white feathers, to the bill, and the eye, and the crest, and laughs. It is the unselfconscious crowing laugh of a creature who has just found the best thing in the world, and puts out both hands to be picked up.

Quill picks it up. She does it with her bill, with a delicacy that you would have said was beyond her, and sets it on her back between the wings. It sits there, delighted, holding two fistfuls of down. And the mother-in-law, to the amazement of the entire village, says in a loud clear voice: 'Well, now. That is the first sensible thing that bird has done.'

By evening, Quill has given rides to nine children, a goat, and the minister. She says it is purely a matter of respect. She says she will not do it again. She is, you think, the happiest you have seen her.

## 6.18  "The Wreck"  (`wreck`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `wreck`.  "Go with Quill to the wreck at {@wreck}."
- **Pays:** 1 Cultivation Pill
- **Words:** 296 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The storm comes at midnight, out of a clear sky, with no warning but the fox's fur standing on end. You wake on the cliff to a sound like the sea clearing its throat. Quill is already on the ledge, a white shape against the dark, with her wings half open. She does not look round.

**Quill:** A ship. The Marigold's sister. I know the sound of her mast.

The next hour is the longest of your life. The wind comes straight up the face of the cliff and tries to take the nest apart. Moss, forty feet below, has gone into his shell like a house with the shutters closed. You cling to a spar and shout something that is lost.

**Closing scene**

There are fourteen on the rocks. You count them twice. Quill takes them one at a time, in her beak or on her back, from a ledge that is awash to a beach that is dry, and each time she goes she is slower. By the end her wings are trembling and her eyes are shut, and she lands badly and lies on the sand like a spilled sack of snow.

The fourteenth is a girl of nine, whose mother has been, up to that moment, her only parent, and who is clutching a hat. She presses it into the crane's feathers with both hands.

**Girl:** I thought it was lost. I wanted her to have it. I thought she'd want to know whose it was.

The crane opens one gold eye. 'Marta,' she says, in a voice so faint it would be lost in a teacup, and then she is asleep. {fox.first} climbs on to her flank and lies down against her ribs, and the two of them breathe together.

## 6.19  "A Price on a White Bird"  (`writ`)

- **Starts when:** 6 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Words:** 333 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The consortium that owns four of the lost ships has decided what it thinks of the white bird. It is a hard thing to say in print, so it has said it in a bounty. Three thousand crowns, payable on the production of the creature, alive or otherwise, to any party able to demonstrate its part in the sinking of vessels. It is a very well-drafted bounty. It names no one it could not afford to name.

You hear of it on the quay at {@town}. Then you hear of the man who has taken it up, and you do not need to be told.

**Closing scene**

He is on the harbour wall, mending a net he does not own, in the cold, with his collar turned up. He looks, you think, much older than he did at the Cracked Egg. He does not stop when you come.

**Brodin:** I took it for the money. I should say that at once, so you needn't wait for it. I've a daughter, and a mortgage on a house I can't sleep in. Three thousand crowns would be everything. I had never heard of the bird.

**Brodin:** And then I started to ask questions, which is a bad habit for a man in my line. Every ship that went down had a clerk aboard who was the last to be seen. Every ship that went down had a policy on the cargo with the same firm. I don't say what I think. I say the numbers are very tidy.

**You:** You think the consortium sank its own ships.

**Brodin:** I think a bird with a crooked beak is a very convenient reason. And I think a court will be happier to hang a bird than to read a ledger.

{fox.first} has jumped up on the wall beside him and put her chin on his knee. He looks at her for a time as if she were a letter he had been expecting. He does not push her off.

Brodin finds the clerk in a pub three streets from the consortium's counting-house, because he has an instinct for pubs. He is a small pale young man in a thin black coat, with ink on his cuffs, and a pint he has not touched. His name is Wilmot Teague, and he has been junior clerk to the Shipping Board for nine months. **Brodin:** I told him we weren't the law. I told him we're a bird and a fox and a tortoise and a man with a grudge. He seems to have found that reassuring.

**Closing scene**

**Teague:** I didn't know what it was. I want to say that first. I copy policies. I'm very quick. I copied four, in the spring, for the Marigold and her sisters, and I noticed the premiums. They were high. Higher than a ship's worth. I thought it was a mistake in the ledger, so I went through the ledger.

**Teague:** Every ship that went down was insured for twice its value. Every cargo for three times. And the same man signed every policy. And the same man, six days later, signed the order for the ship to sail in November.

He stops. He picks up the glass and puts it down. He says, in a flat unsteady voice, that he has not slept since the end of April. He says he knew a boy on the Marigold. A cabin boy, called Eddie, who used to bring him sweets at the quay.

**Teague:** I have the copies. I took them. I'd like it to be known that I'm a coward. I thought about burning them. I thought about it for two weeks. Then I saw the bird on the cliff one evening, in the light, and she didn't look like a witch. She looked like someone who was waiting for something. I went home and got them out of the stove.

The policies are in a flour-sack, in the pocket of his coat. He holds them out in both hands. They are damp and creased and scorched at one corner, and they are the most beautiful papers you have ever seen.

## 6.21  "The Hearing"  (`hearing`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `court`.  "Go to the hearing at {@court}."
- **Pays:** 3,000 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "prewitt")`
- **Words:** 425 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The hearing is in a city a week inland, in a hall with a plaster ceiling and a great many benches. The consortium has hired three advocates and a man to keep the doors. It has not hired anyone to look at the ledgers. Magistrate Prewitt, a grey, tired woman with a pen behind her ear, takes the chair at ten and says, in the voice of someone who has said it before, that she intends to be home by dinner.

The advocate for the consortium is a smooth man in a green coat. He puts four shipwrecks on a table, and a bird made of pasteboard, and a sailor who weeps in exactly the right places, and a petition with eleven hundred names. It is very good. It is the kind of case that you could, if you were not on the other side of it, find rather beautiful.

**Prewitt:** The defence?

There is no defence. There is Quill, on a roof across the street with her head tucked under her wing, because she would not be left behind. There is Moss, in a field. There is {fox.first}, under the bench, eating a clerk's sandwich. There is you.

**Closing scene**

*[only if trial is 1]* Brodin's testimony takes an hour and ends the consortium's case. He lays his own ledger on the table, in his own hand, and reads from it, and by the third page the man in the green coat has stopped smiling. The bounty is struck. Brodin does not look at you as he goes. At the door he stops and lifts one hand, a very little way, like a man testing the weather.

*[only if trial is 2]* The case is over before dinner, and in the way these things go, nobody can say exactly when. The consortium's man withdraws. The Magistrate adjourns. Captain Dray sits on the floor among the hats and cries, and a girl of nine, in the gallery, waves.

*[only if trial is 3]* The court is cleared. The consortium's advocates are, for a week, unable to eat. The case is dismissed, and no one is quite able to say on what grounds, and a rumour starts in the city that there is something on the roof that sees into people. It is a story that will follow Quill for the rest of her life, and in a way, she says, she prefers it to the old one.

On the steps, the Magistrate stops beside you, with her pen behind her ear, and says in a low voice that she is going home to read some ledgers.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `trial`; default: option 1)

> The Magistrate is waiting.

1. Tell it straight: the bird saves sailors, and the consortium is lying.
   - You say it plainly. It takes four minutes. Nobody laughs and nobody gasps, and the Magistrate puts the pen behind her other ear. 'It is a very good story,' she says, 'and I have nothing to set against it but that you say it with a straight face.' The advocate smiles. It is not enough.
   - **Brodin:** May I?
   - He stands. His voice shakes. He says he has read the ledgers.
2. Bring Captain Dray, and a hundred and twelve hats.
   - The hats come in on a cart: a hundred and twelve of them, each with its label, spread over the floor of the court in rows. There is a silence in which you can hear the plaster ceiling think about falling. Captain Dray walks out into the middle of them in his mended coat. He picks up the Marigold's cap, and turns it over, and reads his own name.
   - **Dray:** She took me off the rocks. There were eleven of us. We never saw her. We were told it was shock.
3. Let Quill speak for herself.
   - She does not come in. She does not need to. She lifts her head on the roof across the street, and she speaks, and every person in the room hears her at once, at the back of the mind, in whatever language their mother used. Each hears, in turn, a name and a date and a ship, and the sound of a place where the sea has closed over someone they loved.
   - The Magistrate puts down her pen. The advocate in the green coat is sitting very still, with his hand over his eyes. It is not exactly legal. It is, you reflect afterwards, extremely persuasive.

The week after the hearing is the first quiet one for a year. The consortium's carriages have gone. The streets are full of strangers who stop you to shake your hand. A woman gives you a fish. A boy gives you a stone with a hole in it, for luck.

Brodin comes up the cliff on the third day. Nobody told him he could. He climbs it in the old way, hand over hand, with a bundle on his back and a child's wooden horse tied to the top of it. At the end he sits down at the edge of the nest with the sweat on his face and says that he has brought his daughter's regards.

**Closing scene**

The daughter is eleven. Her name is Ines. She has been ill a long time, with a lung complaint, and she has not been out of the house in the winter. The doctors in town have a name for it, and a price. Brodin has been putting off saying the price. He says it now, flatly, to the sea.

**Brodin:** It was the whole reason, you know. The bounty. I did tell you I took it for the money. I did not say what it was for. You can have a long face, if you like. It is a very ordinary story.

**Quill:** Bring her here.

**Brodin:** I beg your pardon?

**Quill:** The air at the top is clean. It has not been breathed by anyone. I have always thought it a waste. If the girl wishes to come, and is wrapped, I shall carry her up. I do not carry people. I have made an exception of the minister.

He cannot answer. He turns his face to the wall of the nest and stays there, among the hats, with his back to you, while the sea works at the foot of the cliff. After a time {fox.first} climbs into his lap, and he puts one hand on her back, and leaves it there.

The consortium's money has to go somewhere, and Magistrate Prewitt has decided where. It is to go to the hats. Quill's hundred and twelve, each with its label, are to be carried home to the families of the ships. The sum is paid in the hall of the Shipping Board, by a clerk with a very red face, and the hats are loaded on a cart.

It takes the cart eleven days. You walk beside it. {fox.first} rides on top, in a bowler. Quill goes overhead, in wide slow circles, and makes a point of not looking at the cart. At each town the cart stops and you call out a name, from a label, and a door opens.

The first is a woman in a doorway, with flour to her wrists. You give her a sou'wester. She holds it against her chest, as if it were a person, and says nothing. Then she says, 'He hated that hat. He said it made him look like a pudding.' She laughs, and puts her face in it, and you stand in the road with your own hat in your hands.

The second is a boy of six who does not know what he is being given. He holds the cap, and turns it over, and finds a name written inside the band in an unsteady hand, his father's, as if the man had written it for fun. He reads it aloud, slowly, a letter at a time. When he has finished he looks at you with the stern solemn face of a child who has understood a joke at last.

The eleventh day brings you to the last town, which is Salt Landing, and the last hat, which is Captain Dray's own, the one from the Marigold. He has kept it back. He has asked that it be left. It is to hang on a nail in the nest, he says, on the highest ledge, where the weather gets at it, and Quill is to say its name every morning.

**Quill:** I do. I have always done. It is the first thing I say.

## 6.24  "Ines Rides the Wind"  (`ines`)

- **Starts when:** 3 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill

**Opening scene**

She arrives at the cliff on the back of her father, in a blanket, with a cap on, and her thin wrists sticking out of the sleeves. She is eleven. She has never been out of the house in the winter. She has the luminous, cautious stare of a child who has been told a great deal about the world and expects to be disappointed in it.

**Ines:** Is that the bird? She's bigger than I thought. She's whiter. Does she mind if I say so?

**Quill:** I do not mind. It is true.

**Closing scene**

The first flight is short. She is lifted into the nest, among the hats, wrapped in a quilt, and the crane puts one wing under her, like a sort of stair. They go up in a slow spiral round the head of the cliff. She does not cry out. She hangs on with both fists and her eyes screwed up, and for the length of three turns she is entirely silent. Then she opens one eye.

**Ines:** Oh!

It is the whole sea. It lies in a great flat silver sheet under the sun, from the cliff to the end of the world. The little brown boats on it are like crumbs. There is the white line of the surf, and the smoke going straight up from Salt Landing, and the sky above it so wide that it hurts. She says it again, softly, and again. Her father, on the ledge, with his hat in his hand, is not able to speak.

She comes down an hour later, flushed to the ears, with her hair on end and the cap gone, and breathing in great clean gulps. She coughs. It is a small, short, ordinary cough. It does not tear. She looks surprised, and tries again, and then simply stands on the ledge in the wind with her mouth open, inhaling the weather.

**Ines:** It doesn't hurt.

**Quill:** It will take many mornings. I have thought it out. We shall begin with the sea air and proceed to the high.

Brodin turns his face to the cliff wall. He stands there with his forehead against the cold stone until the gulls have gone round twice. {fox.first} goes and sits on his foot. He doesn't push her off.

You hum the six notes. Moss gives you the low ones, a long way down. And then Quill, a little shyly, with her bill pointed at the sky, sings the high end, a note so far up and so sharp that it hurts, like a pin of light. She sings it where your mother always stopped.

The village at the edge of the Burned Wood is called Cinderfold, and it has a churchyard with a field of small stones. Eleven of them stand together at the north wall, in a row, with a rope in front. Fresh flowers are laid at the foot of each. They are changed on Sundays.

You read the names, as you would read a list of the dead in any village. Marten Hale, a carter. Joan Pike, nineteen. Three brothers of the same family, who went up to cut wood on a Tuesday and did not come down. A priest. A woman called Isabel Greave, whose stone has a pair of boots carved on it, small, as for a child. And at the end, in newer stone, GARRICK BRODIN, 19.

A woman is kneeling at the last stone. She is sixty, in a black shawl, with a bunch of heather in her lap and a knife for the stems. She does not look up as you come. She says, in the voice of someone speaking to a child she has known for many years: 'That's the Captain's boy. They put him last. He was the last to come down.'

**Woman:** They tell me you're going to talk to it. The thing in the wood. I'll say this, since nobody else will. I've lost a son. I'm not going to ask you to let it live. I'm not going to ask you anything. I only want you to have seen the stones.

She trims the stems. The knife is very sharp, and her hands are steady, and she lays the heather on the stone in a neat, flat bundle. She says that her own boy is the third stone from the end.

**Woman:** He had a hand like a spade. He'd have been a good man to have by you in a flood. I tell myself he'd have understood the boar. They say it screamed all the way down the hill.

You do not say anything. The wind comes down off the wood, and with it, from far off, the smell of old ash, and from the middle of the stones, quite clearly, as you stand there, the sound of {fox.first} sitting down.

The Burned Wood is two days beyond the last village, past a field of black stones that used to be a farm. The trees stand in rows like the bones of something that was once very large. The air smells of cold fires. The ground is soft with cinders, and every footstep sends up a little cloud that settles on you like a thought.

**Quill:** Nothing alive will go in. I would not blame you if you waited at the edge.

**Moss:** I will wait. I am old, and I have a bad feeling about my legs.

It is {fox.first} who goes first. You have not asked her to. She walks into the ash with her head up, her ears forward, and her tail low, like a very small soldier, and does not look back, and you follow her, because you cannot think of anything else to do.

You feel him before you see him, a heat on the back of your neck, a sense of being watched by something that has been watching a very long time. Then the ash in front of you heaves, and he stands up out of it, like a mountain standing.

He is a boar as large as a house, black as the wood, with tusks like curved swords and a hide cracked with old burns. Small fires still glow in the cracks. His eyes are red and wild and very tired.

**Ember:** FIRE. YOU. SMELL. OF. FIRE.

You do not. You smell of ash and mud and fox. But it is clear that to him everything does, and that this is not a quarrel with you. It is a kind of scream. {fox.first}, at your feet, has planted all four paws in the cinders and is looking up at him without moving, and you realise she is humming.
