You do not say anything, and nobody asks you to. {fox.first} climbs into your lap, a thing she does not do, and puts her face under your arm. After a while Quill spreads a wing over the lot of you, as one spreads a sheet on a bed, and the wood is quiet.

## 6.34  "The Farmer Comes North"  (`farmer`)

- **Starts when:** 3 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 350 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You write to your father in the autumn. It is a short letter. It says that you have found Ember, and the other two, and that your mother is in a lake, and that you have a fox, and an orchard, and that you are all right. It does not say the rest of it. It says: come if you like.

He is on the doorstep eleven days later, with a bag of onions and a bad knee, looking at a boar the size of a house. Ember is looking back. Nobody moves. {fox.first} sits down between them, with the air of a diplomat, and begins to wash her ear.

**Closing scene**

**Ember:** You are the one she went home to.

**Father:** I suppose I am. I did not know she talked about me.

**Ember:** She did not. She went home. It is a different thing. She never talked about the places she was going to. Only the places she had left.

Your father looks at him until the fire cracks. He has never stood in front of a creature like this, and his hands, folded over the bag of onions, are as white as the vegetables. He says at last, in a small voice, that he has been angry for eleven years at somebody who isn't there, and it seems he has been angry at the wrong one.

**Father:** I should like to say I'm sorry. I don't know for what.

**Ember:** For not coming after her. I know. I heard you decide it, on the porch. You were afraid. It was the best thing you ever did.

That night he sits by the fire with the beasts, and tells them what it was to be left. He does it badly. He loses the thread. He asks Moss whether tortoises feel the cold, and is told, at length, that it depends on the tortoise. It is the longest conversation of his life, and when he goes to bed he is humming, flat and unsteady, six notes, and then a seventh, which is not quite the right one, and which Ember hums back.

## 6.35  "Grey at the Muzzle"  (`grey`)

- **Starts when:** 3 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** a technique insight
- **Words:** 372 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You notice it in the spring, on the stone by the orchard, in the light. It has been there a while. A fine line of silver, along the muzzle, and round the eyes, as though someone had gone over her with a sharp white pencil in the night. She is lying on the warm flagstone with her chin on her paws, in the sun, with the apple blossom coming down on her, and she does not get up when you call.

She is twelve, or thirteen, or something. You have never known. A fox is not a creature that tells you its age. She has always been a thing in motion. She has been a flash and a tail and a rumour in the bushes. She has got slow in the way of someone who has decided to, not been made to. She walks a lap of the orchard in the evening, and sits down in the middle of it, and watches the beasts as a retired captain watches the sea.

**Closing scene**

**Moss:** She is not ill. I want to say that at once. I have known many animals who were ill, and she is not one. She has simply understood that there is a great deal of time, and that she does not have to use it all at once.

**Ember:** She sleeps on my back, you know. In the afternoons. I do not mind. It is the one weight I do not mind.

You sit down beside her on the warm stone. She lifts her head, and looks at you, and her eyes are the same eyes, large and amber and ironical, and she puts her nose against your wrist and breathes out, once, through it. It is the longest, most contented breath you have ever seen an animal take.

You hum the six notes, very low, because you can think of nothing else to do. She does not answer. She does not need to. She closes her eyes. The blossom comes down. The beasts in the orchard go on grazing in the long grass, in the sun, in no hurry at all, and you sit there with your hand on her back until the stone has gone cold.

## 6.36  "The Bone Whistle"  (`whistle`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 459 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You have carried it since the letter. It is yellow with age and no longer than your finger, with a tiny hole at each end. It has hung on a cord against your chest through a cliff and a wreck and a courtroom without once being blown. You have told yourself it was not time. You have told yourself it was a thing for a particular night. You suspect now that you have been afraid.

You take it out one evening on the edge of the orchard, with the sun going and the blossom coming down, and you hold it between your finger and thumb, and turn it over. There is something scratched on the side, so worn that you have never seen it. You tilt it to the light. It is a row of tiny marks, like a bird's footprints, and under them a name in your mother's hand. Yours.

**Closing scene**

You put it to your lips. The sound is very small. It is not the six notes, or any notes. It is the sound a breath makes going through a hollow bone, a thin, dry, human sound, like a word said under the covers. It goes out across the orchard and nothing happens.

Then, a long way off, from the line of the hills, a wolf howls. And from the lake, faintly, a deep note. From the cliff, a cry like a rusty gate, so far that it might be a trick of the air. From the burned wood a long low rumble that you feel in the ground. And from the stump at your feet, from a very small, very ordinary animal who has been dozing in the sun, a scratchy flat little answer, once, in the shape of a question.

They are all answering the same thing. It is not a call. You understand that now. Your mother did not use it to summon them. She used it to say where she was.

**Quill:** (from a great way off, faintly, across the sky) Ah. You have blown it. I wondered how long. She used to do it every dusk, on the roof of the farm, to see who was awake.

**Moss:** (from the lake) It is a very small noise.

**Ember:** (from the wood) It's enough.

You sit on the grass with the whistle in your hand. It is warm. Soon you put it to your lips again, and this time you play something: three slow notes, and the same three higher. Then, with your heart going, you play a seventh that you have only ever heard in a dream. It is not the right one. It is close. Across five miles of air, the whole of your family answers, and corrects you.

## 6.37  "Where Isha Lies"  (`lake3`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight

**Opening scene**

You go to the lake in the autumn, alone, on foot, with a flask of tea and a stone from the orchard in your pocket. It is the first time you have been since Ember told you. The water is flat and dark and very still. There is a heron on the far shore. A thread of mist lies along the surface, and the reeds at the edge are the colour of old brass.

Moss is waiting. He has risen, a little, from the middle. His shell is a rounded island of green in the grey, and his old face looks out of it with its usual enormous patience. He has not been asked. He knew you were coming.

**Closing scene**

**Moss:** She is not in the deep part. I have kept her where the sun reaches. I thought she would like to be warm. I put her by the reeds. There is a stone.

You walk along the shore. The stone is flat and plain and very smooth, half under the water. It has no name. It has no carving. There is a small bright pebble on it, and a dead leaf, and a feather: a long grey feather with a white tip. Somebody has been here before you, and often.

**Moss:** The wolf comes. Once a month. I do not know why. He sits on the bank and does not say anything. The first time I thought he was a hunter, and I nearly rose, and then he put down the feather, and sat, and I understood he was doing what I do.

You kneel at the edge. The water is cold on your knuckles. You put the apple stone beside the feather, and say nothing, because there is no word in the language that fits. After a while you find that you are humming the tune. Six notes. Slowly. Then, from under the surface, a long way down, a tone like a bell that is very deep and very sweet. Moss is singing the low one.

**Moss:** She sang that one to me when I was young. I did not know what it was for. I think it is for this: so that one may sing it back.

It goes up at the north end of Nobody's Lake, a green place with a fence made of fallen trees. There is a hut for you, a shed for the hurt, and a big flat rock where a tortoise can sleep. Hunters come out of curiosity, and mostly go away astonished: a cinder boar is eating apples from a child's hand, and a crane the size of a horse is giving flying lessons to a goose.

At dusk you take the bone whistle from your pocket for the first time. You put it to your lips. You blow it, once: three slow notes, and the same three, higher.

She sets it on the gatepost. A thin, yellow, one-eyed cat looks out of it with an air of intense disapproval.

**Closing scene**

**Prewitt:** This is Mister Gavel. He is nineteen. He has been in my chambers since the case of the Rooks. I have decided to ask if he might be allowed to be old with others.

The cat steps out of the basket with great deliberation. He walks the length of the gatepost, down the fence, along the path to the barn. He stops in front of the fox. They regard each other with perfect composure, two creatures who have run a very long way and know it. He sits. She sits. After a minute he lies down beside her in the sun, and begins, harshly, to purr.

**Prewitt:** (stiffly, blowing her nose) I find I have nothing further to say.

When the first rain falls she looks down, once, at you, and you know exactly what she is going to do.

**Closing scene**

She goes up on the first gust. You see her against the cloud, a pale cross, and then she is lost in the grey. The storm closes. The lightning begins, great forked white crowns over the sea, and in the flashes you see her, tiny and bright, wheeling and rising through the black, with the thunder rolling about her like drums. She is singing. You can hear it between the peals: the old storm-crane's cry, hoarse and high and glad.

You wait under the oak for three hours with your coat over your head. The rain comes down in bars. The wind pulls the branches. At last, near dawn, there is a feather on the grass at your feet. It is a long grey pinion with a white tip, singed at the edge, and it is warm. You pick it up. The storm is blowing itself out in the east, and in the thin new light a speck is coming down the sky in long loops.

**Quill:** (in your head, as she lands, wet to the bone, with her crest in rags) I have never been so cold. It was the best night of my life. Do you think they would let me do it again?

You find, by autumn, that the sanctuary is quiet. It is a good quiet. It is the quiet of a house after a long visit, with the beds stripped and the cups in the rack. You walk the paths in the evening with your hands in your pockets and your companions at your heels. You hear for the first time what your mother meant, years ago, when she said that a tamer is a person who has learned how to be left.

## 6.48  "Quill Comes Home"  (`return`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 3 weeks (0 years and 3 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 269 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

She has been away for three weeks. She flew out in the grey of a Tuesday, on a south wind, and did not say where, or why, and you did not ask. The sky has been empty. The roof of the barn has been empty. In the evenings you have looked up at the first stars with a feeling you did not care to examine.

**Closing scene**

She comes down out of the north at sunset on a long, slow, tired glide. She is thin as a rake. Her feathers are ragged, and her crest is gone to a pale tuft, and there is a long white scar down her neck. She lands on the barn roof with a sound like a dropped umbrella, and folds her wings, and does not say anything for a good while.

**Quill:** I have been to the edge of the sky. I thought you should know that it is a very long way, and that it is perfectly all right. There is a place at the top where the blue stops and a sort of grey begins. It has a seam. It hums. I sat on it for a day and listened. I am told by the wind that it is the oldest thing there is.

She stretches out one wing. Caught in the pinions there is a single spangle of pale gold, no bigger than a coin. It is a seed, or a scale, or a splinter of the sky itself. She says she brought it for the lake. She says: 'It's a bit late. I'm sorry. It was a long way.'

## 6.49  "What the Wild Calls You"  (`voice4`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 400 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 224 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The wild has no word for what you are. It never did. Your mother was its Voice, and her mother before her, and the name went down the line like a coat. You are not that. You are, you were told in the autumn that you walked the roads with the four, something else. The wild has been thinking about it for years. At last, on an evening in October, it speaks.

**Closing scene**

It does not come in words. It comes up from the ground, through your boots and your spine. It is a low long hum, and every living thing in the valley takes it up at once. The owl in the beech joins it, and the badger in the sett, and the mice in the barley, and the deer in the long grass. It is the six notes, and the seventh, and an eighth, which is new. The eighth is yours.

It is a plain simple sound, a falling third, like a mother calling a child in at dusk. You know what it means. It means: here is one of ours. It means: she may come in. It is the sound the wild makes for a friend.

**Brodin:** (at the fence, with the whole of the valley humming round him, in a shaken voice) I think you've been given a name.

## 6.50  "A Hundred Years of Sleep"  (`sleep`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 2,000 spirit stones, +3 potential, 4 Potential Pills, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 136 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You go to the lake in the first week of spring. The ice has gone. The reeds are green at the roots, and a heron stands in the shallows on one leg, like a question. The water is flat and clear. At the bottom, a long way down, there is a round dark shape the size of a house, quite motionless, with a faint green light in it. Moss is sleeping.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `farewell`; default: option 1)

> Moss will not wake for a hundred years. You will not be there.

1. Hum him the low note, and leave the lake to its keeping.
   - You hum the low note. It goes out across the water in a long warm line. For a moment the green light brightens, and a thin stream of bubbles rises, one at a time, from the deep, and breaks at the surface. It is, you decide, the closest a tortoise can come to a wave.
   - **Quill:** (from the reeds, dry) He heard.
2. Leave him the apple stone, the feather and the whistle, and promise to come.
   - You lay them on the stone by the reeds: the apple stone, the grey feather, the bone whistle. You say that you will come. You say it aloud, and clearly, to the water, as one says a thing to a friend who has dropped off in a chair. The surface ripples. A single large leaf turns over in the wind and lies, belly up, pale gold. It is the first leaf of the spring. It looks like a hand.
   - **Brodin:** That's a promise. I'll write it down.
3. Say nothing. Sit with him until the light goes.
   - You sit on the flat stone with your knees drawn up. You say nothing. The sun goes down behind the hill and the lake turns from blue to rose to grey. A heron flies over. An owl starts. You sit for ages in the dusk with the cold seeping up through your coat, and you are not sad. You are listening. After a long while you hear it, quite faint, from far down: a bell, very deep, very sweet, very slow.

**Closing scene**

The sanctuary is quiet on the walk home. The old cat sits on the gatepost with one eye open. The kit with the white-tipped tail comes down the lane to meet you, with a feather in her mouth. She puts it in your hand, and sits, and looks up. She says: 'Whose is this?' And you say that you think it is yours.

## 6.I4  Interlude: The Long Quiet  (between season 4 and season 5)

**Interlude**

The four walk the roads slowly now. The cinder boar sleeps through whole weeks. The crane has gone grey at the crest. The lake is where it was. The whistle has not been blown in a year.

One evening the stag from the Palace's gardens comes down the road and stands at the gate. He is not a stag. He is a messenger, and he has the manners of one.

# 6.S5  Season 5: The Door

## 6.51  "The Messenger at the Gate"  (`dr1`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 208 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The stag at the gate is white as a bone and old as the road. He does not graze. He stands in the yard with his head up, looking at nothing, until you come out with the bone whistle in your hand. Then he lowers his antlers and kneels. A strip of bark is tied to the left tine with a thread of moss. It has writing on it.

**Closing scene**

The writing is in no hand you know. It is slanting and clean. It says: Bring them to the plain. There is a gate. It cannot take them through, because it was made for people. It would like to say goodbye. It says the beasts are owed a word, and that the person who is asked to give it is the one they listen to.

*[only if not dead.fox and not slept=1]* The fox, who is very old, comes out of the house and sniffs the bark. She sneezes. She walks twice round the stag, sniffing, and sits down on his foot. It is the clearest approval you have ever seen from her.

The stag rises. He walks out of the yard at a slow dignified pace. At the bend of the road he stops and looks back. You get your coat.

## 6.52  "The Gate Was Made for People"  (`dr2`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `garrison`.  "Go to the Garrison of the Crossed, {@garrison}, with the four."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 225 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The four go with you to the Garrison, one behind the other, on the long road. The cinder boar leads. The crane rides on his back. The tortoise is carried in a cart, and the fox walks beside it, with her tail up, as if she had arranged the whole matter.

**Closing scene**

The line stops at the gate. A woman with a grey plait and a ledger comes down it. She looks at the four. She looks at you. She says that the gate is a muster, and that a muster is for people, and that she has never been asked for a rule about beasts. She says there is no rule. She says it in the voice of someone who has just realised how odd that is.

The boar walks to the gate and puts his nose to the sill. The crane preens. The tortoise withdraws her head and thinks about it. The fox sits down in the dust and begins, very calmly, to wash. They do not go in. They do not need to. One by one they turn, and look at the line, and the line looks back, a hundred soldiers in the rain, and not one of them is afraid.

**Woman:** I will write it down. I will write that they came. It is the first time anyone has asked.

## 6.53  "Six Notes and a Seventh"  (`dr3`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `palace`.  "Go to the Palace of the Oldest Order, at Originis, to the Empty Seat."
- **Pays:** 1,000 spirit stones, +2 potential, 2 Potential Pills, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 123 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Empty Seat is in the great hall of the Palace, under the dome. You have not been in it for years. The Wicks bring a mat and a bowl of water for the beasts, and then, awkwardly, leave you alone. The four settle at the foot of the chair. The whistle is warm in your hand.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `latch`; default: option 1)

> The beasts are at your feet. The Door is under the Seat. Your mother's tune is in your hand.

1. Stay: blow the whistle once, and let the tune go through alone.
   - You blow the whistle. The six notes go out into the hall and down under the flags, and then the seventh, which is not yours. It goes through the Door. You hear it a long way off, small and clear, and then you hear it answered. The beasts lift their heads in a body. The fox, in the dust, begins to sing.
   - **Fox:** (in your head, with immense dignity) That is the right one.
2. Go: sing the six notes, and the seventh, and walk with the tune as far as it goes.
   - You hum the six notes. The seventh comes up out of the floor to meet you. It is a deep slow warmth, like a coat put around the shoulders. You are not afraid. You find that you have never been afraid of this. It is your mother's voice, and the wild's, and it has been calling the whole of your life.
3. Hold the latch: stay by the Door and see the next of the wild safely to the gate.
   - You sit at the Seat for a year. Whenever a beast comes in at the great doors, a stray, a hunted thing, an old bear, you take it by the scruff and say good evening. You show it the water. You show it the Door. You tell it that nobody will mind. By the end of the year you have a very large number of friends and a stiff back.

**Closing scene**

The beasts go home. The fox leads. She does not look back; she is a fox, and has appointments. At the gate of the house she stops and sits and waits for you, and when you come up she butts your knee with her head, hard, once, as she did on the first night. It means: well done. It means: I was never worried.

## 6.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

Your mother was the Voice of the Wild. You are, you are told, something else. The wild does not have a word for it yet.

*[only if calling is 1]* You and the four walk the roads, and the children of every village run out to look. They are not afraid. A cinder boar who loves apples will do that to a village.

*[only if calling is 2]* The gate stays open. The sanctuary has forty residents now and a waiting list. Nobody has ever been turned away.

*[only if calling is 3]* The School of the Open Hand teaches forty students a year to listen. The first rule is to sit still and wait. They say it works better than anything.

*[only if ember is 1]* Ember hums sometimes, when he thinks nobody can hear. Six notes, and then the seventh, which is not his.

*[only if ember is 3]* Ember has a scar on his tusk from the night he threw you into a tree. He shows it to visitors with great pride.

*[only if dead.fox]* The tree by the lake has a stone under it, and a bone, and a smell of apples in the autumn that nobody can explain.

*[only if not dead.fox]* {fox.first} is old, and sleeps in the sun by the lake, and does not leave. If you hum the six notes she lifts her head at the end, and sings the seventh without opening her eyes.

*[only if not dead.brodin]* Captain Brodin keeps the fence. He has told people it is a hobby. A sack of apples comes to the sanctuary every spring, with a note that says nothing, and a belt buckle hangs on the post by the gate.

*[only if latch is 1]* On certain evenings the seventh note comes up out of the ground by the lake, small and clear. Nobody has ever been able to say who is playing.

*[only if latch is 2]* You hum the six notes in the garden. The seventh is already there, waiting, and has been all your life.

*[only if latch is 3]* A stray fox, an old bear, a wounded hawk are all, sooner or later, brought to the Seat. A tall tired person gives them water and tells them they are welcome.

On the night of the autumn storms you sit by Nobody's Lake with a bone whistle in your hand and tell the water about your day. The lake keeps its own counsel. But it is not cold.

## 6.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

The Palace has a courtyard with no animals in it. You fix this at once.

A cinder boar sleeps by the Empty Seat. A tortoise holds court in the fountain. A crane has opinions about the roof.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

The Gardener's army has no beasts. You bring yours. Moss carries the supplies, Quill scouts the sky, and Ember walks at the front, huge and quiet, where fire has always been afraid of him.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You walk out through the Seam, and three great shapes walk out beside you, and the Outside gets a very strange first impression of you.

The first creature you meet there is small and grey with big ears. It sits down in front of you and hums back.

**You are struck down by the array**

The array took you, and the ones you left behind did not forget.

On the evening of every storm, a crane circles the lake, a tortoise lifts its head, and a very large boar leans on the sanctuary gate and hums three slow notes.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden goes out, and the beasts go with it, side by side, a boar and a tortoise and a crane. You are glad they were not alone.

As the light fails, you hum: three slow notes, and the same three, higher.

# 7. The Ghost-Touched  (`ghost`)

*You died once and did not stay dead. People shy away; the dead do not.*

Starts as: any, trait Ghost, Neutral, potential 70, 50 spirit stones.

**What the plan says is the truth of this story:** The Ghost-Touched (9 chapters). Three witnesses give three absurd accounts of your death (a bun, a crab, a poem); the truth is a peach pit, a goose and a bridge. Then the dead come, one at a time, with small unfinished things, and Old Meng tells you that you are not touched but a door. [Old Meng, Dumpling Lu, Captain Foo, Lin Zhaoyu, Bao Tian].

# 7.S1  Season 1: Witnesses

## 7.1  "The Seer of Originis"  (`meng`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** Have 1 friends.  "Be known by the living: make one real friend."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, 1 Cultivation Pill
- **Words:** 333 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

People step out of your way in the street. They do not mean to. They do it the way you step around a puddle. A baby cries when you pass. A dog sits down and refuses to move until you are gone.

You have a terrible feeling that you are cold. Not cold like winter. Cold like a cellar.

You also have a gap in your memory eleven days wide. The last thing you remember is a bright morning, a bridge, and the smell of a peach.

So you go to see the one person in Originis who is said to know about such things.

Old Meng is seventy-seven, tiny, and sits behind a counter with a pot of tea and a lot of cats. She looks you over twice.

**Meng:** Oh, you're dead, dear.

**You:** I'm what?

**Meng:** Dead. A little. Eleven days ago. You came back, which is unusual, and you didn't bring anybody with you, which is lucky. I'm afraid you've been put out of sorts by it. You'll find you have a bit of a chill, and people will shy away. Wear a scarf. It helps.

**You:** How did I die?

**Meng:** Ah. I can't see that. The dead are very unreliable about their own deaths. But three people saw you fall. Find them. Ask them what they saw. Then come back and compare.

**Meng:** First, though, you need a friend. A living one. It will keep you from forgetting the difference.

**Closing scene**

You are not sure what you expected a friend to be like. This one is a thin, stooped man with a basket of onions, who stops to ask whether you are all right.

He does not shy away. He holds out an onion. He says you look as if you could use it.

It is the worst thing anyone has ever given you. It is also the best. You put it in your pocket, and you cry a little, and he pretends not to notice.

## 7.2  "Witness One: The Baker"  (`lu`)

- **Starts when:** 20 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet lu (walk to their tile).  "Find Dumpling Lu, who runs a bun stall in {@bridge}."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> { Chapters.spawn(c, st, "lu"); Chapters.spawn(c, st, "foo"); Chapters.spawn(c, st, "lin"); }`
- **Words:** 201 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Meng gives you three names on a bit of paper, with a small drawing of a cat next to each. It does not mean anything. She just likes drawing cats.

The first is Dumpling Lu, who runs a steamed bun stall at {@bridge}. She was, Meng says, nearest.

**Closing scene**

The stall is wonderful. It smells of ginger and steam. Dumpling Lu is a round woman with flour to the elbows and a loud, happy voice that carries across the square.

**Lu:** Oh, I remember you! I'll never forget it! You came to my stall at noon and bought a pork bun, and you bit into it, and you choked!

**Lu:** Went purple! Dropped like a sack! I tried to help, I really did, I hit you on the back with my rolling pin, and I think that was where I went wrong. You went limp. I was sure you were gone.

**Lu:** Then you got up two minutes later and said you needed a nap. I've felt bad about it ever since. Have a bun. It's free. I'll feel better.

You take the bun. It is excellent. You are almost certain you were not choking. You decide not to say so.

## 7.3  "Witness Two: The Captain"  (`foo`)

- **Starts when:** 12 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet foo (walk to their tile).  "Find Captain Foo of the city watch."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 143 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The second name on the list is Captain Foo of the city watch. He was on duty at the bridge that day, Meng says. Everybody is always on duty at the bridge.

**Closing scene**

Captain Foo is a very straight man with a very straight moustache. He tells it standing at attention.

**Foo:** Sir. Ma'am. Citizen. I saw it clearly. A giant crab came out of the creek at the Mill Bridge. The size of a cart. Eight feet across.

**Foo:** You stood your ground. You drew your ladle.

**You:** My ladle?

**Foo:** It was the nearest weapon. You fought bravely. The crab got you at the last. A terrible loss. The watch will remember it.

**Foo:** The crab escaped. I would be grateful if you did not mention it to my superiors. There has been paperwork.

He salutes. You return it. Neither of you knows why.

## 7.4  "Witness Three: The Poet"  (`lin`)

- **Starts when:** 12 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet lin (walk to their tile).  "Find Lin Zhaoyu, the poet."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 177 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The third name is Lin Zhaoyu, a poet. He lives above a tea house and, according to Meng, is the only witness who has never been wrong. About anything. Ever. He will tell you himself.

**Closing scene**

The poet reclines on a divan with a brush behind his ear and a look of immense, wounded importance.

**Lin:** Ah. The corpse. I wondered when you'd come.

**Lin:** I will be brief. I was on the bridge reciting my new work, 'Ode to a Plum, in Seventeen Cantos.' You were listening. You were riveted. In the ninth canto, I saw your eyes glaze, I saw your knees buckle, and I saw you fall.

**Lin:** It was, I believe, the beauty. I have always feared that the beauty would be fatal to a delicate soul.

**You:** It was boredom.

**Lin:** It was the beauty.

You do not argue with him. It would be like arguing with the weather. You write the three stories down in order. A bun. A crab. A plum.

None of them can be right. All of them are certain.

## 7.5  "The Truth About the Bridge"  (`bridge`)

- **Starts when:** 10 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `bridge`.  "Stand where you fell, on the bridge at {@bridge}."
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **Words:** 310 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You take the three stories back to Meng. She reads them with her tea and says 'Ha.' Then she says 'Hmm.' Then she says 'Well, that is perfectly useless, isn't it.'

**Meng:** Go to the bridge. Stand where you fell. The dead remember the places where they died better than the people who watched. Breathe in. Try not to be sensible.

The Mill Bridge, at {@bridge}, is stone, old, and very ordinary. There is a goose on it.

**Closing scene**

You stand in the middle of the bridge. Nothing happens. The goose looks at you. You look at the goose.

Then it comes back all at once, like a window thrown open.

A warm morning. A peach, which you were eating, juice running down your wrist. A crab in the creek below, which had caught your eye. A man declaiming something about plums in the distance. A steaming bun, on the stall, not yet bought.

And a goose. This goose. Standing in the middle of the bridge, exactly where it is now, with its neck out and its wings half open and the unshakeable confidence of an animal that has never been told no.

You said you were crossing. It said it was crossing. Neither of you was prepared to give way. There was an argument, which you lost. You stepped back to find a better angle, and put your foot on a peach pit.

Your leg went out. The railing was low. You remember a surprising amount of air, and a very small splash, and the goose, peering over the edge, looking pleased.

A peach pit, a goose, and a bridge. The others just happened to be nearby.

**Meng:** (in your head, from far away) Oh, you've remembered. How awful. I'm so sorry. It's very undignified, isn't it. Come home and have some tea.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `goose`; default: option 1)

> The goose is still on the bridge, and still looks pleased.

1. Forgive the goose.
   - You bow to the goose. It honks, once, and moves aside. You are quite sure it has no idea what you were apologising for.
2. Take a firm stand. Cross anyway.
   - You cross. The goose bites you on the ankle, hard. It is, to be fair, a very clean bite. You are not even a little surprised.
3. Leave a peach on the railing as a peace offering.
   - You put the peach on the railing. The goose looks at it, then at you, then at the peach. It eats the peach in three bites and, to your surprise, honks something that sounds very much like thank you.

## 7.6  "A Letter for Mister Pang"  (`pang`)

- **Starts when:** 30 weeks after the previous chapter ended; Major Lvl 1 or more (given up after 6 more years of waiting)
- **Task:** Go to the place `hamlet`.  "Take Mrs. Pang's last letter to her husband at {@hamlet}."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones
- **Words:** 239 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The first ghost comes on a rainy evening. You are sitting in your room with a bowl of rice, and suddenly the rice is cold, and there is a small woman at the foot of your bed.

She is old and tidy and see-through. She has her hands folded in front of her, like someone waiting for a bus.

**Ghost:** Excuse me. You're one of the ones who can hear. I've been trying for forty years. Everyone else just gets goosebumps and leaves.

**Ghost:** My name is Mrs. Pang. My husband never got my last letter. I wrote it on the night I died, and it's in the lining of my sewing box, which is in a hamlet at {@hamlet}. He's still alive. He's ninety-one. I'd like him to read it before it's too late.

**Closing scene**

The sewing box is exactly where she said. The letter is yellow and fragile. You carry it as if it were a bird.

Mister Pang is a tiny, deaf, cheerful man, sitting on a porch in the sun. You hand him the letter. He reads it twice, with his lips moving.

When he finishes, he looks up. He does not look at you. He looks at a spot a little to your left.

**Mister Pang:** Well, dear. You always did have the last word.

The air next to you goes warm. It is the first warm thing you have felt in months.

## 7.7  "The Soldier Who Wanted to Say Sorry"  (`soldier`)

- **Starts when:** 40 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet bao (walk to their tile).  "Find Bao Tian and give him a message from his brother."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "bao")`
- **Words:** 151 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The second ghost has been waiting on a bench in the park for eleven years. He is young, tall, in an old uniform, and he looks very ashamed.

**Ghost:** I was a soldier. I fell out with my brother before the war. Over something stupid. A chicken. I didn't get to say sorry before I went. I'd like him to know. His name is Bao. He lives in {@hamlet}, now, I think.

**You:** I've just been there.

**Ghost:** Have you? Small world. Smaller dead.

**Closing scene**

Bao is a thick, gruff farmer, and he does not believe you for a full minute. Then you say the word chicken.

He sits down very suddenly on an upturned bucket. He covers his face. He says nothing until the bucket creaks.

**Bao:** It was a good chicken, too.

The air by your shoulder gets warm again. It is easier, the second time. You almost enjoy it.

## 7.8  "A Game of Stones"  (`child`)

- **Starts when:** 40 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 3 weeks (0 years and 3 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** +3 potential
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.set(st, "lanterns", read(c, "lanternroad"))`
- **Words:** 204 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The third ghost is the smallest. She is about five. She is sitting in the corner of an inn's courtyard, building a tower of stones that falls over, and building it again.

**Ghost:** Do you want to play? Nobody ever does. They look at me and go away.

*[only if lanterns]* **Ghost:** The old ones on the grey road say somebody puts lights out. Not people. Lights. Will they put mine out?

*[only if lanterns]* **You:** Not yours. Nobody gets yours.

*[only if lanterns]* You are not sure that is true. You said it anyway.

She is so small and so cheerful that it hurts. You are not sure what she wants. It does not seem to be anything. She wants someone to play with.

**Closing scene**

You stack stones with her for three afternoons. Her tower is better than yours. She is very patient with you.

On the third afternoon, she looks up at you with a small serious face.

**Ghost:** I think I can go now. I only wanted somebody to finish one.

The tower is standing. You are almost certain it was your last stone that did it. She waves, and she is gone, and the stones are only stones.

You sit in the courtyard until it is dark.

## 7.9  "What Meng Never Said"  (`tea`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended; Major Lvl 2 or more (given up after 6 more years of waiting)
- **Task:** Reach Major Lvl 3.  "Outlive the whispers: reach Major Lvl 3."
- **Pays:** 2 Potential Pills, a technique insight
- **When it closes, the code:** `(c, st) -> { Character m = Chapters.person(st, "meng"); if (m != null && !m.dead) { m.fatedTo = 0; m.deathCause = "old age (lived " + m.age + " years)"; m.dead(); } }`
- **Words:** 201 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You have not seen Old Meng for a year. When you do, she is thinner, and she has stopped drawing cats.

**Meng:** Sit. Don't fuss. I'm seventy-nine and I've had a good innings. I wanted to tell you something before I go.

**Meng:** You think you're ghost-touched. That you were touched by something. Wrong, dear. I looked at your tea leaves every day for a year. You're not touched. You're a door.

**Meng:** The dead go through. They don't know where else to go. You were a door before you died, and you've been a door ever since. That's all it is. You can keep it open or shut. I never could decide. It's your choice.

**Closing scene**

Old Meng dies on a warm spring day, with a cat on her lap and a pot of tea going cold at her elbow. She is in no pain.

You are at her side. You hold her hand. She does not see you; she looks at the ceiling, and says in a surprised voice: 'Oh. Look at all of you.'

A moment later the room is filled with a quiet, shifting warmth, and for the first time in your life you are not cold.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `door`; default: option 1)

> You are a door, and the dead are standing on the other side.

1. Keep the door open. Let them come.
   - They come all the time. It's noisy and sad and funny. You have never been so busy, and you have never been so well.
2. Open it only for those who need you.
   - You become choosy. A woman with a letter. A man with a grudge. A child with a tower. Each of them is a small fortune.
3. Close it. Rest.
   - The door shuts quietly, like a kindness. The house is silent until dusk. Then you put the kettle on, and you are not alone.

## 7.I1  Interlude: Lost Property  (between season 1 and season 2)

**Interlude**

You died once and did not stay dead. It was, you decided long ago, the best thing that ever happened to you. Just don't tell the goose.

*[only if door is 1]* There is a little shop now at {@bridge}, with a lantern in the window. Its sign says Lost Property (Spiritual). The dead leave things there, and the living pick them up. You run it, in your scarf.

*[only if door is 2]* You keep a small ledger of the ones who came. Mrs. Pang is in it, and the soldier, and a girl with a tower of stones. There are eleven now. You have a tune for each.

*[only if door is 3]* A pale thing sits by the window sometimes, on bright mornings, and watches the street. You leave a cup of tea beside it. It never drinks. It likes to be asked.

*[only if goose is 1]* The goose has retired to a pond. It is believed to be a hundred and four years old. It has never apologised.

*[only if goose is 2]* The goose bites you every time you cross the bridge. You have come to look forward to it. It is the only constant in an uncertain world.

*[only if goose is 3]* A peach appears on the railing each summer. Nobody knows who leaves it. The goose is not saying.

On the night of the Festival of Hungry Ghosts, the whole city lights lanterns on the river. You stand on the Mill Bridge in your scarf. The lanterns drift past.

You do not feel cold at all.

The dead, it turns out, talk. By spring there is a queue.

# 7.S2  Season 2: Dead Letters

## 7.10  "Three Coppers"  (`coppers`)

- **Starts when:** 3 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet rival (walk to their tile).  "Find {rival.name} and collect three coppers for a ghost."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.adopt(c, st, "rival", "rival")`
- **Words:** 480 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It is a wet Tuesday, which is the day the dead do their paperwork. You know this because there is a line of them outside the door and nobody has taken an umbrella, which is the only polite thing about being dead.

*[only if door is 1]* The shop at the bridge has a lantern in the window and a sign that says LOST PROPERTY (SPIRITUAL), and below it, in a smaller hand, NO LIVING PERSON IS REQUIRED TO ENTER. A good many come in anyway, for the tea.

*[only if door is 2]* You keep a ledger, and it has got fat. There are forty-three names in it now. You write each of them down in the evening, with the date, and the thing they wanted, and how it went.

*[only if door is 3]* You closed the door, once. A closed door, you have learned, is only a louder kind of knock.

The first client of the morning is a thin, damp, fussy man in a coat that may have been good, with a leather satchel and the expression of someone who has been told that a thing will take five minutes.

**Quibble:** Quibble. Tax collector, retired, unexpectedly. I was told this was the place for outstanding business. I have a debt. Three coppers. I have been trying to collect it from a person called {rival.name} since the spring of the Long Frost, and I keep missing {rival.him}. First {rival.he} moved. Then I died. I do not propose to let a technicality come between a man and his money.

**You:** Three coppers.

**Quibble:** It is the principle of the thing. The principle is three coppers.

**Closing scene**

{rival.name} turns out to be a large, tired, defensive person who answers the door as though you had come to arrest {rival.him}. {rival.He} listens, and goes red, and then goes pale, and says that it is the stupidest thing {rival.he} has ever heard in {rival.his} life.

**{rival.first}:** He lent me three coppers for a pie. In the year of the Long Frost. I ate the pie. I never paid him the coppers.

**You:** He says it is the principle.

**{rival.first}:** Of course it's the principle. He chased me through four towns. He sent me a letter every spring for eleven years, and every one of them started 'Dear Sir, I regret to remind you'. It was the only post I got. I used to look forward to it.

The coppers are in a jar on the dresser. {rival.He} counts them out onto your palm with a strange slowness, like someone handing over the keys to something. Then {rival.he} stops, and stands in the doorway, and says, in a different voice: 'Is he there? Is he listening?'

**Quibble:** Tell him I forgive the interest.

You tell him. {rival.first} laughs, helplessly, and takes off {rival.his} hat, and holds it against {rival.his} chest in the rain, for as long as it takes a debt to go out of the world.

## 7.11  "The Weight of a Ring"  (`ring`)

- **Starts when:** 10 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet friend (walk to their tile).  "Find your friend {friend.first} and tell them about the ducks."
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.adopt(c, st, "friend", "friend")`
- **Words:** 351 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The second case arrives in a good dress. She is tall and rather cross, with a veil she has pushed back over her hair like a woman who has decided that dignity can wait. Her name is Ilse, and she was to be married on a Thursday, thirty-one years ago, and there was, she explains, a pond.

**Ilse:** I did not die romantically. I would like that on the record. I died because I went to look at the ducks in my wedding shoes. But the person I was marrying is still alive, and has been sorry for thirty-one years. It is the way people are sorry when they have nothing else to do with their hands, and I am tired of watching it.

**Ilse:** It is your friend. {friend.first}. They never married anyone else. They have a ring in a drawer. Tell them it was the ducks. Tell them I wasn't the kind of person who needed protecting, and I'd be furious if they thought so. And tell them to eat something.

**Closing scene**

{friend.first} receives the news with the careful expression of someone who has been told the roof is coming down and is checking whether it matters. You tell the story plainly. The ducks. The shoes. The veil pushed back. The part about being furious.

When you finish, there is a very long silence. Then {friend.first} gets up, and goes to a drawer, and returns with a small ring in a cloth, and sets it on the table between you. They look at it as though it were a verdict that someone else had finally read aloud.

**{friend.first}:** She'd have hated the wedding. All those people. She said so, you know. She wanted to elope to a barn.

**Ilse:** A barn. At last somebody remembered.

You are not sure whether {friend.first} can hear her. You are quite sure that {friend.he} does not need to. {friend.He} puts the ring back in the drawer, and shuts it, and asks you whether you have eaten. It is the first time in thirty-one years that anyone has seen {friend.him} offer food to a guest.

## 7.12  "How Did I Die?"  (`cheese`)

- **Starts when:** 10 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `field`.  "Go to the field at {@field} where Dorrit Hale was last seen alive."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 481 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The third client does not know how she died, and she minds. She is a broad, brisk, weathered woman in her fifties, with the forearms of someone who has hauled things. She stands in the middle of the office with her hands on her hips, like a ship's captain about to complain to the harbourmaster.

**Dorrit:** Dorrit Hale. I've been dead for six weeks and nobody will tell me what of. I've asked the dogs. I've asked the old men on the benches. I've asked Mrs. Pang, who was very nice about it and then talked for an hour about her husband. It's a matter of professional pride. I was never ill. I was never reckless. I'd like to know what I did wrong.

**Mrs. Pang:** I was very nice about it.

Mrs. Pang is in the corner, translucent and satisfied, folding a bit of paper into a smaller bit of paper. She has been with you since the first spring. Nobody knows what she does, exactly. The filing, perhaps. She has, in any case, never been on time, which is an odd quality in a person who has all of eternity.

**Dorrit:** There was a field. That's all I remember. A big green field, and a hill, and a lot of people shouting. After that it's very bright.

**Closing scene**

The field is on a hill above a village, and on the first Sunday in spring the village is the sort of place that people drive in from three counties to be hurt in. There is a banner across the gate. THE GREAT GORGE CHEESE ROLL, it says. Below this, in a newer paint, THE DORRIT HALE CUP.

It takes ten minutes to find the man in the pub who saw it. He tells the story in the flat, careful voice of someone who has told it many times and still has not got it to stop being true.

**Publican:** She won it eleven years running. Eleven. Biggest cheese on the hill, and the best line, and nobody had ever got near her. Last Sunday she took the twelfth. Crossed the line a good ten yards ahead. Turned round to wave. And the second-place cheese, forty pounds of it, which had got a bit above itself, caught her on the ankle.

**Publican:** She went over like a sack. Never woke. The village has been in mourning for six weeks. We've named the cup after her.

Standing in the pub's yard, between a pile of barrels and a goose who is looking at you with a faint, pitying, familiar air, you find you need to sit down. There are many ways to die. You had half hoped for a better one on her behalf.

The goose sniffs. It has seen it all before. It is possible, you think, that it was here on the day. It is possible that it has been everywhere.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `cheese`; default: option 1)

> Dorrit is waiting at the office to hear how she died.

1. Tell her the truth, all of it, including the cheese.
   - **Dorrit:** A cheese.
   - **You:** It was a very big cheese.
   - **Dorrit:** I was killed by a cheese. After eleven years. I have been in the dairy business. There is a certain justice in it, if you stand far enough back. Oh, I'm furious. And it's rather funny. Give me a minute.
2. Tell her she won, and was struck down in her moment of glory.
   - **Dorrit:** I won?
   - **You:** By ten yards. They named the cup after you.
   - **Dorrit:** The Dorrit Hale Cup. Well. I never in my life expected it to be a cup.
   - She says it quietly, and when you look up she is smiling in the way people do when they have decided to go on a long time with something.
3. Tell her it was nothing: she didn't feel a thing.
   - **Dorrit:** Nothing?
   - **You:** It was very quick.
   - **Dorrit:** Hm. I'm not sure that's a comfort. But I'll take it.
   - You are aware that this is the cowardly answer. You are aware she knows.

## 7.13  "The Boundary Stone"  (`boundary`)

- **Starts when:** 6 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones
- **Words:** 565 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The fourth case of the season comes with a living client, which is unusual, and a goose, which is not. The client is a stout farmer called Arbuthnot Gripe, in a coat the colour of a wet field. He sits down on the visitor's chair and says that he has been told this is the place for 'matters of an unfinished character'. He has the look of a man who has tried everything else.

**Gripe:** The south field. It was my uncle Ferris's, and Ferris was the surveyor, and Ferris is dead, and the will says the south field goes 'to him that the goose approves'. I've a neighbour, Mrs. Ploverwick, who says that means her. I say it means me. We've been to the magistrate. The magistrate said, quote, 'What goose?'

**Mrs. Pang:** I do hope it's the goose.

**Closing scene**

The ghost of Uncle Ferris is already in the office when you come back from lunch. He is a thin, upright man in a surveyor's coat, with a chain over one shoulder and a theodolite that he does not seem to have put down since the funeral. He looks at you down the long length of a nose that has measured a great many fields.

**Ferris:** I want it noted that I was perfectly clear. I said the goose. I did not say a goose, or any goose, or the sort of goose that is available. I said the one that saw. I was at the north hedge the day I died, and I stayed there till the light went, and there was exactly one witness to what I did.

**You:** What did you do?

**Ferris:** I moved the boundary stone. Four feet. In Gripe's favour. I felt it was fair. I did it for a reason that I took with me.

The goose, when you find it, is standing on the boundary. It is a large, grey, pitying goose, and it is standing with one foot in each field, exactly on the line, where the stone used to be, and it will not move. It looks at Gripe. It looks at Mrs. Ploverwick. It looks at you with an expression that you have come to know very well.

You walk it down to the stone, which is lying in the hedge. You put the stone back where Ferris said. The goose watches. When the stone has been set in the hole, with four feet of Gripe's field now on Mrs. Ploverwick's side of it, the goose takes one step to the left, plants itself squarely in Gripe's territory, and honks. It is not a happy honk. It is the honk of an animal who has been asked a question at the end of a long day and has decided to answer it honestly.

**Mrs. Ploverwick:** It's me?

**Gripe:** It's her?

**Ferris:** It is neither. It is both. I wished to see them in the same field. They have been quarrelling for thirty years over a hedge. I knew they would have to sort it out between them or sit down with the goose.

They sit down with the goose. It takes the afternoon. By evening there is a pot of tea between them, a drawing of the field, and an arrangement under which each will cut the other's hay. The goose, in the corner, has the expression of a creature who is quite prepared to be paid in grain.

## 7.14  "The Visitor"  (`kin`)

- **Starts when:** 14 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Words:** 317 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The fourth visitor does not come in the usual way. There is no queue, no knock, no damp umbrella. You wake at three in the morning to find a figure sitting on the end of the bed, with its hands folded and its head a little on one side, like a bird that has remembered something.

**Ghost:** Hello, dear. Don't be frightened. It's only me.

It is {=kinrel}, whom you have not seen in a very long time. It is {=kin}. The face is the one you remember, and slightly out of focus, the way a face is when you look at it from the other end of a long hall.

**{=kinfirst}:** I've been standing at the back of the queue since spring. I didn't like to push in. I thought you'd be busy with the people who needed you. I don't need anything. I only wanted to say it, and I'm afraid it's not much.

**Closing scene**

The grave is a plain one, on a slope above a stream, with a stone that someone has kept free of moss. You sit on the grass beside it. The sun comes out, which is considerate.

**{=kinfirst}:** I never asked what you liked to eat. Do you know, I couldn't tell you? All those years. I could tell you the colour of your shoes on the day you were three, and I couldn't tell you what you'd have for supper if I gave you the choice. It's a stupid thing to regret. I've regretted it for longer than most.

**You:** Stew. I like stew.

**{=kinfirst}:** Stew. Oh, that's good. That's very good. I'll write it down.

There is, of course, nothing to write with, and nothing to write on. {=kinfirst} makes the gesture anyway, with a finger, in the air above the stone, slowly and with great care, and for a moment you could swear that the grass bent where it went.

## 7.15  "Forms in Triplicate"  (`tally`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet tally (walk to their tile).  "Hear out Mister Tally of the Office of Returning."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "tally")`
- **Words:** 335 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The man from the Office of Returning arrives on the stroke of nine with a clipboard, a briefcase, an umbrella that he is still wearing as though it were a hat, and a smile that has been ironed. He is polite in the way of a person who has never had to be anything else. His name is Mister Tally.

**Tally:** I'll be brief. I'm sorry to say that my department has noticed an irregularity. Over the last two years a number of persons who ought to have been returned by the usual channel have, I regret to say, been routed through these premises. They have been, if I can put it delicately, completing their affairs. This has an effect on the schedule.

**You:** You're upset that people are saying goodbye.

**Tally:** Upset is a strong word. We are concerned. A person who finishes their affairs does not come back on time, and a person who does not come back on time is a hole in the ledger. I am not a monster. I have a wife, and a cat called Appendix. I am only a man who files things.

**Closing scene**

He lays three forms on the desk. They are for different things: a notice to cease, a notice of intent to cease, and a form requesting that the first two be treated as equivalent. He asks you to sign them in the places marked with a small cross. He has marked them himself, with a ruler.

**You:** And if I don't?

**Tally:** Then I am to inform you that under the Rules of Returning, article nine, a dispute of this kind may be resolved by formal contest. It is a very old rule. I have never seen it used. I did not think anyone would be so unreasonable.

He says it with great regret. He picks up the umbrella. He seems, for a moment, rather like a man who is hoping against hope that you will sign.

**Mrs. Pang:** He's very sweet, really. He sent flowers when I died.

## 7.16  "Appendix"  (`appendix`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 462 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You go to see Mister Tally. It is not a thing you planned. You have a notice on your desk with three forms attached. You also have a cat on your doorstep, a small grey cat with a white bib, who sits there every morning at nine and stares at the door with an air of waiting for something to come out. After the fourth morning you pick it up, and read the tag on its collar, and the tag says APPENDIX, and under it an address.

It is a narrow house in a narrow street, in a quarter of the city that smells of ink. The door is opened by Tally in his shirtsleeves. He is holding a ladle. He looks at the cat, and at you, and at the cat, and the ironed smile slips off his face as if it had never been secured.

**Closing scene**

**Tally:** She does that. She goes out in the mornings. I'd thought she went to the baker's. Please come in. I can't stand on the step with you. My wife will think I'm in trouble.

His wife is a small round lively woman with a laugh that fills a kitchen. She puts you in the chair by the stove, and a plate of something in front of you, and asks nothing for a quarter of an hour. When she does, it is only whether you take sugar. The kitchen is warm and cluttered and smells of onions, and over the mantel is a framed form, in a beautiful hand, with a gilt border. It is his appointment to the Office. He is plainly very proud of it.

**Tally:** I don't enjoy it. I'd like you to know that. It's a post. It's a very small post, in a department nobody has heard of, and I have it because I can add. Forty years of ledgers. Every night I take them home and check the sums, because if a number's wrong, then a person's wrong, and I couldn't sleep.

**You:** You came to my office with three forms.

**Tally:** I was told to. It is the kind of thing I am told. I'm sorry about Article Nine. I didn't know what else to do. I thought if I said it politely enough it would turn out to be a game.

His wife puts a hand on his shoulder. He puts a hand on hers. It is the most natural movement in the world, and he does not notice he has done it. The cat jumps up on the dresser and begins, thoughtfully, to knock a spoon off.

**Tally:** I will fight you if I have to. I'll lose. But I'll do it properly, with the forms. I'd rather that than be the sort of man who doesn't.

## 7.17  "Quibble's Receipt"  (`quibble2`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **Words:** 361 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

He comes back on a Tuesday, in a tidy damp coat, with the leather satchel clasped to his chest. You had thought him gone. He stands on the step with the rain going through him, politely, as it goes through the dead, and he holds up a piece of paper between a finger and thumb.

**Quibble:** I have been remiss. I beg your pardon. I was a tax collector. In forty years I never failed to give a receipt, and I have lately realised that I did not give one for the coppers. It would have been a breach of form.

**Closing scene**

The receipt is written on the back of a hymn sheet in a small cramped copperplate. It reads: RECEIVED OF {rival.name}, THREE COPPERS, IN SETTLEMENT OF A DEBT OF ELEVEN YEARS AND ONE PIE. SIGNED, A. QUIBBLE, COLLECTOR, DECEASED. At the bottom there is a space for a witness. He holds out a pencil.

**Quibble:** I should like you to sign. It is the principle.

**You:** I'll sign it.

**Quibble:** And I should like it delivered. Would you? He will not have kept the letters. I asked, in the spring, in my fashion, and he said that he had kept every one. He had them in a shoebox. He read them out to a cat. I cannot say how that made me feel.

You deliver it. {rival.name} reads the receipt at the door with his reading glasses on his forehead, and then on his nose, and then in his hand. {rival.He} folds it small. {rival.He} puts it in the pocket of {rival.his} waistcoat, over the heart, in the place where a man keeps things. {rival.He} says: 'Tell him I never wanted to be paid back.'

You tell him. Quibble nods, with the grave small dignity of a creature to whom a great thing has been said. 'No,' he says. 'But it was never the debt, you see. It was the receipt.' He puts his hat on his head. It stays there. And he goes out into the rain, a little straighter than he came, and shuts the door behind him very gently, like a man who has finished the books.

## 7.18  "Article Nine"  (`duel`)

- **Starts when:** 2 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Defeat tally (only you can kill them).  "Fight Mister Tally on the Mill Bridge, under Article Nine."
- **Pays:** 2,000 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight

**Opening scene**

The contest is at midnight, on the Mill Bridge, which Tally says is customary and you suspect is merely convenient. He has brought a second, a pale clerk with an ink-stained thumb, and a book in which the proceedings are to be recorded. The goose is there. Nobody invited the goose.

**Tally:** The contest is to be fought to the satisfaction of both parties, under the supervision of the Rules. Neither party may call on the dead. Neither may bring a weapon not described in Schedule C. I must tell you that I am not a fighter. I am, however, extremely well prepared.

He takes off the umbrella-hat, and folds it, and puts it to one side. He rolls up his sleeves. He has the forearms of a man who has lifted a great many ledgers, which is to say that they are rather alarming.

**Mrs. Pang:** I put five coppers on you, dear.

**Closing scene**

*[only if dead.tally]* It is over quickly, and it is not satisfying. He goes down on the bridge with the clipboard under his arm, looking mildly surprised, and the pale clerk closes the book, and writes a line in it, and goes. The goose watches him go. Mrs. Pang is silent for the first time since she arrived.

*[only if not dead.tally]* He yields at the third round, sitting down on the bridge with his glasses crooked and the clipboard across his knees. 'Satisfactory,' he says, with a dignity that surprises you both. 'Entirely in order. I shall note that I was bested.' He takes out a pen, and writes it down, and looks very happy.

**Tally:** I'll be honest, I would have felt worse to be right. There's a sort of relief in losing to a rule.

He leaves a card. It has the name of a department on it, and an address that appears to be under the Palace of the Oldest Order. In a hand like a row of fence posts, he has written: 'You are invited. The Cistern asks for you by name.'

## 7.19  "The Poet's Muse"  (`muse`)

- **Starts when:** 3 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones
- **Words:** 498 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Lin Zhaoyu has come to the office. He lowers himself into the client's chair as if it were a divan and lays one hand on his brow. He has never in his life, he says, asked a favour of anyone, and he would be grateful if that were noted.

**Lin:** I have been dictated to. For three weeks. In the small hours, in my own handwriting, by a person I cannot see. It is the most appalling presumption. The thing is writing my Ode.

**You:** Your Ode to a Plum.

**Lin:** In Seventeen Cantos. I have written nine. The remaining eight have been composed overnight, in my hand, in a better metre than mine. I do not say they are bad. I say it is a question of authorship.

The muse is in the study when you arrive, at the desk, with a brush behind her ear. She is a lean, stooped, ink-stained woman in a robe of a fashion four centuries old, and she is not at all pleased to be seen. She has the harassed face of someone who has been left with the washing-up of a very long party.

**Muse:** I want it understood that I did not ask for this. I was a perfectly respectable poet in the reign of the Third Lantern. I wrote twelve poems and a reasonably good elegy. I died. And I was sent, without any notice, to be the muse of a man who writes odes to fruit.

**Lin:** It is an extremely good plum.

**Muse:** It is a plum. He has spent nine cantos on its skin. He has gone on for eleven pages about its blush. There are people who are dead and are not allowed to rest because they have been given a muse's work, and I am one of them, and I should like to know when it stops.

You put the matter, as gently as you can, to the poet. He is silent for a moment. He rises, and turns his back, and looks out of the window at the roofs until the tea goes cold. His shoulders, in the fine silk, are very straight.

**Lin:** I thought the verses were mine. I thought I had improved. I was so pleased. It was the first time in years that I had been truly proud. I do not wish to be told that I was merely being helped.

**Muse:** You were helped. You were also there. Every word I wrote was a word you had half thought. I merely sharpened it. It is, I will say, a rather good plum.

He turns round. His face is very red. He sits down at the desk, and takes the brush from behind her ear, and, to the amazement of the room, hands her the other end of it. They write the last eight cantos together, in two hands, on the same page, over three nights. They are the best he has done. The plum, in the last of them, is eaten.

**Closing scene**

The house had the quiet that houses have when there is something in them that wants not to be noticed. I walked through it with a lamp. In the kitchen the kettle was warm. On the table was a plate with a single crust of pie, set down neatly, with the fork laid across it. It was the way a man does it who has been told for forty years to put his fork across his plate.

He was in the cupboard under the stairs. He had gone in there on the day of the funeral, and he had been in there since. He was a tall man, with a good moustache, and he was sitting on an upturned bucket among the brooms, with his arms round his knees, trying to look like a coat.

**Ghost:** Don't tell her.

**You:** She knows you're here.

**Ghost:** She knows there's something. She doesn't know I'm ashamed. I owe her a pie. I owe her about three thousand pies. She used to make one every Thursday and I used to say it was nice, and I never once said it was the best thing in my life. Forty years. I thought she knew. And then I was dead, and she was crying in the kitchen, and I stood there with my hat in my hand, and it was too late to start.

I sat down on the stairs. It was cold and the rain was loud. I told him that there was a thing a person could say, even late. That it might not be enough. That it would be better than the cupboard.

It took two hours. He came out at last. He stood at the kitchen door with his hat in his hand, looking at the back of his wife's head as she did the washing-up. I held the door of the world open behind him. He said, in a low, stiff, unpractised voice: 'Maud. It was the best pie.'

She did not turn round. Her hands went on in the water. After a moment she said, to the window, in a perfectly level voice: 'It was a bit dry.' And then she put her wet hands over her face. I let myself out.
