**Opening scene**

The hearing is long, absurd, and moving in about equal parts. Mrs. Fortune presents the ledgers. A clerk from the Department reads aloud, with a stammer, from the section on 'irregularities of unassigned origin'. Wilbur reads his report and has to stop twice. Pip reads from the Chronicle of Wonders, which takes an hour, and on which nobody has the heart to interrupt him.

??? listens to it all with the greatest attention, nodding, with his soup going cold. Twice he writes something down. Once he stops the proceedings to ask what a 'cousin Ellis' is. He is told. He is quiet for a moment.

**???:** I find that I am a poor judge of luck. I have none. I was made, you see. There is nothing left to chance in me. I am all quite intended. It is an odd thing to be, in a room full of people like you.

**Closing scene**

**???:** But I can tell you what the gap is. I have looked at the books. I am not allowed to say how I know. I am allowed to say that there are places in the Garden where nobody decided. The one who made it was in a hurry. He was fighting a war. He did not fill in every page. There are blanks. There are a very few people who were made on the blanks, and for them, things are not settled. They can go either way.

**???:** It is not luck. It is not good fortune or bad. It is only the freedom of the thing. You were born in a place where the future had not been written. And you filled it in, as you went, with friends.

The hall is silent. Somewhere at the back, a very large goose, who has no business being there, honks, once, in a tone of vindication.

**Mrs. Fortune:** So it was never a clerical error.

**???:** It was a gap. I think that is much better. A clerical error is something wrong. A gap is somewhere to put things.

## 8.27  "The Recess"  (`recess`)

- **Starts when:** 1 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **Words:** 385 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The hearing is adjourned at noon for soup. It is the only adjournment in the Palace's history, and nobody is quite sure of the form. They are shown, by a young Wick, to a long stone corridor with a bench along one wall, and there they sit, the whole Society, in their tall black hats, in a row, eating dumplings out of a basket.

It is a kind of hush. For the first time in two hours nobody has anything to say. Marigold passes the dumplings. Captain Barnacle polishes his compass on his sleeve. Master Gu, at the end, has the carp in its bucket on his knees and is looking into the water with a deep and professional attention.

**Closing scene**

**Fenn:** Do you think they'll close it? The gap?

**Marigold:** I think it depends on what they think it's for.

**Barnacle:** I never knew I was lucky. I thought I was just old. Thirty years of sailing and I never once went down. I always put it down to the rum.

**Gu:** I spent my life believing a person was the sum of what he did. I trained for forty years to be a certain weight. Then a bar of soap. I was in the pond for ten minutes. It was the finest ten minutes of my life.

They look at one another. Nobody is embarrassed. It is the kind of thing that can only be said in a corridor, on a stone bench, with a mouth full of dumpling. Fenn takes off his hat and turns it over, and looks inside, as if for an answer.

**Fenn:** I used to think I was the unlucky one. Six years of failing. And then it turned out that was where I met all of you.

**Marigold:** That's what a gap is, dear. It's where a person falls through and lands on the others.

The young Wick comes to say that they are ready. They file back in, one by one, in their hats. At the door stands the Prior of the Bare Head, who has been outside the whole time with his notebook. He looks along the line of them. In a very small voice he says that he should like a dumpling, if there is one left, and that he will not make a speech about it.

## 8.28  "The Canteen"  (`canteen`)

- **Starts when:** 1 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **Words:** 369 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Department of Seeds and Weather has a canteen, and it is the only room in the whole of Heaven that smells of boiled cabbage. It is a long low whitewashed hall with benches, and on the benches clerks in their hundreds, large and small, and the hum of them is the hum of any office at noon. A heron queues for a tray.

Mrs. Fortune takes you in by the side door. She has a table. It is by the window. It has a cloth on it with a pattern of small, worried umbrellas, and four chairs. She sits. She says that everyone has to eat, even in Heaven, and that she can recommend the pie.

**Closing scene**

The clerks come up to the table in ones and twos. They stand at a respectful distance. They are not allowed to speak to the subject, and so they speak to the table, and to the pie, and to the weather. A tall thin clerk in a bow tie murmurs, to the sugar bowl, that he once filed a report on a man who fell into a pond and came out with a purse. 'Very well put,' he says to the sugar. 'Very sensible. I enjoyed it.'

A very old clerk, who has been at the Department since the foundation, comes to the next table and sits with her back to you. She says, to the wall, in a voice that carries: 'I have been filing luck for four hundred years. I have never once met anyone it was for.' And she drops a small folded paper over her shoulder on to your pie. It says: THANK YOU FOR THE HAT.

**Mrs. Fortune:** They talk about you, you know. In the corridors. There's a sort of cult. Nobody can find the form that explains why. It's the best thing that has happened to the Department in my lifetime.

You eat the pie. It is good. It is very ordinary. It is the best pie you have had in your life, and the heron, at the next table, with its tray, looks at you with a bright knowing eye and says in a flat, polite, entirely human voice: 'Hat's off.'

## 8.29  "Pip's Statement"  (`pipwords`)

- **Starts when:** 1 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 405 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Pip is the last witness. He has been waiting at the back with the others, in his hat, with a roll of paper in his fist that he has been twisting for an hour into a damp baton. When the clerk calls his name he does not hear it. He has to be nudged by Marigold. He gets up like a man in a dream.

**???:** You are Pip Tallow, editor of a newsletter.

**Pip:** I am, sir. Your Mastership. I mean, Master. I don't know what to call you.

**???:** I am not sure either. Please go on. I've been looking forward to this.

**Closing scene**

He does not use his notes. He stands at the foot of the table with the roll hanging from his hand and he tells it in the plain, rapid, stumbling voice of a person with no stage manner at all. He says that he met the Master eleven years ago, when they were boys. The Master was sitting on a wall in the rain, eating a peach. The peach was not his, and the Master did not seem to mind.

**Pip:** I thought: there's someone who can't be hurt. Everything lands on him and bounces. I was so jealous I couldn't see straight. And then I thought: I'll stay close. Maybe it'll rub off.

**Pip:** It didn't. It never rubs off. I wanted to say that. I've never been lucky. Not once. I've never found a purse. I get every cold that goes round. I have the worst feet in the province.

**Pip:** But I've been to more places than anyone I know. I've seen a whale lift a boat. I've seen a man fall in a pond so well that two hundred people clapped. I've been at the middle of the most absurd and wonderful life I've ever heard of, and the only qualification I had was that I'd sat down next to someone on a wall.

He looks at the paper in his hand. He looks at the Master of the Palace, at the little gavel, at the cold soup. He puts the paper on the table.

**Pip:** So if it's a gap in the books, I'd like to say I think it's a very good one. And if you're going to close it, I'd ask you to leave the wall. Just the wall. There's a bit of the world that's always been there. I like to think it's the same one.

**Opening scene**

Mrs. Fortune calls in person this time. She comes up the path in a flowered hat and a mackintosh, with a briefcase and an umbrella, and rings the bell. She is very old. She is also, you gather, a good deal older than that. She sits down at your kitchen table and takes out a ledger the size of a paving stone.

**Closing scene**

**Mrs. Fortune:** It's only the final tally, dear. I like to do it in person. Let me see. Luck, ninety-eight, which was never yours. Friends, a great many. Hats, nine hundred and four. I find the sums come out very well. There is a small balance in your favour of one life, which you may spend as you please.

**You:** What happens if I don't?

**Mrs. Fortune:** It goes back into the books. Somebody else gets it. A person who needs a little luck will find a purse on the road one day and not know why.

She shuts the ledger. She sips her tea. She says, rather shyly, that she has put in for retirement, and that she would like it very much if you would come to the party. It is to be held at the Garrison, on the plain. There will be cake.

The Empty Seat has a hat on it. You find it there when you come in, in the cool grey light of the great hall, set a little crooked on the cushion of the chair that nobody sits in. It is a tall black hat with a silver cloud on the brim, and a tag in the lining in a hand like a spider's: For the Host. Return when wanted.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `latch`; default: option 1)

> The hat is on the Seat. The Door is under it. You have a life to spend as you please.

1. Stay: put the hat on, and spend the life on being ordinary.

The goose has followed you from the Palace gates, or a goose very like it. It sits on the steps in the sun. It has the expression of a being that has seen everything. As you pass it says, in a flat polite human voice, as it did once before: 'Hat's off.'

## 8.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

Everyone agrees you have no talent. Everyone also agrees that you are the happiest person they know.

*[only if ruling is 1]* You are, by any measure, an ordinary person now. You drop things. You miss boats, and they sink. You have never been so interesting.

*[only if ruling is 2]* Things go your way, as they always did. A purse on the road. A roof that falls the day after you move. A friend at the end of a rope. You have stopped asking why.

*[only if ruling is 3]* The gap is open. A good many strange and lucky things happen in the neighbourhood, and nobody can say why. A woman finds the cousin she thought she had. A dying business finds a customer. A hat finds a head.

*[only if wronghat is 1]* The Society of the Fortunate Hat has two thousand members now. They still think you are a Hidden Master. You have stopped correcting them. It is easier, and there is a lovely tea service.

*[only if wronghat is 2]* The Society knows you are not a Hidden Master. They have kept the hats anyway. They say the hat is the point. They may be right.

*[only if gu is 1]* Master Gu visits every year with fish. He sits by the pond where he fell in and tells you about his students. They are very good at falling in ponds.

*[only if gu is 2]* Master Gu has told everyone you are a Hidden Master. You have given up trying to stop him. He is in the fourth edition of the Chronicle.

*[only if hexgift is 2]* Wilbur sleeps in the teapot, which has been mended, and has opinions on the garden.

*[only if not hexgift=2]* A very small man in a rusty suit comes to tea on the first Tuesday of the month, on the back of a snail. He is always late. He is never refused.

*[only if latch is 1]* You are, by any measure, an ordinary person. You wear a hat. It is the luckiest thing you own.

*[only if latch is 2]* A tall black hat with a silver cloud hangs on a peg by the door. It is waiting for you to go through. It has been very patient.

*[only if latch is 3]* A person in a tall black hat stands at the Empty Seat. They tip it to everyone who goes by. The Wicks have never seen them leave.

Every so often, in a quiet moment, you open the inner pocket of your purse. It is empty. It is warm again, just a little. You close it, and you put on your hat, and you go out to see who is at the door.

## 8.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

The Palace has a notice board. You are the only person ever to win its raffle five years in a row. The Elders want to investigate.

Pip says it is skill.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

You are the least qualified soldier in the Gardener's army. You are also the only one who has never been wounded.

The generals have given up asking why. They put you in the middle, where everyone can see you.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You leave the Garden with a purse, a hat, and a friend. The Outside is huge and strange and you have no talent for it whatever.

Within a week you have found a free supper.

**You are struck down by the array**

The luck ran out at the array. It had run out before, on a mountain, and your friends caught you.

They are standing on the far side of the Seam, in tall black hats, looking up.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden goes out. Somewhere in the dark a very small woman in a grey dress straightens her spectacles.

'Well,' she says, with great dignity, 'that is the final form submitted.'

# 9.S1  Season 1: The Crane's Clan

## 9.1  "The Last of the Cranes"  (`hall`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** Have 5 friends.  "A clan needs people: make five friends."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, gear a Major above you
- **Words:** 511 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Silver Crane Clan lived in a valley hall for four hundred years. They were not famous. They were not rich. According to their neighbours, they were a bit too fond of tea.

Nine days ago Baron Hexley's riders came in the night. By morning the hall was a heap of black beams and eighty-three members of the clan were gone. The valley smelled of smoke for a week, and the tea, when you tried to make it, tasted of it for a month.

You are what is left of the main line, which means that three people are looking at you as though you knew what to do.

**Tamsin:** We have a ruined hall, forty silver coins, and a goat. Go on, then.

Tamsin is your cousin, six years older, broad in the shoulder, and has never in her life been told anything twice. She tends the herbs. She has made a list of everything the fire left and it is a short list. The goat is item four.

**Joren:** Dig?

**Tamsin:** We're not digging.

**Joren:** A small one.

Joren carries a shovel the way other men carry a sword, and for the same reason, which is that it makes him feel prepared. He is a miner, and cheerful in a way that borders on alarming. He sleeps well. He has slept well through the whole of it, and you have not decided if you envy him or are afraid.

**Isla:** I saved the banner.

The youngest says it as if it were an apology. She unrolls it on a stump: a silver crane on blue, standing on one leg, scorched at one corner. Under the bird, in faded thread, the clan's motto. Stand on one leg, see far. Isla is a tailor, and eighteen, and has a needle in her sleeve at all times, in case.

It is the first time any of you has laughed in nine days. It is not a good laugh. Nobody minds.

**Closing scene**

They come slowly. A ferryman called Poll, who owed your grandmother a favour and has come to pay it in the only coin he has, which is unlimited complaining about the weather. A widow called Marta, who makes dumplings in a pan the size of a cartwheel and refuses to be thanked. Two brothers from the next valley, Dunn and Dunnock, who never liked Hexley and are not sure why. A retired schoolmaster named Pilcher, who arrives with a cat called Verdict and a trunk of books and sets up a school in the shade of the burned wall for the six children who have no school.

On the day the fifth one comes, Isla hangs the banner on a pole above the tent. It flaps in the wind like a bird trying to take off. Poll says that it looks as if it wants to be somewhere else, and Marta tells him it does not, it only wants a bit of encouragement, and gives him a dumpling.

**Tamsin:** Well. That's a clan, I suppose.

**Joren:** Can I dig now?

Of course Tamsin finds out. She reads it over your shoulder, and her only comment is a long, heavy, ironic silence, which is the form of speech she uses for her cousin.

**Closing scene**

There are eleven holes in what used to be the kitchen garden. Tamsin has fallen into two of them. She sits on the edge of the largest with her arms folded, saying nothing, while he shows you the twelfth.

It goes down through the cellar floor and the clay, and down into rock. At the bottom is a cave, and in the cave there is a light. It is pale, and silver, and slow, and it comes out of the rock itself, like breath on a cold morning. It hums. It is a note so low that you hear it in your teeth before your ears.

**Joren:** Uncle Aldous told me never to dig in the cellar. He said it was flooded. I thought it was a funny thing to say about a cellar. I asked what it was flooded with. He said tea.

**Tamsin:** It's a spirit vein. A big one. Hexley wanted this.

The light moves over your face, and for the first time in nine weeks you feel rested, in the middle of the afternoon, standing up.

**Isla:** Stillspring. That's the name. Uncle Aldous said it when he thought nobody was listening. I thought it was a prayer.

**Joren:** It might be. It's a nice hole for one.

## 9.3  "Isla's Banners"  (`banners`)

- **Starts when:** 30 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet isla (walk to their tile).  "Ask Isla about the coin on the banners."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 211 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Isla sews when she is afraid. By now there are forty banners hanging in the tent, and each is slightly different from the others, and one of them is wrong.

You do not see it at first. Then you do. On the edge of every banner, in tiny stitches, is a coin with an animal's head. It is not part of the clan crest. You have never seen it on anything.

At night, in the tent, the banners hum. It is very faint. If you put your ear to the cloth it is the same note as the cave.

**Closing scene**

**Isla:** I don't know. My hands just make it. A wolf, I think. Or a boar. I can't see the whole thing, only the nose. It's a bit like trying to remember a face.

**You:** How long have you been doing it?

**Isla:** Since the fire. Before that, a little. I thought I'd got it from the pattern book.

You write the coin on a scrap of paper and put it in your pocket next to the forty silver coins. Later, in a market in the next valley, you see the same wolf-headed coin carved above a doorway. A passing trader says, without being asked: 'Hexley's mark. Don't stand under it.'

## 9.4  "Baron Hexley"  (`baron`)

- **Starts when:** 1 year(s) after the previous chapter ended; Major Lvl 2 or more (given up after 6 more years of waiting)
- **Task:** Meet hexley (walk to their tile).  "Meet Baron Hexley at his castle in {@castle}."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "hexley")`
- **Words:** 327 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

There comes a day when you can't go on guessing, and you write to Baron Hexley. You expect no answer. He answers in two days, in a clear, formal hand: 'Of course. Come to my castle. I shall be glad to explain.'

It is the politest thing anyone has said to you in a year, and it frightens you more than a threat would.

**Closing scene**

The Baron is a grey, handsome man of fifty-five, very upright, with a trace of weariness about the eyes. His study has one picture in it, of a boy on a pony. He pours the tea himself, and the tea is excellent, which you resent.

**Hexley:** You think I am a villain. I don't blame you. Allow me one document.

The contract is three pages long. At the bottom of the third, in a hand you know from a hundred birthday cards, is the signature of Aldous Crane, Head of the Silver Crane Clan.

**Hexley:** Three years ago your uncle rode to me. The southern raiders were burning the border villages and he could not hold the valley. He offered me the guardianship of the vein beneath it in exchange for two hundred spears. I sent them. They held your border two winters. Then he changed his mind. He barred my steward from the gate and wrote that he had made a mistake.

**You:** And you burned us for it.

**Hexley:** I sent my captain to demand what I had paid for. My captain went further than I told him. I hanged him the following week. It did not bring anybody back, and I did not expect it to.

He turns the cup in its saucer. His hand is perfectly steady.

**Hexley:** I do not ask to be forgiven. I would like to be understood a little. I made a bargain, and I could not bear to see it broken, and the second of those is the only thing I am sorry for.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `believe`; default: option 1)

> Baron Hexley says your uncle sold your home.

1. Believe him. The paper is real.
   - **You:** That's his signature.
   - **Hexley:** It is. I'm sorry.
   - You walk out of the castle in a daze. Nobody warns you that the worst part of hating a man is finding that he is telling the truth.
2. Call him a liar to his face.
   - **You:** My uncle would never have done it.
   - **Hexley:** Your uncle did what frightened men do. I would not blame him, were I you. I would blame the raiders.
   - You leave without finishing the tea. You go on hating him, and you know a little more now about why.

*[only if keeper is 1]* Tamsin reads it. She sits down slowly, the way a person sits who has been told the chair is not there.

*[only if keeper is 2]* Joren reads it. The shovel he has carried for nine years slides out of his hand and clangs on the ground, and it is the first time you have seen him without a joke.

*[only if keeper is 3]* Isla reads it. Her needle drops from her sleeve and rolls under the table, and nobody picks it up.

2. Tell them it hurts, and that you will get through it together.

The hall goes up in a single summer. It is plain and strong, with a very large well. The well is Joren's hole, number twelve, with a stone rim round it and a small crane carved on the stone. Pilcher's school has a room now, with a stove, and Verdict has been given the whole of the windowsill as a mark of rank.

## 9.I1  Interlude: Too Fond of Tea  (between season 1 and season 2)

**Interlude**

The Silver Crane Clan is not famous. It is not rich. According to its neighbours it is a bit too fond of tea. It has a spring, a well, and four hundred years of reasons to be stubborn.

*[only if clan is 1]* The school at Stillspring has two hundred students. They arrive muddy and leave able to see in the dark. Nobody is turned away. Nobody is told what to believe.

*[only if clan is 2]* The clan keeps the vein honest. Each year it chooses a dozen guests and teaches them what it knows. It is a small circle, and a true one.

*[only if clan is 3]* The stone over the cavern has a crane on it, standing on one leg. Children sit on it to eat their lunch. Nobody tells them what lies below. Some secrets are better as benches.

*[only if believe is 1]* You sent Baron Hexley's family a Midwinter card, once. It said only: we are both still here.

*[only if dead.hexley]* Edric Hexley visits once a year, quietly, and brings flowers to a grave that is not yours. You do not talk about it.

*[only if keeper is 1]* Tamsin's garden has thirty kinds of chamomile now. Her tea is terrible, and everyone drinks it.

*[only if keeper is 2]* Joren dug a second well, and a third. He found a fourth hole in a field. It was only a hole. He was delighted.

*[only if keeper is 3]* Isla's banners hang in the halls of four clans now. Nobody knows who makes them. They have a crane on the edge, and nothing else.

On summer nights you sit on the flat place on the roof of the hall, with the banner turning below you, and listen. The hum has not stopped. Lately it has started to rise, a very little, at the end of the note, as if it were about to ask something.

## 9.9  "The Shift Bell"  (`bell`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> { Chapters.spawn(c, st, "marta"); Chapters.spawn(c, st, "poll"); Chapters.spawn(c, st, "pilcher"); }`
- **Words:** 339 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

There are rules in the Deep, and they were not written down. They were passed along the way rules are, from one tired mouth to another, with a nod and a nudge on the ladder. Don't whistle. Don't count the dead. Don't say the word 'collapse'; say 'the shift'. Count your lamps going down and count them coming up, and if the numbers differ, say nothing, and go up anyway.

It is called the Deep because no one in the clan has been able to agree on another name. It is the old cavern, widened by two summers of work into a shaft with a timber frame and a wheel. A hundred and thirty people of the clan go down it, in three shifts, to take the pale stone of the vein: the dust of it, the grit, the cold bright crumbs that people grind for their cultivation.

The bell goes at five. Clang, clang, clang. Boots on the boards. Lamps on the hooks. Marta's dumplings steam on the lid of the stove, and Poll, who has retired from the river and taken up complaining as a trade, says that it will rain, and it does not.

**Joren:** Count your lamps.

**All:** Counted.

It is the shift's whole liturgy. You have said it a hundred times. This morning, for the first time, you notice that there are always one more voices than there are men.

**Closing scene**

You do the sums on the stairs, going up, with the dust on your lips. A hundred and thirty-one lamps went down. A hundred and thirty came up. You count again in the yard. It is the same.

**Poll:** Don't. Don't go counting it twice. That's how it gets in your head.

**You:** How what gets in?

**Poll:** Nothing. I'm a ferryman. We say that about water.

He stumps off. Clang goes the bell for the end of the shift, and the noise goes out across the valley, and the hum underneath it, steady and slow, goes on as if nothing had interrupted.

## 9.10  "Rules of the Deep"  (`rules`)

- **Starts when:** 6 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **Words:** 329 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The children have a rhyme for it. They sing it skipping, on the flat stones by the wheel-house, with two girls turning the rope and a third in the middle. The words go like this: Lamp up, lamp down, count the ones that came to town. Say it low, say it true, if there's one that's not for you. Bring your boots and keep your head, and say good night before you're dead.

Pilcher collects them. He has a book. It has eighty rhymes in it already, and a section on omens, and one on what to do about the smell. He writes down each rule as it is told him, with the name of the teller and the date. Beside it he draws a small square, to show whether the rule has ever, so far as he can tell, been broken without consequence.

**Closing scene**

The squares are almost all blank. There are three that are filled. The first is a rule about the left boot, and the filled square beside it is for a man named Dunn, who put on the left first, and lost his supper. The second is a rule about not saying the word 'snake', and the filled square is for the cat, which does not know the word and fell into a bucket.

The third square is next to a rule that has no name beside it. Nobody can say who told it. It is the first rule in the book, in Pilcher's neatest hand, and it says: Say good night to the dark. And under it, in a handwriting that is not his, small, in pale ink, there is a single word, added later, and it is Good night.

**Pilcher:** I did not write that. I have asked everybody. I assure you I do not forget my own sentences. I have looked at it every day for a week. It is a little warm, if you hold your hand over it.

## 9.11  "The Sleepers"  (`sleepers`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `hall`.  "Keep watch at the shaft head of the Deep, at {@hall}, through the night."
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill
- **Words:** 360 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It begins with Dunnock. He is found at four in the morning at the head of the shaft, in his nightshirt, with his arms at his sides, looking down. His eyes are open. He is asleep. He is humming, very softly, the same note as the Deep, and he does not stop when Tamsin slaps him, nor when she pours a bucket on his head.

The next night it is two. Then six. They come out of the huts barefoot, in ones and twos, in the dark, as quiet as cats, and they go down the paths to the shaft head and stand there. They do not fall. They do not try to climb. They only stand and hum and sway a little, and when the sun comes up they wake with no memory at all and a grave, apologetic hunger.

**Marta:** It's not a sickness. I've nursed sickness. It's more like being called.

**Pilcher:** I took the liberty of keeping a register. It is, I regret to say, in alphabetical order. I do not know how to record a thing like this without being orderly.

**Closing scene**

You sit on a barrel by the wheel with a lantern and a flask. Joren is beside you, whittling a stick to a point. By midnight there are fourteen of them at the head of the shaft, in their nightshirts, in a loose ring, humming. The moon is up. Under their feet, the boards of the shaft cover are warm.

Isla comes out of the tent with her sewing. She sits beside the sleepers, cross-legged, in the light of the lantern, and begins to stitch. She does not look up. After a while the humming slows, and rises, and finds her note, the way a choir finds its pitch.

**Joren:** She's doing it right, isn't she. Look. She isn't fighting it. She's going along with it.

The ring of sleepers sways. The needle goes in and out. The note rises one tone and holds. And from below the boards, a very long way down, something answers it, in a voice that has no words, with a sound like a great lazy breath.

## 9.12  "Count Your Lamps"  (`lamps`)

- **Starts when:** 6 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** a technique insight
- **Words:** 283 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You go down the next morning with the first shift. You have been down a hundred times, and it has never taken so long. The ladder is the same ladder. The rungs are the same rungs. But the numbers on the lamp hooks, which are painted in white, have changed. The hooks that said 41, 42, 43 now say 41, 42, 43, 43, 44.

**Marta:** Don't look at them. Look at your feet.

There is a crowd of you at the bottom, the whole shift, with lanterns, on a ledge of grey rock, looking at a wall. The wall is the vein. It is not like stone. It is the silver of a cold sky, and it moves very gently, in and out, in and out, as the wall of a sleeping animal moves.

**Closing scene**

Poll counts the lamps. Twice. Out loud, which is against the rules. He gets to the end of the line, and stops, and wipes his mouth with the back of his hand.

**Poll:** Hundred and thirty-two.

**Joren:** We're a hundred and thirty-one.

**Poll:** I know what we are, lad.

The extra lamp is a small one, at the very end of the ledge, hanging from a hook that was not there yesterday. It is not one of yours. It burns with a clear, still, unfamiliar flame. It has been lit by someone who knew exactly how much oil to put in, and did not need a wick.

None of you touch it. Nobody says it is a good sign. Nobody says anything at all. You go up the ladder, one by one, and count yourselves on the stairs, and the number is right, and nobody feels any better.

## 9.13  "The Baron's Heir"  (`edric`)

- **Starts when:** 10 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet edric (walk to their tile).  "Hear what Edric Hexley wants."

- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "edric")`

**Opening scene**

The rider who comes to the gate on the fourth morning is young, in a plain cloak, with a satchel and a bad cough. He has the Baron's long jaw and his father's way of sitting a horse, as if he were at a funeral and the horse were the deceased. He will not give his name to the sentry. He asks for the head of the clan, and when told, he gets down and walks the last half mile on foot.

**Edric:** I'm Edric Hexley. I'll say it plainly, since there's no good way to say it. I know what my father did. I know what the contract said. I've come to see the spring. I've heard it all my life.

**Closing scene**

He tells it in the kitchen, over Marta's soup, with his cloak off and his sleeves rolled, like a man giving evidence. He grew up in the Baron's castle fifty miles away. On the east side, in a cold room, he heard a note. It came up through the floor on still nights, and no one else heard it. His father said it was the wind. His nurse said it was a draught. His mother, who died, said nothing.

**Edric:** I heard it from the age of four. I think I'm the one who told him where to look. I mentioned it to him once, at supper, as a child does. He went very quiet. He asked where in the room it was loudest. I said the north wall, by the window. He put down his spoon and looked at the map.

The kitchen is silent. Marta stops stirring. Pilcher, in the corner, takes off his spectacles.

**Edric:** It's not a story I'm proud of. I think I'm the thing that began it. I didn't want to hide that. I wanted you to hear it from me, and then decide whether I'm to be allowed to hear the note again.

## 9.14  "The Dumpling Rota"  (`rota`)

- **Starts when:** 4 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **Words:** 361 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The trouble starts, as such things do, in the kitchen. A hundred and thirty people work three shifts, which means a hundred and thirty people want to eat at seven different times, and there is one pan. It is a very large pan. It has been in Marta's family for five generations, and it can hold forty dumplings at once, and she has not yet been persuaded to buy a second.

**Marta:** It's not the pan. It's the principle. If I buy a second pan I'll have two pans to keep clean, and the day after that someone will want a third. It's how it begins. First it's the pan, then it's the cook, then it's a committee.

**Poll:** Aye, and then it's bureaucracy.

**Marta:** It's a dumpling.

**Closing scene**

By the second week there is a rota on the kitchen door. By the third, there is a sub-rota, for the people who have been excluded from the rota on grounds of quarrel. The night shift says the day shift gets the fresh ones. The day shift says that the night shift gets the hot ones. A small, curly-haired boy of seven writes a petition and delivers it to the pan. It says, in a careful hand: MORE.

On the fourth Thursday, with the dumplings an hour late, the entire night shift lays down its tools and sits on the floor of the kitchen with its arms folded. It is the first strike in the history of the clan. There is a long silence. Marta looks at them over the rim of the pan with an expression like a dam being considered.

**Marta:** Right. Well. If it's to be a dispute, it'll be done properly. Pilcher! Fetch the register.

The dispute is settled by Tuesday. It takes eleven resolutions, a motion of thanks, and the purchase of a second pan. Marta announces that she has not changed her mind. She says she has merely been outvoted by a pan. She cooks a double batch that night, in both, with her sleeves up, and her face in the steam, and her mouth set in the line of a woman who is, quietly, very happy.

## 9.15  "Old Poll Goes Down"  (`pollside`)

- **Starts when:** 3 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 1 weeks (0 years and 1 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 412 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Poll has not been down the Deep. In all the years of the shifts he has stayed at the head, with the wheel, and the bell, and the cart-horse. He is a ferryman, he says. He knows water, and air, and the thing that lies between a boat and the bottom. He does not hold with holes. The clan has stopped asking. He has gone grey in the shaft house, and his boots have never been wet by anything but the rain.

On the day the pit boy falls ill with a fever at the end of a shift, the bell for the last cage goes unrung. There is nobody on the ladder but the old man himself. He puts down his pipe, and takes off his coat, and says that somebody has to bring the lad up.

**Closing scene**

He goes down the ladder like a man walking into cold water, one rung at a time, with his hands tight and his face white, counting. You go behind him. You count with him. At the sixtieth rung he stops, with his forehead against the rail, and says in a flat small voice: 'I was four. I was in the river, in the spring flood. They fished me out. I was under for what they said was a minute. It was the best minute of my life.'

**You:** What do you mean?

**Poll:** I mean I wasn't afraid. I should have been. I was under the ice, with my eyes open, and the whole river was singing. It was a low note. A long one. I've been listening for it ever since. Why do you think I took up the ferry?

You reach the bottom. The lamps of the ledge are burning in a row, and at the far end, hung from the hook that was not there, is the extra lamp. It burns clear and still. Under it, on a bench, wrapped in a blanket, is the pit boy, asleep, with his mouth open. And the wall behind him is breathing, a slow silver surge and sigh, and the note is in the air, the note, as clear as a bell in a well.

Poll stands in front of it with his hat in his hands. His face is wet. He is not ashamed. He says: 'Well, there you are.' And the vein, in a voice that every person on the ledge hears at once, says, with great gentleness: 'Hello.'

## 9.25  "Ask the Cup"  (`cup`)

- **Starts when:** 4 weeks after the previous chapter ended

**Opening scene**

The tea ceremony is the oldest custom of the clan, older than the hall, older than the motto, older than the name. Every night, at midnight, the head of the clan takes a cup of tea down to the cellar, and sets it on the flat stone by the well, and says three words: 'Sleep, grandmother. Sleep.' Then he drinks half and pours half out on the floor. Nobody remembers why. It is just done.

You have done it a hundred times. This night you leave it undrunk. You sit on the flat stone with the cup between your hands and ask it. It is an ordinary cup. It is chipped at the rim. It has a pattern of small blue cranes.

The cup is warm. It is warmer than the tea. And the hum comes up through the stone, up through the soles of your feet, up into the china, and the cup begins, very quietly, to speak.

**Closing scene**

It is not a voice. It is a pressure on the mind, like a hand laid very gently on the top of the head. It says: grandmother. It says: sleep. It says: four hundred years. It shows you, one after another, in the cup, the faces of the heads of the clan who have gone down these steps with a cup in their hands.

The first is a woman in a cloak, in the dark, with a torch, kneeling beside an opening in the rock, weeping. She is not afraid. She is sad. She pours the tea from a cup into the pale light and says three words. And in the vein, a great way down, something very large, turning in its sleep, settles.

It is not a spring. It is not a vein. It is a bird. It is lying on its side in the earth, folded, with its neck curled round and its head tucked under its wing, as cranes do, and it is as long as a valley. It is breathing. The silver light is the shine of its feathers. The hum is its sleep.

**Joren:** Oh. Oh, I see. That's why the hole was so good.

At the eighth hour, someone asks Isla. She has not spoken once. She sits at the end of the long table with the great banner in her lap, sewing the border, with her head down. She says, without looking up, in her small clear voice: 'I think it's not about her. I think it's about whether we're afraid. And I think we've been afraid for four hundred years, and it was a very good reason, and I should like to stop.'

The room is quiet. Poll clears his throat. He says that he has changed his mind, for the first time since the Flood. He says a clan which has had a good reason for four hundred years has earned the right to try another.

The vote is carried by a hundred and nineteen to twelve. The twelve are asked to say why. They say that they would simply like it noted that they were against it, so that if it goes wrong they may say so. Marta writes it on the door of the pan.

## 9.30  "Pilcher's Last Rule"  (`lastrule`)

The book of rules is full. He tells you so with a sort of dry astonishment, as if it had happened without his consent. Two hundred and eleven rhymes, ninety-three omens, nine recipes for the dumplings, and the entire history of the clan's quarrels, set out in chronological order. There is one page left. It is blank. He has put a ribbon in it, and has been looking at it for three days.

**Pilcher:** I cannot think what to write. It seems wrong to leave it empty. I have been a schoolmaster for forty years. A blank page is the one thing I cannot abide.

**Closing scene**

He tries a number of things. He tries 'Always say good night to the dark', and crosses it out. He tries a rhyme, which he writes and reads aloud and tears into small pieces. He tries to put down an entire account of the history of the clan, in a paragraph, and gets as far as the second line. He sits with the pencil in his teeth until the cat gets onto the desk, and onto the page, and sits down in the middle of it.

**Pilcher:** Verdict. I beg of you. This is a very serious book.

The cat does not move. It looks at him. It is the yellowish, steady, tolerant look of a creature that has watched a man try to get something right for a very long time. It puts out one paw, slowly, and sets it on the page, and leaves the faint round print of a pad in a little smudge of ink.

Pilcher looks at the paw-print until the candle burns down a finger. He takes off his spectacles. He wipes them, and puts them on again, and looks again. Then he picks up the pencil, and under the print, in his small, precise hand, he writes the last rule of the book. It is four words long. It says: Let the cat decide.

**Pilcher:** It has the great merit of being true.

## 9.32  "The Last Night of Tea"  (`lasttea`)

If it is to be done it will be done at midnight, as it has always been, in the cellar, with a cup. The clan comes down the steps in a long line with lanterns, a hundred and thirty-one of them, one after the other. They line the walls of the old cave until the whole of the Deep seems to be wearing a necklace of lights.

Tamsin has made the tea. She has made it in the old pot, the blue one with the cracked lid, as her mother did, and her mother's mother, and so on back through the generations to a woman in a cloak with a torch. You take the cup. It is warm. You stand on the flat stone by the well with the cup between your hands. The long soft silver breath of the sleeper goes in and out behind the rock. You find that you have nothing prepared to say. You had thought of a speech. You had thought of something about duty. All you have is a cup of tea.

**Isla:** You don't have to say anything. She knows who's there.

So you say the old words, one more time, the three of them, as they were said. 'Sleep, grandmother. Sleep.' It is a simple thing. It is the plainest thing in the world. A hundred and thirty-one people breathe out. And you add, at the end, because there is room, three more words that you had not known you were going to say. 'Thank you. Wake.'

You pour the tea out on the stone. It does not run away. It stands in a small round pool of dark gold, quite still, in the lantern light. Then it begins, very slowly, to shine.

The hum stops. It stops the way a held note stops in a church, not with a cut but with a settling. The silence that follows is so wide and so clean that nobody moves. Then you hear above you, through the rock, from a very long way up, a sound you have never heard in your life. It is the sound of a wing being unfolded in the dark, one feather at a time.

They look up. They stand in the rain, a hundred of them, with their lamps, and watch a house descend from the clouds with a goat on its roof. Nobody cries out. A woman near the front, with a grey plait and a ledger, lifts one hand to shade her eyes. She smiles. It is a small, tired, startled smile. She lifts the hand, and waves.

**Marta:** (leaning far over the rail, with the dumpling pan in both hands) Have they eaten?

She tips it. A hundred and forty dumplings fall in a long fragrant shower on the plain, bouncing, rolling, steaming, among the boots of the line. Nobody moves for a moment. Then a boy of sixteen stoops, and picks one up, and bites. His face changes. He says something. A rumble goes down the line like a wave, and the whole file, to the last man, is laughing.

## 9.45  "Landing"  (`land`)

- **Starts when:** 4 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 2 weeks (0 years and 2 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 2,000 spirit stones, +3 potential, 4 Potential Pills, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 156 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You bring the hall down on the third of April in a thin cold drizzle, on the walls of its own foundations, with a bump like a wooden spoon dropped on a table. The beams settle. The slate sighs. The hum fades to a low murmur, and then to a whisper, and then to nothing. In the silence you can hear the river, and the wind in the poplars, and the goat.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `flight`; default: option 1)

> The hall has flown, and come home, and can fly again.

1. Keep it: a hall that can lift whenever the clan wishes, kept on a short rope.
   - You keep it. You add a chain to the corner posts, thick as a man's arm, and a set of brass rings. The hall rises a few yards, on summer afternoons, to catch the breeze, and the school takes its lessons on the roof. The Baron's son has a hammock slung from the beam. It becomes the best-known house in the province, and nobody has ever been able to find the Silver Crane Clan's address.
   - **Joren:** (with a spanner) It's all right. It's very well balanced.
2. Ground it: pin the roof to the walls with iron, and make the flight a story.
   - You ground it. You drive twelve iron bolts through the beams, into the walls, with Joren's own hammer. The hum sinks. The banner hangs. The hall sits down on its foundations like a hen settling on eggs. The school children draw it, in chalk, on the flagstones of the yard: a house with wings. It becomes a tale. In fifty years nobody believes it.
   - **Pilcher:** It is the best-attested incident in the clan's history. I have it in four hands, two of which are drunk.
3. Give it away: offer the hall and its banner to the Palace of the Oldest Order.
   - You send word to the Palace. A grave, polite reply comes in a week from a man in an apron. It says that the Palace has a great many halls, and none that fly, and he has long thought one would be useful. It says that the Silver Crane Clan would be most welcome to bring it. It says there is a field. It says the soup is ready. You do, in the spring. It is the single most extraordinary arrival the Wicks of the Outer Court have ever seen.
   - **???:** (in the doorway, delighted, wiping his hands on his apron) It has a goat on it.

**Closing scene**

The clan sits down to supper in the great hall that evening, at the long table, under a roof that is, at the moment, exactly where it ought to be. The tea is poured at midnight in the cellar. The hum is in the stones. Nobody says anything about it. On the beam over the table, in silver thread, in Isla's hand, a new stitch has been added to the motto. Stand on one leg, see far. And underneath, smaller: Or fly.

## 9.I4  Interlude: The Long Quiet  (between season 4 and season 5)

**Interlude**

The hall is a house of two hundred and a very large well. The vein hums in the stones, the banner turns in the wind, and the tea is poured at midnight in the cellar by the head of the clan. It is you, still. You have not been replaced.

The hum changes key on a Thursday. Joren is the first to notice, from the bottom of the well. He says it is going somewhere.

# 9.S5  Season 5: The Door

## 9.46  "The Hum Changes Key"  (`dr1`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 175 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It goes up a step. It goes up another. By the end of the week the vein under the hall is singing, not humming, a long clear bright note, and the banners in the hall ring with it like glasses at a feast. Pilcher's school sits in the yard with its fingers in its ears and its faces bright. Isla has stopped sewing. She sits on the steps with her needle in her lap and her head back.

**Closing scene**

On the seventh day the note stops. In the silence you can hear every sound in the valley: the wind, the well-rope, a cat on a roof. The three cousins stand in the yard with their faces turned to the north, where the sky is the colour of a pearl. Tamsin says, quietly, that it is not a note. It is a name.

**Joren:** It says: come. It says it nicely.

**Isla:** (with her needle held up like a candle) It's the First Crane. She's calling the clan. She's asking if we'd like to see the roof.

## 9.47  "Stand on One Leg"  (`dr2`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `garrison`.  "Go to the Garrison of the Crossed, {@garrison}."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 208 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The clan goes to the Garrison. It is a small procession, by the standards of the road: forty-one people, a goat, a pan the size of a cartwheel, and a banner on a pole. Marta walks in front with the dumplings. Poll brings up the rear, complaining of the weather. Pilcher carries the school's cat.

**Closing scene**

They stand in the rain and watch the line go in. Tamsin has her arms folded. Joren has his hat in his hands. Isla holds the banner up, and the silver crane on it, standing on one leg, catches a gleam of light from the open gate. A tall woman with a grey plait stops in front of the banner and reads the motto. She reads it twice.

**Woman:** Stand on one leg, see far. I've never had that from a clan before. I shall put it in the ledger.

One by one the clan of the Silver Crane goes in at the gate. They do not go all at once. They go as people go to dinner, in twos and threes, talking, with their plates and their jugs. Marta is the last of the first batch. She puts a dumpling on the sill, as she always did, for the road.

## 9.48  "The Roof of the World"  (`dr3`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `palace`.  "Go to the Palace of the Oldest Order, at Originis, to the Empty Seat."
- **Pays:** 1,000 spirit stones, +2 potential, 2 Potential Pills, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 117 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You go to the Empty Seat last. You go alone, on a clear cold evening, in the dark blue coat the clan wears at funerals. The hall is empty. The nine lamps burn without wavering. You sit on the flags with your back against the cold stone of the Seat, and look up into the dome. The dome, as you look, goes thin as glass, and you see a sky with no roof.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `latch`; default: option 1)

> The First Crane is above you. The Door is under the Seat. The clan is, in part, already through.

1. Stay: keep the hall, and the vein, and the tea.
   - You keep the hall. The hum sinks back to its old steady note. The tea is poured at midnight by the head of the clan, who is you, in a tin cup, with one sugar. Joren, who stayed, digs a hole in the north meadow and plants an apple tree in it. It is the happiest day of his life.
   - **Joren:** It's a good hole.
2. Go: ride the First Crane up through the glass, and see how far one can see.
   - A long white shape comes down from the glass. It is as big as a hill and as soft as a cloud, and it has an eye like a pond. It lowers a wing. You climb on. The whole of the valley falls away beneath you. The last thing you see, as the dome closes behind, is a banner on a pole, standing on one leg, seeing far.
3. Hold the latch: stay by the Door and help the clan's last stragglers on with their luggage.
   - You sit by the Door for a season. Every few days a straggler arrives, a cousin, a goat, a schoolmaster's cat, and you help them with their bags. Tamsin comes through from the other side now and then with a message and a pie, and goes back again. You have the oddest sense, as you sit there, of being exactly where you were put.

**Closing scene**

On the roof of the hall, the next morning, there is a single silver feather as long as a spear. Someone has stuck it upright in the thatch like a flag. The children say it grew. Nobody asks them to prove it.

## 9.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

The Silver Crane Clan is not famous. It is not rich. It is a bit too fond of tea, and nobody now remembers why, and everybody says it is because of the bird.

*[only if wake is 1]* The First Crane is somewhere in the Outside, in a sky that has no roof. Sometimes a silver feather comes down in the spring, in the north meadow, as long as a spear. It is kept in the school.

*[only if wake is 2]* The tea is still poured at midnight, in the cellar, by the head of the clan. The three words have changed. They are now: 'Sleep well, grandmother. Thank you.'

*[only if wake is 3]* The First Crane lives in the valley. She sleeps most of the day in a field with her head under her wing, and the cows walk round her with tact. The tea is poured at midnight. She drinks it.

*[only if sleeper is 1]* Letters come, in long loops, from a place where nothing is written in the same hand twice. Joren has dug a very good hole.

*[only if sleeper is 3]* The old and the young are somewhere warm. A banner hangs in the window of the hall.

*[only if dead.nought]* A small brass snuffer hangs on a nail above the hall door. It says NOW. Isla keeps it polished, as a reminder.

*[only if not dead.nought]* A grey rider is sometimes seen on the road at dusk. He never comes closer than the gate. Marta leaves a dumpling on the wall.

*[only if latch is 1]* The apple tree in the north meadow gives sour apples. They make the best tea you have ever had.

*[only if latch is 2]* The hall is empty, and swept, and warm. A banner hangs in the window. The tea is on the stove.

*[only if latch is 3]* Tamsin comes back through the Door on Thursdays with a pie, and has never once been late.

Stand on one leg, the motto says. See far. You can see a long way from the roof, these days. You can see the whole of the valley, and the hall, and the place where a bird once sat, and the road that goes on past it, and the sky.

## 9.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

The Palace has a hundred kitchens. You choose the smallest and put a kettle on.

Tamsin turns up the next day and rearranges all the jars.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

The Silver Crane banner goes to the front. It is blue, with a crane on it, on one leg.

It is the one banner in the whole army that people can find in the dark.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You leave through the Seam on one leg, so to speak. See far, the motto said.

You see a very long way.

**You are struck down by the array**

The array took you, and the clan stood on the roof of the new hall and watched the banner turn in the wind.

'They would have been terrible at this,' says Joren, and puts the kettle on.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden goes out. The hall, the well and the spring go out. The last thing to go is the banner, a silver crane on blue, standing on one leg, seeing far.

# 10.S1  Season 1: Three Moves

## 10.1  "Three Drunken Moves"  (`moves`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** Reach Major Lvl 1.  "Master the first of the three moves: reach Major Lvl 1."
- **Pays:** a technique insight
- **Words:** 321 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You remember it the way you remember a smell. Not clearly. All at once.

You were ten. It was an inn courtyard, at night, with paper lanterns and a smell of spilled wine. An old man sat on a barrel, scratching his beard, with a red gourd on his lap that was never empty.

You were watching him because everyone else had stopped. He was swaying, humming, and you were sure he was drunk. Then he stood up, and he was not drunk at all.

**Old man:** Watch. Don't try. Just watch. Once. Twice. Three times.

He showed you three moves, slow as honey, in the lantern light. When he finished, he sat down on his barrel and looked at you for a long time.

**Old man:** That's all of it. It isn't much. Don't try to be clever with it. A clever person will improve the moves and lose what they are for.

In the morning he was gone. All that was left on the barrel was a small clay cup, and a rice-paper note in his terrible handwriting: 'Be good. Don't drink on an empty stomach.'

You have never forgotten the moves. You have never learned his name.

Now you are eighteen, and you are ready to learn what they are for.

**Closing scene**

The first move is easy now. It was never hard. It was only quiet.

It is called Cup Raised to the Moon. You hold up one hand, as if holding a cup, and you tilt your head back, and you let the whole sky tip in.

As you finish it, another memory surfaces, small and sharp. You asked him his name that night. You were ten, and not shy.

**Old man:** My name? Ask the moon, lad. She's known me longest.

You look up. The moon looks back. She does not say anything. You think, though, that she has a good idea.

## 10.2  "The Corner Seat"  (`inn`)

- **Starts when:** 30 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `inn`.  "Visit the old inn at {@inn}, where an old man sat for thirty years."
- **Pays:** 500 spirit stones
- **Words:** 272 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It takes a year of asking. Most people look at you as though you had asked for the loan of a unicorn.

Then an innkeeper, in a far town, says something strange over a cup of cold tea.

**Innkeeper:** An old man with a red gourd? Oh, aye. He had the corner seat for thirty years. My father's inn, then mine. Never aged a day. Nobody saw him arrive. Nobody saw him leave.

**Innkeeper:** You'd better come and see. He left something.

**Closing scene**

The inn is a long, low, warm building, full of people laughing. In the corner is a table with one chair. Nobody sits there. A little brass plate on the table says Reserved, in a hand very like the one on your rice-paper note.

**Innkeeper:** I never took the plate off. He asked me not to. He said he'd be back, only he didn't say when. I don't like to disappoint a regular.

**Innkeeper:** He paid in coins I've never seen before. Small, gold, with a picture on them of a bird I couldn't name. I kept them. Here.

She puts one in your hand. It is warm. On one side is an animal like a crane. On the other, in small letters: the writing is not any alphabet in this country.

**Innkeeper:** He used to hum, too. Always the same tune. Slow, a bit sad. I've heard it in my sleep.

You sit in the corner seat for a quarter of an hour. Nobody stops you. The chair is exactly the right height. You feel as though you have been here before, and as though somebody has just left.

## 10.3  "The Second Move"  (`pass`)

- **Starts when:** 30 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** KILLS 15.  "Test the moves where they were meant for: fifteen kills."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 199 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The second move is harder to remember. It is not hard to do. It is hard to want to do. It looks like a drunk man falling over.

You know exactly what it is for, though, and you know where to try it. The Weeping Pass is an old trade road, and the bandits there have been waiting a long time for something to do.

**Closing scene**

It takes a season. It is not what you expected. You do not strike. You stumble. You turn, you sway, you lunge toward the man you want, and fall into him, and he is on the floor and you are not.

It is called The Stumble That Is Not a Fall. Never aim, the old man told you. Fall toward the one you want to stop.

On the fifteenth night, in a roadside shrine, you remember the rest of the lesson.

**Old man:** The road. You can ask the road, too, if you've a mind to. Everything I know I learned on foot.

He was pouring wine into the shrine's little offering bowl while he said it. He did it every night. The god, he said, was a lonely type.

## 10.4  "A Taste of Somewhere"  (`wine`)

- **Starts when:** 1 year(s) after the previous chapter ended; Major Lvl 2 or more (given up after 6 more years of waiting)
- **Task:** Hold 20,000 spirit stones.  "Even immortals drink: hold 20,000 spirit stones to buy what the merchant keeps."
- **Pays:** gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 178 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

A wine merchant in the city has been talking in the market. She says she bought a gourd of something extraordinary from a peddler who traded it for a song. She says it cannot be priced. She says that once you taste it, ordinary wine tastes like water.

You know before she says it. She has a red gourd.

**Closing scene**

She names a price. You have it in your hand. She pours you a thimbleful, as though handing over a baby.

You taste it. It is not sweet. It is not strong. It tastes like a place. It tastes like a long, long way from here, in the evening, with the windows open.

You cannot say what the place is. You can only say, with total certainty, that you have never been there, and that he has.

**Merchant:** The peddler said something odd as he left. He said, 'A year isn't very long, where I come from.' I thought he meant he was old.

You buy the gourd. It is heavy. It never empties.

## 10.5  "The Road That Is Not Finished"  (`road`)

- **Starts when:** 1 year(s) after the previous chapter ended; Major Lvl 2 or more (given up after 6 more years of waiting)
- **Task:** Reach Major Lvl 3.  "Rise far enough that he might return: reach Major Lvl 3."
- **Pays:** 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 314 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You dream. It is not a dream you have had before.

You are on a road at the edge of the world. It runs on ahead into a mist. The paving stones are good at your feet and thin ahead, and then not stones at all, just a faint grey suggestion of the way.

Far in front of you is an old man in a ragged coat, with a red gourd at his hip. He is walking slowly, and testing the air with his hand, like someone feeling for a draught under a door.

**Old man:** (not turning) Is that you, lad? Don't come any closer. The road's a bit thin here. Wait till you're ready.

**Old man:** I'm nearly there. I think I've found the crack. It's very small. I've been looking for years.

You try to speak. The dream will not let you. He stops, and tilts his head, and you think he may be smiling.

**Old man:** Third move. You know it. You've always known it. I only had to remind you.

**Closing scene**

The third move is called Empty Gourd, Full Sky. You tip the gourd all the way over, and there is nothing in it, and you let your arms fall wide, and you are not afraid.

It is not a movement to hit anybody. It is a movement to be hit by. You let the whole world come in, and you do not close.

On the night you finish it, you remember the last answer. He gave it very late, on the night he left, when he thought you were asleep.

**Old man:** If you want to know my name, ask the gourd. It's the only thing that never lied to me.

You hold up the red gourd. You turn it over. There is a name scratched under the stopper in tiny letters, so worn you can hardly read it.

## 10.6  "The Last Cup"  (`cup`)

- **Starts when:** 30 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `inn`.  "Go back to the corner seat at {@inn}."
- **Pays:** 5,000 spirit stones, 2 Potential Pills, a technique insight
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.set(st, "sawgourd", read(c, "garrison"))`
- **Words:** 374 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You go back to the inn. You did not decide to. Your feet decided.

The corner table has a lantern on it tonight, and the lantern is lit. The Reserved plate is gone.

The innkeeper stands in the doorway, wiping her hands on her apron, and she looks at you as though she wants to say something and cannot find the first word.

**Closing scene**

He is sitting in it. He is exactly the same. The beard, the coat, the red gourd at his hip, the look of a man who has just remembered a very good joke.

**Old man:** Ah. There you are. You've gotten tall. Sit. Don't stand there like a stork.

You sit. He pours into the little clay cup, and hands it to you. It is the cup he left behind, years ago. It has been mended with gold.

**Old man:** You kept it. Good. Most don't.

**You:** You never told me your name.

**Old man:** Didn't I? How rude. It's Wen Jiu. Warm Wine. It isn't the first one. The first wouldn't fit in your mouth. Ask me again when you've seen the sky from the other side.

You do not ask what he means. You have the feeling you are not meant to.

*[only if sawgourd]* You think of a long stone in an empty fortress, and a small drawing of a gourd beside the words The Wandering Immortal. You don't ask. You have the feeling he knows what you saw.

**Old man:** I've signed a few margins in my time. 'A guest.' People think it's modest. It's only accurate.

**Old man:** I can't stay. I've left it too long. I only came to see if you'd got there. You have. Almost.

**Old man:** There's no fourth move. I never found it. Perhaps you will. That's the thing about a teacher, you see. He's only the first pair of hands.

He stands. The chair scrapes. He pats your head, absently, like a boy's. He is humming, softly, a slow tune you have heard all your life.

**Old man:** If you ever meet a quiet man in a very big garden, tell him I found the crack. And that I'm sorry I'm late.

The lantern flickers. When it steadies, the chair is empty. The cup in your hand is warm.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `cup`; default: option 1)

> He is gone, and the cup is still warm.

1. Pour the first cup out onto the floor, for him.
   - The wine soaks into the boards. For a moment the whole inn smells of somewhere else. Then it is only an inn again, and you pour another.
2. Drink it yourself, to the dregs.
   - It tastes of a place you have never been. You swallow. For one long moment, you stand at an open window at evening, in a country with a different sky.
3. Put it back on the table where it was.
   - You set it on the corner table, on the brass plate. The innkeeper nods. She will not move it. Nobody will.

## 10.I1  Interlude: Empty Gourd, Full Sky  (between season 1 and season 2)

**Interlude**

You are not a great master. You are a person who falls toward the one they want to stop, and tips the whole sky into a cup.

*[only if cup is 1]* On the night of every full moon you pour a cup out for him on the inn's boards. The innkeeper pretends not to see. Her daughter has started to do it too.

*[only if cup is 2]* You drank that cup, and you have never again tasted anything quite like it. You have never stopped trying.

*[only if cup is 3]* The cup is still on the corner table. People say it is warm. Some say they have seen it refill.

Sometimes, in the evening, you take out the red gourd and look at the name scratched under the stopper. It does not say Wen Jiu. It says a word in a country you do not know.

You hum a tune. Slow, a bit sad. You find you know it better than you thought.

# 10.S2  Season 2: The Fourth Move

## 10.7  "A Student, Against Advice"  (`student`)

- **Starts when:** 3 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "nettle")`
- **Words:** 351 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

She is thirteen and she has been sleeping in the corner seat. Nobody has told her she may not. The innkeeper, who is old now and has opinions about everything but this, says that the girl came in out of the rain in the spring and sat down in the one chair nobody sits in. When the innkeeper went to tell her off, the words did not come.

She is called Nettle. She has a face like a closed fist and a pair of very large, very steady eyes. She watched you practise the first move in the yard last night, from the kitchen window, with a heel of bread in her hand. She has come to say that you are doing it wrong.

**Nettle:** You tip your head back too soon. The sky doesn't come in until you've finished the wrist. You do the wrist after. I've seen it done properly, I think. I mean, I haven't. But I know where it goes.

**You:** I'm not anyone's teacher.

**Nettle:** I haven't asked you to teach me. I've told you what's wrong with your wrist.

**Closing scene**

You teach her nothing. You do the moves in the yard every morning at dawn, in the cold, and she sits on the step with her chin on her knees and never blinks. After a month she has stopped telling you what is wrong. After two, she has started, very slightly, to move her own wrist.

One evening you find her in the stable, by herself, with the lantern on the wall, trying to fall toward a bale of straw. She falls. She gets up. She falls again. She is not graceful. She is a thirteen-year-old with skinned knees and a chin like a spade, falling toward straw with a look of the most profound concentration.

**Nettle:** I'm doing it wrong, aren't I?

**You:** Yes.

**Nettle:** Good. Then I'll know when I've got it.

You hear yourself say, in a voice that is not entirely yours: 'Don't aim. Fall toward the one you want to stop.' She looks round at you, and you are both rather startled.

## 10.8  "The Beggar Prince's Song"  (`funeral`)

- **Starts when:** 14 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `village1`.  "Go to the village of Lower Teng, at {@village1}, and hear their story of the singing drunk."
- **Pays:** a technique insight
- **Words:** 343 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

They tell it in a village called Lower Teng, at the foot of a hill, in the evening, to anyone who will sit still for it. A man came through in the year of the long drought. He was old, and drunk, and wore a coat that had more patches than coat. The village was burying its headman that day, and the village did not know how to cry.

It was a hard people. They had buried a great many in a great many droughts, and had got into the habit of burying quickly and without noise. The old man stood at the grave with his gourd. He listened to the silence. Then he sang a song.

**Closing scene**

**Village elder:** It was a terrible song. I want that known. He had no voice, and he had no tune, and he forgot the words in the second verse and made up the rest. It was about a goat. A goat that wanted to be a bird. And the more he sang, the more we laughed. And the more we laughed, the more we wept. And by the end the whole village was in the churchyard on its knees, howling, and he went away.

**Village elder:** We've sung that song at every funeral since. It is a very bad song. It's the only song we have. You'll find that when we do it right, the dead sit up for a bit and listen.

Nettle is beside you on the wall, swinging her heels. She has been given a cup of cider. She says, in her solemn way: 'He was teaching them the second move.'

**You:** What?

**Nettle:** The stumble that isn't a fall. He made them fall toward the thing they were afraid of. That's all that was. He just did it with a goat.

The elder tells you the moral of the tale, which is that a village which weeps together will not starve. It is a plain little moral, and slightly wrong. The village starved the next year. But it did it, they say, remarkably well.

## 10.9  "Rain Follows Laughter"  (`rain`)

- **Starts when:** 10 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 329 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The second village is high and dry and unlucky. It has not rained there in four years. The wells are down to their last yard of mud. The people have the careful, polite, frayed look of a household that has stopped quarrelling because there is no water in it to quarrel with.

They say a man came through. They say he sat down in the dry square beside the dry fountain with his red gourd, and poured the wine out on the ground. All of it. A whole gourdful, glug by glug, on to the cracked clay. And he said, so they remember, in a loud cheerful voice: 'There. Now that's one of us that's drunk.'

**Closing scene**

The headwoman is a spare, brown, humorous person with a face like a pressed leaf. She leads you to the square and shows you the spot. It is a flat paving stone, a little darker than the rest. Moss grows in a perfect circle where the wine was poured, the only moss for forty miles.

**Headwoman:** It rained the next night. I want to be fair. It might have rained anyway. But it rained the way it rains in a story. It rained for three days, quietly, in a straight line, and not a drop of it fell on the stone. Everything else in the valley was drowned. We had to bail out the church. But the stone was dry.

**Headwoman:** And the old man was sitting on it with his coat over his head, laughing, and the water running off in a ring.

She tells you the moral, which is that the sky is fond of a joke. It is a poor moral. The next drought came in nine years and the stone made no difference at all. But on certain evenings, the headwoman says, the moss glows. You do not see it. Nettle, who has an unusual gift for seeing things that are not there, says that she does.

**Tobiah:** He paid me with it. Thirty years ago. A cup of tea and a bowl of noodles. I put it in the till. In the morning it was in my pocket. I put it in the till again. On the near side, as you left, a man was waiting for the ferry with a pack and a stick. He was in the queue behind you. He is not there now.

**Ferryman:** I said no. I never take a fare from a man who looks as tired as that. He sat down in the bow and said, 'Then I'll row.' And he took the oars out of my hands and rowed me across, and back, and across again, until the moon was up. He wouldn't stop. He said it was the only fair way. He rows on in silence. Nettle looks at you.

**Nettle:** That's the fourth thing. Isn't it? That's what it looks like.

**You:** What does?

**Tailor:** There was a rip in the sky once. Not a big one. A rip about so. It came from a very hard winter, you see, and the heavens had worn thin at the seam. It let the rain in. People looked up and said it's a pity, and went in, and nobody did anything about it.

**Tailor:** It took him three days. It was an ugly stitch. You can see it still, on a clear night, a sort of wobbly line of stars across the north, where it doesn't match. The villagers call it the Drunkard's Seam. They say if you look at it long enough you can feel the wine.

He tells you the moral, which is that a thing doesn't have to be done well to be done. It is a poor moral. The judge pauses. His dog sighs. A log falls in the grate.

The second is small and sharp and shuffles the cards of a game she is not playing.

**Second:** He drank it.
