# 13.S1  Season 1: The Dress Code

## 13.1  "Seven Hems"  (`hems`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** Go to the place `quarter`.  "Go to Seven Hems in the Lantern Quarter, {@quarter}."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, 1 Cultivation Pill
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "orla")`
- **Words:** 327 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The shop is called Seven Hems. It sits in the Lantern Quarter of Brass Ford, between a lamp-maker and a tea merchant who sells nothing but one very dull tea. The sign is a gold needle on green. The window holds a headless dummy in a good grey coat, which has stood there so long that the neighbours greet it.

Madam Orla Vane has run the shop for forty years. She wrote to you in the spring, on a card, with a pin stuck through the corner. It said: I am too old to bite the thread. Come and learn to do it properly. Bring your own scissors.

**Closing scene**

Madam Vane is sixty-eight and as upright as a ruler. She wears a black dress with a pincushion strapped to the wrist like a bracelet. Her hair is white and pinned in the shape of a small neat cabbage. She looks you up and down once, from the hat to the boots, as a surgeon looks at a patient she has already decided to save.

**Orla:** Stand there. Don't move. You've a shoulder an inch higher than the other, and you've been told not to slouch, and you do it anyway. Hold out your arm. Mm. You'll do.

**You:** I only came to see the shop.

**Orla:** The shop is the least of it. Look at this.

She turns up the hem of her skirt. It is neat and flat and very dull. Then she turns it up again, and again, and you see that it has not one hem but seven, folded inside each other, each a little narrower than the last, each stitched in a different thread. The seventh is a hair's breadth wide. It is stitched in silver.

**Orla:** Six you can see. The seventh holds a promise. Every garment I have ever made has had one. Nobody knows. That's the point of a promise, dear. It does its work whether or not you remember it.

## 13.2  "A Sleeve for Every Sect"  (`sleeve`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Make 8 items **since this chapter began**.  "Learn the codes: cut and sew eight garments."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `TaleTailor::mark`
- **Words:** 243 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Brass Ford has nine sects, and every one of them has a code of dress. The Cobalt Order wears blue only, and never below the knee. The Vermilion Hall wears red, in a cut that was fashionable at the time of the flood. The Grey Brotherhood wears anything, so long as it is grey, and they take this very seriously. The shop makes their sleeves.

**Orla:** You'll learn the codes by heart. You'll learn them before you learn the stitches. A sleeve that offends a sect is a sleeve that gets burned, and a tailor who has had two sleeves burned is a tailor who is not asked back.

**Closing scene**

By the eighth garment you have made three mistakes. A Cobalt robe, three inches too long. A Vermilion cuff, with a yellow thread by accident. A Grey tunic that, when held to the light, turns out to be fractionally green. Orla finds all three in a single glance and says nothing. She picks up the green tunic, and unpicks it, and hands you the thread.

**Orla:** Again. Slowly. A stitch is a small decision. Don't make it twice.

You make the Grey tunic again. It is correct. It is grey as a pigeon's back. When you hold it up, Orla runs her thumb along the cuff and stops at the seam, and for a moment her mouth twitches at one corner. It is the most extravagant praise you have had in your life.

## 13.3  "The Seventh Hem"  (`seventh`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** a technique insight
- **Words:** 150 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It is a Tuesday, and you have been sewing for nine hours, when Orla puts down her scissors and says that she thinks you are ready for the seventh. She says it as one might say that the tide is turning. She takes a bolt of undyed linen off the shelf, cuts a length, and lays it on the long table between you.

**Closing scene**

**Orla:** The seventh hem is yours to fill. It can be a word, a wish, a name. It must be true when you stitch it. It has to be small enough that nobody feels it and honest enough that the garment can carry it. I have stitched four thousand and eleven. I have never told anyone what any of them said.

**You:** What happens when it comes true?

**Orla:** The garment is worn out. Not before. That's why one must be so careful what one asks of a coat.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `promise`; default: option 1)

> The seventh hem of your first real garment is empty, and the silver thread is in your hand.

1. Stitch a kindness: may the wearer be forgiven something.
   - You stitch a kindness. It takes an hour, and three false starts. When it is done it looks like nothing: a line of silver no wider than a hair. You press it flat with the iron. Orla holds the coat up to the lamp, and runs a thumbnail down the inside of the hem, and says, 'Ah,' very softly, as a person says it who has had a thing confirmed.
   - **Orla:** Good. It will be forgiven. I hope it is something small.
2. Stitch a warning: may the wearer be told in time.
   - You stitch a warning. It takes forty minutes. You are quite sure it is crooked. Orla holds it up, and looks at it for minutes, and says that it is rather a stern little hem, but that the world needs a few. She hangs it on the rail in the window. It sells within the week to a sergeant of the City Guard.
   - **Orla:** He has a long face. He'll need it.
3. Leave the seventh hem plain. Some promises should not be made on another's behalf.
   - You turn up the seventh hem, and press it, and leave it plain. Orla looks at it. She looks at you. She says nothing at all for a minute, and then she says that, in forty years, she has seen perhaps six apprentices do this, and that four of them became very good tailors.
   - **Orla:** And the other two went into politics. I wouldn't worry.

## 13.4  "Thimble"  (`thimble`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Have 2 friends.  "Take on an apprentice and make a second friend."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "thimble")`
- **Words:** 227 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The girl on the doorstep is twenty and wears a coat made of four other coats. She has a basket, a tin whistle and a placard saying, in careful capitals, HAND TO HOLD. She has no hands to hold of her own, she explains, since the last tailor she worked for threw her out for singing. She would like to be taken on. She would like it explained that she does not need paying. She needs a bed, and a dictionary.

**Closing scene**

Her name is Thimble, which she says is a nickname, and which she will not explain. She learns the pins in a morning and the pressing in an afternoon. By the end of the week she has reorganised the button drawer by mood. Orla finds the new arrangement baffling and quite right.

**Thimble:** I don't talk much, you know. People think I do. It's only that I'm in a good mood. Do you want me to hem that?

**You:** It's a curtain.

**Thimble:** I like curtains. They're hems with a view.

She sings, too. You had been warned. She sings when she presses, and when she sorts thread, and in her sleep, and she is flat on every note. It is one of the most cheerful sounds you have ever heard. Next door, the lamp-maker has stopped complaining. He says it makes the lamps burn higher.

## 13.5  "The Shop Across the Lane"  (`kestra`)

- **Starts when:** 32 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet kestra (walk to their tile).  "Call on Kestra Dray, across the lane."
- **Pays:** nothing

**Opening scene**

The shop that opens across the lane at Michaelmas is called Dray & Co. It has plate glass, brass fittings, a doorbell like a cathedral and a window of dummies in the latest cut. They are all faceless. They are all in the colours of the nine sects, tastefully blended into a fashion nobody has asked for. By ten in the morning there is a queue.

**Orla:** That's a young person with money and ideas. I do hope they are going to be tiresome.

**Closing scene**

{kestra.He} receives you at the door with a tape measure round {kestra.his} neck and a pin in {kestra.his} mouth. {kestra.He} is about twenty-nine, narrow and bright and impatient, with ink on {kestra.his} cuff and a way of standing that makes the room look slightly out of date. {kestra.He} takes the pin out and says that you must be the old shop.

**Kestra:** Don't take it personally. I've nothing against tradition. I only think it ought to be cut on the bias. Do come in. Do you want to see my patterns? I've a way of sewing three codes into one garment that no one's thought of.

**You:** That sounds like a loophole.

**Kestra:** It's not a loophole. It's an interpretation. I've a licence from the Guild.

{kestra.He} shows you a sleeve. It is blue on the outside, red inside, and grey in the lining, and it can be turned in the hand to present any of the three. It is the cleverest garment you have ever seen. It is also, you realise, exactly the sort of thing that gets a tailor burned. You tell {kestra.him} so. {kestra.He} laughs, and says that is what they said about the buttonhole.

## 13.6  "The Gala Robe"  (`gala`)

- **Starts when:** 32 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Make 6 items **since this chapter began**.  "Cut the gala robe: sew six pieces of it."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill
- **When it opens, the code:** `TaleTailor::mark`
- **Words:** 246 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The letter comes from the Guild of Hems in a cream envelope with a gold seal. Dame Thrale, President of the Guild, requests the honour of a robe for the Convocation Gala at the Palace of the Oldest Order. It is to be worn by the Master of Ceremonies. It is to honour all nine sects. It is to be ready in six weeks. The letter ends with a postscript: Do not attempt anything original.

**Closing scene**

The robe takes six weeks and eleven yards of silk. It has nine panels, one for each sect, and each panel is perfect. You sew them together in the long room at the back of the shop with Orla standing over you and Thimble holding the lamp. By the third week you can hear your own pulse in the needle.

Dame Thrale arrives on the day with two clerks and a trunk. She is seventy and as dry as paper, with a voice like a drawer being slid shut. She walks round the robe twice, without a word. She lifts a cuff. She turns up the hem. She runs a thumbnail along the inside of the seventh, which is bare, and stops.

**Thrale:** You have left it plain.

**You:** I thought it was for the wearer to fill.

**Thrale:** Interesting. It is also against the Guild's rules. A seventh hem must be stitched, or it is not a hem. I shall let it pass. I shall mention it to the committee.

## 13.7  "The Stain"  (`stain`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 12 weeks (0 years and 12 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 292 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

A man comes into the shop every Thursday with a white linen shirt and a tragic expression. He lays it on the counter. It has a stain on the cuff, a wine stain, a deep plum purple. He asks if you can get it out. You can. You do. He pays, thanks you, and goes. The following Thursday he returns with the same shirt, and the same stain, and the same expression.

**Closing scene**

This goes on for five weeks. Thimble starts to keep a tally on the back of the door. Orla says nothing, with a gleam. On the sixth Thursday you take the shirt, and look at the stain, and say, 'I can get this out, but I'd like to know how it keeps getting back in.'

He stands there for a moment. He has a long grey face, like a patient horse. He says that his wife died in the spring. He says she was a clumsy woman and spilled wine on his cuff at their last dinner. He says he cannot get himself to wash it. He says he comes here to have it cleaned, and then he goes home and puts it back.

**You:** Would you like it to stay?

**Man:** I would like it to be cleaned, and I would like it to be there. I know it makes no sense.

You take the shirt. You sew a small purple flower into the cuff, in silk, exactly where the stain was, and press it flat. It looks like nothing. It looks like the cuff of a shirt. He holds it up to the window for ages. He says thank you in a voice that is much younger. He never comes back, and he never needs to.

## 13.8  "Three Codes, One Coat"  (`code`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 212 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Three sects send commissions on the same morning for the same occasion. The Cobalt Order requires a coat in blue, to the knee, with no ornament. The Vermilion Hall requires red, with a high collar and a gilt button. The Grey Brotherhood requires grey, in any style, but with a mourning band. They are to be worn at the same funeral. They are to be worn by the same man. He has been adopted by all three.

**Closing scene**

You spend a night with the three letters spread on the table, and a pot of tea, and Thimble asleep in the corner with a pin in her mouth. In the morning Orla comes down at six and reads them in her dressing gown, with her glasses on the end of her nose. She says that she has seen this before. She says in 1873 she dressed the Duke of Marsh for his own wedding and his own divorce on the same afternoon.

**Orla:** It can be done. It can be done honestly, if you've a great deal of patience. It can be done cleverly. It can be done in a way that will make three tailors across the city furious. You'll have to decide how to make a man look like three things.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `loophole`; default: option 1)

> Three sects want one man in three colours.

1. Make it honestly: three coats, one over the other, so that he wears all three.
   - You make three coats. The blue goes over the red, which goes over the grey, each a little shorter than the last, so that he wears them in order, like layers of a pastry. He looks ridiculous. He looks, also, absolutely sincere. The funeral is a great success. The Cobalt Order says it was tasteful. The Vermilion Hall says it was bold. The Brotherhood says it was grey.
   - **Orla:** It is the only time I have seen three sects agree, and it was because they couldn't see each other's faces.
2. Make it cleverly: Kestra's turning sleeve, in your own cloth.
   - You go across the lane and ask Kestra for the sleeve. {kestra.He} is so pleased that {kestra.he} drops a pincushion. Together you make a coat that turns, blue to red to grey, and fits three codes. It is the cleverest thing either of you has ever made. It is also, as Orla says afterwards, the beginning of a long and complicated friendship.
   - **Kestra:** I think we ought to work together more often. I think we are annoying each other in a good way.
3. Refuse the commission and tell the three sects to come to an agreement themselves.
   - You send a polite note to each sect, saying that the Shop would be honoured to dress the man in whatever they agree upon. You do not hear for a fortnight. Then three clerks arrive at the same time, glaring at each other, with a joint document of seven pages. They have agreed on grey, with a blue lining and a red button. It is, you think, the first time in the history of the city.
   - **Thimble:** Did you do that on purpose?

## 13.9  "The Fitting"  (`fitting`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** nothing
- **Words:** 254 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Kestra comes across the lane on a Sunday evening with a bundle under {kestra.his} arm and an air of elaborate unconcern. {kestra.He} says that {kestra.he} has a problem with a sleeve. {kestra.He} says that it has been bothering {kestra.him} for a week, and that Orla has always said you are good with sleeves. {kestra.He} puts the bundle on the counter and unwraps it. It is a coat for {kestra.his} own back. It is the best thing {kestra.he} has ever made. It has one very small error in the left shoulder.

**Closing scene**

You pin it on {kestra.him}. It is a long business. You walk round {kestra.him} three times, with pins in your teeth and chalk in your hand, saying 'Turn' and 'Arm up' and 'Don't breathe, please'. {kestra.He} stands very still, as people do, with the faintly stunned look of a person being fitted by someone they dislike a little less than they expected.

**Kestra:** I should say that I am not good at this. Being measured. I am all right at measuring. I have never been quite certain how to stand.

**You:** Like that. You're fine.

**Kestra:** Mmm.

There is a short silence. The pins are very small. Thimble, from the corner, with a needle in her mouth, makes a noise that might be a cough. Orla, who is supposedly asleep in the armchair, opens one eye, and closes it again. You mend the shoulder. It is done in five minutes. Kestra says, 'I'm not in any hurry,' and does not leave until nearly eleven.

The Guild of Hems holds its Mastership examination on the first Friday of May, in a long bare hall with seven tables, seven chairs, seven candles and seven examiners in grey. It is said to take three days, three nights, and three kinds of patience. Orla drives you there herself in the shop cart, and sits in the front row with her knitting, and does not say a single word.

**Closing scene**

The first day is the cutting. You are given a length of striped silk and told to make a coat without a pattern. The second is the sewing. You are given a needle with no eye and told to thread it. The third is the fitting. You are given a stranger from the street, an old man with a hump and a dislike of tailors, and told to make him comfortable.

You do not pass at once. The examiners confer. They confer for an hour, in a corner of the hall, in murmurs. At the end of it the eldest comes over and says that the coat was correct, the sewing was correct, and the fitting was admirable. He says the seventh hem of the coat was blank. He says that is irregular. He says they have decided to overlook it, in view of the fact that the old man has asked to keep the coat.

**Examiner:** He says it is the first thing in forty years that did not itch.

The gala is held in the great hall of the Palace of the Oldest Order. There are nine hundred guests, in nine hundred colours. It goes wrong at the third toast. It goes wrong in a small way: a button. The robe, from the left cuff to the right, begins gently to smoke.

Thimble is on the dais before you have understood. She has a bucket. She has a damp towel. She has, for no reason, a tin whistle. She tears off the Cobalt panel with a single pull, and stamps on it, and the whole hall watches a girl of twenty in a coat of four coats put out the Master of Ceremonies. There is a silence.

Then Kestra, from the back, calls out, 'Hems to the rescue!' and starts to clap. The hall laughs. The Master, who is unburned, looks down at his robe: eight panels, and a hole where the ninth was, and a broad stripe of white lining showing through. He begins, slowly, to smile. He says it is the best robe he has ever worn.

**Thrale:** (at your elbow, in a very dry voice) I shall be mentioning this to the committee. I shall be doing it in the warmest terms.

**Opening scene**

The courier is a lanky youth of nineteen called Dunstan, who carries letters for the Guild of Hems. On a Monday morning he sets out with a satchel and a new brown overcoat, a gift from an uncle, and instead of turning left to the Guild he turns right. He walks through the Lantern Quarter at a steady pace. He walks down Mill Street. He walks into the weir, in his overcoat, with his satchel on, and the current takes him.

He is found two days later. The coat is intact. The satchel is intact. A boatman, who has seen a good many drowned men and is not easily shaken, says the lad was smiling. Inside the collar of the overcoat is a neat green label. It has a gold needle on it. It says: SEVEN HEMS.

**Closing scene**

You go to the weir yourself. A rope has been stretched across the bank and a constable stands at it, stamping, with his hands in his sleeves. Inside the rope, on a trestle, the overcoat is spread to dry. You are let through because the constable says the Sergeant expects you.

You turn the collar back. The label is green, with a gold needle. The lettering is perfect. The stitches in the border run clockwise, four to the inch, with a very slight lean to the right. It is your hand. You stand there with the collar in your fingers and a sort of cold taking hold of your wrists.

**Constable:** Is it yours, then?

**You:** I didn't make this coat.

**Constable:** That's what I told the Sergeant you'd say.

You put the glass down. Thimble has stopped humming. She is sitting very straight on her stool with her hands in her lap and her face quite white. She says, in a voice you have never heard from her, 'That's a stitch.' She says, 'That's a stitch I've seen.'

**You:** Where?

**Thimble:** I don't remember. I only know it. It's like a tune. I've seen it done by hand, once, a long time ago, and I couldn't sleep afterwards.

## 13.25  "Brass Ford Closes Its Gates"  (`gates`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended

**Opening scene**

The Ninth Banner comes over the hills on a bright cold morning in March, ten thousand strong, under a flag of a black wheel on a white field. Its commander is Warlord Grist, who was once a quartermaster and is now a good deal more. He has a reputation for paying his soldiers on time. It is, the Guild says, the most frightening thing about him.

The city council meets in the Guildhall for four hours and decides to shut the gates. They are shut at dusk with a sound like a great sigh. The next morning, from the top of the Lantern Quarter, you can see the camp: ten thousand small fires, in rows, as neat as a ledger.

**Closing scene**

The shop is full of people by noon. Soldiers of the City Guard, with torn sleeves. Merchants who want banners. Women who want warm things for their sons on the wall. A lamp-maker who has brought a tray of tea, since he cannot think what else to do. Thimble has arranged the customers in a queue by the colour of their anxiety, and is moving among them with a tape measure and a calming word.

**Kestra:** Right. I've closed the shop across the road and put the dummies in the cellar. I've sixty yards of grey wool, forty of red flannel and a roll of oilcloth. Where do you want me?

**You:** Cutting table.

**Kestra:** Brilliant. I've always wanted to be useful in a catastrophe.

It is the first time since the courier that the two shops have worked as one. It is a strange, quick, frightening pleasure. The lamps burn late. At midnight Orla's old dog, who has come in the post-cart from the country with a note round its neck, lies down on the cutting-room floor and goes to sleep.

He says the men are cold, and the wind off the camp is bitter, and half of them have no cloaks. He says the Master of the Hall has authorised the purchase of two hundred, and he would like to know whether the shop can supply them by Friday.

**Closing scene**

You set the cutting table in the street. You set the pressing table beside it. You borrow the lamp-maker's cart, and the net-mender's boys. The whole of the neighbourhood's sewing circle, sixty old women in black who have been stitching shrouds for forty years and are delighted at last to make something warm. They sit in rows in the lane. They sing. They sing flat.

On the third night, in the light of a hundred lanterns, you realise what you are doing. You are not stitching a cloak. You are stitching a cloak with something in the lining: a small array, a pattern of silver thread no larger than a thumbnail, sewn into the shoulder where the wearer will not feel it. It is a thing you have never been taught. Your hands have simply known how.

**Thimble:** That's a seventh hem.

**You:** It's a lining.

**Thimble:** It's a hem that's moved.

The first cloaks go up to the wall at dawn on Friday. The soldiers put them on. A big sergeant with a squint says, to nobody, that it's the warmest thing he has ever had on his back. Then he says, a minute later, in a voice of surprise, 'I'm not afraid.' He looks at his hands. He says: 'I'm not afraid at all.'

The assault comes on the ninth night. It is a grey bitter night with a thin cold rain, and the camp is alive with torches. Warlord Grist's men come up the slope in long files with ladders and hooks and a great rolling tower of oak. The City Guard stands to. You are on the wall at the north gate with a basket of thread and a lantern, because someone has to mend the cloaks, and because Kestra has refused to leave your side.

It lasts until dawn. You stitch, and run, and stitch. A cloak torn at the shoulder, a sleeve slashed, a hood on fire. Kestra is beside you with a needle between her teeth, and a pair of shears, and a face as bright as a coin, hemming soldiers where they stand. At two in the morning a ladder strikes the wall six feet away and a man in a black wheel surcoat swings a leg over the parapet and sees the two of you, kneeling in the rain, repairing a boot.

He stops. He looks very puzzled. Kestra looks up with a mouthful of pins and says, quite calmly, 'Do you mind? We're in the middle of something.' The man opens his mouth. Then a sergeant of the Guard cuts him down with a billhook, and the moment is gone, and you are both laughing in a hysterical, helpless way, and you have to stop to thread the needle again.

The needle wants thread, and the Palace's blue light is not enough. Mending a sky requires seven kinds, one for each hem, and each must be made by hand. You take the bowl of blue light to the long table in the Wardrobe and spend a week making the other six. Dawn thread, spun from the first light of a winter morning. Salt thread, drawn from the sea. Iron thread, twisted from the filings of a forge. Rain, glass, hunger, and the seventh, which you make last.

**Closing scene**

The seventh thread is the hardest. It is not spun from anything you can name. You work at it for three nights, and on the third you give up, and put down your tools, and look at your hands. They are shaking. They are very tired. You have made, in your life, four thousand and some coats, and in every one you have put something into the seventh hem, and you have never once asked yourself what it was.

You take the silver thread that Orla sent you, the very small last scrap of it. You wind it round the card. You look at it. You put it, finally, in the bowl. It spreads, and glows, and settles, and in a moment the seventh thread is a pale clear silver, as bright as a tear. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever made, and you did not make it.

**Thimble:** That's the promise, isn't it? That's what's in the hem. It's every promise you've ever kept.

The Thin Sky is a mountain peak in the far country under a cracked blue dome. The air is clear and cold and tastes of iron. The crack is a long thin line across the heavens, from one horizon to another, and through it comes a dim far light, and a wind that smells of nothing you can name. Kestra and Thimble climb the last of the ledge behind you. Mister Snip walks beside them with his hands behind his back.

**Closing scene**

You thread the needle at the summit with all seven threads, one after the other, in order. It takes an hour. You stand on the very top of the world with the silver needle lifted above your head. It is nine feet long and weightless. You reach up. You put it into the sky.

It goes in like a pin into silk. The crack parts, and closes, and parts again. The wind drops. The thread hums, a huge slow note, like a bell heard from underwater. You draw it through. You turn the needle. You sew the sky, stitch after stitch, with long strokes of your arm, and wherever the thread goes, the dome is whole.

The seventh thread is last. It is the brightest of all. It hangs in the air before you, pulsing, and you see, quite clearly, that there is one filament in it that is slightly different from the rest. It is thin as a hair. It is yours. Snip is standing at your elbow, with the silver scissors in his hand, and an expression of kindly inquiry.

A man in an apron watches you work, from a stool, and learns to thread a needle.
   - **???:** I find that I like it. I did not know it could be so quiet.

**Closing scene**

You sit that evening at the long table, in the lamp's yellow circle, with the dog on your feet and a coat across your knees. You turn up the hem. You turn up the seventh, a hair's breadth wide, and take a length of silver thread, and think, for a long moment, of what to put in it. You know it will be true. You know it will come true, in its own time, and the coat will be worn out. Then you begin.

## 13.I3  Interlude: The Long Quiet  (between season 3 and season 4)

**Interlude**

The shop has a queue on Mondays and a dummy in each window. The silver thread on the shelf has not been touched. You have made four thousand and some coats, and you have not once been bored.

A letter comes from the country, in an upright hand. It is not Orla's. It is from the dog's new owner. It says Madam Vane has gone to see about a hem.

# 13.S4  Season 4: The Door

## 13.37  "The Last Hem"  (`dr1`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 195 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Orla's cottage is neat and plain and smells of lavender. The dog's new owner, a stout vicar's wife, lets you in with a wave and goes back to her baking. On the table by the window, folded, is a coat. It is grey, of a good plain cloth. It has never been worn. There is a label in the collar, in the old border: SEVEN HEMS. Under it, in silver: for the one who asks.

**Closing scene**

You turn up the hem. You turn up the seventh, a hair's breadth wide. It is stitched in the thread you hoarded, the last of the silver. It is the only seventh hem you have ever seen that is not a promise. It is a question. It says, in letters so small that you have to hold it to the window: Is it finished? Please say when.

You put on the coat. It fits as if it were poured. You stand a moment in the cottage kitchen in the afternoon light with the cloth warm against your back. Outside, in the garden, the vicar's wife is hanging out sheets, singing, flat. You find you cannot stop smiling.

## 13.38  "A Coat for the Line"  (`dr2`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `garrison`.  "Take the cloaks to the Garrison of the Crossed, {@garrison}."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 240 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The line at the Garrison has no cloaks. You have read it in a pamphlet. A hundred and eleven men and women stand in a long wet file in the thin clothes they came in, and the rain, off the plain, is cold. Thimble finds you at the shop with a handcart. She has her own apprentice now, and a coat made of eleven others. She says: 'We should take them something.'

**Closing scene**

You have made them in a week, all night, with the whole of the Quarter at the table. Four hundred cloaks, plain grey, with a ring of silver thread in each shoulder. You hand them down the line. The soldiers take them one by one and put them on. Some say thank you. Some laugh. A boy of sixteen says it is the warmest thing he has ever had on his back, and then, in a lower voice, 'I'm not afraid.'

**Dray:** (who has come with the cart and a face like a candle) I stitched the hems. Seven each. I put in a thing. I won't tell you what.

They go in at the gate in the grey cloaks, in rows. The last is a woman with a plait who carries a ledger. She stops at the gate and turns up the hem of her cloak. She looks at the seventh. She looks at you. She says: 'It's a question.' She says: 'I'll answer it.'

## 13.39  "Is It Finished?"  (`dr3`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `palace`.  "Go to the Palace of the Oldest Order, at Originis, to the Empty Seat."
- **Pays:** 1,000 spirit stones, +2 potential, 2 Potential Pills, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 117 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You wear the coat to the Empty Seat. The Palace's robed Wicks look at it as you cross the great hall, and look away, and look again. Some of them touch their own cuffs. You stop in front of the Seat, in the lamp-light, with your hands in your pockets. You turn up the hem of the coat. It says: Please say when.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `latch`; default: option 1)

> The coat has asked you a question. The Door is under the Seat.

1. Stay: say not yet, and go back to the shop.
   - You say not yet. You say it aloud, to the coat, in the empty hall. The silver thread in the seventh hem brightens a very little and then goes dim, like a lamp turned low. You go home. The shop is open. The queue on Monday is round the corner.
   - **Dray:** You've come back. I thought you might. I've put the kettle on.
2. Go: say now, and walk through in the coat.
   - You say now. It is a plain word. It comes out very easily. You turn up the hem and run your thumb along the seventh and feel it loosen, a thread of silver coming away from the cloth, and drifting down into the dark under the Seat. The coat is only a coat. You walk to the stair.
3. Hold the latch: say when to the next, and the next, and stitch each of them a hem.
   - You sit by the Seat for a season with a needle and a spool. Each person who comes, you take their sleeve, and turn it, and put in a hem. Seven. The seventh is a question. It is the same for all of them. They put it away, and go down. It is the most useful work you have ever done and it takes four seconds.

**Closing scene**

Thimble, who is forty now, runs the shop on Mondays. She has the dummy in the window. She has put a new coat on it, in the Quarter's grey. The seventh hem of the coat, on the inside, in silver, in her own flat unmusical hand, says one word. It says: Yes.

## 13.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

Seven Hems has a gold needle on a green sign, and a grey dummy in the window, and a dog on the doorstep that nobody remembers acquiring.

*[only if hem is 1]* The queue on Monday goes round the corner. The coats are lucky. Nobody knows why, and everybody has stopped asking.

*[only if hem is 2]* The school in the lamp-maker's yard turns out two hundred tailors a year. Each one learns the stitch for the seventh hem, and the rule that goes with it.

*[only if hem is 3]* In the cedar room under the Palace a lamp burns late. A man in a plain apron has learned to thread a needle with one hand.

*[only if stitch is 1]* The sky above Brass Ford is whole. Children say it is the best-kept sky in the country. They do not know why they say it.

*[only if stitch is 2]* One thread in the seventh hem is loose. You can feel it sometimes, on the highest ground, on a still evening, like a hair across the face. You do not mind. It is gentle work.

*[only if stitch is 3]* Somewhere above the highest mountain there is a small neat buttonhole in the sky. It opens only from the inside. Once a year, in the spring, a single feather comes through it, from nowhere, and lands on the sill of the shop.

*[only if siege is 1]* A short square man visits in the autumn with a ledger. He is still a very careful tailor's client. He pays on time.

*[only if siege is 2]* The north wall of Brass Ford has a row of hooks along it, on which hang a hundred and twenty cloaks, in oilcloth, each with a small ring of silver in the hem. Nobody wears them. Nobody takes them down.

*[only if siege is 3]* The black wheel flag still hangs in the Guildhall, reversed, in a glass case. A small card beneath it says: Not authorised.

*[only if love is 1]* Kestra keeps the books of the shop across the lane, and sleeps on the right-hand side.

*[only if love is 2]* Kestra has a key to both doors.

*[only if love is 3]* Kestra and you share a cutting table, a kettle and a joke which nobody else has been told. It has taken a great deal of thread.

*[only if latch is 1]* The shop is as it was. The queue goes round the corner on Mondays. The coat hangs on a peg in the back, and the seventh hem has never been looked at since.

*[only if latch is 2]* A grey coat hangs on the peg by the door of the shop. The seventh hem is gone. The coat is warmer than it has any right to be.

*[only if latch is 3]* There is a stool by the Empty Seat with a needle on it. People who go down the stair stop to have a hem put in. The Wicks call it the Last Fitting.

The last coat you made this year had a plain grey outside and a plain grey lining. In the seventh hem, in silver, in very small letters, you stitched: Come back. It is the only promise you have ever made that was not meant for the wearer.

## 13.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

You stay in the Garden. The Palace's Wardrobe has a new tenant in the cedar room under the stair, and every robe that comes out of it has a seventh hem.

The Master of the Palace wears a plain apron with one stitch in it that is not plain. He will not say what it promises.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

The army of the Outside marches in uniforms you did not make, and on the night before a battle you sew a hem into the nearest coat. You do not say what it promises. It always comes true a little.

The soldiers call the coats lucky. You let them.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You step through the Seam with a pincushion on your wrist. On the far side there is a street with a lamp-maker, a tea merchant who sells only one dull tea, and an empty shop with a window.

You hang the grey dummy in it. You say: Seven Hems.

**You are struck down by the array**

The array took you. In the dark a hand turns up a hem, and then the next, and the next.

The seventh is silver, a hair's breadth wide, and it says your name.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden goes out. The shop, the lane and the long table go out, and the sign with the gold needle.

The last thing to go is a dog asleep on a doorstep, with a coat across its back.

# 14.S1  Season 1: Nothing Works as Meant

## 14.1  "Gearwheel Lane"  (`lane`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** Go to the place `lane`.  "Go to the workshop in Gearwheel Lane, {@lane}."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, 1 Cultivation Pill
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "orlop")`
- **Words:** 276 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Uncle Barnaby Crank left you a workshop, a debt, and a note that said: Sorry about the smell. The workshop is at the bottom of Gearwheel Lane in the city of Tallowmere, next door to a bakery. It has a crooked chimney and a door that opens outward, because the first time it opened inward it took the porch with it.

Everyone in the lane calls the workshop the Crank, and everyone in the lane calls you the new crank. They say it with affection. They say it from a safe distance, with their hands over their ears.

**Closing scene**

The workshop smells of hot oil, singed hair and mild disappointment. There are forty-one half-finished machines on the benches. A brass kettle on legs is walking slowly in circles round the stove. A wind-up umbrella has got itself stuck in the rafters and is opening and closing in a hopeless fashion.

**Orlop:** Oh, you've come. You're the image of him. He was a lovely man. He set fire to my oven three times.

Mrs. Orlop is sixty, floury to the elbow, with a bun of grey hair that has a pencil stuck through it and an air of having forgiven everybody in advance. She puts a hot loaf in your hands and tells you the rule of the lane. You may build what you like. You may blow up what you like. But not before seven in the morning or after ten at night, and never on Sundays.

**Orlop:** And if it's going to be loud, put a sign on the door. Your uncle put a sign. It said BRACE. I thought that was very considerate.

## 14.2  "The Self-Kneading Dough Machine"  (`dough`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Make 8 items **since this chapter began**.  "Build the kneader: make eight contraptions."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `TaleInventor::mark`
- **Words:** 249 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Mrs. Orlop wants a machine to knead dough. She asks politely, with a plate of buns. She says her wrists are not what they were. She says she would be most obliged if it did not talk, explode, or escape, as the last one did, in 1869, and was found three streets away working as a pastry chef.

**Closing scene**

You build eight machines before you build the right one. The first kneads too hard. The second kneads too soft. The third refuses to knead at all, and sits on the bench, humming, in a sulk. The fourth, a pretty thing with brass paddles and a small array in the base, kneads a perfect dough, and then, with a sigh, keeps kneading.

By the end of the afternoon the dough is three feet high. It has filled the bakery. It has crept up the stairs. It is gently and patiently kneading itself against the ceiling, and a baker's boy is hanging from a beam, shouting for his mother. Mrs. Orlop surveys it with her hands on her hips.

**Orlop:** It's a very good dough. I've never seen one so well worked. Is there an off switch?

**You:** There was.

**Orlop:** Well. I suppose we'll have to make a great many loaves.

The whole lane eats bread for a week. A famous baker from the next district comes to look at the machine, and goes away shaking his head, and orders two. Nobody has ever been so pleased with a catastrophe.

## 14.3  "Biscuit"  (`duck`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended

It starts as a spare-parts project, on a wet Thursday, to take your mind off the dough. You have a drawer of gears, a biscuit tin, a pair of tin cymbals and a small array that boils water. You put them together without a plan. At eleven at night there is a duck on the bench. It is brass, the size of a loaf, and it has one blue glass eye and one brown.

**Closing scene**

It does not move. You wind it. You tap it. You say, 'Hello,' in a foolish voice. Then, very slowly, as if remembering something it had once been told, it turns its head and looks at you with both its eyes. It makes a small clicking noise, rather like a throat being cleared, and waddles across the bench and settles on the open page of your uncle's notebook.

**Fitch:** Is it alive?

**You:** It's a duck.

**Fitch:** It's looking at the notebook.

It is. It is pecking, softly, at a drawing on the page, a plan for a thing called a Lifting Engine, with the word MAYBE written beside it three times in your uncle's hand. You put the duck on your shoulder. It sits there, peering about, as though it had always lived in this room.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `duck`; default: option 1)

> You have built a duck, and it has opinions. You can still change what it is.

1. Give it a voice: a small brass reed in the throat.
   - You fit a brass reed in its throat. It takes the whole night. In the morning the duck opens its beak. It says, in a clear small voice like a spoon in a cup, 'Good morning'. It says it eleven times, with minor variations, and spends the rest of the day saying 'Interesting' to the furniture.
   - **Fitch:** I think it's the best thing you've ever made. I think it might also be the worst.
2. Leave it silent. Some things are better with a mind of their own.
   - You leave it silent. It takes to the workshop at once, and follows you from bench to bench, and sits on whichever machine is about to go wrong. It has never been wrong yet. Mrs. Orlop says it has the manner of a retired judge.
   - **Orlop:** It's a kind of companionship. You don't have to say anything.
3. Sell it to the toymaker down the lane for a very good price.
   - You sell it. The toymaker pays twenty silver and takes it away in a box. By the following morning it is back on your bench with a note pinned to its wing: Returned. Does not like the shop. Refund enclosed. The duck settles on your shoulder as if nothing had happened. It is the nicest thing anyone has ever done to you by not leaving.
   - **Fitch:** It's a good duck.

## 14.4  "The Petition"  (`noise`)

**Opening scene**

The petition arrives on a Saturday, delivered by a very small boy in a very large hat. It has forty-three signatures. It complains of noise, smoke, sparks, the smell of burnt hair, a continual ticking at night, and a duck. It asks the Crank to desist. It asks very nicely. At the bottom someone has written in a different ink: P.S. Please do not desist. It is the only exciting thing here.

**Closing scene**

You do not desist. Instead you go from door to door with a box of small gifts you have built for the purpose. There is a self-trimming candle, a boot that cleans itself, and a toasting fork that tells you when the bread is done. They do not all work. Some of them work in unexpected ways. A tiny spinning top given to the widow at number nine plays a lullaby so beautiful that her cat is found weeping in the larder.

By the evening forty petitioners have been to the workshop. They stand about in a ring, with their hands in their pockets, drinking tea out of whatever cups come to hand. The very small boy in the very large hat tells the duck his name. The duck says nothing. It bows.

**Orlop:** There. That's the lane. It's not much, but it's ours, and we'll put up with a great deal.

The Clerk of Patents calls on a damp Tuesday in an umbrella and a long grey coat. The umbrella is of the old pattern, black, with a hooked handle. The coat is buttoned to the chin. The clerk has a briefcase, a notebook, a pair of round spectacles, and the sort of narrow, tidy face that has never in its life been late for an appointment.

**Closing scene**

**Mott:** Lysandra Mott, Clerk, Second Grade, the Conservatory of Right Arrays. I should like to say at once that this is a courtesy visit. The Conservatory has had a number of reports about your premises, and I am obliged to inspect. It is a formality. I do not expect to find anything.

{mott.He} finds the duck. It is sitting on {mott.his} briefcase. {mott.He} looks at it. It looks at {mott.him}. {mott.He} writes something in the notebook, and crosses it out, and writes something else. {mott.He} asks, in a slightly strangled voice, whether it is registered.

**You:** It's a duck.

**Mott:** That's a category. Is it an Automaton or an Array-Assisted Domestic Animal? I'm afraid the forms are different.

{mott.He} stays two hours. {mott.He} inspects forty-one machines, writes eleven citations, and is shown the kettle that walks in circles. {mott.He} laughs at it, unwillingly, one short surprised bark, and then looks appalled at having done so. At the door, {mott.he} turns, and says that {mott.he} has seldom seen so many violations in one room, and that {mott.he} does not expect to find that they are as bad as {mott.he} had been led to fear.

## 14.6  "The Conservatory of Right Arrays"  (`conserv`)

**Opening scene**

The Conservatory occupies a grey marble building in the middle of Tallowmere, with a portico, nine columns and a clock that is never wrong. It is the guardian of the Right Way of Making: the only licensed method of building arrays, taught in a seven-year course, in a set of forty-one volumes, by a faculty of grey men. It regards inventors as it regards weeds.

**Closing scene**

Master Dimmock is sixty, tall, beautifully dressed, with a voice like a church organ and a profile on a medal. He receives you in a long panelled room with a table the length of a boat and a portrait of himself, on the wall behind him, looking slightly younger and slightly more pleased. He invites you to sit. He does not offer tea.

**Dimmock:** I understand that you build. I understand that you build without a licence, a diploma or a mentor. I understand that you have a pet duck. I want to say that I do not regard this as a crime. I regard it as a condition. It is a thing that happens to certain young people. It passes.

**You:** Does it?

**Dimmock:** Almost always. The Conservatory has a very good rehabilitation programme. Seven years. Forty-one volumes. You would be amazed what a young person can learn when there is no choice.

You thank him. You decline. He smiles, with every one of his teeth, and rings a small silver bell. A clerk appears with a cup of tea. The cup has a crack in it. You are not sure whether it is an accident.

## 14.7  "The Array in the Teapot"  (`teapot`)

**Opening scene**

The idea comes at three in the morning, as ideas do. You are lying awake in the loft with the duck on your feet, thinking about nothing, when it arrives whole. It is a tiny array, no larger than a thumbnail, that heats water by a fraction of a degree for each turn of a wheel. You are out of bed before you have finished the thought. You do not stop till dawn.

**Closing scene**

The first prototype boils a teacup in four seconds, then the table, then the ceiling. The second goes off like a firework. The third makes a high, sweet, ringing note and sets every glass in the workshop vibrating until it shatters. The tenth, which you build at sunrise, with burnt eyebrows and a quivering hand, boils a pot of water in exactly three seconds, quietly, politely, without exploding.

You pour a cup of tea. It is perfect. You sit at the bench and drink it, with the duck on your knee, and weep a little, in the way of a person who has been wrong forty-one times and right once. Fitch comes in at nine and finds you asleep with your head on the table and a cup in your hand.

**Fitch:** Did it work?

**You:** Yes.

**Fitch:** Everything?

**You:** Just the one thing.

**Fitch:** That's usually the way, isn't it? One thing. And then you find out what it was for.

The Conservatory sends a formal letter of inspection. It will be conducted by a panel of five, led by Clerk Mott, on the first Friday of the month. It will be a full examination of all premises, devices and animals. The letter is signed by Master Dimmock, with a flourish. At the bottom it says: A cheerful demeanour will be noted.

You spend the week hiding things. By Thursday you have crammed eleven machines into the cellar, six into the loft, and a self-ironing board into the coal scuttle. You put the walking kettle out in the yard under a bucket. You lock the umbrella in a cupboard. You tell Biscuit to be a normal duck.

The panel arrives at nine. It is led by Mott, in the long grey coat, with Dimmock's three assistants behind. They examine the benches. They examine the shelves. They examine the loft, where a self-ironing board escapes from the coal scuttle and chases a clerk down the stairs. The kettle gets out from under the bucket and walks into the room, calmly, with a cup on its lid, and comes to rest at Mott's feet.

**Mott:** (after a very long pause, to the panel) It appears to be making tea.

It is. It is making a perfect pot of Assam. Mott takes the cup. {mott.He} sips it. {mott.He} sets it down on the saucer without a sound. The three assistants stand there, in a row, like members of a jury who have just been shown the murder weapon and found it is a cake.

**Mott:** I shall record that the premises are in order. I shall record that the kettle is an exemption. I shall record, if I may, that this is the best cup of tea I have had in this city.

## 14.9  "The Great Lane Race"  (`race`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended

**Opening scene**

The race was Fitch's idea. It is to be held on the first Sunday in June, down the whole length of Gearwheel Lane, from the bakery to the canal. The entries are anything with wheels. The rules are that there are no rules. The prize is a golden spanner, made by the lamp-maker, and a barrel of Mrs. Orlop's best cider.

**Closing scene**

By the day, there are eleven entries. A coffin on skates. A wheelbarrow with a sail. A tea-trolley with a boiler, driven by the vicar. The biggest crowd the lane has ever seen is packed along the pavements, cheering and eating buns, and Biscuit sits on the bakery roof wearing a tiny flag. You enter a four-wheeled cart with a small boiler array in the back and a handle in the front. You call it the Stately.

It does not go well. The start-gun is a firework. The vicar's trolley takes off. The coffin is overtaken by a goat. You are in the lead for the first fifty yards, with the wind in your hair, laughing like a lunatic. Then the Stately's array, which you have set to Cautious, decides it has been Cautious long enough. It switches itself, without asking, to Furious.

You cross the finish line at forty miles an hour, backwards, in a cloud of steam. You go through the canal fence. You come to rest, with a splash, in four feet of mud. The crowd is silent. Then, from somewhere, a single voice shouts, 'Again!'

**Fitch:** (hauling you out) That was the best thing I've ever seen. I wanted you to know that. That was incredible.

## 14.10  "The Lifting Engine"  (`bridge`)

The Weaver's Bridge falls in on a Tuesday. It is a grey stone arch, three hundred years old, over the canal at the foot of the lane, and it falls without warning, in the middle of the morning, with a sound like a stack of plates. A cart is on it. A horse is on it. A baker's boy, who has stopped to tie his shoe, is on it. The whole thing goes into the water, and the baker's boy goes with it, and does not come up.

**Closing scene**

There is no time. The horse is screaming. The cart lies on its side across the stones. Under it, in the dark water, among broken arches and baulks of timber, there is a space where a small boy might be, alive, if the weight could be taken off. The Guard has sent for a crane. The crane is an hour away. You look at the duck, on your shoulder, and the duck looks at you.

**You:** Fitch! The Lifting Engine!

**Fitch:** It's a plan! It's only a drawing! It says MAYBE!

You build it in eleven minutes, on the bank, with a plank, a barrel hoop, a spare wheel, and the little array you made in the teapot. It is ugly, and it works. It takes the cart on its brass arm and lifts it, with a long groan, a foot, two feet, three. Fitch goes into the water. He comes up with the baker's boy over his shoulder, coughing, alive.

The crowd gasps, and then roars. The boy's mother runs down the bank with her apron over her face. Mrs. Orlop is crying. The horse is led out, trembling. Biscuit, on your shoulder, makes a very faint, very clear sound that you have never heard before: not a click, but something nearer a laugh.

## 14.11  "An Offer from Master Dimmock"  (`offer`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones

**Opening scene**

He calls the next morning, in person, in a carriage with a coat of arms. He stands in the doorway of the workshop in his beautiful coat, with his gloves in one hand, and he looks at the Lifting Engine on the bench with an expression you cannot read. He says that the Conservatory has been following events with interest. He says it would like to make an offer.

**Closing scene**

The duck, on the bench, has turned its head to watch him go. When the carriage has rattled out of the lane it looks round at you and gives, very distinctly, a click. It is the click that means: well, then. It is also, you are fairly sure, the click that means: look out.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `offer`; default: option 1)

> The Conservatory wants the Lifting Engine, and is willing to pay.

1. Sell it to the Conservatory for a fortune, and walk away.
   - You sell it. The Conservatory pays four thousand in silver and a seat on the Committee of Mechanical Methods. It is the most money you have ever seen. It is delivered in a box. It is very heavy. You feel, signing the paper, as if you had given away a coat and been paid for the buttons.
   - **Fitch:** It's a lot of money. It's a lot of money for something that isn't ours any more.
2. Share it: give the plans to anyone who asks, free, and let the lane build its own.
   - You give the plans away. You run off a hundred copies on Mrs. Orlop's bread-wrappers and hand them out on the quay. Within a week there are nineteen Lifting Engines in Tallowmere, and a team of boys in the canal with one, rebuilding the bridge. Dimmock is livid. The newspapers are charmed.
   - **Orlop:** That was a lovely thing to do. It's going to make you awfully unpopular.
3. Keep it: refuse, and register it in your own name at the Patent Office.
   - You refuse. You write to the Patent Office the same afternoon, on a sheet of foolscap, in a very formal hand, with the duck's footprint in the corner as a seal. The reply arrives in three days. It says that the application is received, and that the examiner will be a Clerk of the Second Grade named Mott.
   - **Dimmock:** (in the doorway) You have made a mistake. I shall be sorry to see how it goes.

## 14.12  "The Patent"  (`patent`)

- **Starts when:** 32 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Reach Major Lvl 1.  "Qualify for the Register: reach Major Lvl 1."
- **Pays:** 1,000 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **When it closes, the code:** `(c, st) -> { int l = Chapters.flag(st, "love"); Chapters.bond(c, st, "mott", l == 3 ? 1 : 3); if (l == 1 || l == 2) Chapters.wed(c, st, "mott"); }`
- **Words:** 288 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Patent Office is a low yellow building at the top of Quill Street with a great many steps. The queue goes round the corner. You wait six hours with a flask and a duck, among inventors of every degree: the mad, the prudent, the obsessed, a man with a bird cage on his head. When your number is called you carry the Lifting Engine up the stairs in your arms, in a blanket, like a baby.

**Closing scene**

Mott receives you in a small bare office with a table, two chairs and a window onto a brick wall. {mott.He} examines the Engine for forty minutes, with a lens, a ruler and a notebook, not speaking. Then {mott.he} sets down the lens and says that, in {mott.his} professional opinion, it is the most original device {mott.he} has examined in eleven years.

**Mott:** It is also, I am sorry to say, entirely illegal. It lacks an approved array. It lacks a certificate of provenance. It has been built by an unlicensed person, using unlicensed methods, from salvage. I have no discretion. I am obliged to reject it.

**You:** I see.

**Mott:** I should like to say that I had to read the regulations three times to be sure. I should also like to say that there is a clause in section nine, which has never been used, which permits a Clerk to waive the licensing requirement in the case of a device that has saved a life.

{mott.He} stamps the form. The stamp is a very loud, final noise. It says: GRANTED. Under it, in {mott.his} handwriting, tiny, in the margin, is a note that makes your face go hot. It says: I have wanted to do that for eleven years.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `love`; default: option 1)

> Lysandra Mott has just broken the rules for you, and has gone slightly pink.

1. Ask {mott.him} to dinner, and mean it.
   - You ask. It comes out wrong, at the wrong speed, with a sort of squeak in the middle. Mott stares at you for a very long moment. Then the narrow tidy face breaks up into something astonishing, a smile that has clearly been kept in a drawer for minutes, and {mott.he} says, 'Yes. Seven o'clock. I shall wear the other coat.'
   - **Mott:** It is not a good coat. I want you to know that in advance.
2. Send a thank-you with a small clockwork bird that sings the date.
   - You send the bird. It is a small brass thing the size of a walnut. It arrives at the Patent Office on Monday and sings the date in a high clear voice at the start of every hour for a week. The whole Office is in uproar. Mott takes it home in a pocket and writes a note, on a card, in a very upright hand, which says: Thursday?
   - **Fitch:** I think you've been outflanked.
3. Say thank you, shake hands, and leave it there.
   - You say thank you. You shake hands. It is a stiff, brief clasp, over a desk, and both of you let go a little too fast. You go out into the cold afternoon with the Lifting Engine under your arm and the duck on your shoulder, feeling clever and a bit of a fool. From the window above, if you looked up, you would see a narrow face watching you go.
   - **Mott:** (in a small voice, to the window) Well. That's that.

## 14.I1  Interlude: Patent Pending  (between season 1 and season 2)

**Interlude**

The Crank has a plate on the door now, in brass, from the Patent Office. It says: MECHANICAL INVENTIONS. It says it in three languages. Under it is a bell that rings if you pull it, which is rare, since people mostly knock and shout.

*[only if duck is 1]* Biscuit says 'Interesting' to the furniture, in a high clear voice, and has been known to say it to a bishop.

*[only if duck is 2]* Biscuit says nothing. It sits on whichever machine is about to go wrong, and nobody has yet found a way to make it move.

*[only if duck is 3]* The toymaker has sent seven more notes. They all say the same: the duck is not wanted, and would you take it back.

*[only if offer is 1]* The Lifting Engine is in the Conservatory's courtyard, on a plinth, with a small brass plaque that spells your name wrong.

*[only if offer is 2]* There are nineteen Lifting Engines in Tallowmere. Three of them work properly.

*[only if offer is 3]* The Lifting Engine is on a shelf in the workshop with a label: PATENT NO. 1. A small crowd of schoolchildren is brought to look at it every Thursday.

Biscuit sits on the windowsill in the evenings and looks at the stars. It does this with one blue eye and one brown. Nobody has ever asked what it is looking for. The kettle walks in a circle round the stove. In the dusk, if you listen closely, you can hear a very faint sound from somewhere in the roof. It is the sound of an idea, still on its way, getting off its horse.

**Opening scene**

The letter comes in a cream envelope by a footman in a powdered wig, who hands it over at arm's length, as though it were hot. It is from the Conservatory of Right Arrays. It says that the Lifting Engine, Patent No. 1, is an infringement of Conservatory Patent No. 40,011, filed on the fourth of March. It says that you are required to cease. It says that the penalty is the seizure of all machines.

You read it three times. Patent No. 1 was granted on the ninth of June. The Conservatory's was filed on the fourth of March, three months before you built the thing, by a clerk who had never seen it. You show it to Fitch. He says it is the most beautiful lie he has ever read.

**Closing scene**

The duck is on the bench looking at the envelope with an expression of grave interest. It pecks it once, very hard, in the middle of the seal. Fitch says that there is nothing to be done. He says the Conservatory has an army of lawyers, a hall full of precedents, and a master who has not lost a case in thirty years.

**Mrs. Orlop:** (leaning in the doorway with a plate of buns) It sounds to me like a case of someone stealing your pie.

**You:** It's more complicated than that.

**Mrs. Orlop:** It's never more complicated than that, dear. It's only longer.

## 14.14  "Prior Art"  (`priorart`)

**Opening scene**

The first thing to do, Mott says, is prove prior art. It must be shown that the Lifting Engine existed before the fourth of March. Since it did not, it must be shown that something very like it did. Mott comes to the workshop in the evening, off duty, in an overcoat, with a satchel of old catalogues, and spreads them across the long bench.

**Closing scene**

You spend a fortnight asking. You ask in the lane, and the market, and the old men's club at the canal. You find a retired bridge-builder who remembers a lifting rig from his father's day. You find a widow who has a diary with a drawing. You find a ship's carpenter, a clockmaker, and a woman who sells chestnuts and has, for some reason, a very large collection of old patents in a trunk.

By the end of the second week the workshop is full of witnesses, sitting in rows among the half-finished machines, drinking tea. Mott takes down their statements in a neat shorthand. {mott.He} does it with the air of a person at last doing the thing {mott.he} trained for, which is to be on the side of the truth.

**Mott:** I should say I'm not meant to be doing this. It is a conflict of interest. I'm employed by the Conservatory, and I'm helping to prove it wrong. I have never felt so well.

The Court of Patents sits in a hall with a roof like the inside of a drum. There are forty benches, a gallery, and a high judge's chair on a platform, under a banner of a golden gear. Master Dimmock sits at the table on the left with six lawyers. You sit at the table on the right with Fitch, a duck, and a satchel of statements. The judge is a very old man who falls asleep during the oath.

**Closing scene**

You lose. It takes forty minutes. The lawyers speak in a long calm cadence, like water in a drain. They show the filing date. They show the clerk's stamp. They show that the Lifting Engine, as described in the Conservatory's patent, uses a crossed pulley, and that yours uses a crossed pulley, and that crossed pulleys are the property of the Conservatory by prior grant. The judge wakes up and says, 'Quite.'

On the steps afterwards Dimmock stops beside you in a long coat, with his gloves in his hand. He says that he bears no ill will. He says that the Engine will be put to excellent use. He says the Conservatory will build a hundred. He says it is a pity to be on the wrong side of progress, and that you will recover. People generally do.

**Dimmock:** Give my regards to your duck.

The duck on your shoulder turns slowly, and looks at him. It makes the click that means: noted.

## 14.17  "The Locksmith"  (`lock`)

**Opening scene**

Old Cobb has a shop on Tinker's Row, a cupboard of a place, hung with ten thousand keys on ten thousand nails. He is sixty-six and small and bent, with a square white beard and hands like a pair of old gloves. He sits at a bench in the window with a lens in his eye and a lock the size of a plum in his fingers. He will not look up.

**Closing scene**

**Cobb:** The Conservatory vault. I've had my eye on it for forty years. It's a Bramah, with a double-bolt and a seven-lever tumbler. I've never seen it opened. They had it put in by a foreigner, who died. It's said to be perfect.

**You:** Can you open it?

**Cobb:** It's not that. I can open anything. It's that I've promised not to. I've promised a lady. It's a long story.

He puts down the lock and looks at you for the first time. His eyes are small and bright and very blue. He asks what it is you want out of the vault. You tell him. He listens, nodding, picking at a splinter in the bench. When you have finished he says: 'It's a funny thing. The lady I promised was my wife. She died in the spring. I've been wondering what the promise was for.'

He gets up and takes a long black case from a shelf. It is lined with red baize and holds seventeen picks of various sizes. He closes it. He puts on his hat. 'You'd better tell me about this duck,' he says.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `drawer`; default: option 1)

> The vault holds nine thousand drawers, each with a name, a date and a bundle of plans.

1. Take the proof of your own engine and expose the vault to the whole city.

Then it clicks, once, and the sound is, you could swear, an enormous sadness.

**You:** What is it?

**Fitch:** It's another duck.

## 14.23  "Prior Art, Again"  (`again`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 1,000 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 257 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Court of Patents sits again, in the hall like a drum. The gallery is full. The judge is awake. Dimmock does not appear. In his place there is a pale young lawyer who stands up, and sits down again, and mumbles. The old judge asks, in a mild voice, whether he proposes to contest.

**Closing scene**

He does not. The register is produced. The papers are read. The old judge listens with his chin on his hand. When it is done he takes off his spectacles and wipes them on his sleeve, and says that in sixty years on the bench he has never been so ashamed of an institution.

The Conservatory is not abolished. It is not that sort of country. But it is stripped of the licensing power, and the patent system is handed to a new body, with a panel of inventors and a dean who has never owned a lawyer. The first act of the new Board is to restore Patent No. 1. The second is to ask whether you would be willing to serve as a member.

**Mott:** I shall resign the Conservatory. I should like to say it was a very good job. I should also like to say I hated it.

Dimmock is seen later that week on the canal path, in a plain brown coat, feeding the ducks. He looks smaller. He lifts his hat to you as you pass. His hands are shaking a little. You find, to your annoyance, that you are sorry for him.

## 14.I2  Interlude: Patent Granted  (between season 2 and season 3)

**Interlude**

Gearwheel Lane has a new sign at the top: THE LANE OF INVENTIONS. It has been hand-painted by Mrs. Orlop, with a bun in the corner. She says it is not a pun. She says it is a mark of respect.

*[only if plan is 1]* The rocket that went through the roof of the orangery was recovered in a field outside the town, intact. It is on display in the bakery window, with a label: GLADYS.

*[only if plan is 2]* The bishop's mitre is on a peg in the workshop, with a duck-shaped hole in the top. The duck likes to sit in it on Sundays.

*[only if plan is 3]* The seventeen-page application is framed over the bench. It is considered by lawyers to be the best-drafted request in the history of the city.

*[only if drawer is 1]* The register of the vault is on display in the Hall of Records. Visitors may read it. They do, in large numbers, and sometimes weep.

*[only if drawer is 2]* Your uncle's drawing hangs over the stove with a card: MAYBE, MAYBE, MAYBE. It is generally agreed to be the best-looking piece of paper in the lane.

*[only if drawer is 3]* There are nine thousand inventions out in the world that were not there before. Some of them work. A small number of them are dreadful. A few of them are changing everything.

The small brass bird from the vault sits on the workshop mantel. Fitch has mended the wing. It does not move. It does not sing. But on certain evenings, at dusk, when the light comes in sideways, it turns its head, and Biscuit, on the sill, turns its head to match. The two of them look at each other, in a long grave silence, like cousins at a funeral.

This one walks in through the roof, sits on the end of the bed, and says: Wall. A wall of bells, round the whole of a city. Each bell tuned to the next. **You:** Nobody. It just arrived.

**Fitch:** Ideas don't just arrive. They have to come from somewhere. They come from a postmark. This one's the first I've ever seen that didn't come with a stamp.

Mott is in the doorway. {mott.He} has been awake all night, too, on the other side of town, with a feeling {mott.he} could not name, and has come across at dawn in {mott.his} coat over a nightgown. {mott.He} looks at the sheet. {mott.He} goes white. {mott.He} says, 'Where did you get that?' in the voice of someone who has seen a ghost in a library.

## 14.25  "The Shed in the Wood"  (`shed`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight

Mott knows where it comes from. {mott.He} has read it, in the Conservatory's archive, in a bound book nobody opens, in a chapter called Provenance. Ideas, the chapter says, are not made. They are lent. They are issued from a store, to those who can use them, on loan, for a term. The store is in a shed, in a deep wood, in the north. Nobody has seen it for three hundred years.

**Closing scene**

It is a plain, low, weathered wooden hut at the end of a path that was not there yesterday. It has a door with a latch and a window with a cracked pane. Inside, on racks and pegs and hooks, in long dusty rows, hang tools. They are the strangest tools you have ever seen. There is a plane that planes time. There is a pair of tongs for lifting light. There is a hammer, the size of a thimble, whose head is a small closed fist.

You walk along the racks, with Mott behind you, holding a lantern. The duck is on your shoulder. It has gone completely silent. Every tool has a label, tied on with string. The labels have names, and dates, and a line in small neat capitals: ON LOAN TO.

**Mott:** (in a whisper) These are the ideas. These are all of them. The wheel. The lever. The clock. The array. They are tools. They are tools for building a world, and they have been left here, on loan, for anyone who needs them.

You find your own name three-quarters of the way down the long rack. It is on a small brass drill. The label says: ON LOAN TO: CRANK, B. And under it, in a different ink, in a newer hand, so fresh that it has not yet dried: AND TO HIS HEIR.

## 14.26  "On Loan To"  (`loan`)

There is a ledger in the shed, on a high desk at the end of the room. It is bound in black cloth and as big as a church Bible. Its pages are ruled in columns: Tool, Borrower, Date, Term, Returned. Mott opens it at the beginning. The first entry is in no language either of you can read. The last is in yours, and says that the Wall has been issued, on a term of nine years, for use in the city of Tallowmere.

**Closing scene**

You read down the page. Every entry has a column marked Purpose. The wheel was lent for carrying. The lever was lent for lifting. The clock was lent for waiting. The array, you read, was lent for protecting, and for no other thing. At the very bottom of the page is a line in a hand like a row of nails: These tools are lent to be used. If they are not returned they are not lost. They are owed.

**Mott:** I have spent eleven years of my life guarding patents for ideas that were never ours. I find I am not as angry as I should be.

**You:** What's it owed to?

**Mott:** To whoever lent them. And to anybody who might need them next.

The duck, on the ledger, walks slowly down the page with its head cocked, reading. At the last entry it stops. It taps the line with its beak, three times. Then it looks at you. You have the unsettling sense that it has read something you have not, and is deciding whether to tell you.

## 14.27  "Fitch Builds a Prototype"  (`build`)

The prototype takes a month. It is a single bell the size of a hat, with nine silver rings round the rim, and a clapper made from a spoon. You and Fitch build it in the yard behind the bakery, under a canvas, with a great many wooden pegs and a pot of glue. Mrs. Orlop brings buns. The lane watches over the wall. Nobody makes a joke.

**Closing scene**

You set the bell on a trestle in the yard on a cold bright evening, and Fitch strikes it, softly, with a wooden mallet. It makes no sound at all. Then the air round it begins to hum. It is a low, steady note, so deep that it seems to come out of the ground. Mrs. Orlop sits down very suddenly on a barrel. The lane's forty-one cats come out of the cellars, one by one, and sit in a circle round the trestle with their eyes shut.

A pane in the bakery window shivers and goes to dust. The note does not rise. It does not fall. It rings on and on, in the ground and in your teeth, and where it reaches the evening light stands very clear, as though a lamp had been lit in the air.

**Fitch:** (in a hoarse whisper) That's it. That's the one.

The duck, on your shoulder, begins to hum, very faintly, a single note. It is the same note. It has a brass throat, and no reed, and has never made a noise but a click, and it is humming.

He wears a pair of spectacles with very thin gold rims, and a badge that says CLERK. He enters the workshop with his hat in his hand, and stands by the door, and waits to be offered a chair.

**Closing scene**

**Quire:** Mister Quire. I am here as a Clerk of the Court. I represent a party you may have heard of. I should explain at once that I am not a hostile presence. I am an administrator. There has been a regrettable irregularity in the matter of an invention.

He opens the case. He takes out a printed form. It is the colour of a pale cheese. It has nine boxes and a small neat title in capitals: FORM 9. DECLARATION OF ORIGIN. He lays it on the bench and smooths it with the flat of his hand, the way a man smooths the sheet on a sickbed.

**Quire:** The Court has noticed that a device of considerable power has been proposed within this city. It has no recorded origin. It is not registered with any approved source. The Court is concerned that it may have been acquired without authority. I am obliged to ask you to complete the form.

**You:** And if I don't?

**Quire:** Then the item is deemed to be unclaimed, and is returned. To the place it came from. It is quite painless. It simply stops having been.

## 14.30  "Form Nine"  (`form`)
