**Opening scene**

You read the form for a day and a half. It is the most thoroughly baffling document you have ever seen. It asks for your name, your trade, your place of birth, the place of birth of your invention, the place of birth of its parts, and the place of birth of the idea of its parts. It asks you to state whether the work is wholly your own. It asks, in the last box, in a tiny italic, whether you have at any time been Lent To.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `form`; default: option 1)

> The Clerk waits at the door with a pen, and a pot of ink, and a patient face.

1. Fill it honestly: write that the Wall was lent, by the Shed, for protecting.
   - You write the truth. It takes forty minutes. You put Origin: the Shed in the north. You put Term: nine years. You put Purpose: to protect. Quire reads it with faint surprise, and, to your astonishment, nods. 'That is perfectly in order,' he says. 'It is not often that a form is filled in so correctly.' He stamps it with a small iron stamp, and sighs. 'I had rather hoped you would lie.'
   - **Quire:** It would have been so much simpler.
2. Fill it falsely: write that the work is wholly your own, and sign.
   - You write: wholly my own. You sign it with a flourish. Quire takes it, and reads it, and puts it carefully in the case. He says nothing for a moment. Then he says, in an almost gentle voice, that he is obliged to inform you that, in the opinion of the Court, a falsehood on Form 9 is a very serious matter. It forfeits the term. It does not forfeit the tool. It forfeits you, a little.
   - **Quire:** I shall be back. I shall bring a longer form.
3. Refuse to sign, and say that an idea cannot be filed.
   - You refuse. You tell him that an idea cannot be filed. It cannot be owned, or borrowed, or declared. It can only be had. Quire looks at you for ages over the thin gold rims. Then he picks up the form, and tears it neatly in half, and in half again, and puts the pieces in his pocket. 'Nobody has ever said that to me,' he says. 'I shall have to go away and think about whether it is true.'
   - **Mott:** I have the strangest feeling you have just won a point.

**Closing scene**

He stays to tea. It is a stiff, formal, curious tea. He sits on a stool in the workshop with a cup in one hand and the document case on his knee, looking round at the forty-one half-finished machines with an expression of mild distress. He admires the walking kettle. He asks if the duck is registered. He says, in a low voice, that he used to have a hobby once.

The cards come out with a crisp new click. When you have done, the woman with the plait takes the last card and reads it. She smiles. It is the first time you have seen her do so.

The card says, in a tiny print, in the machine's own flat tone: Thank you. Under it: Please come again.

## 14.38  "The Gear in the Seat"  (`dr3`)

- **Starts when:** 26 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `palace`.  "Go to the Palace of the Oldest Order, at Originis, to the Empty Seat."
- **Pays:** 1,000 spirit stones, +2 potential, 2 Potential Pills, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 133 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You find it under the Empty Seat, wedged in a crack in the flags, where the latch should be. It is a small brass wheel with eleven teeth, one of them chipped, no bigger than a coin. The duck hops down from your shoulder and looks at it. It makes a sound like a held breath. It says: 'It is the last piece of the first bird.'

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `latch`; default: option 1)

> The wheel is in your palm. The Door is under the Seat. The duck is waiting.

1. Stay: put the wheel back in the bird in the vault, and mend her.
   - You mend her. It takes a year at the bench in the workshop, with a loupe, and a hundred tiny files. When the wheel goes in, the brass bird shivers on the mantel and lifts her head. She looks at the duck. The duck looks at her. They sit on the sill, side by side, in the sun, and nobody in the lane has ever seen anything so quiet.
   - **Mott:** (with a plate of buns) Neither of them is going to explain.
2. Go: take the wheel and the duck through the Door together.
   - You close your hand on the wheel. The duck climbs onto your shoulder. The stair is dark. The latch is a plain iron thing, with a handle like a bird's head. You say that you will take the duck. You say it to the stone. A tiny voice, from the pocket of your coat, says: 'I was going to say that.'
3. Hold the latch: build a small machine to keep the Door open, and sit beside it.
   - You build a machine. It is the simplest you have ever made: a spring, a lever, a weight. It holds the latch up. You set it by the Door and sit down on a stool beside it, with the duck, and a flask of tea. People go through. A soldier says it is the first Door he has ever seen that had a doorman. You tell him it is a doormat.

**Closing scene**

The workshop in the lane has forty-one machines. One of them works. It stands on the bench, by the window, a plain brass thing the size of a loaf. It has a lamp, a crank and a single dial. The dial has three marks. They say: MAYBE. MAYBE. MAYBE. Nobody knows what it does. Everyone says it is the best thing in the lane.

## 14.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

Gearwheel Lane smells of hot oil, new bread and mild disappointment. It has forty-one half-finished machines in the Crank alone. One of them works.

*[only if wall is 1]* The Ringing Wall rings once a year, on the first night of spring. Nobody forgets anyone in Tallowmere. They say it is a feature of the climate.

*[only if wall is 2]* The note of the Wall carries a hundred miles, and the villages leave a lamp in every window. Travellers say they can hear it from the road, at dusk, a low steady hum like a cat.

*[only if wall is 3]* The Wall rings in the Palace as well. In the Under-Kitchen, on certain evenings, a man in an apron stops stirring the pot, and listens, and smiles.

*[only if form is 1]* A grey Clerk calls every year with a form. He fills it in himself. He has begun to leave a sprig of lavender on the bench.

*[only if form is 2]* A grey Clerk calls every year with a longer form. You fill it in wrongly. He thanks you.

*[only if form is 3]* A grey Clerk comes to tea on Thursdays, and has taken up the hobby of repairing clocks. He is not good. He is happy.

*[only if loan is 1]* The tools are back in the Shed, on their racks, in the dust. The ledger says Returned. Sometimes in the evening an idea comes up the lane on foot, sits on the step, and waits to be asked in.

*[only if loan is 2]* The brass drill is warm on certain nights. You do not mention it.

*[only if loan is 3]* Every child in Tallowmere knows how to make a lever. Some of them know how to make an array. A few of them are already working on a thing called a duck.

*[only if love is 1]* Lysandra Mott keeps the accounts of the Crank and has never once filed them correctly.

*[only if love is 2]* Mott has a key to the workshop, and an opinion on every machine in it.

*[only if love is 3]* Mott sits by the stove on Thursdays, at a respectful distance, and corrects the spelling on the labels.

*[only if latch is 1]* Two brass birds sit on the sill of the Crank, one with a mended wing and one with a mitre. They look at the lane. Sometimes, at dusk, they hum.

*[only if latch is 2]* The workshop has a bench with a gap on it the shape of a duck. Nobody puts anything there.

*[only if latch is 3]* A brass spring and a lever hold the latch at the Seat, and there is a stool beside it. The Wicks call the man on it the Doormat. He answers to it.

At night, when the lane is quiet, Biscuit sits on the windowsill and looks at the stars with one blue eye and one brown. From time to time, very faintly, it hums the note of the Wall. On the mantel behind it a brass bird with a mended wing turns its head to listen.

## 14.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

You stay in the Garden. The Palace's forge has a bench in the corner, a brass duck on the shelf above it, and a man in an apron who is learning, very slowly, how to open a clock and shut it again.

*[only if not dead.mott]* {mott.He} visits on Thursdays and corrects the labels.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

In the Gardener's army you are the person who is handed the thing that does not work. You put it on a bench, look at it for an hour, and make it work in a way nobody meant.

The soldiers call it luck. The duck says nothing. The duck is, as always, right.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You step through the Seam with a toolbox and a brass duck on your shoulder. On the far side there is a lane, and a bakery, and a workshop with a crooked chimney and a door that opens outward.

You put a sign on it. BRACE, it says.

**You are struck down by the array**

The array took you. In the dark something is ringing, very low, below hearing, and you know the note.

You hum along. It is the first thing you have ever built that nobody else could take apart.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden goes out. The lane goes out, and the bakery, and the forty-one machines on the benches.

The last thing to go is a small brass duck, on a windowsill, looking at the stars with one blue eye and one brown.

# 15.S1  Season 1: The Road Song

## 15.1  "Thirteen Strings"  (`strings`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** Go to the place `inn`.  "Take the zither to the Fiddler's Rest, the inn at {@inn}."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, 1 Cultivation Pill
- **Words:** 286 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The zither came in a flat box, by the carrier, with a note in shaky capitals: FOR WHEN YOU ARE READY. It is a long narrow instrument of dark wood, as old as a grandmother and as scarred as a doorstep. It has thirteen strings. Twelve are steel. The thirteenth is something else. It is pale, and thin, and when you touch it, it does not sound. It listens.

Your grandmother played it at weddings and wakes, in the days when you were small enough to sit under it. She never once let you touch it. She never said why. She died in the winter with the lid shut and her hands folded on it, and the doctor said her last words had been about a tune.

**Closing scene**

The Fiddler's Rest is a long low inn at a crossroads, with a roof like a hat and a sign of a fiddle with a wooden leg. The landlord is a heavy grey man called Brewster, who looks at the box, and the road, and your boots, and asks if you can play.

**You:** A little.

**Brewster:** A little is plenty. I've had a great deal of nothing. Sit by the fire. If it's good, I'll feed you. If it isn't, I'll feed you anyway, but I'll look sad.

You tune it in the firelight with the wind in the chimney. The twelve steel strings come up one by one to a clear bright pitch. The thirteenth does not move. You leave it alone. You begin to play, something simple, a song your grandmother hummed over the washing-up, and the room goes quiet, and halfway through the second verse, very faintly, the pale string begins to hum.

## 15.2  "A Hat on the Ground"  (`hat`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Have 2 friends.  "Play for your supper: make two friends."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **Words:** 233 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You have eleven coins and a zither. The road runs three ways. You choose the one with a village at the end, because villages have markets, and markets have crowds, and crowds, in your experience, will give a person a coin to stop. You play at the cross in the square on a Saturday morning with your hat on the ground in front of you and your heart in your mouth.

**Closing scene**

The first hour is nothing. The second brings a dog. It sits in front of you with its head on one side and its tongue out, and a small boy comes to fetch it, and stays. By noon there is a ring of faces. A woman with a basket of eggs. A man with a ladder. Two girls who have been told to go home and are pretending not to hear.

You play every song you know. You play them badly and then less badly. At the end of the afternoon the hat is half full of coins and one boiled egg. The woman with the basket has said that you have a nice touch, and that it is a pity about the thirteenth. You ask what she means. She says she could hear it, all afternoon, under the rest, like somebody humming in another room.

**Woman:** I thought it was the wind. But the wind doesn't know the words.

## 15.3  "Pocket"  (`pocket`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet pocket (walk to their tile).  "Hear what Pocket has to say."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "pocket")`
- **Words:** 196 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The drummer finds you. He is twenty, thin as a rail, in a coat too big for him, with a pair of sticks in his belt and a snare drum slung on his back with a bootlace. He has been following you for three streets. He says his name is Pocket. He says it is because he keeps everything in them, including, at present, a pigeon.

**Closing scene**

**Pocket:** I heard you in the square. I couldn't help it. You've got something under the tune. Something low. I tried to hit it on the drum and I couldn't find it. I'd like to come with you. I don't need paying. I eat very little. The pigeon eats more.

**You:** I don't need a drummer.

**Pocket:** Nobody needs a drummer. That's what makes it fun.

He taps a rhythm on his knee. It is a plain beat, two slow and one quick, the sort you would hear in a market. The thirteenth string, from the box at your feet, hums to it. It is the first time it has answered anyone but you. Pocket stops. He goes white. He says, 'It's got a pulse,' and sits down on the kerb.

## 15.4  "A Wedding Without a Band"  (`wedding`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 174 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The village of Haldane has a wedding on the first Saturday in May, and the band has got drunk. The fiddler is in the ditch. The piper is in the pond. The bride's father, a vast red man, comes out to the road in his best waistcoat and stops you with a hand like a shovel. He says that his only daughter is being married in an hour. He says that he has been told you can play.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `wedding`; default: option 1)

> A whole village is waiting in a barn with garlands and no music.

1. Play the old dances: the ones everyone knows, just as they know them.
   - You play the old dances. The reels, the jigs, the long slow waltz that goes round the barn like water round a stone. Pocket keeps time on the snare. The whole village is on its feet by the second tune, grandmothers and children and the bride's father, who dances like a bear, and cries, and tells everybody it is the smoke. It is a wedding like every other, and for that reason perfect.
   - **Father:** That's the way it ought to be. That's how it was in my day.
2. Play something new, written on the spot, for the bride and groom.
   - You write it as you go. A tune for two people: one slow, one quick, running together, each finishing the other's phrase. You make it up in the corner of the barn with your eyes shut and the string humming under your hand. When you finish there is a silence. Then the groom, a shy young man in his father's coat, walks across the floor and shakes your hand without being able to speak.
   - **Bride:** Nobody's ever written me anything before.
3. Play the song your grandmother hummed, the one with the thirteenth string.
   - You play it. It is the song your grandmother hummed over the washing-up, with nothing added. The thirteenth string joins in on the third line. The sound is not loud. It goes through the barn like a draught through a keyhole, and at its touch every person in the room stops, and looks up, and for a moment sees someone they love who is not there. A man weeps. A child laughs. The bride, who has not wept all day, takes her husband's hand.
   - **Pocket:** (low, afterwards, behind the drum) What was that?

**Closing scene**

They pay you in cheese and cider and a ham. The bride's mother wraps the cheese in a cloth. The father gives you the whole of the wedding cake, in a box, and tells you that if you are ever in Haldane you will never pay for a bed. When you leave, in the grey of the morning, a child runs after you, down the lane, with a bunch of cowslips, and says shyly that he heard the string. He says it sounded like his dog. He says his dog died in the winter.

## 15.5  "The Academy of Sweet Sounds"  (`academy`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet lamberd (walk to their tile).  "Answer Master Lamberd's invitation at the Academy of Sweet Sounds."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "lamberd")`
- **Words:** 274 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Academy of Sweet Sounds stands in the town of Saltwick, a tall white building with a glass dome and a clock with a different tune for each hour. It teaches the Proper Way to play. It has done so for two hundred years. It has a faculty of thirty masters, a hall of a thousand seats, and a rule on the door: No instrument may be played in this establishment that is not in tune.

**Closing scene**

Master Lamberd is a tall precise man in a black coat with a white stock and a face like a metronome. He receives you in a long panelled room with a grand piano and a cabinet of glass jars, each with a label, each holding a little faint pearly light. He circles the zither without touching it. He says that it is a very old instrument. He says it has one string that is out of tune.

**Lamberd:** I should be glad to retune it for you. It would be a favour to the instrument. It's a matter of principle. A string that cannot be tuned is a string that does not wish to be part of the music.

**You:** It's not for tuning.

**Lamberd:** Everything is for tuning. That is the nature of a string.

He smiles. It is a thin, courteous, hungry smile. As you leave, you pass the cabinet of jars again. One of the labels reads: The Lullaby of Fennel Cross. Another: A Marching Song, Anonymous. Another, in a smaller hand: Nan Hollin's Third Verse. You stop. The little light in the last jar flickers, and for a moment hums a note you know.

## 15.6  "A Tune for the Dead"  (`funeral`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 270 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The old miller dies at Fennel Cross in the second week of June, and the village sends for the zither player. There is nobody else. The funeral is held at dusk in the churchyard, under a yew. The miller's widow stands at the graveside in black, a small stout woman with a face like a closed door, and asks you to play the only tune her husband ever whistled. She cannot remember it. She says it will come if you play.

**Closing scene**

You play every tune you know. None of them is right. The widow shakes her head. The mourners shuffle. The light is going. You are about to give up when, under your hand, the thirteenth string sounds, quite clear, one note. It is a note you have never played. Then another, and another. It is the tune. It is a plain, slow, cheerful whistle, ten notes long, with a skip in the middle, and a stop at the end where you can hear a man putting on his cap.

The widow lifts her head. She sings it. She sings all ten notes, quite steady, in a cracked high voice, with her eyes shut. When she gets to the stop at the end she says, 'There you are, then,' to the open grave, as one speaks to a husband who has come in late. The mourners sing it after her. The yew trembles. The thirteenth string goes quiet, as a person does who has finished what they came to say.

**Pocket:** (very softly) It knew it. How did it know?

**You:** I don't know. I don't think it's mine.

## 15.7  "The Listener"  (`listener`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended

**Opening scene**

There is a person in the third row at the Fiddler's Rest on a wet Tuesday who is not listening to the music. They are sitting very straight in a grey coat with a notebook on their knee, their head slightly tilted, and their eyes closed. They are not writing. They are doing something else, something a good deal harder, with the whole of their face. When you stop, they are the last to open their eyes.

**Closing scene**

**Ilse:** I am sorry. It is bad manners to listen with my eyes shut. I am Ilse Ferrant. I am a Listener of the Convocation Choir. I hear the Convocation. That is my entire function. I have heard every instrument in the Palace of the Oldest Order and I have never heard that.

{ilse.He} is about twenty-seven, long and thin, with a high forehead and a quick uncertain smile, like a person who has just remembered someone is watching. {ilse.He} says {ilse.he} has perfect pitch, and no ear whatever for people. {ilse.He} says it has been explained to {ilse.him} that this is a flaw, and that {ilse.he} has never been able to see why.

**Ilse:** That thirteenth string. It is not in any scale. It is a quarter-tone below the lowest note the Palace's organ can reach. And it is in tune. I have never heard anything so exactly in tune with nothing at all.

{ilse.He} puts a hand out to the zither, and stops, and draws it back, and says, 'May I?' You nod. {ilse.He} touches the pale string. It hums, once, a long way down. {ilse.He} stands there with {ilse.his} hand on the wood and tears in {ilse.his} eyes, and does not seem to notice.

## 15.8  "Three Songs for a Hat"  (`songs`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended

The fair at Reedmarch has a contest, a thing called the Hat, where three players are given three songs, and whoever fills the most hats wins a silver fiddle. It is held in the big marquee on the green, with fifty benches and a crowd of five hundred and a stout man in a striped waistcoat who calls the turns. There are eleven entries. You are the tenth.

**Closing scene**

You play a hornpipe, a lament and a ballad. Pocket accompanies on the drum, and on the third song, without warning, on the pigeon, which has learned to flap in time. The hat goes round. It comes back heavy. You do not win; you come second to a girl of twelve with a penny whistle, who plays with her eyes shut and a look of perfect indifference, and wins by a margin of eleven pennies.

**Pocket:** She's very good.

**You:** She is.

**Pocket:** Do you mind?

**You:** Not in the least. I think it's the first time I've lost and enjoyed it.

The girl comes over afterwards, to shake your hand, with the silver fiddle in the crook of her arm. She says she liked the thirteenth string. She says her mother plays one. She says her mother is a long way off, and that she can hear it humming when she has her eyes shut, on certain nights. She says, 'Is it the same one?' You say you do not know. She nods, gravely, and goes away to her supper.

## 15.9  "The Duel of Strings"  (`duel`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended

**Opening scene**

The challenge comes on the Academy's good grey paper, in the Master's own upright hand. It proposes a duel. It will be held in the Academy's great hall on the evening of the autumn equinox, before an audience of a thousand, with a champion of the Academy against a player of your choosing. The loser's instrument is to be retuned by the winner. It adds, in a postscript, that the Academy's champion is its best student, a young woman named Clarice Quill. It adds that she is nineteen.

**Closing scene**

The hall is a glittering oval, white and gold, with a thousand velvet seats and a stage the size of a pond. Clarice Quill walks out in a white dress with a cello, bows to the audience with the grace of a swan, sits, and plays a piece of such technical splendour that Pocket, in the wings, forgets to breathe. It is flawless. It is as clean as a cut diamond. It has not one note in it that has ever been a mistake.

You walk out with the zither on your knee. You play for ten minutes. You play the funeral tune, and the wedding tune, and a part of the song your grandmother hummed. It is not flawless. It is not clean. But at the third verse the thirteenth string comes in, from nowhere, and the whole hall goes silent, as a room does when a door has opened somewhere behind it. When you stop, nobody claps. A woman in the front row has her hand over her mouth.

**Lamberd:** (from his box, very clearly, into the stillness) Retune it.

## 15.10  "After the Duel"  (`result`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 156 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The judges retire for an hour. They come back in a body, five old men in black, with the faces of men carrying a bag of snakes. The chief judge reads the verdict from a card. He says that the Academy's champion played a perfect performance. He says that the visitor did not. He says that in the opinion of the panel, after careful consideration, the question of which was the better cannot be answered by the rules. It will be left to the audience.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `duel`; default: option 1)

> The hall of a thousand is on its feet, and the audience has been asked to decide.

1. Accept the audience's verdict, whichever way it falls.
   - The audience votes with their hands. It takes ten minutes. The count is close. It is announced as a thousand and four to nine hundred and ninety-six, in your favour, by a clerk who is plainly in pain. Lamberd's face does not change. Clarice, in her white dress, looks at you across the stage, and bows, very low, and straightens. Her face is not the face of a loser.
   - **Clarice:** (low, as she passes) I'd like to hear that string again. Some day when no one's watching.
2. Concede to Clarice Quill: she played better, and you know it.
   - You concede. You say it clearly, into the silence. You say that Miss Quill played the better performance, and that the zither should be retuned, if the Master insists. Lamberd's mouth opens. Clarice stands very still. Then she says, in a high clear furious voice, 'I will not accept that,' and puts down her bow. 'I did not win. I played a recital. She played a duel. I will not be given a thing that I did not earn.' The hall erupts.
   - **Lamberd:** (in a strangled voice) The result stands.
3. Offer to play with her: a duet, the two of you, on stage, and let the music decide.
   - You ask Clarice to play with you. She stares. Then she stands, slowly, and carries her cello to the centre of the stage, and sits beside you. You begin together. It is the strangest sound that hall has heard. The cello is precise and dark. The zither is rough and gold. They fight, and agree, and the thirteenth string comes in, a long way down, under both. A thousand people sit without moving. At the end she takes her bow off the string and says, 'Again.'
   - **Lamberd:** (very quietly, to himself, in the box) No. Not that. Anything but that.

**Closing scene**

The zither is not retuned. Lamberd does not insist. He does not speak to you again that evening. As you leave by the stage door a clerk presses a note into your hand. It is on Academy paper, in an upright hand, and says: You have something I have been looking for since I was a young man. I shall not stop. Please accept that I mean it kindly.

## 15.11  "The Thirteenth"  (`tuning`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 307 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

A letter comes from the country, by a carrier who has been three weeks on the road. It is from a farmer's wife in a village you have never heard of. It says that she has your grandmother's box. It says it was left with her, forty years ago, with a request that it be kept for a grandchild, and that the grandchild be told something when the time came. She is old now. She says she thinks the time has come.

**Closing scene**

The farmhouse is small and white, with a pear tree and a dog. The farmer's wife is ninety, as bent as a hook, with a voice like dry leaves. She leads you into a kitchen with a stove and a rocking-chair, and sits you down, and gives you a cup of something hot and dark, and says nothing for so long that you wonder if she has forgotten.

**Wife:** Your grandmother couldn't tune it either. She tried all her life. She said it was waiting to be answered. She said the thirteenth string was a rope with the other end somewhere else, and that you couldn't tune a rope that was tied to a thing so far away. She said you had to play it to someone who could hear.

**You:** Who?

**Wife:** She never said. She only said she'd heard it answer once. In the Palace, at the Convocation, in the year of the great snow. She said it answered for a moment and then went quiet. She said she thought it was the best moment of her life, and the saddest.

She gives you a folded paper. It is in your grandmother's hand, a few lines in pencil, a fragment of a song. The last verse. It breaks off in the middle of a line, like a person who has been called away.

## 15.12  "The Road Ahead"  (`road`)

## 15.I1  Interlude: The Road Song  (between season 1 and season 2)

**Interlude**

The road is a long one, and it goes everywhere. There are three of you on it, and a pigeon, and a zither with a pale string that hums at night. It is the happiest you have ever been.

*[only if wedding is 1]* The village of Haldane still dances the reels exactly as they were, and has declared a holiday on the first Saturday of May. They call it Zither Day. They have not asked your permission.

*[only if wedding is 2]* The tune you wrote for the bride and groom is now played at every wedding in the county. Nobody knows where it came from. They say it is a very old one.

*[only if wedding is 3]* People in Haldane say that on the first Saturday of May, near midnight, if you stand in the barn, you can hear a child's dog bark.

*[only if duel is 1]* Clarice Quill left the Academy in the spring. She sends a postcard, each month, from a different town, with a drawing of a cello and one word: Again.

*[only if duel is 2]* Clarice Quill refused the Academy's prize and plays now in a tavern in Saltwick, where she is, by all accounts, appalling and magnificent.

*[only if duel is 3]* A cello and a zither duet is played every year at the equinox in the great hall at Saltwick. Master Lamberd has never once come to hear it. He sends flowers.

At night, in the camp, when Pocket is asleep and the pigeon is on his chest, Ilse sits with {ilse.his} notebook on {ilse.his} knee and writes down the note of the thirteenth string. It is always the same note. It is always, to the fraction of a hair, a little lower than it was the night before. {ilse.He} says that it is not going flat. {ilse.He} says it is getting nearer.

**Opening scene**

The invitation is printed on pale green paper, with a silver fiddle at the top. It says that the Festival Circuit of Nine Towns will run from the spring to the autumn, and that its tournaments of strings are open to all players of good character, in the old forms. It says the prize is the Silver Fiddle and a seat on the Convocation Choir. It says that the loser of each duel will surrender the tune they were playing.

**Ilse:** That is a very odd rule. It has been in the charter for three hundred years, and nobody has ever asked what it means to surrender a tune.

**Closing scene**

You read it at the long table in the Fiddler's Rest with the zither across your knees. Pocket reads over your shoulder, his lips moving. The pigeon has grown old and fat and sleeps on the dresser. Ilse has put down her tea. She says it is the most interesting thing she has seen in ten years.

**Pocket:** Are we going?

**You:** I think so.

**Ilse:** I think we have to. The Silver Fiddle comes with a seat in the Choir. The Choir sings at the Convocation. I have never heard what it sings at the Convocation. They won't tell Listeners. It is considered too loud.

The thirteenth string hums, once, from its case on the table, a low long note, and stops.

## 15.14  "Pocket's Drum"  (`drum`)

- **Words:** 275 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The snare drum has a hole in it. It is a small neat round one, the size of a coin, in the middle of the head, where for ten years Pocket has hit it in exactly the same place. He holds it up in the morning light and puts a finger through. He says it is fine. He says it is a drum with a window. He says it with a face that is not fine at all.

**Closing scene**

Mending it takes a week. You go from town to town looking for skin, and for a man who knows how to stretch it. You find him at last in a cellar behind a tannery, a huge hairy old drum-maker called Orlo, who takes one look at the hole and says that it is the finest hole he has ever seen. He says he will not touch it. He says a hole like that is a drum's signature.

He gives Pocket a new drum instead, a great round barrel of a thing in ash and goatskin, with a bass like a church bell. He asks no money. He asks only to hear it played. Pocket plays. Orlo sits on a stool with his hands over his face. When it is over he says, in a muffled voice, that he made his first drum in 1843, and that this is the first time he has been sure it was worth it.

**Pocket:** (to you, in a whisper, afterwards, in the street, with the drum in his arms like a baby) I'll never be this good again. I'll never be this happy. I'd like to keep it.

The first town of the Circuit is Reedmarch, on the river, a pretty place of boats and bridges, with a green that runs down to the water and a bandstand in the middle. Eleven players have entered. They sit on benches under a striped awning, drinking beer, glaring. A herald in a tabard reads out the rules in a voice like a goose.

**Closing scene**

You draw a piper, a gaunt young man called Dace, with a bag the colour of old leather and a way of closing his eyes when he plays. He is good. He plays a jig so quick that the dancers on the green fall over each other, and a lament so slow that a woman in the crowd faints. When he has finished the herald turns to you.

You play the funeral tune, the ten notes with the skip in the middle. The pipes cannot follow it. They are too high and too bright. By the sixth note Dace has taken his lips from the mouthpiece, and by the tenth he is standing quite still, staring at his hands, as a man stares at a thing he has dropped and cannot find. The herald declares the contest. Dace bows. He walks off the green in silence.

**Ilse:** (afterwards, low) He has lost it. He doesn't know what he was playing. I watched his face. It simply went.

At the edge of the green, Dace sits on a bench with his pipes on his knee. A girl in a blue frock goes up to him with a cup of water. He thanks her. He turns the bag over in his hands. He says to nobody, 'I know I used to play this.'

## 15.16  "The Rule of the Duel"  (`rules`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 240 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Ilse reads the charter at the inn that night, line by line, with a pencil, by the light of two candles. She does not speak for an hour. She marks passages. She writes in a notebook. When she looks up her face is greenish, and her hands are shaking, and she says she thinks she knows what a surrendered tune is.

**Closing scene**

**Ilse:** The charter is not a metaphor. It says that the losing player shall surrender the tune. It says to the victor. It means it. When a duel of strings is played in the old form, the loser's tune is not defeated. It is taken. It goes into the winning player's ear, and out of the loser's. There is no way to give it back. It is in the charter. It is called the Quiet.

**You:** Then Dace is...

**Ilse:** Dace has lost the jig and the lament. He has not lost his hands. He has not lost the pipes. But he has lost whatever it was that made him play, and he may never get it back. I think the Circuit was meant to be a competition. I think it has been a harvest.

Pocket has gone very quiet. He says: 'Where do they go? The tunes. After they've been taken?' Ilse turns over a page. 'To the Academy,' she says. 'To the Master. There is a cabinet.' She says it in the voice of someone naming a disease.

## 15.17  "A Village That Forgot"  (`fennel`)

**Opening scene**

The letter comes to Ilse by the Circuit's post, forwarded from the Choir. It is from the schoolmistress of Fennel Cross, in a cramped anxious hand. It says that there is something wrong with the village. It says nobody can sing. It says the mothers have forgotten the lullaby, the one their own mothers sang, and the babies will not sleep, and there is a kind of exhaustion in the place. She asks whether the Choir can help.

**Closing scene**

Fennel Cross is a street of low grey cottages by a stream. It is very quiet. It is quiet in a way you have never met: not the quiet of sleep, but the quiet of a house where a clock has stopped. In every window there is a pale tired face. In every doorway there is a mother with a baby, jiggling, walking, humming something that is not quite anything.

The schoolmistress is a brisk worn woman in spectacles who has been up for nine nights. She shows you the churchyard and the well and the old green door. She says the lullaby is called Fennel Cross. She says it has been sung to every child born in the village for four hundred years. She says that on the first of March she woke and could not remember how it began.

**Ilse:** I remember the label on a jar.

**You:** I know.

**Pocket:** Is this what it is? Is this what he does? He takes a village's song, and they just stop?

**Schoolmistress:** (looking at the zither) I don't understand what you are saying. But if you can bring it back, I'll give you anything I have.

The second town on the Circuit is Saltwick, which is where the Academy stands. The tournament is held in the great hall with the glass dome. The crowd is larger than before. The champions of the nine regions sit in a row on the platform, in white. At the end of the row, in a plain grey dress, with a cello between her knees, sits Clarice Quill.

**Closing scene**

*[only if duel is 1]* **Clarice:** (stopping by you in the interval) I have been practising. I did not want to lose to you, and I have been careful not to be flattered. But I should tell you I have not slept since the autumn. I keep hearing the thirteenth string in the middle of the night.

*[only if duel is 2]* **Clarice:** (stopping by you in the interval) I told you I would not accept it. I want to know whether I was right. I do not play for the Academy now. I play for myself, and I have never been so frightened.

*[only if duel is 3]* **Clarice:** (stopping by you in the interval) We played well, you and I. I have been doing nothing but duets since the autumn, and I find I am bad at everything else.

The duel is brief. You draw a bass viol, a man you do not know, a retired concert master of sixty-three with a white moustache. He is gracious. He plays a nocturne of such sweetness that the entire hall sighs. You play a country dance, plain as bread. When you have finished he rises, and bows, and walks off the platform with his instrument under his arm like a man leaving a house he has loved.

**Clarice:** (in a low voice, as he passes) Don't. Don't take it. You don't have to. He doesn't even know what he's giving up.

You look at the tune in your head. It is there, small and bright, like a coin in a pocket. It is a beautiful nocturne. It is not yours. You find, for the first time, that you do not want it.

## 15.19  "The Cabinet"  (`cabinet`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 293 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The cabinet stands in Lamberd's study at the top of the Academy, behind a locked glass door, in a pool of lamplight. It is mahogany, with nine shelves, and each shelf holds forty glass jars with a cork and a label. There are three hundred and sixty. They glow faintly in the dusk, each a different colour: pearl, rose, pale gold, grey. You stand before them, with Ilse beside you, and for a moment neither of you can speak.

**Closing scene**

Ilse puts her ear to a jar. She listens. She straightens. 'It is a nocturne,' she says. 'It is the nocturne of the old concert master. It is quite complete. It is alive.' She moves along the shelf. 'And this is a drinking song. This is a hymn. This is a march that was played by a regiment that no longer exists.' She stops at one jar, small and pale, with a label in a faded hand. She says: 'This is a verse.'

It reads: Nan Hollin's Third Verse. You open the cork. A thread of silver light rises, as thin as a hair, and hums, very faintly, a phrase of three notes. You know it at once. It is the end of the paper your grandmother left. It is the missing line.

**Lamberd:** (from the doorway, in a flat quiet voice) I would rather you did not do that.

He stands in the door in his black coat, with a lamp in one hand. His face is in shadow. He is very still. The lamp does not shake. He says: 'I have been in that room every night for forty years. I have never once let anyone else in. I should like to explain, before you decide what to think.'

## 15.20  "Master Lamberd's Story"  (`lamberd`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 284 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

He tells it at the little table by the window, with a pot of tea gone cold, in a level voice, looking at his hands. He was a boy of eleven in a mining town, he says. He had a whistle. It was a tin one. He could play a hundred tunes on it. He entered the Circuit at twelve, and lost. He gave up a tune that his mother had taught him, a plain slow song she sang at the stove. He woke the next morning and could not remember how it went.

**Closing scene**

**Lamberd:** She died that spring. I could not sing it to her. I have been looking for it ever since. I built the Academy to look for it. I found that the tunes go somewhere, when they are taken. They go into the winner, or they go out of the world. I found I could catch them, in a jar, if I was quick. I have caught three hundred and sixty. I did not find mine.

**Ilse:** (very gently) Why did you keep them?

**Lamberd:** Because nobody else would. I have never been able to bear the idea of a thing being lost. I have forgotten a great deal about why I started. I am told I am very cruel. I have heard that it is true.

The thirteenth string hums softly in its case on the floor. He turns his head. For the first time in your acquaintance his face is naked. He says, 'That string is not in my cabinet, because I could not catch it. It is the only one I ever tried to take and could not. I have thought about it every day since the autumn.'

## 15.21  "Ilse's Ear"  (`ear`)

There is something that Ilse can do that no one has known. She does it first at Fennel Cross, on the third night, in the churchyard, with a lantern and a mother with a baby on her shoulder. She stands with her eyes shut and her head tilted. She listens to the jar in her mind. Then she opens her mouth, and sings.

**Closing scene**

It is not a good voice. It is thin, clear, a little flat, with a catch in the third line. But it is the song, all of it, every note, in the right order. The mother with the baby takes a long shaky breath. She lifts her head. She sings the second line, and then the third, and the baby, on her shoulder, takes its fist out of its mouth and looks at her, and shuts its eyes.

By morning the whole village has it. Women in doorways. Men at the well. An old man on a bench by the stream. They sing it to one another. They sing it to the children, and the children to the dogs. The schoolmistress cries, in the road, in front of the whole street, without trying to hide it.

**Ilse:** (hoarse, with a half-smile) It turns out I was never listening for the notes. I was listening for the people who needed them.

## 15.22  "The Seventh Town"  (`seventh`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Words:** 284 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Circuit's seventh town is Gravenhall, a grim black market-town with a cathedral. The tournament is held in the nave, under a ceiling of stone ribs, in front of an audience of two thousand. The Duke's Bandmaster is the champion of the region. He is a tall man in a scarlet coat with a beard like a spade and a trumpet the length of an arm. He has never lost a duel.

**Closing scene**

He plays a fanfare. It shakes the windows. It brings the dust down from the ribs of the roof in a fine grey rain. When it is done the whole nave is ringing, and the crowd is on its feet. You sit with the zither, small as a sparrow, in the middle of a pool of silence, and do not play a note.

The Bandmaster waits. The crowd waits. A baby cries. You close your eyes, and put your hand on the thirteenth string, and let it find its own note. It comes up out of the floor like a spring. It is not loud. It is simply there, a long soft sound, as large as the building, and where it passes the dust stops falling, and the echoes of the trumpet fold themselves up and go to sleep.

The Bandmaster lowers his horn. He stands for ages with his mouth slightly open, listening. Then he does a thing no one has ever seen him do. He takes off his hat, and holds it against his chest, and bows his head. The two thousand people in the nave do not move. The sound goes on. After a time, from somewhere very far away, a second sound answers it.

## 15.23  "Master Lamberd's Offer"  (`trade`)

He comes to you on the road to the eighth town, on foot, alone, without his coat. It is raining. He stands in the road in his shirt-sleeves, with water running down his face, and asks if he might speak. He has a new voice, a hoarse humble one, as if he had been practising it. He says he has a proposition, and that he does not expect you to like it.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `trade`; default: option 1)

> Master Lamberd offers every jar in his cabinet, all three hundred and sixty, in return for the thirteenth string.

1. Refuse. The string is not for sale, and the jars are not his to trade.
   - You refuse. He takes it quietly, with a slight bow, in the rain. He says he understands. He says it was a wretched thing to ask. He says he would be very grateful if you would do him the honour of considering a duel. He says it is the only way he knows how to ask for what he wants.
   - **Lamberd:** I have never asked anyone for anything. I find it is much worse than taking.
2. Accept: three hundred and sixty tunes are worth more than one string.
   - You accept. It is the hardest thing you have ever said. You say it with the zither in your arms and the rain in your face. Lamberd closes his eyes. When he opens them he is smiling, a terrible, tender smile, and he says, 'Thank you,' and your stomach turns over. The string, in the case on your back, goes cold. It does not hum again that night.
   - **Ilse:** (very low, appalled) What have you done?
3. Ask for a night to think, and a duel in the morning to settle it.

In the morning he is still there, soaked, sitting on a stone, quite calm. He says that the duel would be at noon.
   - **Pocket:** I think I'm starting to like him. I think that's a mistake.

**Closing scene**

The rain stops at midnight. The sky comes out in a field of stars. By the road, in the wet grass, the thirteenth string begins, faintly, to hum, in a note a little lower than it has ever gone. Ilse lies on her back with her notebook on her chest and her eyes open. She says, 'It is much nearer.' She does not say what.

## 15.24  "The Last Duel of the Circuit"  (`final`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 600 spirit stones, 2 Potential Pills, a technique insight
- **Words:** 155 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The last duel is held in the Palace of the Oldest Order, in the great hall, before the Choir of the Nine Bells. It is the oldest custom of the Circuit. The final two players stand on the black-and-white floor with their instruments, in a ring of candles. The Choir sits in its stalls along the wall, nine hundred voices in grey robes, absolutely silent. Above them, in the shadow of the dome, hangs an empty chair.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `final`; default: option 1)

> Master Lamberd stands across the floor with a viol in his hands, and a cabinet of tunes behind him in a cart.

1. Win the duel, and take the cabinet: let the jars be broken, and the tunes go free.
   - You win. It is not a close thing. When Lamberd's viol falters on the third bar you press, and the thirteenth string comes in, and the hall rings like a struck glass. The jars in the cart shatter, all three hundred and sixty, one after another, in a chain of small sweet sounds. The tunes rise like smoke and go out through the windows, in a cloud of pale lights, to wherever they belong.
   - **Lamberd:** (on his knees, not looking) I did not know they would be so beautiful.
2. Win the duel, and open the jars quietly: give each tune back to the one it was taken from.
   - You win. You say nothing about it. That night, with Ilse and Pocket and a cart, you take the jars one by one to the people from whom they were taken. It takes a year. You find the piper, and the old concert master, and the mother in the mining town. Each time you open a jar they stand a long time in silence. Then they begin, with a stumble, to sing. Lamberd drives the cart. He does not speak.
   - **Lamberd:** I am only the driver. I should like that to be clear.
3. Play with him: a duet of the viol and the zither, and let the music decide who is beaten.
   - You play with him. You ask him, in front of the whole Choir, to put down his bow and take it up again beside you. He hesitates. He is shaking. Then he lifts the viol. The two instruments find each other in the first four bars. It is a strange, slow, cumbersome thing, like two old men walking together. Halfway through, Lamberd begins to hum, without knowing, a tune. It is a plain slow song a woman sang at a stove.
   - **Ilse:** (a whisper, in the stalls, with her hands over her mouth) That is the one. That is his mother's.

**Closing scene**

The silence at the end is the silence of a church. The Choir does not move. Then, from the stalls, from nine hundred throats, in a single great breath, there comes a sound that is not applause. It is a low unanimous hum, a chord, which holds, and swells, and holds. It is the Choir's note. It is the note that it sings at the Convocation, which is not a hymn. It is the thirteenth string.

## 15.25  "What the Tune Was For"  (`tune2`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 1,000 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, gear a Major above you, a technique insight

**Opening scene**

The tunes go home. It takes a year, and a thousand miles, and a great deal of walking. Pocket keeps a ledger. He writes down every name in a schoolboy hand, with a drawing of the tune beside it. By the end he has filled four notebooks, and his drum is worn nearly through, and he has learned, to his surprise, that he can read.

**Closing scene**

*[only if trade is 2]* The thirteenth string is quiet now. It hangs on the zither pale and loose, and hums only when you are asleep. Ilse says it is waiting. She does not say for what. She sits by the fire at night with her ear to the wood, and her face, in the firelight, is calm, and sad.

*[only if trade is 1]* The thirteenth string hums every night, a little lower. Ilse sits with her ear to the wood and writes in her notebook. She says it has stopped being a note. She says it has become a direction.

*[only if trade is 3]* The thirteenth string hums every night, a little lower. Ilse says it is as near as a neighbour's door. She says that if you listened very hard you could hear someone on the other side, putting down a cup.

On the last night of the Circuit, at the Fiddler's Rest, there is a small party. Brewster has put out a ham. Orlo the drum-maker has come in a new coat. Clarice plays a duet with Pocket, a cello and a snare, that no one thought could work. At midnight Lamberd, who has been sitting in the corner with a glass of water and a face like a convalescent, stands, and asks if he might sing.

It is a plain, slow, wobbly little tune. He sings it in a cracked tenor, with his eyes shut, to the end. When he has finished nobody speaks. Then Brewster says: 'Is that all of it?' And Lamberd says, 'I believe so,' and sits down quite suddenly, and puts his face in his hands.

## 15.I2  Interlude: The Quiet  (between season 2 and season 3)

**Interlude**

The charter of the Circuit has been amended. A tune surrendered may be given back. It is the first change in three hundred years. It was proposed by a Listener, seconded by a drummer, and carried by an old man with a viol.

*[only if final is 1]* The jars were broken and the tunes flew out of the windows. For a week afterwards, all over the country, people woke at night humming something they could not place.

*[only if final is 2]* The jars were opened one at a time. It is said that if you stand in Fennel Cross on the first of March, at dusk, you can hear every mother in the village sing the same song, in the same key, to a different baby.

*[only if final is 3]* Master Lamberd plays the viol on Sundays in the Fiddler's Rest. He is not good. Brewster says he is the best the place has ever had.

Clarice Quill has taken the Academy. She has taken the clocks off the tower. She has taken the rule off the door. A new one has been put in its place, in brass, in her own hand: Any instrument may be played in this establishment that can be heard.

In the cabinet at the top of the Academy there is one jar left. It has not been opened. It is pale, and small, and sealed with black wax. The label says, in a hand like a row of wire: The Last Verse. Under it, in smaller letters: Do not open until the Door.

# 15.S3  Season 3: The Song at the Door

## 15.26  "The Note Wakes"  (`wake`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 238 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It has been humming for thirty years. On a night in October, in the barn at Haldane, with the wind in the thatch and Pocket asleep on a hay-bale with his arm round the drum, the thirteenth string stops. It does not fade. It stops, as a voice stops when a person has been told to wait. Ilse sits up in her blanket. She puts her ear to the wood. She is silent for so long that you think she has gone to sleep with her eyes open.

**Ilse:** It is not humming. It is counting.

**Closing scene**

She writes it down by lantern light. It is nine notes, repeated, with a rest between. Low, low, high, low, low, high, high, high, low. She plays it on your spare fiddle, and it is a phrase you have heard a hundred times in your life without knowing. You have heard it in the bell at Originis. You have heard it from the Choir. It is the first line of the muster call.

**Pocket:** (waking, with straw in his hair) What's the muster?

**Ilse:** It is what you play for the people who are about to go through.

The thirteenth string takes up the phrase again, very quietly. This time it does not stop. It runs through the nine notes and starts at the beginning. It sounds, you think, rather like someone knocking, from a long way off, politely, on a door.

## 15.27  "The Lowest Pipe"  (`organ`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `palace`.  "Go to the Palace of the Oldest Order, at Originis, and ask for the organ loft."
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 313 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Palace of the Oldest Order has an organ in the great hall, nine storeys high, with five thousand pipes and a console like the bridge of a ship. It is played once a year at the Convocation. It has a pipe that nobody uses, at the very bottom of the case, as wide as a well. Ilse has wanted to hear it since she was nine. She asks the Master of the Choir. The Master of the Choir goes the colour of tallow, and says that it is not played.

**Closing scene**

The Master relents. He takes you up through the dark behind the pipes, along a catwalk, past the great gleaming shapes. At the bottom of the case, in a niche of black stone, there is a pipe thirty feet long with a stop of unpolished iron. It has a note painted on it in white. The note is a quarter-tone below the lowest A of the organ. It is the note of the thirteenth string.

**Master:** The Choir does not sing a hymn at the Convocation. It never has. The Choir holds one note. It holds it for the length of the Convocation, nine hundred of us, in relays, without a pause. It is the only thing the Palace does that is older than the Palace. We do not know why. We were told it was a tuning.

**Ilse:** Tuning what?

**Master:** We were told: the Door.

He lays his hand on the great iron stop and does not pull it. His fingers are trembling. 'It was last sounded,' he says, 'in the year of the great snow. Someone brought a stringed instrument to the Convocation, and it answered, and the pipe answered it. The Master of the day had it sealed. He said it was an interference.' He looks at the zither on your back. 'He did not say with what.'

## 15.28  "The Roll of the Crossed"  (`roll`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `garrison`.  "Go to the Garrison of the Crossed, {@garrison}."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 280 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Garrison of the Crossed stands on a bare plain at the edge of the world. It is a fortress with its gates open, whole and empty, with the beds made and the lamps trimmed. In the muster hall there is a long stone carved with names in a hundred different hands. THE CROSSED, it says at the top. You have not come to read it; you have come because the string has been pointing here since the barn.

**Closing scene**

You walk the length of the stone with a lantern. Ilse follows, reading aloud in a low voice, like a woman reading the lesson in church. Some of the names are only initials. Some are in languages that are no longer spoken. About halfway down, in a small upright pencil hand, scratched rather than cut, there is a line you know. It is a signature you have seen on the flyleaf of a hymn-book: N. Hollin. Under it, in the same hand: Gone to see about a string.

**Pocket:** (reading over your shoulder, with the drum silent for once) That's your gran.

**You:** It can't be.

**Ilse:** It is the same hand. It is the same paper. Look at the date.

The date is the year of the great snow. You stand there with the lantern, in the cold, in a long empty room that smells of lamp oil. The thirteenth string, on your back, makes a small, terrible, clear sound, like a person catching their breath. Your grandmother did not die in the winter. She was called. She went through the Door with a zither on her knee, and left the other end of the string behind her, with you.

## 15.29  "What the Garrison Sings"  (`hymn`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 243 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

They are about to muster. A line forms in the yard at dusk: a hundred men and women in good boots, with their blades at their sides and a small lamp apiece. They stand in rows. They do not speak. A tall woman with a grey plait walks along the line with a ledger, checking names. When she has finished she nods, once, to nobody. Then from somewhere in the ranks, a single voice begins to sing.

**Closing scene**

It is the muster hymn. It is plain and slow and not at all warlike. It has three verses and a refrain. It goes through the yard like a river through a field, rising, until a hundred voices hold it, low and steady and quite without fear. You stand at the back with the zither across your arm, and Ilse puts a hand over her mouth. The refrain has nine notes. The thirteenth string joins it, softly, on the fourth.

They stop at the end of the second verse. There is a pause, a gap in the shape of a verse, and then they sing the refrain again and begin to file out through the gate. Ilse's face is wet. She says: 'There is a third. They do not sing it. They have never sung it. Listen to the shape.'

**You:** I have it.

**Ilse:** What?

**You:** Three lines, in pencil, on a piece of paper from a farmhouse. And a last verse, in a jar.

## 15.30  "Mister Rest"  (`rest`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet rest (walk to their tile).  "Hear what Mister Rest has come to say."
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "rest")`
- **Words:** 270 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

He is waiting at the foot of the stair, a tidy bald man in a grey suit with a tuning-fork in his waistcoat pocket and a silence about him like a closed door. He lifts his hat. When he speaks, you notice, there is a faint hush after every word, as if the air round him had been taught to listen.

**Rest:** Mister Rest. I am a Guest of the Court. I have come about the string.

**Closing scene**

He walks beside you for a mile under the stars, without hurry. He says that the Court has no quarrel with music. He says it is a perfectly respectable art. He says it has, however, a difficulty with one note, a note that has been sounded in the Garden for as long as the Garden has been, and has been answered, he says, from the other side. It keeps a door ajar. The Court would be extremely grateful if it were allowed to close.

**Rest:** I take one thing. It is a rule of my trade. I only ever take a sound. I should like to take that one. I would leave you every other note you own. I would leave you the zither, and the drum, and the cello. You would play to the end of your days. Only the thirteenth would be gone.

**Ilse:** (very quietly) You would take the Door's ear.

**Rest:** I would take its voice. It is a great kindness to a door to let it stop calling.

The thirteenth string, in the case on your back, goes quiet. It is the quiet of an animal in a hedge.

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `rest`; default: option 1)

> A Guest of the Court asks for the thirteenth note, and offers the rest of your music.

1. Refuse him to his face, and play the note.
   - You play it. It is as loud as you can make it, in the dark, in the road, with the whole of your body. The note rolls out over the plain and comes back from the stones. Mister Rest does not flinch. He stands with his hat in his hand and his head a little on one side, hearing it out, and when it dies he says in a tone of the deepest respect: 'Ah. That is a good deal harder than it looks.'
   - **Rest:** I shall be back. I do hope you will keep your tuning.
2. Ask what the Court wants the Door shut for, and listen to the answer.
   - You ask. He is delighted to be asked. He tells you, at length, over a mile of road, in a low pleasant voice, that the Court is tired. He says the Garden has been ringing for a very long time, and nobody has had a night's sleep. He says it is not malice. It is exhaustion. He says if the door were shut, and the calling stopped, a great many people on the other side could rest. You listen. When he has finished you find that your eyes are wet.
   - **Rest:** You see the difficulty. I do not hate it. I only want it quiet.
3. Offer him a song instead: one note of your own, freely given.
   - You offer him a song. You take the fiddle from the hay-cart, and play, for a single minute, the plainest tune you know. When you finish he is standing very still. He has taken the tuning-fork from his pocket and is holding it in both hands, looking at it. 'I have never been given one,' he says. 'I take, you see. Nobody has ever thought to give.' He puts the fork away with great care.
   - **Rest:** I shall keep that. I should like to say that it is a great deal more than I deserve.

## 15.31  "Rounding Up the Players"  (`ensemble`)

**Opening scene**

You need an ensemble. The thirteenth string is a rope, and the Door is a long way off, and a rope can be pulled harder by many hands. Ilse draws up a list, in her upright script, of every player you have met on the Circuit. There are forty names. It begins with Clarice, goes through Orlo and Brewster and the old concert master, and ends, in a smaller hand, with the words: Lamberd (if he will).

**Closing scene**

You write forty letters. Thirty-one answer. They arrive at Haldane in carts and on foot, a straggle of fiddlers, pipers, fifers, drummers, cellists, one man with a harp the size of a door. They fill the barn. They fill the lane. They sleep in the hay and the stable and the church. The bride's father, now a very large grandfather, feeds them all, and weeps when he is thanked.

**Clarice:** I brought the cello. I brought seven students. I told the Academy I was going on a walking holiday. They were very understanding. I think they assumed I'd gone mad.

Lamberd is the last to arrive. He comes at dusk on foot, in his best black coat, with a viol under his arm and a very small hat. He stands in the doorway of the barn. Thirty-one people turn round. Nobody speaks. After a long moment Pocket gets up from the straw, crosses the floor, and says: 'You're late. We've saved you a bench.'

## 15.32  "Rehearsal in the Rain"  (`rehearse`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 279 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It rains for nine days. The ensemble rehearses in the barn, thirty-two players on straw bales and upturned buckets, in a noise like a barn on fire. Nobody can agree on the key. The harpist, a mild man called Fenwick, plays everything in a mode that has not been heard since the Flood. The pipers refuse to sit with the viols. Pocket, who is conducting because nobody else will, has made a baton from a wooden spoon.

**Closing scene**

On the sixth day it all falls apart. Clarice and Lamberd have a row about tempo, in front of everyone, in clipped voices, with the cello and the viol held across their bodies like swords. The pipers go out. The drummers go after them. The harp falls over. A hen walks across the stage. Ilse puts down her notebook, walks to the middle of the barn, and says in a high clear voice, 'Please, will you all be quiet.'

They are. It is the first time she has ever raised her voice. She stands there, very straight, in her grey coat, with ink on her cuff and her ears pink. She says that she has listened to every one of them for three weeks. She says that each of them is a very good player. She says that they have not yet noticed that they are all playing the same piece. She says: 'Hear the note under it.'

She lifts her hand. She nods to Pocket. He raises the spoon, and counts four. And thirty-two players, who have not once played together in tune, find the thirteenth string under their feet, like a floor, and stand on it.

## 15.33  "The Last Jar"  (`jar`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 331 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Lamberd brings it on the last night of the rehearsal, in a handkerchief, from an inner pocket. It is a small glass jar sealed with black wax. He holds it out on the flat of his palm, like a boy with a bird's egg. He says he has carried it for thirty years and has never once opened it. He says it is not from the Circuit. It was left at the Academy by a woman, on a night of snow, with a note.

**Closing scene**

**Lamberd:** She said: keep this until somebody comes who can hear the string. She said I would know them. I did not. I thought it would be a Master. It is a young person with a hat on the ground. I have been unfair to you, and a great fool. I should like to be allowed to apologise.

You break the wax. A thread of silver light rises and loops in the air above your head. It is a voice. It is thin, and old, and very close. It is your grandmother's. She is humming. She is singing a verse, low and slow and a little off the note, as she sang over the washing-up. It is three lines, and it ends the way the hymn ends in the yard of the Garrison, and the pencil fragment, and the song.

**Nan Hollin:** (in the light, faint, from a long way off) If you are hearing this, my dear, it means you have come far enough. I never could tune it, you know. I tried. I thought it was my fault. It was a rope, and I was the other end. I went through to hold it. I am in a dim long room with a great many others, and we are all humming it. It is very restful. Come when you are ready. Play it at the Door.

The light folds up, and goes out. The barn is utterly silent. After a time Pocket blows his nose.

## 15.34  "The Concert at the Door"  (`concert`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 600 spirit stones, 2 Potential Pills, a technique insight
- **Words:** 146 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The ensemble marches to the Garrison in the first week of spring, thirty-two players in a long file, with carts of instruments and a cook-wagon. They set up on the plain, under the grey sky, in front of the open gates. The line is there, as always, patient, in boots, with lamps. A tall woman with a grey plait stands at its head. She watches the players unpack. She says nothing at all. When Pocket sets up his drum, she turns her head and looks at the horizon.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `tune`; default: option 1)

> The ensemble is in place. The string is a rope, and the Door is at the other end.

1. Play it to tune the string: send the full note down the rope and let it settle.
   - You play. The thirteenth string rings, and thirty-one instruments take its note and give it back. For the first time in the world it sounds against something and does not echo. It settles. It is as if a lamp in a window has been trimmed to its proper height. The string is in tune. Ilse takes the zither, afterwards, in her hands, and holds it a long time, and says: 'Quiet. It's so quiet. Is it supposed to be so quiet?' It is. It is a rope with the weight taken off.
   - **Clarice:** That is the most beautiful noise I've ever made, and I'm no longer sure it belongs to us.
2. Play it for the line: a muster hymn with its third verse, for the called, whatever else happens.
   - You play the muster hymn, all three verses. It is the first time the third has been heard on the plain. The line stands, in boots, with lamps, and listens. At the third verse a woman at the head of the file puts her hand to her mouth. By the refrain the whole line is singing. They sing it a hundred strong, in the cold, in the rain that has begun, and then they file in through the gate, one after another, with their lamps held high. Not one of them looks back. Not one of them is afraid.
   - **Lamberd:** I have conducted four thousand concerts. That is the only one I would call music.
3. Play it as a message: ask the other end, plainly, to answer.
   - You play it as a question. It is a single phrase, nine notes, rising. You send it down the string with every instrument you have. for ages there is nothing. Then, from very far away, a single answer comes up the rope. It is a voice, humming, on the same nine notes, a fraction lower. It is a woman's. It is a woman who has hummed the same phrase for forty years, patient and steady, in a long dim room, to anyone who might hear.
   - **Ilse:** (a whisper) She answered.

**Closing scene**

The rain falls. The plain is silver. At the edge of the line, the tall woman with the plait turns to you, at last, and inclines her head. It is a small, formal, courteous movement. She says nothing. She puts her hand over her heart. Behind her the gates stand open on a corridor of lamps.

## 15.35  "Mister Rest Listens"  (`listens`)

He stands at the back of the plain after it is over, alone, under his hat, in the rain. He does not come forward. He is holding the tuning-fork in both hands. When you go to him he is looking at the gate. His face is, for the first time, quite without its courtesy.

**Closing scene**

*[only if rest is 1]* **Rest:** I shall not take it. I should like you to know that. I came to take it, and I found I could not. I have taken the sound of two thousand things. I never once heard one of them. I am not at all sure what to do.

*[only if rest is 2]* **Rest:** You were right to let me say it. I should like to say it was not an argument. It was a confession. I have been tired for a very long time. I had not noticed that the tiredness was a sound.

*[only if rest is 3]* **Rest:** I have your tuning-fork. I mean, you have mine. I mean, I have been given a note, and I do not know where to put it.

He lifts his hat. He walks away across the plain in the rain, a small grey figure with a tuning-fork, humming. He is a little flat. He stops, and tries again. He gets it, on the third go. He goes on, a tiny tuneful shape against the horizon, and is gone.

**Pocket:** (watching him go) I think he'll be all right. I think he's going to learn the drum.

## 15.36  "Tuning"  (`verse`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 2,000 spirit stones, +3 potential, 4 Potential Pills, gear a Major above you, a technique insight

**Opening scene**

The thirteenth string is still. It hangs pale on the zither, quiet as a thread. It is the first time in your life you have seen it at rest. You sit with it across your knees on the bench in the barn at Haldane in the blue of the evening, with the swallows going over the roof, and look at it for ages. You have one verse left, and one choice.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `verse`; default: option 1)

> The last verse is yours: three lines, in a jar, in a pencil fragment, in your grandmother's hum.

1. Keep it. Some tunes are better held than given.
   - You keep it. You say it aloud once, to the barn, in a low voice, and then never again. It lives in your head like a coin in a pocket. Clarice asks, once, what it was. You say it was a verse. She nods. She says it is the sort of thing that is better asked about than answered.
   - **Ilse:** It is the first secret you have ever kept. I think it suits you.
2. Teach it to the Choir, so that the Convocation can sing it with the rest.
   - You teach it to the Choir. It takes a winter. Nine hundred voices in grey robes learn it from a Listener and a drummer and a young woman with a cello, in the great hall, in the evenings, by lamplight. At the next Convocation they sing it. It is not loud. It is the quietest thing the hall has ever heard. In the stalls, a man in a plain apron puts down his spoon.
   - **???:** (afterwards, very faint) I have heard that. I have heard it somewhere. I cannot think where.
3. Take it to the Door, and sing it yourself, when your turn comes.
   - You carry it with you. Years go by. On a clear evening in autumn, at the end of a long life, you stand at the Door with the zither on your back and Ilse's hand in yours. The line has gone in. The gate is open. You put the zither to your knee and play the three lines. It is not a good performance. It is not meant to be. At the end the thirteenth string answers, in a voice that is half an octave lower, and you walk in.
   - **Pocket:** (gruff, at the gate, his drum on his shoulder) We'll keep the fire lit.

**Closing scene**

The zither has thirteen strings. Twelve are steel. The thirteenth is pale and thin and does not sound unless it is spoken to. Ilse says it is perfectly in tune. She says she has checked it eleven times. She says that it is in tune with something, and she does not mind what.

You hang it on the wall of the barn at Haldane over the hearth. At night, when the fire has burned low, it hums a little, softly, as a cat does, in its sleep.

## 15.I3  Interlude: The Long Quiet  (between season 3 and season 4)

**Interlude**

The zither hangs over the hearth. The thirteenth string is quiet and perfectly in tune. Pocket's drum has a hole in it. Ilse listens to the evening with her eyes shut.

One night the string begins to count again. Nine notes, with a rest between. It is the muster call. It is, this time, being played on purpose.

It is a road, and it has been laid very carefully by somebody who wanted you to find it.
