   - You play it once. It is three lines. The pipe, nine storeys down, takes up the thirteenth note and holds it under your voice, and the Choir rises and sings. It is the quietest thing the hall has ever heard. At the last line the thirteenth string breaks, with a small clean sound, and lies curled on the wood like a hair.
   - **Ilse:** (a whisper) It's done. It's been tuned. By being let go.
2. Go: play it through to the end, and go where it goes.
   - You play it to the end. The sound goes down under the flags, and something answers: a woman humming, a long way down. You rise. Ilse takes the zither from your hands, gently, and holds it against her chest. She says: 'I'll keep it for you.' You walk down the stair. The note goes with you, getting nearer, until it is all around you, and you are in tune.
3. Hold the latch: sit with the Choir and play the muster for each line, for as long as it comes.
   - You sit with the Choir all winter. Each time the line files in at the gate, you play them through, the hymn and the third verse. It is the humblest music you have ever made. It is never once applauded. A soldier stops, near the end, and puts a coin in your hat, and says it is for the zither. You have never, in your life, been paid better.

**Closing scene**

The barn at Haldane has a new sign over the door, hand-painted. It says: ZITHER DAY, FIRST SATURDAY OF MAY. Under it, in smaller letters: All instruments welcome. Do not tune them. There is a pigeon on the roof of the barn with a bit of green ribbon on its leg. It has the look of an animal with an appointment.

## 15.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

The zither hangs over the hearth in the barn at Haldane. It has thirteen strings, and one of them is in tune.

*[only if tune is 1]* The string is quiet. When you play it, the sound goes down the rope and does not come back. Ilse says that is what it is for.

*[only if tune is 2]* On the plain at the edge of the world a line forms every dusk. It sings three verses now. Nobody can say who taught it.

*[only if tune is 3]* On certain evenings, at dusk, the thirteenth string hums a phrase of nine notes. Some distance away, very faintly, a woman hums it back.

*[only if rest is 1]* A bald man in a grey suit has been seen at the back of the Choir's stalls with a tuning-fork. He never sings. He is said to be learning.

*[only if rest is 2]* A bald man in a grey suit sits at the end of a bench in the Fiddler's Rest with a glass of water, listening. He tips generously.

*[only if rest is 3]* Mister Rest plays the triangle, on Sundays, in a chapel in the north. It is a very small triangle. He plays it a little flat.

*[only if verse is 1]* There is a verse that you have never sung. You know it by heart.

*[only if verse is 2]* The Choir of the Nine Bells sings a quiet verse after the muster hymn, once a year. Nobody has told them where it came from.

*[only if verse is 3]* Your grandmother's third verse was the first thing the line sang, on the day you went in.

*[only if love is 1]* Ilse Ferrant listens to you with her eyes shut. She does it still, every evening, as though it were a thing worth the trouble.

*[only if love is 2]* Ilse walks beside you on the road, a little behind, with a notebook. She says she is writing a book about listening. It has no first chapter.

*[only if love is 3]* Ilse keeps a perfect fifth in a drawer of her desk, on a card, in her upright hand. She says she will frame it. She does not.

*[only if latch is 1]* A single string lies curled on the mantel in the barn at Haldane, pale as a hair. It hums when it is spoken to.

*[only if latch is 2]* The zither hangs over the hearth. Nobody plays it. In the evenings, if you are quiet, you can hear it answering a note from very far away.

*[only if latch is 3]* The Choir of the Nine Bells sings a third verse after the muster hymn. A zither player sits at the back, in grey, and nobody has ever asked her name.

Pocket drums at weddings. His drum has a hole in it, a small neat one, in the middle of the head. He says it is a window. Through it, if you put your eye to it on a clear night, you can see a line of lamps going in at a gate.

## 15.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

You stay in the Garden. The Choir of the Nine Bells has a new member in the back stalls with a pale-stringed zither, and at the Convocation it holds the quarter-tone under the organ without a rest.

*[only if not dead.ilse]* {ilse.He} listens to you with {ilse.his} eyes shut, still.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

In the Gardener's army you are the one who plays at the muster. The hymn has three verses now. Nobody knows who taught the soldiers the third.

On the night before a battle you play it quietly, and the line sings.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You step through the Seam with a zither on your back. On the far side there is a long dim room full of people humming one note, and one of them looks up.

You sit down beside her. You play the verse you have been keeping. She says: you took your time.

**You are struck down by the array**

The array took you. In the dark, very low, below hearing, a string is being played by someone who is not you.

It is perfectly in tune with nothing at all. You join in.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden goes out. The barn goes out, and the Fiddler's Rest, and the green in Reedmarch with its bandstand.

The last thing to go is a note, a quarter-tone below the lowest pipe of the organ, still sounding.

# 16.S1  Season 1: The Debt

## 16.1  "Born Owing"  (`owing`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** Go to the place `mine`.  "Report to the pit-head at Cinder Deep, {@mine}, for your first shift."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, 1 Cultivation Pill
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "kell")`
- **Words:** 297 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Cinder Deep is a town of four hundred houses built on the lip of a silver mine, all of them the same grey, all of them the Company's. The Company built the houses. The Company built the chapel. The Company built the shop, the school, the pump and the graveyard, and it charges rent on every one of them, payable in scrip, which is good in the Company's shop and nowhere else.

You were born in house 211 on a Tuesday in the wet season. The midwife was a Company midwife. The cradle was a Company cradle. By the time you were a week old you owed the Lode Company eleven scrip, four pennies and a farthing, and the sum was written in the ledger under your name in a clerk's brown ink. It has been growing ever since.

**Closing scene**

The pit-head is a grey wooden tower with a wheel on top and a cage underneath, and round the foot of it, at five in the morning, a hundred people in canvas coats stand in the dark with their lamps. Nobody talks. The wheel turns. The cage goes down with a clank. It comes up empty, and the next forty go in, and you are among them.

**Kell:** Name?

**You:** You know my name.

**Kell:** I know your debt. Name's what I call you when I like you. Lamp.

Foreman Kell is fifty-five, as broad as a door and as grey as the stone, with a black moustache and a voice that has never been raised in its life. He hands you a lamp, a pick and a tin of dripping. The lamp is rented. It is the Company's. It is half a scrip a week, and he does not apologise for it, and neither do you.

## 16.2  "The First Shift"  (`shift`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Have 2 friends.  "Work your first month: make two friends."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **Words:** 250 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The cage drops four hundred feet in a minute and a half, with a sound like a wet cough. Then there is the gallery. It runs left and right into the dark, as low as a church pew and as long as a street, lit by a string of lamps every thirty feet. The air is hot and tastes of copper. Somewhere far off a pick is going, clink, clink, clink, steady as a pulse.

**Closing scene**

You learn the work in a week. You learn the rhythm: swing, strike, rest, swing. You learn to read the seam by the colour of the dust, and to hear a bad roof by the way the timber ticks, and to eat with your hands black and not care. You learn that the coal-tits in the tool shed are unlucky and the mice are lucky and that you do not whistle underground.

The man on your left is called Dob Pennyfeather, a lanky cheerful lad of twenty-two with a gap in his teeth and a pony he calls Marmalade. The woman on your right is a thin silent widow who works the face with a short pick and has not been seen to speak since the spring. They are both fast. You are slower. They never say so.

**Dob:** You get used to it. It takes three weeks. After that you stop noticing the dark and start noticing the other thing.

**You:** What other thing?

**Dob:** The quiet. It's got a sound. You'll hear it.

## 16.3  "Company Scrip"  (`scrip`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Hold 500 spirit stones.  "Save against the debt: hold 500 spirit stones."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "dob")`
- **Words:** 263 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Pay day is the last Friday of the month, at the pay-window in the Company shop, through a brass grille. A clerk with a green eyeshade counts out your wages in scrip. He counts it twice, so that you may see him do it. Then he counts out what you owe: rent, lamp, oil, the doctor, the chapel, the school, the pump, and the interest. He counts that twice as well. He pushes the remainder under the grille. It is eleven pennies.

**Closing scene**

It takes you a year and a half to get the first five hundred. You do it by working double shifts, by picking up spilled ore after the loaders, by catching rats for the shop at a farthing a head and cutting your own hair. You sleep four hours. You eat at the Company canteen, where the stew is grey and the bread is damp, and you send up a prayer of thanks for the day the cook went on strike.

When you have it in your hand you walk to the window and ask for the figure. The clerk looks at the ledger. He turns a page. He turns another. He says that the Company has been pleased to note a rise in expenses in the previous quarter, owing to the price of oil. He says that, with allowance, the debt stands at eight hundred and sixty. It was nine hundred and ten.

**Dob:** (at your elbow, in the queue, softly) Forty-eight less. That's good. That's actually good. My dad took thirty years to get under a hundred.

## 16.4  "The Company Medic"  (`medic`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet ottoline (walk to their tile).  "Visit the Company medic at the infirmary."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "ottoline")`
- **Words:** 294 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The infirmary is a whitewashed hut by the pit-head with six cots and a stove and a smell of carbolic. It is run by the Company's medic, a tall, quick, untidy person in a stained white coat who is paid to keep the workforce at its work and has, as far as anyone can tell, never done so. They sit on the edge of a cot bandaging a boy's hand and singing to him under their breath. They look up. They do not stop singing until the knot is tied.

**Closing scene**

**Ottoline:** Harl. Ottoline Harl, M.D. I'm told that makes me a doctor. I've been here two years. I'm not allowed to prescribe rest, which is the only thing the men need, so I prescribe cough linctus and tell them to take it lying down.

{ottoline.He} is about thirty, with ink on {ottoline.his} cuffs and straw in {ottoline.his} hair and a wry crooked mouth. {ottoline.He} listens to your chest with a cold steel trumpet. {ottoline.He} says that your lungs are good, your heart is good and your back is a disgrace. {ottoline.He} says that in eight years you will be coughing black. {ottoline.He} says it in the voice of a woman reporting the weather.

**Ottoline:** I keep a book. It's not the Company's. It's mine. Every man and woman in the pit, with the date of every cough. I've been sending copies to the Medical College for two years. They haven't answered. I'd be grateful if you'd come and look at it some evening and tell me whether I'm mad.

You say you will. You go on the Wednesday, with a bag of apples. It is a long thin book, in a small crabbed hand, and every page is a roll of the dead.

## 16.5  "A Tapping in the Wall"  (`tap`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 248 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It starts in the fourth gallery in the wet season. A man puts his ear to the rock to hear for water and hears a tapping. It is slow and regular, three and a pause, three and a pause, like someone with a knuckle, a long way off. He thinks it is the next shift. It is not. The next shift is at the top of the shaft, eating.

**Closing scene**

By the end of the month it is the talk of the pit. The old hands say it is the Knockers: the little dead men of the mine, who tap to warn of a fall. The young ones say it is water in the pipes. Kell says it is nothing, and puts a lamp on it, and goes away. The widow with the short pick lays her cheek flat against the rock and listens, and straightens, and goes quite white, and crosses herself.

**You:** What does it say?

**Widow:** (the first words she has spoken since the spring) It's counting. It's counting us.

You put your ear to the wall that evening, alone, with the lamp turned low. The rock is cold and slightly damp. For a long minute there is only the sound of your own pulse. Then it comes, very faint, deep down, in the dark. Three and a pause. Three and a pause. And then, quite clearly, a fourth. It is a different rhythm, and it is faster, and it has your name in it.

## 16.6  "The Fall in Number Six"  (`cavein`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 159 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It goes at ten past two on a Thursday afternoon, with a sound like a door slammed in the next county. The floor jumps. The lamps swing. A long rolling thunder runs down the gallery from the north, and then there is dust, and in the dust there is a cry. Dob was at the face of Number Six. You were thirty yards back with the cart. You run.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `rescue`; default: option 1)

> Dob Pennyfeather is under a fall in Number Six, and the timbers are groaning.

1. Dig him out by hand, now, with the others, and never mind the roof.
   - You dig. Forty people, with picks and shovels and their bare hands, tearing at the rock in the dust and the dark. It takes fifty minutes. You get him out with a broken leg and a cracked skull and a smile on his face, and as the last stone comes away the roof behind you drops with a roar. You are nearly under it. Kell hauls you out by the collar and swears for the first time in your acquaintance.
   - **Kell:** Never again. Do you hear me? Never again. Not even for him.
2. Shore the roof first, even if it takes the hour he may not have.
   - You shore. It is the hardest thing you have ever done. You stand in the dust and give orders, quickly and in a flat voice, and cut props with the saw and set them with the maul while a man's voice, somewhere under the stone, calls for his mother. It takes an hour and ten. When you reach him he is grey and cold. He is breathing. The roof holds, over all of you, for the whole time, and you could weep.
   - **Ottoline:** (afterwards, on the surface, with a bandage in her teeth) That was either the bravest or the coldest thing I have ever seen. I'd say both.
3. Send for the medic and wait: she knows what a body will stand.
   - You send for the medic. It is the longest eight minutes of your life. Ottoline comes down the shaft on the cage with a bag and a lamp and an expression of cold fury. She crawls into the hole, flat on her stomach, with Kell holding her ankles. She says in a calm voice that he has lost a lot of blood and that if you move that rock he dies. She works for forty minutes. You cut the stone away on her word.
   - **Dob:** (faintly, as they lift him) Is the pony all right?

**Closing scene**

They bring him up on a hurdle at dusk, grey with dust, bandaged to the eyes, and lay him on a cot in the infirmary. The whole town stands in the yard in the half-dark, without speaking, in canvas coats, holding lamps. The widow with the short pick is at the front. She has her hand over her mouth. When the doctor comes out, wiping her hands, and says he will live, nobody cheers. A great breath goes out of them, like wind going out of a field.

## 16.7  "The Meeting in the Shed"  (`shed`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Have 6 friends.  "Raise the shed: make six friends."
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `TaleMiner::mark`
- **Words:** 281 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The meeting is held in the tool shed on a Sunday night, in secret, with the door barred and a lamp in a bucket. Forty people crowd in among the picks and the coils of rope. Ottoline stands on an upturned crate with the long thin book in her hands. She does not make a speech. She reads out names. She reads out the date of every death in the pit in the last two years, and the cause, and the Company's estimate of the cost.

**Closing scene**

She reads for twenty minutes. By the end there is no sound but the lamp. A man at the back is weeping without any noise at all. The widow with the short pick is holding her lamp in both hands and staring at it. When Ottoline closes the book she says that she is not a union man and does not know how to run a union. She says she knows how to count.

**Ottoline:** It's thirty-one in two years. Thirty-one dead, out of four hundred. And the Company has paid out, in compensation, a total of forty scrip. I put it to you that this is not a mine. It is a slaughterhouse with a chapel.

It is a short meeting. At the end of it they take a vote, by hands, and carry a motion which is read out, rather unsteadily, by Dob from his hurdle in the corner, with a bandaged head. It says that the Cinder Deep Miners' Fellowship shall be formed this night. It says that there shall be a committee. It says that nobody shall sign anything, or say anything, to anyone, without the others being told.

## 16.8  "The Strike"  (`strike`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 400 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 190 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Company hears of the Fellowship in a week. It is, after all, a small town. By Monday Mister Sable is on the morning coach from the city, a plump bland man in a bowler hat and a silk waistcoat, with a case of papers and a smile. He receives the committee in the Company office, in a room with a carpet, and tells them that he is delighted to hear of their interest in safety. He says the Company will consider it. He says in the meantime wages are cut by a fifth.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `strike`; default: option 1)

> The Fellowship has called a vote on whether to strike, and you have the casting voice.

1. Vote to strike, now, all four hundred, and shut the pit.
   - The pit shuts at noon on the Tuesday. Four hundred people walk out of the cage into the daylight and stand in the yard, blinking, with their lamps in their hands. Nobody says anything. There is a quiet that is not a defeat. The wheel on the pit-head stops turning for the first time in ninety years. Sable comes to the window of the office, and looks down, and for a moment loses his smile.
   - **Kell:** (low, at your shoulder, with his moustache working) I've been thirty years waiting to see that wheel stop. I'll be damned if I'll start it.
2. Vote to wait: gather more, and strike in the spring when the stocks are low.
   - You vote to wait. The Fellowship grumbles, but the vote carries. For four months you meet in the shed in secret, and keep the cuts, and put by what you can, and write letters. In March, when the Company's stocks of silver are as low as they will ever be, you strike. The pit stops. The Company has no ore to fill its orders. Sable is on the coach by the end of the week, with an offer.
   - **Ottoline:** Patience is a terrible thing in a cause. It is also, I find, devastatingly effective.
3. Vote against, and negotiate: put the case to Sable in writing and bring the Medical College in.
   - You write to Sable. It is a long polite letter, in a clear hand, listing the deaths, the figures and the reforms asked. Ottoline writes to the College. The College, to everyone's astonishment, answers. Within a month a Commission of three grave elderly doctors is on the coach to Cinder Deep, with notebooks, and spends a week underground, and goes back to the city saying nothing at all. Sable's smile has gone grey at the edges.
   - **Ottoline:** It's the first time in two years anybody has answered me. I wanted you to know I had a small cry.

**Closing scene**

at last it is not one thing but all of them. The pit is closed for six weeks, or the stocks are low, or the Commission has reported, or the press in the city has taken an interest. Whatever it is, on a grey Friday in spring, Sable comes to the pit-head with a paper. It is a short paper, and he reads it aloud in a thin high voice, looking over the heads of the crowd. It says that the Company, in recognition of the loyalty of its workforce, will recognise the Fellowship.

## 16.9  "Sable's Offer"  (`offer`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Hold 2,000 spirit stones.  "Stand on your own feet: hold 2,000 spirit stones."
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **Words:** 235 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

He calls on you privately, on a wet evening, at house 211, with his hat in his hand. He sits on the one chair. He accepts a cup of tea. He says, in a pleasant reasonable voice, that he has been very impressed. He says he has had his eye on you for minutes. He says the Company is looking for someone to be the Fellowship's representative to the Board, with a salary and a house on the hill, and that your debt would be struck off at once.

**Closing scene**

You say no. It takes you a night to say it, and the next morning to mean it. You send him your answer in a note, on a page torn from Ottoline's book: that the debt is a lie. The Company a larger one, and that you will take no house on the hill while there are four hundred in the valley. He does not reply. A week later you receive a second note in a different hand, from a clerk, in brown ink, which says only that your debt has been revised.

The revision is an increase. The sum is eleven thousand. It is, as Dob says, with a rueful grin, the first compliment you have ever had from the Company. You laugh until you cry, in the road, with a loaf under your arm. Then you go home and begin again.

## 16.10  "The Lamp Count"  (`lamps`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 293 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Company has a way of settling disputes. It counts the lamps. Every miner has a rented lamp, numbered on the base. On the first Friday after the recognition the Company calls a muster at the pit-head, in the rain, and requires every lamp to be handed in for inspection. Three hundred and ninety-seven are brought up. There should be four hundred.

**Closing scene**

The missing three are Dob's, the widow's, and yours. Sable reads their numbers aloud from a list in a flat voice, and then the numbers of the lamps that were issued to the dead and to the sick and to the departed, and then a sum. It is a large sum. It is the sum of the lamps that have been lost, in ninety years, which the Company proposes to recover from the Fellowship's funds.

It is not true. It is perfectly legal. The lamps are in the Company's own ledger as lost, and the ledger is the Company's own. Kell stands at the back with his arms folded, looking at the sky. Ottoline begins to speak, and you put a hand on her arm. You walk forward, in the rain, to the table. You put down the three lamps, one after another. They are warm. They are still lit.

**You:** That's three. And the rest of the sum is a lie, and everybody here knows it, and I think you do.

The crowd does not make a sound. But somewhere at the back a lamp is raised, and another, and then a hundred, all lit, a long wet river of small flames, held up in the dark above the heads of the Company's men. Sable looks at them. He says nothing. He folds the list, and goes.

## 16.11  "Paid Down"  (`paid`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Reach Major Lvl 1.  "Clear your name: reach Major Lvl 1."
- **Pays:** 500 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **Words:** 220 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The last payment is made on a Friday in November at the pay-window, through the brass grille. The clerk in the green eyeshade counts it twice, as always. He looks at the ledger, and turns a page, and turns another, and then he sits quite still for a time with his pen above the paper. He looks up. His face is, for the first time in your acquaintance, a face. He says: 'It's nothing.'

**Closing scene**

He writes it in brown ink in the margin. He turns the ledger round on the counter so that you can read it. It says, beside your name: PAID. You have owed the Lode Company something every day of your life. You stand there, at the window, with the pen and the paper, and have no idea what to do with your hands.

**Dob:** (behind you, quiet, with his cap in his fist) Well. That's you out. That's the first one out in our street in thirty years.

You walk out into the yard. It is raining, a thin cold drizzle. The wheel on the pit-head is turning. The cage goes down with its clank. You stop in the middle of the yard with your face turned up, and the rain on your eyelids, and stay there for ages. Nobody tells you to move.

## 16.12  "Daylight"  (`daylight`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended

Ottoline is packing. There is a trunk on the floor of the infirmary, and a stack of books, and a tin of bandages, and the long thin ledger, wrapped in oilcloth. The Medical College has written at last, offering a post in the city and a laboratory. {ottoline.He} has not yet said yes. {ottoline.He} says that {ottoline.he} has been standing in the doorway for four days, looking at the pit-head, and has not had one useful thought.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `love`; default: option 1)

> Ottoline Harl has been offered a place in the city and has not said yes.

1. Ask {ottoline.him} to stay, and mean it.
   - You ask. {ottoline.He} stares at you. Then {ottoline.he} sits down on the trunk, rather suddenly, and laughs, and wipes {ottoline.his} eyes with a bandage. {ottoline.He} says: 'I wanted to be asked. I did not want to be the sort of person who needed to be.' {ottoline.He} writes to the College that evening. The reply says that the post may be held for a year.
   - **Ottoline:** I'll do my research here. There's a mine, after all. It's the best laboratory I've ever had.
2. Tell {ottoline.him} to go, and that you will write: a laboratory is no small thing.
   - You tell {ottoline.him} to go. It is the hardest thing you have said. {ottoline.He} looks at you for a very long moment. {ottoline.He} says, quietly, that it is the kindest thing and the worst, and that {ottoline.he} will write every week. {ottoline.He} does. The letters are long and dense and full of cheerful scorn. They end in a single line, different each time, and you keep them in a tin under the bed.
   - **Ottoline:** (in the first letter) The city is too tidy. There is nobody to be rude to.
3. Go with {ottoline.him} for a while, and see the city, and decide there.
   - You go with {ottoline.him}. You take a month, and a train, and a room in a lodging-house in a city of a million people who have never been underground. It is loud and bright and strange. You see the sea. You eat an ice. On the last night you stand on a bridge at dusk, with the lamps coming on along the river, and agree, in a few short words, that you will go home.
   - **Ottoline:** I think I like it better when it's ours. I think I'd rather be needed than admired.

**Closing scene**

On the first Sunday after, the whole of Cinder Deep goes up the hill. It is a soft clear spring morning. They walk in a long straggling line, in their Sunday best, with children on their shoulders. They stand at the top in the long grass and look out. They can see the sea. Most of them have never seen it before. They stand there in silence for an hour, in the sun, with their lamps in their hands, unlit.

## 16.I1  Interlude: Paid  (between season 1 and season 2)

**Interlude**

Cinder Deep is a town of four hundred grey houses. Most of them are the same. The Company still owns the shop, and the chapel, and the pump. But the Fellowship owns the rota, and the safety book, and the sound of the wheel.

*[only if rescue is 1]* There is a brass plate on the wall of Number Six with a list of names. Dob's is not on it. Dob's is on the hurdle, which hangs over the door of the infirmary, with a pony shoe nailed beside it for luck.

*[only if rescue is 2]* The props in Number Six are set in a pattern now called the Dob. It is in the regulations. It is on the wall of every gallery.

*[only if rescue is 3]* The doctor's rule is chalked in the cage: the first person to reach a trapped miner shall be the one who knows how to touch them.

*[only if strike is 1]* The wheel stopped for six weeks in the spring of that year. Children are born who are told it as a legend.

*[only if strike is 2]* The Fellowship has a reserve fund of eleven thousand scrip. It is in a tin in the vestry.

*[only if strike is 3]* The Commission's report hangs in the pit-head, in a frame. Nobody has read it. Everybody knows what it says.

In the lowest gallery, behind the timber props, in the dark, the tapping goes on. Three and a pause. Three and a pause. It has not changed. It has not stopped. In the evenings, when the shift is done and the cage has gone up, Dob sits on the edge of the shaft with his legs hanging over the dark, and taps back.

# 16.S2  Season 2: The Counting Below

## 16.13  "The Tally on the Wall"  (`tally`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 12 weeks (0 years and 12 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> { Chapters.spawn(c, st, "agnes"); Chapters.spawn(c, st, "dob"); }`
- **Words:** 277 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The marks appear in the third gallery in the dry season. They are scratched into the rock at shoulder height in a column, five to a bundle, the way a prisoner scores a wall. Nobody sees who made them. They are fresh every morning, a hand's width lower than the day before, and by the end of the month there are four hundred and eleven.

Dob counts them on the Monday. Then he counts again. Then he sits on an ore-cart with his lamp in his lap and says nothing. The workforce of Cinder Deep, children included, is four hundred and eleven. It was four hundred and eight last spring. Three have been born since. The marks have kept pace.

**Closing scene**

On the Tuesday one mark is struck through. It is a clean, firm, downward stroke, with a long tail. The same day a man in the sixth gallery steps back to let a cart go by, and a loose stone the size of a loaf falls forty feet and takes him in the neck. He is called Wilf. He had two girls.

**Dob:** (white, in the cage on the way up) It's a tally. It's counting us. And when it strikes you out, you're gone.

**You:** That's superstition.

**Dob:** Is it? Go and look at the wall. Wilf's is struck. It was a hundred and twelve.

You go. You hold the lamp to the stone. Number one hundred and twelve has a line through it. Under the line, in very small letters, scratched with a fingernail or a nail, someone has written the name: WILF. Whoever it is, they were polite enough to spell it right.

## 16.14  "The Eleventh Level"  (`eleven`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, a technique insight

**Opening scene**

The mine has ten levels. Every miner knows it. It is on the Company's maps, in the Company's regulations, painted in white on the lintel of the cage: LEVELS 1-10. The tapping comes from below the tenth. The tally marks are scratched in a hand that is not human. On a Thursday night after the shift, Dob takes you to the very bottom of the shaft and shows you a staircase that is not on any map.

**Closing scene**

It starts behind a stack of rotten timbers in the corner of the tenth gallery, in a niche of black stone. It is narrow, and very steep, and cut straight down in the living rock with a tool you have never seen. The steps are worn in the middle by feet. They have been worn very deep. Whoever used them did so for a very long time.

**Dob:** I found it by chance. I fell against the timbers. I was chasing Marmalade. I went down eleven steps and there was a door.

**You:** What was behind it?

**Dob:** I don't know. I didn't open it. I heard someone counting on the other side. I heard it say my name.

You hold the lamp over the stairs. A cold draught comes up, smelling of old stone and old dust and, very faintly, of something you cannot name. It is something warm and animal, like a stable. From far below, in the dark, three taps come up the stair. They stop. They begin again, and the fourth tap is yours.

## 16.15  "The Company Seals the Shaft"  (`sealed`)

- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones

**Opening scene**

Sable is back on the morning coach. He stands in the yard of the pit-head, in the rain, in a mackintosh, with two clerks and a man with a crowbar. He announces that, in the interests of safety, the tenth level is closed for inspection. He announces it with a smile. It is the first time in a long time that he has been seen to have a purpose.

**Closing scene**

The Fellowship objects. The Fellowship has the right to inspect. Kell, standing in the door of the office with his moustache bristling, points out that the regulations allow a joint inspection by a committee of three. Sable says that the matter is covered by a clause. He produces the clause. It is in a book that is older than the town, and it says that the Company reserves the right to close any gallery that is, in the opinion of the Company, a hazard.

They seal it that afternoon. The stairs are bricked up with eleven courses of brick, and the brick plastered over, and the plaster painted the colour of the rock. Sable stands over them, watching. He does not look at the wall. He looks at you. He says: 'It is better for everyone.' It is the only time you have ever believed him.

**Ottoline:** (low, in the shed afterwards) He's afraid. He's not afraid of the men. He's not afraid of the Fellowship. He's afraid of something that's down there.

Ottoline puts the long thin book on the table in the shed and opens it to a page near the back. She has drawn lines in red ink across the rows of the dead. She has made notes in the margins. She has been up all night. She says she noticed it when Wilf died, because he was her eleventh that year and it was an odd number. She says she began to look.

**Closing scene**

**Ottoline:** It is not random. I have plotted it. The deaths in the pit fall on the hundredth day, to the day, from the last count. Every hundred days, someone is struck. Not always the same sort of accident. Not always the same gallery. But always, to the day, on the hundredth.

**You:** Since when?

**Ottoline:** Since the Company opened the mine. Ninety-one years. There are three hundred and thirty-two deaths, and they fall on a count of a hundred days, every time, like a clock. And before the first count there is a gap of about a hundred days, in the Company's own records, where the mine did not open. A gap marked: Surveying.

She turns the page. On the last leaf she has drawn a diagram. It is a spiral. It goes down, and down, and at the bottom there is a small neat circle, and inside the circle a figure that you cannot make out. She says it is from a map she found in the Company's archive. She says it is a map of the mine as it was in the year before the Company came. She says the figure is a word.

## 16.17  "Down"  (`down`)

**Opening scene**

You break the wall on a Sunday night, with Dob and Ottoline and the widow, who has insisted. You take a pick, a crowbar, forty feet of rope, a thermos of tea and a lamp apiece. The brick is thick but old. The mortar is soft. It comes away in a dusty sheet, a course at a time, and the stair opens before you: black, steep, silent. The draught that comes up from it smells of a stable.

**Closing scene**

The stair is two hundred and eleven steps. You count them, because there is nothing else to do. At the bottom there is a door, round, of dark wood, bound with bronze. It is not locked. It is not even closed. It stands an inch ajar, with a thin line of yellow light along the edge. And through it, quite clearly, comes the sound of voices: a murmur, a clink, the rattle of tin mugs, the ordinary hum of a shift going off.

**Agnes Marrow:** (the widow, for the first time in a year, in a trembling voice) That's Tom.

**You:** Who?

**Agnes Marrow:** My husband. He went down in 'forty-nine. They never found him. That's his laugh.

She puts her hand on the door, and pushes, and it swings open on a long low gallery, lit by lamps. It is full of men.

## 16.18  "The Gallery of the Eleven"  (`gallery`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 273 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

They are eleven in number, in old canvas coats and caps of a cut that went out before your grandfather's day. They sit on benches along the wall, eating bread and cheese out of handkerchiefs, drinking tea from tin cans. A pit-pony is asleep in the corner. The lamps burn with a steady yellow flame. It is a perfectly ordinary mine at the end of a shift, except that the shift has been going for seventy years.

**Closing scene**

They look up when you come in. They do not look surprised. A broad old man with white whiskers and a face like a friendly ham rises, wiping his hands, and says in a deep voice that they were beginning to wonder. He says the foreman has been late with the wages for minutes. He says it is not like the Company. He asks if you are the new man.

**Tom Marrow:** Evening. I'm Tom. We're the Eleven. We came down in 'forty-nine for the day shift, and the roof came in behind us, and the lads said, never mind, we'll sit it out. We've been waiting for the relief ever since. They've forgotten us, I think. Would you tell the foreman we'd like our money?

Agnes makes a sound you will never forget. She is across the gallery before anyone can stop her. She takes his face between her hands. She says his name. He looks at her, politely puzzled, in the manner of a man who has been spoken to by a stranger. Then he says, slowly, in a different voice, 'Aggie?' And all along the bench, the others set down their cans.

## 16.19  "What Counts"  (`counter`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 247 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Eleven tell it plainly, over the tea. The roof fell in, they say, and they were cut off, and they sat in the dark. After a time they heard a sound in the rock. It was a slow regular tapping, like a heart. It said, in a voice they could feel in their ribs: I am keeping count. They have been counted ever since. They do not grow old. They do not grow tired. They do not die. They have not seen daylight in seventy-two years.

**Closing scene**

**Tom Marrow:** It doesn't mean harm. I'll say that. It's like a clerk. It writes us down. When one of the lads upstairs goes, it marks him off, and we feel it, down here, a sort of cold in the chest. We call it the Counter. It's not a bad sort. It's only that it has nobody to tell.

**Ottoline:** (quietly, to you, with her hand over her notebook) It's a record. It is the world's oldest ledger. Somebody is keeping track of the living, and has been since before the Company.

The wall at the end of the gallery is covered with marks. They run from floor to ceiling, in bundles of five, in tens of thousands. Some are struck out. Most are not. At the very bottom, in a corner, in very small tidy scratches, there is a column of names. It begins with Tom Marrow. It continues for eleven lines. It ends, very recently, with a twelfth: yours.

You find him in the gallery of the Eleven, sitting on a bench, quite calm, with a cup in his hands. He looks up with a puzzled smile. He says that he came down for a drink. It is a long clean downward stroke, very black, and still wet.

**Dob:** Oh. Is that what's happened? That's not so bad. I thought it would be worse. I'd like to tell Marmalade. Is there somewhere I could send a note?

You say that he is coming with you. He says, kindly, that he does not think he can. You can see the faint mark, on the back of his hand, where the line has been drawn.

## 16.21  "Agnes Speaks"  (`widow`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight

**Opening scene**

Agnes Marrow has not spoken in a year. She speaks now. She sits with you in the gallery, at the end of the bench, with her short pick across her knees and her husband's cap in her lap, and tells you, in a low steady voice, what she knows. She has been listening to the tapping since the day he went. She says she understands it. She says it is not a language. It is a counting, and a counting is a kind of kindness.

**Closing scene**

**Agnes:** It's not to hurt us. It's to keep us. A person who is counted is a person who is not forgotten. Do you understand? That's all it's ever done. It couldn't bear that nobody was keeping track. It's been writing us down since the beginning, in case we're needed. It's only that it writes us down in a ledger that has one column. It doesn't know about the other.

**You:** What other?

**Agnes:** The one that says: going home.

She stands. She puts the cap on her husband's head, gently, over the white hair. She looks at the wall of marks. She says that she thinks the way to stop it is not to fight it. She says she thinks the way to stop it is to answer. She says: 'It's been counting alone for ninety years. Somebody ought to count back.'

## 16.22  "Counting Back"  (`count`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Make 10 items **since this chapter began**.  "Answer the Counter: make ten marks."
- **Pays:** 500 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **When it opens, the code:** `TaleMinerSeasons::mark`
- **Words:** 151 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You do it in the gallery of the Eleven at midnight, by lamplight, with the whole of the Fellowship standing in the stair behind you and every lamp turned up. Ottoline has the book. Kell has the names. Agnes stands at the wall, with her hand flat on the rock, as a woman stands at a bedside. You take a piece of chalk. You write, under the Counter's last scratch, in a clear bold hand, a number.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `count`; default: option 1)

> The Counter has been counting for ninety years. You can answer it with a count of your own.

1. Count the dead: read out every name struck, and say that they were here.
   - You read the names of the dead. All three hundred and thirty-two. It takes an hour and a half. Kell reads half, and Ottoline the rest. At every name the knocking in the rock answers, once, like a hand on a door. When you finish there is a long silence. Then, from every side, the rock begins to hum, very softly, as a church organ does when the last note has been played and the pipe is still sounding.
   - **Agnes:** (very quietly) There. That's the first time it's been thanked.
2. Count the living: read out every name on the town's roll, and say that they are not yours.
   - You read the living. Four hundred and eleven names, and the babies born that spring. You say after each, 'Here,' and the Fellowship says it after you, and the rock says nothing. When you reach the end you say, aloud, that none of them belongs to the Counter. You say that they belong to themselves. For a moment the tapping stops. Then it begins, much faster, anxiously, like a clerk who has lost his place.
   - **Kell:** I'd say you've upset it. I'd say it deserved it.
3. Do not count: put down the chalk, and say plainly that a person is more than a tally.
   - You put down the chalk. You say that a person is not a number. You say that you do not mean to be struck out, or kept, or counted at all. The wall is silent. You can hear your own breathing. Somewhere in the rock, a very long way off, a sound begins, a low grinding groan, like a great stone shifting. It is the sound of something that has never been refused.
   - **Ottoline:** (whispering) I think we've hurt its feelings.

**Closing scene**

The marks on the wall begin to fade. They go one after another, in order, from the top. The scratches soften, and blur, and dissolve into the rock like breath on glass. When the last has gone, the wall is smooth, and grey, and quite blank. The tapping has stopped. The Eleven stand up from their benches. They look about, in puzzlement, like men who have woken from a long afternoon sleep.

Down in the lowest gallery, where the Counter's last mark was rubbed out, someone has chalked three words on the bare rock, in a large rough hand: SHIFT ENDED. THANKS.

## 16.I2  Interlude: Shift Ended  (between season 2 and season 3)

**Interlude**

The tally is gone from the wall. The tapping in the rock has stopped. For the first time in ninety-one years nobody in Cinder Deep is counted by anything but a clerk.

*[only if count is 1]* On certain nights at the turn of the shift you can hear the rock hum a long low chord, softly, and every miner stops, and lifts his head, and nods.

*[only if count is 2]* The Counter has gone quiet. Some say it is sulking. Dob leaves a lamp lit at the bottom of the shaft on the first of every month, in case it wants company.

*[only if count is 3]* Something in the rock groans on a Thursday evening, once a month, and then is still. Nobody has said what. Everybody knows.

*[only if seal is 1]* The lintel at the sealed stair reads THEY WERE COUNTED. On the first Sunday of the month somebody leaves a cup of tea at the foot of it.

*[only if seal is 2]* The Gallery of the Eleven has a visiting day. A child sits on Tom's bench with a piece of chalk and writes his own name, and counts to eleven.

*[only if seal is 3]* The Eleven lie in a row on the hill. There are twelve stones. The twelfth is blank, and has a lamp on it.

Far below, at the very bottom of the mine, under the last scratch of the vanished tally, in the dark, the rock is warm. If you put your ear to it, you can hear, very faint, not a tap, not a count, but something much slower. It is the sound of a very large thing, turning over in its sleep.

# 16.S3  Season 3: The Floor of the Garden

## 16.25  "The Rock Is Warm"  (`warm`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 12 weeks (0 years and 12 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 257 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The warmth starts in the autumn. It begins in the lowest gallery, where the last tally was rubbed out, and creeps up through the rock a foot a month. By midwinter the walls of the tenth level are as warm as a loaf. The ice on the pit-head melts. The ponies sweat. Dob takes off his coat in January, and comes to work in his shirt, and says it is like working in a kitchen.

Ottoline measures it with a thermometer and a notebook. She goes down every day. She sits on a barrel in the lowest gallery with her ear to the rock, and her instruments laid out on a cloth, and writes. She says it is not the sun. She says the mine is breathing.

**Closing scene**

**Ottoline:** It has a pulse. Fifty-two beats a minute, slow and steady, and very strong. It comes from below. It comes from a long way below. I've taken readings from the sixth level and the tenth, and the pulse arrives at the sixth seven seconds later. I make the depth of the source about eleven thousand feet.

**You:** Eleven thousand? The mine is only four hundred.

**Ottoline:** Quite. It is not our mine. We have been working the top of something else.

She turns the notebook round. She has drawn a long thin tree, upside down, with its branches spread under the town and its trunk going down and down off the bottom of the page. At the top, small and neat, is the pit-head. She has labelled it: Twig.

The vote is carried by every hand in the shed except one, and that one belongs to a man who is asleep.

**Closing scene**

It takes four months. They sink it in the old fashion, with a windlass and a bucket, a foot at a time, every hand in turn. The rock is dense, and dark, and strangely smooth. It does not splinter. It comes away in long curling shavings, like wood, and smells of resin. Where the pick goes in it bleeds a little clear gold sap that runs down the face and sets like amber.

On the hundredth day, when the shaft has reached the depth of a church spire, the windlass runs slack. The bucket comes up empty and clean. Dob leans over the edge with a lamp and cannot see the bottom. He says: 'I think it's gone through.' Ottoline says nothing. She has gone completely white. She is holding up a hand, as a person does at a concert when the music is about to begin.

He goes through. He does not fall. He stands, upside down, on the air.

It is daylight. You stand on a mountain top in a cold clean wind. The sky is wide and pale and the sun is a long way to the left of where it should be. All round you the world falls away in blue folds, and far below, on the plain, tiny and exact, you can see a grey town with a wheel on a tower. It is Cinder Deep. It is a thousand miles below, and it is directly overhead.

**Kell:** That is not possible. That is geometrically absurd.

**Ottoline:** (with a little hysterical laugh) No. It's a loop. I've read of it. It's a thing that happens at the edge of a made world. If you go far enough in any direction you come back to where you began. We have dug through the floor of the Garden, and out into its roof.

A long way off, at the edge of the plain, there is a wall. It runs from horizon to horizon, grey and high and as fine as a weaver's cloth. You can see, from here, the threads.

It runs away into the distance in both directions. Where you touch it, the squares tremble and close up again, like water.

**Closing scene**

There is a door in it, a little way along. It is small and low and brown, with a latch of horn. It has been left ajar. You peer through. On the other side is a plain, with wheat on it, and a road, and a town with a wheel on a tower. It is the same plain as the one you are standing on. It is the same road. If you went through, you would be where you began.

**Ottoline:** The Garden is a loop. That's all it is. It has no edge. You walk to the border and the border puts you back. It is the neatest thing I have ever seen, and I have never been so frightened.

The widow Agnes has put down her pick. She is standing with her hand against the weave of the wall, staring at it, with her lips moving. After a time she says: 'It's counting, too. Listen.' You listen. Very faint, from the threads of the Wall, deep in the weave, there is a ticking, regular and slow, three and a pause, three and a pause.

The man who comes out of the Wall is square and quiet, with a face like a closed fist. He wears a plain grey coat with a captain's braid, and a sapper's leather apron, and carries a short spade over one shoulder. A line of men and women in similar grey comes after him, silent, in file, each carrying a pick and a coil of fuse. They stop. They stand at ease.

**Closing scene**

**Ashgrove:** Captain Ashgrove. Sappers of the Hollow Court. I should say at once that we are not here for you. We are not here for the town. We have been digging up this floor for eighty years, from the other side, to put out the root. You have been so good as to dig down to meet us. I am rather obliged.

**You:** The root?

**Ashgrove:** The thing you have been calling the vein. The Counter. The warm. It is the Garden's root, the oldest part. It is the one place in the Garden that touches the real earth. If it is cut the Garden will wither from the bottom. We have a good many men down there, and the work is slow. You are three weeks ahead of schedule.

He looks at the five of you in your canvas coats with your lamps and your bread. He nods, slowly, as a man nods who has reached a decision he does not like. He says: 'I shall be perfectly honest. I would rather not do it. But I have my orders, and I have never in my life disobeyed one.'

There is no shouting. It is a patient scrupulous contest in the dark, fought with timber and rope, and the only casualty is time. The Captain sends a note each morning by a corporal. It says: Good morning. We have advanced a yard.

On the ninth day you are working the same gallery from two sides without knowing it. You set a prop and hear a prop set. You set another and the sound answers. at last you reach the middle, a pair of hands on either side of the same beam, and a pair of eyes meet yours through a gap in the rock. They belong to a sapper of eighteen with a dust-grey face and the weary politeness of a boy brought up in a barracks.

**Sapper:** Excuse me. Is this your beam or ours?

You pass him a flask of tea through the gap. He takes it with both hands. He drinks. He passes it back. Neither of you says anything for a time. Down the tunnel the sound of picks has stopped, on both sides, and the only noise is the soft crack of the timber settling under the whole world.

She says the rat is now eleven years old and has taken up with a hamster.

**Closing scene**

**Ottoline:** It is life. It's not a cure. It's what cures come from. Every herb, every pill, every medicine in the Garden is a thin dilution of this. It's the Garden's own blood. It's the stuff the world is made of. I've been practising medicine for twelve years and I've never once understood what it was for.

She gives a drop to the old stoker, who has had the black lung since he was nineteen. In an hour he is sitting up in bed, breathing like a man at the top of a hill, laughing and asking for tobacco. She gives a drop to a baby with the fever. The baby sneezes, once, and goes to sleep, and in the morning it is pink.

**Ottoline:** It's the thing the Company has been after for ninety years. It's not the silver. It never was the silver. It's this.

The Fellowship meets that night in the shed. They agree, without a vote, that the sap shall belong to nobody. It shall be given to anyone who asks. It shall be kept in a plain jug by the door of the infirmary, with a tin cup, and a notice. The notice reads: Take what you need.

Up on the surface a house in the High Street leans, quite gently, to one side, like a drunk, and a chimney slides off the roof.

The whole of Cinder Deep turns out. Four hundred miners, and the sappers, and the corporals, and the clerks in their eyeshades, with timber and rope and bread. They work for nine days. They work in shifts, by lamp, in the dark, sinking props and bracing beams, sweating in the warm, while the ground groans under them like a ship in a gale. The Captain works the face with his coat off, a grey man with a spade, and does not say a word.

On the ninth night the last beam goes in, with a sound like a church door. The groaning stops. The tremor dies. The Captain wipes his face with a dirty hand, and looks at you through the dust.

## 16.37  "Four and a Pause"  (`dr1`)

You go down the old shaft in the cage at the end of the shift. The wheel is quiet. The gallery is lit with a string of lamps, and at the end of it the rock is warm, and green with something that glows. You put your ear to the wall. Four taps. A pause. Four taps. It is a rhythm that you have never heard, and that you feel in your body as an old song.

**Closing scene**

You tap back, four and a pause. The rock answers, at once, and a seam in the wall opens, like a mouth, and a faint warm wind comes out of it that smells of rain on a hot road. There is a staircase on the other side. It goes up. It goes up for a very long way. At the top of it, far off, small and clear as a coin, there is a gate.

**Dob:** (in the cage, with his cap on his chest) I know it. That's the Garrison. I've seen it in a dream. It's a day's walk from here, up the root. They've been calling us for a hundred years. They didn't know our name.

Ottoline puts a hand on your arm. She says that she has been reading the Counter's ledger for a decade. She says it has one column. She says that at the foot of it, in the last line, in the Counter's own tiny scratch, it has added a second heading. It says: Going Home. It has your name under it.

## 16.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

Cinder Deep is a town of four hundred houses, built on the lip of a mine. Nobody owes anybody for the cradle.

*[only if root is 1]* The shaft is sealed under a plate of brass. Children put their ears to it on the first of March and swear they can hear a heart.

*[only if root is 2]* The hospital on the hill treats nine thousand a year. The sappers of the Hollow Court, in grey coats, guard the door. They are very polite.

*[only if root is 3]* A forest grows from the pit-head to the sea. The wheel turns on Sundays, for the visitors. The root comes up in the gardens in the spring, and the roses are the size of cabbages.

*[only if sable is 1]* Mister Sable keeps a stall in the market, selling medicine at cost. His daughter helps him. She is almost entirely well.

*[only if sable is 2]* A hat hangs on a hook in the pit-head office. Nobody wears it. Nobody moves it either.

*[only if sable is 3]* Mister Sable works the night shift at the lowest level, with a pick. He is not good at it. He says it is the best job he has ever had.

*[only if count is 1]* On the first of the month Agnes Marrow reads out the names of the dead at the pit-head. The rock hums.

*[only if count is 2]* Dob leaves a lamp lit at the bottom of the shaft. In the morning it is always out.

*[only if count is 3]* Something in the rock groans on a Thursday evening, once a month, and then is still.

*[only if love is 1]* Ottoline Harl keeps a laboratory in the old infirmary. She writes a monthly report to the Medical College. The College has stopped being surprised.

*[only if love is 2]* Ottoline's letters arrive every Friday from the city. They end in a different line each time. You keep them in a tin under the bed.

*[only if love is 3]* Ottoline Harl has a room in the city and a room in Cinder Deep, and has never once been sure which she is going home to.

*[only if latch is 1]* There is a bench by the pit-head with a name on it. The town sits there at the end of the shift and looks at the sea.

*[only if latch is 2]* A lamp stands on the sill of the house on the hill, and is lit every evening, for someone who has not yet come home.

*[only if latch is 3]* The lowest gallery under the Seat is lit from end to end. The Wicks call it the Safest Mile.

The tapping goes on, down at the very bottom, under the sealed stair, in the warm. Three and a pause. Three and a pause. Dob sits on the lip of the shaft in the evenings, with his legs hanging over the dark, and taps back.

## 16.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

You stay in the Garden. The Palace's lowest floor has a shaft in it, four hundred feet deep, with a cage, and a man in an apron rides it down on Tuesdays to listen to the root.

He says he has stopped being afraid of the dark. He says it has a sound, and the sound is a kind of company.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

In the Gardener's army the sappers are the ones who go first and come back last. You dig the trench the line stands in. Nobody thanks you. You prop it anyway.

On the night before a battle you tap three and a pause on the wall of the tent. Somewhere, very far away, someone taps back.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You step through the Seam with a lamp at your belt. On the far side there is a hill, and a sea, and a very long seam of something dark under the grass.

You light the lamp. You say: first shift.

**You are struck down by the array**

The array took you. In the dark someone is counting, patiently, a long way down, and you are on the list.

You say: here. It is the first time you have ever said it and meant it.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden goes out. The town goes out, and the wheel, and the four hundred grey houses.

The last thing to go is a slow tapping in the rock, three and a pause, and then, for the first time, a fourth.

---

*A blue panel has appeared at the edge of your sight. It says you are special. It is wrong about nearly everything else, but it does seem to know what happens next.*

Starts as: any, trait Cheater, Neutral, potential 70, 100 spirit stones.

**People of the story** (real characters in the world; "fated" means only you can kill them):

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| vesna | Vesna Hartley | Alchemist | Good | +4 | place:village | when a chapter needs them |

# 17.S1  Season 1: Level One Human

## 17.1  "Loading"  (`loading`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** Go to the place `village`.  "Go to the village, {@village}, and find out whether anyone else can see it."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, 1 Cultivation Pill
- **Words:** 272 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You are shelling peas on the back step of your mother's house when the world goes blue at the edges. A rectangle appears in the air in front of your face. It is semi-transparent. It has rounded corners and a drop shadow. It says, in a friendly sans-serif font: [Status Window (Loading...)]. A small bar underneath fills slowly from left to right, and stalls at eighty-eight per cent.

You put down the peas. You look behind you. Nobody is there. You look in front of you, and the rectangle is still there, and you have the very clear sense that it has arrived, in the manner of an unexpected relative.

**Closing scene**

The bar reaches a hundred per cent. A chime sounds, inside your head, a bright little ping like a tea-spoon on a glass. The panel clears and shows a column of text. [NAME: ______] [CLASS: Human (Level One)] [HP: 11/11] [MP: --] [TRAIT: Special]. The word Special is in gold. It has a small animated sparkle. It is the most self-satisfied sparkle you have ever seen.

A line of text scrolls up the bottom of the panel in bold. [Welcome, Host! You have been selected. You are one of a kind. Please enjoy your stay.] Under it, in smaller letters, the way an apology is typed: [Terms and conditions apply.]

**Nib:** (the innkeeper's lad, two doors down, watching you stare at nothing) You all right? You've been looking at that bit of air for a good while.

**You:** Can you see anything?

**Nib:** Air. A bit of dust. Is it a ghost? You can tell me. I'm very good with ghosts.

## 17.2  "Daily Quest: Eat Breakfast"  (`daily`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Have 2 friends.  "Make friends with the neighbours: make two friends."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "nib")`
- **Words:** 216 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The first quest arrives at seven in the morning, with a fanfare. [QUEST RECEIVED: Daily Routine (0/1). Objective: Eat breakfast. Reward: +1 Vitality (Hidden). Penalty for failure: Mild Hunger.] You read it twice. You are, at the time, holding a piece of toast. You eat it. A trumpet sounds. [QUEST COMPLETE! +1 Vitality (Hidden). You feel a little more alive. Not noticeably.]

**Closing scene**

They come every morning after that. [Daily Quest: Brush Teeth (0/1).] [Daily Quest: Say Good Morning to a Stranger (0/3).] [Daily Quest: Do Not Step on a Crack (0/1). Warning: This quest is a trap.] You do them all, at first, in a spirit of cautious obedience. Then you begin to suspect that the panel is not so much guiding you as keeping you busy.

**Nib:** So the thing says to say good morning three times, and then you get a thing?

**You:** A hidden stat.

**Nib:** What does it do?

**You:** It's hidden.

**Nib:** (after due consideration) That's the best thing I've ever heard. Can I have one?

The panel pings. [HOST HAS ACQUIRED AN ALLY: Nib Fennimore (Level 2). Relationship: Loyal. Special Ability: Believes You.] Under it, in italics: [This is a rare trait. Please handle with care.] Nib reads it over your shoulder, which he cannot do, and goes pink to the ears.

## 17.3  "Stats"  (`stats`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 226 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Stats page unlocks on a Thursday. It arrives with a cheerful riff and the words [Congratulations! You have unlocked: Character Sheet!] in a spinning gold font. You open it with a thought. It lists STRENGTH, DEXTERITY, INTELLIGENCE, VITALITY, LUCK and CHARISMA, each with a number. The numbers are: 4, 5, 3, 6, 98 and -2.

**Closing scene**

You study the page for an afternoon. You sit on the well with a mug of tea and move your eyes about, trying to find an Accept button. There is not one. There is a small gear icon in the corner that opens a menu called Settings, which contains only one option: Font Size. You make it bigger. The panel makes it smaller again, with a faint air of reproach.

**Nib:** What's Luck?

**You:** It says ninety-eight.

**Nib:** That's very good. I think. Is it very good?

**You:** I think so. I've been struck by lightning twice this month.

**Nib:** That's not luck.

**You:** It says it is. [LUCK: 98 (Excellent). Hint: High Luck increases the frequency of Fortunate Events.] I've also dropped a cart on my foot, fallen in a ditch, and lost my hat in a river. Five fortunate events in a month.

The panel flashes. [Fortunate Events: 5. Misfortunate Events: Not Applicable. Please contact Support if this seems wrong.] There is a link at the bottom. It is greyed out.

## 17.4  "Skill Acquired: Lie Detection (Faulty)"  (`skill`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **Words:** 223 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The skill comes in the middle of a conversation with the tax-collector. He is explaining, with great warmth, that the new levy is entirely for your benefit. The panel pings in the corner of your eye. [SKILL ACQUIRED: Lie Detection (Level 1). Description: Detects statements that are untrue. Success rate: 50%. Hint: Do not rely on this.] You glance at the tax-collector. A small red icon shows above his head. [LIE.]

**Closing scene**

It works on everyone. It works on the baker, who says her bread is fresh. It works on the priest, who says he is at peace. It works on your mother, who says she is not upset. It works, in a rather ghastly series of encounters over the next week, on every person you love, and in each case the red icon shows up with the sound of a small buzzer.

On the Sunday you realise it is also working on you. You say 'I'm fine' to Nib, who has asked how you are, and a red [LIE] flashes above your own head in the reflection of the well. You say, 'I'm fine,' again, with more conviction. The icon flickers. It turns yellow. It says: [LIE (Probably).]

**Nib:** Is it doing something?

**You:** It says I'm not fine.

**Nib:** Oh. Well, I could've told you that. I just didn't have a skill.

## 17.5  "A Possible Love Interest"  (`vesna`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet vesna (walk to their tile).  "Visit the alchemist's apprentice on the hill."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "vesna")`
- **Words:** 264 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The alchemist's shop on the hill has a new apprentice. The panel notices before you do. [NEW CHARACTER DETECTED: Vesna Hartley (Level 4). Occupation: Alchemist's Apprentice. Disposition: Neutral. Special Tag: POSSIBLE LOVE INTEREST (Unconfirmed).] You stare at the tag. It pulses gently. It sparkles. It is, you feel, the most embarrassing thing that has ever been done to you in a public place.

**Closing scene**

{vesna.He} is behind the counter in a stained apron, grinding something green in a mortar, with a pencil in {vesna.his} hair and a look of wary, humorous intelligence. {vesna.He} looks up. {vesna.He} sees you looking at the air above {vesna.his} head. {vesna.He} looks at it too, with real interest, and says: 'Is there something there?'

**You:** No.

**Vesna:** You're lying. You went a very odd colour.

The panel says: [LIE.] You close it with a thought. {vesna.He} puts down the pestle and leans on the counter. {vesna.He} says that {vesna.he} has been in the village for three weeks and has already heard about the person who stares at things. {vesna.He} says that in {vesna.his} experience the people who see what nobody else sees are either liars or poets, and that {vesna.he} cannot decide which is worse.

**Vesna:** I'd like to buy you a drink. Not for the reason in your tag. I'm curious. Whatever you can see, I would like to know what it says about me.

The panel flashes. [Warning: Do not reveal the Tag. The Tag is private. Revealing the Tag may lower Relationship by up to 40.] Underneath, in small grey type, as an afterthought: [Good luck.]

## 17.6  "The Boss Encounter"  (`rat`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **Words:** 264 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The cellar of the inn has been invaded. The landlord hires you to clear it. There is a pay of ten silver and a pie. You go down at dusk with a candle, a broom and Nib, who has brought a saucepan. The panel is silent on the stairs. At the bottom, as the candle lights the dark, there is a chime and a cry of trumpets. [BOSS ENCOUNTER! The RAT KING (Level 3). HP: 40. Weakness: Cheese.]

**Closing scene**

He is the size of a large dog. He wears a crown made of a bottle cap. He is surrounded by his court, an assembly of twenty-odd rats, who stand on their hind legs in a respectful ring. The King regards you from a barrel with small shrewd red eyes and the faintly pained expression of a monarch whose subjects have been kept waiting.

The panel is jubilant. [BATTLE START! Select a command: ATTACK | DEFEND | ITEM | RUN.] You select nothing. You are a person with a broom. The Rat King squeaks, and his army advances, and the next ten minutes are a confusion of brooms and saucepans and shrieking in the dark.

It ends when Nib throws a wheel of cheese. It is a good throw, and it lands on the barrel, and the Rat King takes it in both hands and sits down. The court sits with him. They eat. The panel is baffled. [BOSS DEFEATED?] it says. [Experience gained: ???.] Then: [Error: Experience source not recognised.]

**Nib:** I don't think we won.

**You:** I think we made a treaty.

## 17.7  "The Chosen One"  (`rival`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet aldwin (walk to their tile).  "Meet the stranger on the market square."
- **Pays:** nothing
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "aldwin")`
- **Words:** 266 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Chosen One arrives in the village on the market day with a horse and a sword and a sunbeam that follows him about. He is tall, golden-haired, square-jawed and twenty-four. He is called Sir Aldwin of the Bright Lance. People turn to look. Small children follow him in a line. A dog sits up and begs. The panel, in the corner of your eye, pings in alarm. [WARNING: PROTAGONIST DETECTED. YOUR STATUS HAS BEEN DOWNGRADED TO: SUPPORTING CHARACTER.]

**Closing scene**

**Aldwin:** Good day. I am told you are the one who sees things. I have a quest. It has been given to me by a voice in the sky. I am to find the nine keys and open the Door. I wonder whether you might assist.

He holds up his hand. In the air above it, clear and brilliant, hangs a panel like yours. It is bigger. It has gold edges. Its font is a graceful serif. It lists his STRENGTH as 87, his DEXTERITY as 91, his LUCK as 100, and his CHARISMA as an upward-pointing arrow. Under his name there is a small icon of a crown. Under yours there is a small icon of a potato.

**You:** I see you've got a better one.

**Aldwin:** Do I? I never compare. I'm told it is rude. Yours is perfectly adequate, I'm sure.

The panel flashes. [NOTE: THIS PERSON IS NOT A THREAT. THIS PERSON IS A PROBLEM.] You have the odd sensation that the panel is, for the first time, on your side. It adds, in a smaller font: [Please do not tell him this.]

## 17.8  "Patch Notes"  (`patch`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 199 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You wake one morning to find that everything has moved. The panel is a different colour. The font has changed. A fanfare sounds and a banner scrolls across your eyes, in letters of gold. [PATCH 1.0.2 HAS BEEN APPLIED! Please read the notes below.] The notes are eleven pages long. You read them at breakfast. They contain no information whatsoever.

**Closing scene**

[Fixed: A bug whereby the Host could not see the Host]. [Fixed: A bug where the colour blue was not blue enough]. [Added: Daily Quest: Be Kind to a Cat]. [Changed: The meaning of the word Special]. [Known issues: The Host may experience occasional feelings] You read it again, and a third time. At the end there is a line in a different font, which looks, you think, a little like handwriting. [We are sorry for the inconvenience. We are doing our best.]

**Nib:** Does it say sorry?

**You:** It says it's doing its best.

**Nib:** (with great sympathy) Poor thing. It sounds like it's had a hard week.

The panel is silent for minutes. Then a small line appears, in the corner, for no reason, like a hand held up from the back of a room. [Thank you.]

## 17.9  "Side Quest: The Lost Cat"  (`cat`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 304 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The old woman at the end of the lane has lost her cat. The panel announces it. [SIDE QUEST: The Lost Cat. Objective: Find Mister Whiskers. Reward: ???. Difficulty: Easy. Hint: He is not what he seems.] The old woman is called Mrs. Pargeter. She has a house full of clocks and a voice like a creaking gate. She is sure he has gone to the churchyard. He goes to the churchyard on the first of every month.

**Closing scene**

You find him on a tombstone at midnight, a large black cat with a white bib and a ring of keys on a ribbon round his neck. He looks at you without hurry. The panel goes off like a firework. [WARNING! HIDDEN BOSS! MISTER WHISKERS (Level 99). HP: ???. Defeat him to unlock: THE TRUE ENDING.] A chime, and then, anxiously: [Please do not attack him.]

He yawns. He stretches. He walks across the grass and leans against your shin, and begins to purr, in a note so low that the gravestones hum. The keys on his ribbon jingle. There are nine of them. They are made of old brass, and each is cut with a different pattern.

**Mister Whiskers:** (in your head, mildly, with the voice of a retired colonel) Don't be alarmed. I was only passing through. I was told someone here could see me. I hadn't hoped for it. Is there any chance of a sardine?

You give him your supper, which is a pasty. He eats half. He says it will do. He says that he has been looking for the Host for nine hundred years, and has had a great deal of trouble getting an appointment. He pads away across the graves with his tail up, and the panel, after a long baffled silence, says only: [Side quest complete?]

## 17.10  "The Tutorial Ends"  (`tutorial`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
