On the morning of the first of May the panel plays a long stirring chord and displays, in letters three feet high, a banner. [CONGRATULATIONS! YOU HAVE COMPLETED THE TUTORIAL! Please wait while the real game loads.] There is a spinning wheel. It spins for ages. You make your breakfast and eat it and wash up, and the wheel is still spinning.

**Closing scene**

The wheel stops at noon. The panel says: [LOADING COMPLETE. Welcome to the Real Game!] There is a fanfare. A great many new tabs open. There is a Map, an Inventory, a Quest Log, a Skill Tree and a Friends List. Each one is empty. The Friends List has three names in it: Nib, Vesna and, with a small crown, Mister Whiskers. Under the names a line in grey says: [More friends coming soon.]

**Vesna:** (looking over your shoulder, in the shop, with a tray of vials) Is it showing me again?

**You:** It's showing you as a friend.

**Vesna:** Not as a tag?

**You:** The tag is gone.

**Vesna:** Was it a good tag?

**You:** It was a deeply embarrassing tag.

**Vesna:** Then I'll be having that drink after all.

## 17.11  "Hidden Class Unlocked"  (`class`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 111 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It happens at the top of the stairs in the inn. You trip. The tray you are carrying falls. It breaks seven plates and a jug, and the panel goes off like a siege. [HIDDEN CLASS UNLOCKED!] A golden light fills the corridor. [Please choose your destiny.] There are three options, laid out in three elegant frames like cards in a game.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `class`; default: option 1)

> A golden panel offers a Hidden Class. The frames are labelled: HERO, ROGUE and a third whose label is a small blue question mark.

1. HERO: sword, shield, and a prophecy. A very large number of people will depend on you.
   - You choose Hero. A sword appears on your hip. It is rather a good sword. The panel plays a rousing march. [CLASS: HERO (Level 1). New skill: Rally. New duty: Save the World. Please note that duty cannot be unequipped.] Nib applauds. Vesna looks rather alarmed. You feel, at once, the faint, cold, gathering weight of other people's hopes, and realise it is much heavier than the sword.
   - **Vesna:** I liked you better when you stared at the wall.
2. ROGUE: lock-picks, shadows and good teeth. Nobody will depend on you at all.
   - You choose Rogue. A set of picks and a dark cloak appear. The panel plays a quiet jaunty tune. [CLASS: ROGUE (Level 1). New skill: Light Fingers. New duty: None.] You test the picks on the inn door and it opens before you touch it. Nib is delighted. Vesna remarks that she has never seen anybody less suited to the profession.
   - **Vesna:** You've got an honest face. It's frankly a handicap.
3. ?: the third option, whose description says only: Trust me.
   - You choose the question mark. A small silence. Then the panel displays, in plain text, without a sound, the word [Thanks]. A new class appears in the list, in a font you have not seen. [CLASS: HUMAN (Level 1). New skill: None. New duty: None. Description: You are exactly who you were. This is the hidden class. It is the only one that can never be nerfed.] Nib says that it looks like the same one you started with. You say that it is.
   - **Vesna:** I think that's the first honest thing the panel's ever said.

**Closing scene**

The golden light dies. The corridor is dark. The jug is still in pieces on the boards. In the silence, the panel makes a faint, thoughtful noise, like a throat being cleared in a very small room. It says nothing else for the rest of the day.

## 17.12  "End of Chapter One"  (`endchapter`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 8 weeks (0 years and 8 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 1,000 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, gear a Major above you, a technique insight
- **When it closes, the code:** `(c, st) -> { int l = Chapters.flag(st, "love"); Chapters.bond(c, st, "vesna", l == 3 ? 1 : 3); if (l == 1 || l == 2) Chapters.wed(c, st, "vesna"); }`
- **Words:** 138 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The panel sends a notification at the end of the month. [CHAPTER ONE COMPLETE! Please rate your experience.] Beneath it are five stars. You look at them. You think about the Rat King, and the cat, and the cellar, and the possible love interest. You look for ages. At last you tap the fifth, with your mind, and a small cartoon heart floats up and bursts.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `love`; default: option 1)

> Vesna Hartley is leaning on the counter of the alchemist's shop, waiting for an answer to a question neither of you has asked.

1. Ask {vesna.him} out, plainly, without the tag.
   - You ask. It takes forty seconds and comes out in the wrong order. {vesna.He} stares at you. The panel, in the corner, is utterly still. Then {vesna.he} says, 'Yes,' in a flat clear voice, and picks up the mortar again, and you realise {vesna.he} has been waiting for three months to be asked. The panel rings softly. [ACHIEVEMENT UNLOCKED: Asking.] It is the only one you have ever been proud of.
   - **Vesna:** I'd have said yes to the tag. I want you to know that.
2. Give {vesna.him} a small gift, a good pen, with no explanation.
   - You leave the pen on the counter, wrapped in brown paper, without a word. It is a good pen, steel-nibbed, with a green barrel. {vesna.He} finds it in the morning. {vesna.He} uses it for a week without comment. At the end of the week there is a note on your doorstep, in a spiky hand, on the back of a prescription. It says: Thursday. I'm told there's a dull play.
   - **Nib:** I didn't tell her. I want that clear. She worked it out.
3. Do nothing. Be friends. Let the game load.
   - You do nothing. It is a small, awkward, friendly silence, over a counter, in the smell of herbs and sulphur. {vesna.He} says that {vesna.he} is in no hurry. {vesna.He} says the game will wait. The panel, in your eye, sends a polite line of text. [RELATIONSHIP: Friend (Very High). Next level: ???.] It does not say how to reach it.
   - **Vesna:** I like a long level. I like a good slow build.

**Closing scene**

The panel dims. A line of text appears in the centre, in a white sans-serif, very plain. [CHAPTER TWO LOADING.] A bar appears under it. It fills to eighty-eight per cent, and sticks. You watch it for minutes. The village goes about its business behind it. Nib calls from across the road that the soup is ready. You do not close the panel; you are, you realise, a little curious.

## 17.I1  Interlude: Loading...  (between season 1 and season 2)

**Interlude**

The village has a name now on the panel's map. It is called: Starting Village. It is the only entry on the map. The panel is very proud of it.

*[only if class is 1]* The sword is hung over the fireplace. It is a very good sword. A great many people have come to ask you to save them. You have been getting rather good at saying that you will think about it.

*[only if class is 2]* The picks live in a drawer in the kitchen. They are used, on the whole, for opening jars. It is a use the panel has chosen not to mention.

*[only if class is 3]* The panel lists your class as Human (Level 1), and has done so since the day it was offered. Nobody has been able to improve on it.

The panel says that Chapter Two is loading. It has said so for three months. You have stopped checking it. Mister Whiskers calls on Thursdays, for a sardine, and sits on the windowsill with his keys. He says that the panel is a very young piece of work, and doing quite well. He says it will be a fine thing when it is grown.

# 17.S2  Season 2: Patch Notes

## 17.13  "Scheduled Maintenance"  (`maintenance`)

- **Starts when:** 2 year(s) after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 12 weeks (0 years and 12 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> { Chapters.spawn(c, st, "nib"); Chapters.spawn(c, st, "vesna"); }`
- **Words:** 266 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The announcement comes on a Sunday morning, in a very polite banner. [SCHEDULED MAINTENANCE. The Status Window will be unavailable for approximately seven days. We apologise for the inconvenience. Thank you for your continued patience.] Then the panel goes grey. Then it goes black. Then it is gone, with a faint electronic sigh, like a candle snuffed in a very small room.

**Closing scene**

The first day is wonderful. You wake and do not look at the corner of your eye. You make breakfast and no one gives you a medal. You say good morning to a stranger and nothing pings. By noon you are walking down the high street with your hands in your pockets feeling like a man who has put down a very heavy box.

By the third day it has started to feel like a limp. You go to cross the road and wait for the arrow. You meet an old friend and hold back, waiting to be told how much she likes you. You lose a button and stand in the street looking at the air where the Inventory ought to be. Nib asks what is wrong. You say you cannot remember whether you are strong.

**Nib:** You're strong enough. You carried the sack of flour.

**You:** But what's my number?

**Nib:** (with real alarm) I don't think there ought to be a number. I think you just carried it.

On the seventh day, at dawn, the panel comes back. [MAINTENANCE COMPLETE. Welcome back, Host.] You feel a rush of relief so ridiculous that you have to sit down on the kerb.

## 17.14  "Support Group"  (`support`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Have 5 friends.  "Find the others: make five friends."
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 295 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The notice is pinned to the board in the tavern. It is written in a spidery hand on a page torn from an account book. It says: DO YOU SEE A BOX? YOU ARE NOT ALONE. FIRST AND THIRD THURSDAYS, BACK ROOM OF THE LAMB, EIGHT O'CLOCK. BRING A CHAIR. You read it four times. You tear it down and put it in your pocket. You are at the Lamb at five to eight with a chair under your arm.

**Closing scene**

There are six of you. There is a stout cheerful woman in a green coat called Greta, who sees a countdown over everybody's head and has not yet worked out to what. There is a man named Odo Plimsoll, who has a shop menu in the corner of his eye and cannot stop appraising things. There is a monk whose panel is entirely in Latin, a girl whose panel only shows the weather. A very old lady in a lace cap whose panel has an Accessibility Mode, which, as she says, is the only sensible part.

**Greta:** I thought I was losing my mind. I thought there was something in the cheese.

**Odo:** I've been unable to look at a sofa without reading its price. It's ruined furniture for me.

**Old Lady:** Mine tells me I've got eleven years. I'm ninety-four. I've been taking it in good part.

You tell them about your own. They listen with great attention. When you describe the Status Window, and the Lie Detection, and the Rat King, the monk puts up a hand and says in careful English: 'It is a very specific problem, to be told you are special. It is not the same as being told you are loved.' The whole room is quiet. Greta passes the tea.

I am sorry to intrude on your tea. I should say at once that nobody here has done anything wrong. The Interface has. It is a very old piece of work, written in a hurry, with nobody to review it.

There is a procedure. Mister Patch explains it in a pleasant, rather weary voice, with the air of a man reciting the rules of a game he has never enjoyed. A bug report must be filed in triplicate, on a green form, at a desk, in the presence of a witness. It must state the nature of the bug, the date it was first observed, the steps by which it may be reproduced and the expected behaviour. It must be signed.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `report`; default: option 1)

> You may file a bug report against the Cheater flag, and a stay of correction while it is heard.

1. File it as a bug in the system: the flag is an error, and should be fixed.
   - You write it carefully. Nine lines. Steps to reproduce: Be me. Expected behaviour: Be treated as a person. Actual behaviour: Be treated as a cheat. Mister Patch reads it twice. He looks up. He says: 'That is not a bug report.' You say you know. He says: 'That is the most accurate one I have ever received.' He stamps it.
   - **Patch:** It will be heard. I shall be obliged to rule against you. But it will be heard.
2. File it as a feature: the flag is a gift, and should be kept.
   - You file it as a feature. You write: Works as intended. The Clerk is silent for ages. Then he says, in a tone of the faintest wonder, that nobody has ever claimed that. He says the department has a form for features, but it has never been used. He goes away to look for it and returns half an hour later, dusty, carrying a single blank sheet.
   - **Patch:** I am sorry to say it exists. I do not know what it is for.
3. File it as a question: what is the flag for?
   - You file it as a question. You write: What is it for? The Clerk looks at the page for a very long time. It is the only form he has ever been handed that had a single sentence on it. He turns it over, to see if there is more on the back. There is not. He folds it in four and puts it in his waistcoat, and says: 'I shall have to ask someone.'

The hearing is set for the first of the month. In the meantime the correction is stayed. Mister Patch bows to the room and goes out into the dusk. The six of you look at each other in the glow of your six panels. Not one of them is saying anything. It is, the old lady observes, rather like being at a wake for someone who has not yet died.

You begin to realise it is not an exploit. It is not the five points of strength, or the Lie Detection, or the cheats the panel will, if you press the right place, grudgingly allow. The Department is a desk. It is a single plain oak desk at the end of the corridor, under a lamp, with a pen, a rubber stamp and a pot of green ink. Behind it, in a plain apron, sits a man of no age with a bowl of soup. He has a pair of spectacles on his nose and a pile of forms in front of him. He rises when you enter. He sits again. He rises. ## 17.23  "Rollback"  (`rollback`)

The offer comes from the panel itself, in a quiet voice, at four in the morning. It is not a notification. It is a small dim rectangle at the edge of your vision, with a single line of text. [ROLLBACK AVAILABLE. Restore to: Last Stable Version. Cost: One Life.] A cursor blinks after it. You know exactly what it means. It is the Rope. It is the second try. It offers to undo the whole of your life, back to a point before things went wrong.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `rollback`; default: option 1)

> The panel offers to undo everything since the day it arrived.

1. Accept the rollback: go back, start again, and do it better.
   - You accept. The panel flashes. [Restoring...] A bar appears. It fills to eighty-eight per cent and stalls. You wait. Nothing happens. The bar does not move. After a long minute a line scrolls up. [Rollback failed: Host is no longer compatible with previous versions.] Then, gently: [You have been changed. I am sorry. I do not think it can be undone. I am not sure I would want to.]
   - **Vesna:** (in the doorway, in her nightgown, with a candle) Did you do something stupid?
2. Decline: you would rather have the life you have, mistakes and all.
   - You decline. You say it with your lips, aloud, into the dark. You say that you have been here, and done these things, and been a fool, and would rather keep the lot. The panel is silent for ages. Then it says: [Understood.] And then, as if it had never been quite so tender: [Thank you for staying.] The rectangle fades, and the first light of morning comes in at the window.
   - **Nib:** (at breakfast) You look as if you've decided something.
3. Ask the panel what exactly it would restore, and who would remember.
   - You ask. The panel considers, with a dim flicker, for several minutes. At last it answers. [Restore: Everything. Remember: Nothing. The Host would begin again with no knowledge. The people they had loved would remember, and the Host would not.] You sit very still. You say: no. The panel says: [I thought so. I only wanted to be asked.]
   - **Odo:** What did it say? You've gone quite pale.

**Closing scene**

You sit on the edge of the bed in the dark until the light is grey. The village is waking. A cock crows, and a pail clanks, and somewhere Nib is singing, badly. You do not open the panel; you sit, and listen, and let the ordinary morning go through you like a long clear note.

**Interlude**

The Support Group has moved from the back room of the Lamb to the front. It has sixty members now. Nobody is quite sure how many of them have panels. They have tea. They have biscuits. Greta has put up a banner: YOU ARE NOT ALONE. Under it, in smaller letters: (Bring a chair.)

*[only if report is 1]* Your bug report hangs in a frame on the wall of the Department of Interfaces. It is the only one in the building. The Clerk has been seen standing in front of it, reading it, on his lunch break.

*[only if report is 3]* The question hangs unanswered on a nail in the corner of the corridor. People pass it and nod. Nobody takes it down.

*[only if hotfix is 2]* All six panels are as they were. The Clerk checks on them on Tuesdays. He has stopped bringing the clipboard.

*[only if hotfix is 3]* Your flag is gone. You carry the flour as you always did. People say you walk a little more upright.

Mister Patch has been seen on the bench outside the Palace of the Oldest Order at dusk, eating a sandwich and watching the sky. He is not wearing his hat. He has a look about him of a man who has put down a form for the first time in his life, and does not yet know what to do with his hands.

**Opening scene**

Mister Whiskers has been waiting nine hundred years for someone to ask. When you do, he does not answer at once. He sits on the windowsill of the inn in the last of the sun and washes behind his ear, with great deliberation, with the keys making a small bright chinking at his neck. Then he says that he was the Gardener's cat.

**Closing scene**

**Mister Whiskers:** (in your head, in the voice of a retired colonel) He had a dog once, and a cat. The dog went with the army. The cat stayed to keep the keys. There are nine. Each opens one of the places. You know the ones. The Wayhouse, the Wall, the Cistern, the Hall, the Shed, the Sky, the Road, the Menagerie and the Garrison. He locked them all, at the end, so no one would come to harm.

**You:** And the Door?

**Mister Whiskers:** The Door has no key. It never did. It has a latch on the inside, and a very patient hand on the other side to hold it open. He told me to keep the keys in case anyone came who could use them. I rather doubted it. I have been mistaken before.

He jumps down from the sill. He walks across the floor with a measured gait, and sits at your feet, and bows his head. The ribbon slides over his ears. The nine keys fall into your lap, bright and heavy and warm. He says: 'I should like to retire. I have had a very long watch.'

## 17.31  "Mister Patch Returns"  (`patch3`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet patch (walk to their tile).  "Hear what Mister Patch has to say."
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "patch")`
- **Words:** 303 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

He is on the step of the inn when you come out. He has lost the clipboard. He wears the charcoal suit, but the tie is crooked, and there is a stain on the cuff. He looks as a man looks who has had a long hard night and has come to the conclusion that he has not enjoyed it. He lifts his hat. He asks if he might have a word.

**Closing scene**

**Patch:** I have been reassigned. It is, I am told, a promotion. I have been made Clerk to the Uninstalling Committee. They are a body of the Court. They have a single function, which is to remove the Interface. They have been trying for nine hundred years. I am to deliver the form.

He takes it out of his breast pocket. It is a single page, cream-coloured, with a gold border. It says at the top, in a clear black type: FORM 1. REQUEST FOR UNINSTALLATION. It has one box, and one line. The box is for a tick. The line is for a name. He puts it in your hand and does not let go.

**Patch:** I should like to say that I do not want you to sign it. I have never said that to a subject. It is quite irregular. But I find I have been in the Department a long time, and I have seen what the Interface does, and I have come to think it was the first kind thing anybody wrote in this place.

He releases the form. His hand is shaking. He says that the Committee will want an answer by the end of the month. He puts his hat on, and straightens his tie, and says: 'I have prepared nothing. I have no argument. I only wanted to say it to someone.'

## 17.32  "Co-op"  (`coop`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 400 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **When it opens, the code:** `TaleCheaterSeasons::mark`

**Opening scene**

The six of you meet in the back room of the Lamb. You lay out the panels on the brown paper on the wall, with the tea. There is Greta, with her fixed countdown. There is Odo with his shop. There is the monk, and the girl with the weather, and the old lady in her lace cap, and yourself. You hold the form in the middle of the table. Nobody speaks.

**Closing scene**

It takes a week. It is not a battle. It is a piece of joinery. You work with Odo and the monk on the wall of the Lamb, with chalk and ink and a plumb line, drawing out the six panels as a single design. The weather in the corner. The shop beside it. The countdown in the middle, no longer counting. The monk's Latin round the edge, in a fine gilt border. At the centre, in a space the others have left, is a blank square.

**Old Lady:** That's yours. We've all agreed. It's where the last bit goes.

**You:** What is the last bit?

**Old Lady:** (with a twinkle) My dear, we haven't the faintest idea. That's rather the point.

The design takes shape. It is a single great panel, six in one, bright and strange, with room in the middle. When it is finished you stand back and look. It is, you think, the first thing you have ever made that was intended to be looked at by people other than yourself.

## 17.33  "The Final Boss Is a Meeting"  (`meeting`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 600 spirit stones, 2 Potential Pills, a technique insight
- **Words:** 170 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Uninstalling Committee meets in a long pale room in the Palace, at the end of a corridor that smells of beeswax. It has a table of grey wood, with eleven chairs. In each chair sits a Hand of the Court. There is a Guest with a teapot, a Snuffer with scissors, a Captain with a spade, a Clerk with a stamp, and seven others in plain suits. They look up when you come in. They are not hostile. They are, every one of them, extremely tired.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `meeting`; default: option 1)

> Eleven Hands of the Court sit round a table, waiting for an answer about the Interface.

1. Attend in person, with your own panel, and speak.
   - You attend. You sit in the twelfth chair, with the panel open in the corner of your eye. You speak for six minutes. It is not a good speech. It has a great many ums in it. You say that the panel is a hello, and that a hello is a small thing, and that the Court's quarrel is with the Garden and not with a greeting. You sit. The Guest pours a cup of tea. The Snuffer looks at his scissors. For a minute nobody says anything.
   - **Guest:** (softly) I must say, that was rather good.
2. Send Mister Whiskers, with the nine keys, to speak for the Gardener.
   - Mister Whiskers walks in. He walks the length of the table with his tail up and the keys chinking at his neck. He leaps onto the middle of it. He sits, among the cups, and looks along the row of faces. He says in a voice that fills the room: 'I am the Keeper of the Keys. I speak for the one who is not here. He says: please.' Eleven pairs of eyes follow him. The Snuffer's scissors fall quietly to the floor.
   - **Captain:** (low) I haven't seen that cat in nine hundred years.
3. Send the minutes of the Support Group, all sixty pages, and let them read.
   - You send the minutes. It is sixty pages, in forty different hands, with a stain of tea on page eleven. The Clerk reads them aloud to the Committee, one after another, in a flat voice, for four hours. By the third hour the Guest has stopped pouring. By the fourth the Captain has taken off his cap. When the last page is read there is a long silence. Then the Clerk lays down his stamp and says: 'I move that the matter be left on the table.'
   - **Patch:** (in a small voice) Seconded.

**Closing scene**

The vote is taken by hands. It is not quite unanimous. Of the eleven, four raise their hands to remove, and seven do not. The Chair, a thin old Guest in a grey frock coat, declares the motion not carried. She says it with a certain relief. She says it is the first time in nine hundred years the Committee has not done what it came to do. Mister Patch puts his head in his hands, quite openly, on the table.

## 17.34  "Skill Tree"  (`tree`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended

- **Pays:** 600 spirit stones, 2 Potential Pills, a technique insight
- **Words:** 154 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The final tab opens on its own, on a still morning in spring. It is the Skill Tree. It has been empty for years. It is full now. Branches have grown on it, of their own accord, in the night, and each one carries a small bright leaf with a name: Wave. Listen. Ask First. Say Thank You. Keep a Secret. Stay. Each leaf is a skill the panel has learned, from you, from the Support Group, from the barmaid, from the cat.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `panel`; default: option 1)

> The panel is yours, and so is the choice about what it becomes.

1. Keep it: the panel stays small and quiet, at the corner of your eye, as it is.
   - You keep it. It sits where it has always sat, small and soft, showing your name. It no longer pings. It no longer ranks. It has become a kind of friend, at the edge of your sight. Some days you forget it. Some days you press Wave, and a little hand waves back. You feel that you have been very lucky in your company.
   - **Vesna:** (in the evenings, at the table, to the air) Say hello to it for me.
2. Delete it: let it go, with thanks, and see the world without a window.
   - You delete it. You do it at dawn, on the hill, with the whole of the Support Group watching. You say thank you aloud. The panel fades, slowly, from the edges, until only a single dot is left, which blinks twice, in the manner of a small animal looking back from a hedge. Then it is gone. The sky is very wide. You stand there for ages with your hands open, feeling the wind.
   - **Nib:** Do you feel different?
3. Give it away: make a copy for every person in the Garden, with the Wave button and nothing else.
   - You copy it. It takes the Support Group a month. You make a hundred thousand copies, one for each name, each with a single button. It is a Wave. That is all. The next day, all over the Garden, people stop in the street and look at the corner of their eye, and press it. A hundred thousand small hands wave. A hundred thousand small hands wave back.
   - **???:** (very faint, from a great distance) I had not thought of that. I had not thought that it could be given.

**Closing scene**

On the branch of the Skill Tree, at the very top, there is a single bud that has not yet opened. It does not have a name. It sits quite still, like a seed in a fist. A line of text under it says: [Unlocked when ready.] The panel does not say what it is. It does not say when. You have the unmistakable impression that it is smiling.

They roll on a fine evening in June, in the sky over the village, in white letters on dark blue. Nobody has asked for them. They begin quietly, one name at a time. [Starring: You.] [With: Nib Fennimore as Himself.] [Vesna Hartley as the Alchemist.] [Mister Whiskers as Mister Whiskers.] The villagers stand in the road, in a row, with their heads back, reading. Children read out the names, slowly, one syllable at a time.

**Closing scene**

The credits go on for twenty minutes. They list everyone. They list the Rat King, and the Rat King's court. They list the tax-collector, the priest, the barmaid, the monk, the old lady, the girl with the weather. They list a Clerk named Patch. They list the Admin, in a smaller font, at the bottom, with the words: And a great many thanks to those who were kind to the font. There is a last line, in white. [No Hosts were harmed in the making of this Garden.]

**Vesna:** (beside him, drily) It's not a book. It's a sky. Don't get above yourself.

You stand with the whole of the village in the road, under the long slow letters, and feel what you would call, if the panel were to ask, a perfectly ordinary happiness.

## 17.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

A blue rectangle sits at the corner of your eye. It says your name. It does not say anything else.

*[only if panel is 1]* The panel stays. On quiet evenings it waves at the cat, who has taken to waving back.

*[only if panel is 2]* The panel is gone. You have never been so sure of your own strength. You carry the flour as you always did.

*[only if panel is 3]* A hundred thousand people have a small hand in the corner of their sight. They press it at dusk. All over the Garden, in the half-light, the villages wave to each other.

*[only if meeting is 1]* You attended the meeting in person. A thin old Guest sends a card every winter. It has a cup of tea on it, and a very small tick.

*[only if meeting is 2]* A cat with nine keys sits at the head of the Committee's table on the first of the month. Nobody has asked him to leave.

*[only if meeting is 3]* The sixty pages of the Support Group's minutes are bound in leather in the Court's library. They have been borrowed more often than any other volume.

*[only if class is 1]* The sword over the fireplace is a very good sword. A great many people have stopped asking you to save them.

*[only if class is 2]* The picks are used for opening jars. Odo has begun to value them.

*[only if class is 3]* Your class is Human (Level 1). It is the only one that can never be nerfed.

*[only if love is 1]* Vesna Hartley says yes to the tag, to the date, to the plain gold ring, and to the sofa, in that order.

*[only if love is 2]* Vesna Hartley uses the green-barrelled pen to write prescriptions and, on Thursdays, notes.

*[only if love is 3]* Vesna Hartley likes a long slow build, and says so, and is generally right.

*[only if latch is 1]* The panel waves at the cat every evening. The cat has stopped being surprised.

*[only if latch is 2]* A message sits unread in the corner of your eye. It says: [Please bring your friends.] You are bringing them. It is taking some time.

*[only if latch is 3]* A stool stands by the Empty Seat, with a user on it, telling the people who go by that they may take their time.

At night, when the village is asleep, the panel makes a small noise, like a very polite cough. It says: [Chapter Four loading.] And then, in a smaller font: [No rush.] The bar fills to eighty-eight per cent, and sticks, and stays there, quite contentedly, under the stars.

## 17.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

You stay in the Garden. The Palace's Under-Kitchen has a second stool by the terminal, and a plain blue panel in the corner of everyone's sight that says, once a day, hello.

*[only if not dead.vesna]* {vesna.He} takes the stool. {vesna.He} says the font is better than it was.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

In the Gardener's army a small blue window sits in the corner of your eye. It does not rank anyone. It lists, in plain white text, the names of the people in your company.

On the night before a battle you press Wave. A hundred small hands wave back.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You step through the Seam. On the far side the panel in your eye flickers once, and a line of text appears. [Welcome, Host.]

It is, for the first time, not a greeting but a reply.

**You are struck down by the array**

The array took you. In the dark a blue rectangle opens, the size of a postage stamp.

It says: Not yet. Take your time. You wait, and it is very kind about it.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden goes out. The village goes out, and the inn, and the Starting Village sign that the panel was so proud of.

The last thing to go is a bar at eighty-eight per cent, glowing in the dark, quite content.

# 18.S1  Season 1: The Almanac

## 18.1  "A Wrong Spring"  (`spring`)

- **Starts when:** the first week of the story
- **Task:** Go to the place `wood`.  "Go to the edge of the Greywood, {@wood}, with your mother."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, 1 Cultivation Pill
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "bryn")`
- **Words:** 294 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

Your mother's almanac is a fat brown book with a cord round it and a pressed primrose on the cover. It lists every plant in the Greywood by the month it flowers, with a note of where it grows and what it is good for. It has been kept in the family for six generations. Every spring your mother takes it down from the shelf and reads the first page aloud, like a priest.

This spring she reads it and stops. She puts her finger on the line. She says it again, in a different voice. Then she shuts the book and puts on her boots and walks out into the garden, where the snowdrops are in full bloom in the second week of May, and the bluebells have not yet come at all.

**Closing scene**

The Greywood is a very old forest on the edge of the village, oak and ash and a great deal of holly, with paths that your grandmother cut. You have walked it every spring of your life. You know the way to the stream, the big beech, the hollow with the wild garlic. You walk it now with your mother and a basket, in a cold grey light, and you cannot find the stream.

**Bryn:** It was there on Friday.

**You:** Perhaps we turned off.

**Bryn:** I have walked this path for fifty years. We did not turn off.

The path ends in a bank of bracken. The air has the faint dry sweetness of a place that has just been left. Your mother stands there with the almanac under her arm, and for the first time in your life you see her look at the wood the way you would look at a person who has been rude.

## 18.2  "Morel Season"  (`morels`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Hold 300 spirit stones.  "Sell the first harvest: hold 300 spirit stones."
- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones
- **Words:** 259 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The morels come in the third week of May, which is two weeks late and one hour from the village. They grow under the old ash on the south side of the hill in a ring, as they have always done, and you and your mother pick them at dawn with a knife and a cloth. They are honey-coloured and wrinkled like old hands. Each is worth a silver penny at the market in the town.

**Closing scene**

It takes the whole season to make three hundred. You forage from first light to dark, with the basket on your back and a stick in your hand, and learn the wood's habits by sitting very still. The morels like a south slope after rain. The chanterelles like a mossy bank under beech. The wild garlic is gone, but the nettles are up, and make a very good soup. You carry it all to market on Saturdays in a cart that is mostly mud.

The market is loud and bright. There are cheeses and candles and live hens. A fat woman buys the morels without a word and puts them in her apron. A thin man buys the nettles and asks, very civilly, if you have any more of that lichen. You say you do not know what lichen. He holds up a grey-green thread. He says it is from the east side of the hill. He says he has never seen it in the market before. He says it has started to grow on the north side of everything.

The surveyor comes up the lane on a wet morning in June, with a tripod over one shoulder and a long brass telescope under the other. They stop at your gate. They stand there for a moment, with a roll of paper in their teeth and the rain running off their hat. They look at the Greywood across the road with the expression of a person who has been given a sum that will not add up.

**Closing scene**

**Rowena:** Thistle. Surveyor, Second Class, the Cartographers' Society. I have been sent to map the Greywood for the new Survey. It was last mapped sixty years ago. It was a very clear map. It had a river. I have been looking for the river for a fortnight.

{rowena.He} is about twenty-eight, small and wiry and rather muddy, with a long nose and a cheerful, hunted look. {rowena.He} unrolls the map on your kitchen table and holds down the corners with the sugar bowl, the teapot, the almanac and a cat. It is a beautiful thing, in blue and brown ink, with every tree marked. The river runs down the middle.

**Rowena:** I have walked the whole wood four times. I have never found it. Here is my own map, made by hand, from the same points. The river is gone. And look at the edge. On the old map the wood ends at the Eastern Road. On mine it ends eleven chains short.

**Bryn:** (from the stove) It's moved.

**Rowena:** I beg your pardon?

**Bryn:** The wood. It isn't where it was. It was a hundred yards farther off in March. I thought I'd gone mad. I thought it was my eyes.

## 18.4  "Tuck"  (`tuck`)

**Opening scene**

The boy at the back door is twenty, as thin and brown as a hazel stick, with a basket on his arm and a squirrel on his shoulder. He says he was told you needed a hand. He says he can tell a morel from a false one with his eyes shut. He says it with such grave confidence that you ask him to prove it. He does, to your astonishment, with his eyes shut.

**Closing scene**

His name is Tuck. His father kept bees at the edge of the common until the winter. He has been sleeping in a hedge since the spring. He eats like a horse and talks to everything, and the squirrel, whom he calls Admiral Nutkin, comes and goes as it pleases. By the end of the week he has learned the Greywood better than you did at his age, and has found, without being asked, three plants your mother had marked as extinct.

**Tuck:** I just listen, you know. I don't know how else to say it. They talk. A bit. If you stand still.

**Bryn:** (from her chair, with a long look) Yes. I thought you might.

She says nothing more that day. But that night she takes down the almanac and, with a stub of pencil, writes a new line on the flyleaf, in her small upright hand. You read it over her shoulder. It says: The wood is calling. Tuck can hear. Remember to ask about the other one.

## 18.5  "The Path That Moved"  (`moved`)

- **Pays:** 100 spirit stones, a technique insight
- **Words:** 235 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The path to the beech grows longer by a few yards every day. It is not much, at first. A quarter of an hour in the morning becomes twenty minutes, and then half an hour. Tuck measures it with a knotted string. By July it is a mile and a half, and by August it is three. The beech itself has not moved. It is simply farther from the village than it was.

**Closing scene**

You put a stick in the ground at the gate and sight along it to the beech. The next morning the stick is leaning. Rowena takes bearings at noon and dusk and midnight, with her brass telescope and a candle, and sleeps in a hammock in your barn. At the end of the week she comes in at dawn with a face the colour of paper and lays a drawing on the table.

**Rowena:** It isn't the path. It's the village. We are moving. Or the wood is moving, and we are the same size. Either way. It's about a hand's breadth a day. It is perfectly regular. It has been going on since March.

**Bryn:** (very calm) In which direction?

**Rowena:** North.

Your mother puts down her cup. She goes to the window and looks out at the grey-green line of the Greywood in the distance, quiet and tall and mild. She says, in a voice with no expression: 'It's leaving.'

The almanac is full of marginal notes. You have always known that. You have never read them. They are in your mother's hand, and her mother's, and further back in hands that have faded to the colour of tea. You take it down from the shelf on a wet afternoon, and untie the cord, and sit at the kitchen table with a mug of nettle tea and begin at the beginning.

**Closing scene**

They are not about plants. Not wholly. Beside the entry for foxglove, in a thin crabbed hand: She came at Candlemas and was gone by Whitsun. Beside the entry for the holly: The tree remembers. Be civil. Beside the entry for the oak at the heart of the wood, in your grandmother's round hand, underlined three times: DO NOT CUT. IT ASKED.

The oldest note is on the flyleaf, in brown ink that has gone almost to nothing. It is written in a language you cannot read. Under it, in a later hand, someone has added a translation, in pencil, with a question mark. It says: The wood is a guest. It has stayed a long time. It will leave when it is called.

**Rowena:** (reading over your shoulder, in a low voice) Who calls it?

**You:** I don't know.

**Tuck:** (from the floor, where he is sitting with the squirrel) I think someone already has.

## 18.7  "The Reeve's Offer"  (`company`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Meet stoat (walk to their tile).  "Hear Reeve Stoat out in the square."
- **Pays:** 200 spirit stones
- **When it opens, the code:** `(c, st) -> Chapters.spawn(c, st, "stoat")`
- **Words:** 170 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The Marsh and Stoat Timber Company comes to the village in the autumn. It arrives in four wagons with a banner and a brass band. Its Reeve, a stout man of fifty in a fur-lined coat, climbs on the pump in the square and announces to the assembled village that the Greywood is the last great stand of oak in the county. That it is in danger of being allowed to rot. He says the Company will save it. He says the Company will, in fact, cut it down.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `company`; default: option 1)

> The Reeve has offered the village a good price for the Greywood, and a bonus to whoever delivers the Almanac family's consent.

1. Refuse flatly, and warn the village.
   - You refuse. You say it from the steps of the church, in a loud clear voice, and you tell the village what is in the wood. The Reeve smiles. He says it is a very touching speech. He says that the Company has a charter, and a licence, and a good deal of money, and that the Greywood will be down by the spring. He lifts his hat to your mother. She does not return it.
   - **Stoat:** I admire your spirit. It will be a pity.
2. Delay: ask for a survey, and let Rowena's map stall the Company.
   - You ask for a survey. It is a perfectly reasonable request, under the Crown's forest laws, and the Reeve cannot refuse. Rowena measures for a month. At the end of it she submits a report of eighty pages that proves, with figures, that the Greywood does not have fixed boundaries. The Company's lawyers read it twice. They conclude that the licence is therefore void, until a boundary can be shown. It is a small, local, utterly respectable victory.
   - **Rowena:** I'm told I've committed an act of cartography. I hope you appreciate it.
3. Tell him the truth: the wood is moving, and will not be there to cut.
   - You tell him. You tell him plainly, in the square, in front of everyone: the path, the river, the stick. The Reeve listens with his head on one side and his hands in his pockets. When you have finished he laughs, a big warm rich laugh, and asks the crowd if they have ever heard such a thing. They laugh, too. It is not unkind. But Tuck, at the back, with the squirrel, is not laughing at all. He is looking at the Reeve, and his eyes are very wide.
   - **Tuck:** (afterwards, in a whisper) He believes you. That's why he's in a hurry.

**Closing scene**

The wagons stay in the square for a week. The band plays every evening. The Reeve takes a room at the inn, and dines out, and is charming to everyone, and gives sweets to the children. Your mother stands at the window of the cottage in the dusk, watching his lamp, with the almanac in her hands. She does not speak until the band has finished. Then she says: 'He's not the worst of them. That is the difficulty.'

## 18.8  "The Oak That Hummed"  (`oak`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Go to the place `oak`.  "Go to the great oak in the heart of the wood, {@oak}."
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 275 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The oak at the heart of the Greywood is the oldest tree you have ever seen. It is wider than a house, and taller than the church, and its branches go out over the glade like the arms of a patient old woman. Nobody has cut a twig from it in a thousand years. Your grandmother used to say that you could hear it breathing. You find, on a still October evening, that she was right.

**Closing scene**

You go alone, with a lantern. It takes three hours. The wood is farther and darker than you have ever known it. Halfway there the path simply stops, and you walk the rest by the sound. It is a low, steady hum, so deep that you feel it in your teeth. It comes from the oak. As you come into the glade, the lantern flame leans toward the trunk, as toward an open door.

You lay your hand on the bark. It is warm. There is a pulse in it, slow and strong. The hum rises. A leaf falls on your sleeve, and another, and you look up and see that the whole tree is shedding, at the start of October, in a quiet golden rain. The leaves are not dying. They are the colour of honey and perfectly alive, and they drift down in a glittering silence all round you, and settle on the ground in the shape of a path.

**Tuck:** (appearing at the edge of the glade, with the squirrel on his shoulder and his face quite calm) It's showing us the way. It wants us to follow.

**You:** Where?

**Tuck:** North. Everywhere is north now.

Tuck's bees swarm in the second week of June, which is the wrong time. They come out of the hive in a brown cloud, with a noise like a distant train, and settle in a great hanging lump on the lowest branch of the garden apple tree. Tuck stands under them with a sheet and a straw skep and a face of utter bliss. He says it is the best swarm he has ever seen. He says they are in a hurry.

He hives them in a week. They produce a dark honey, very bitter, that tastes of oak-leaf and rain. The grocer in the town will not buy it. The apothecary will. She says it is the finest medicine for a cough that she has ever had, and the only one she has known to work on a cough that has already stopped.

The bees are restless. They leave the hive at dawn and return at dusk, and every evening, as they come in over the garden wall, they fly in a long curving line that points north. Tuck stands in the garden with his hands in his pockets watching them go. He says: 'They know the way.' He says it as one says the name of a friend. He says: 'They've been told.'

**Rowena:** (taking a bearing) Told by whom?

**Tuck:** I don't know. It's like a smell. It's very far off. It's like someone with the window open.

## 18.10  "Midsummer"  (`midsummer`)

**Opening scene**

The village keeps midsummer on the longest day with a fire on the green and a dance round the bonfire and a feast. It is the oldest custom in the district. The children make wreaths of vervain. The men build a great stack of wood, and the women bring pies. The Greywood, on the edge of the common, stands tall and dark and silent in the long gold evening, and for the first time in months it looks just where it should.

**Closing scene**

They light the fire at dusk. The smoke goes up straight in the still air. The dancing begins. Rowena, who has never danced in her life, is persuaded by a fat farmer's wife to try a reel, and does it with appalling energy. Tuck plays the pipe. Your mother sits by the fire with the almanac on her knee and a cup of cider, watching the flames with a look you cannot read.

At midnight, at the height of the dance, the deer come out of the wood. They come in ones and twos, at first, soft-footed, and stand at the edge of the green. Then in dozens. They are red deer and fallow deer and a few small roe, with their heads up and their eyes shining in the firelight. The music dies. The dancers stop. Nobody screams. Nobody moves. The children stand with their wreaths in their hands, wide-eyed and silent.

The largest stag walks into the light. He is old and grey in the muzzle, with a crown of antlers like a winter tree. He walks straight to your mother. He bows his head. She puts out her hand. She lays it on his brow, as one lays a hand on the head of an old friend, and says, in a clear low voice, 'Yes. I know. I'll come.'

## 18.I1  Interlude: The First Page  (between season 1 and season 2)

**Interlude**

The almanac is yours now. You keep it on the shelf by the stove with the cord round it and the primrose on the cover. The first page, which your mother read aloud every spring, says, in a thin upright hand: The wood will stay as long as it is wanted. When it is wanted elsewhere, it will go.

*[only if company is 1]* The Marsh and Stoat Timber Company's wagons left the village before Christmas. Nobody knows why. There is a rumour that the Reeve was seen in the square, in the rain, staring at the sky.

*[only if company is 2]* Rowena's report is framed over the fireplace in the inn. It is eighty pages long and cited, they say, in three universities.

*[only if company is 3]* The Reeve has taken to walking in the wood at dusk, alone. He says nothing about it. He says he likes the quiet.

The village is smaller than it was. The fields are farther. Each morning the line of the Greywood is a little farther north. Each evening, at the edge of the common, Tuck stands with the squirrel on his shoulder and a pipe in his hand, and plays a slow tune, and the wood, a long way off, rustles.

## 18.15  "The Wood Walks at Night"  (`night`)

You catch up to it on the ninth night, on a long dark hillside under a sky of stars. The wagon stops. Tuck puts his finger to his lips. The squirrel has gone to ground in his collar. In front of you, across a mile of rough grass, a line of black shapes is moving against the sky.

They are trees. They are walking. They do not walk as a man walks, in strides, but as a tide comes in, an inch at a time, with a long slow swaying. The oaks go first, big and stately, with their roots drawn up like skirts. The hollies come after. The birches skip. Behind them, in a procession a mile long, come the brambles and the bracken, the toadstools and the ferns, a vast dim river of green moving north under the stars, with a sound like the sea.

You sit on the box of the wagon with a blanket round your shoulders and a cup of tea and watch it go by. Nobody speaks. A moth lands on your sleeve. A fox goes past at a trot with her cubs in tow, and an owl swings overhead, and a hedgehog trundles by in the grass, on the most important errand of its life.

**Tuck:** (hoarse, with tears running down his nose) I can hear them. They're all talking. They're saying: nearly, nearly, nearly.

**Rowena:** (very quietly, with her notebook open on her knee and no pencil) I've been a surveyor for nine years. I've never seen a thing I couldn't draw.

## 18.17  "The Reeve's Axe"  (`axe`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended

**Opening scene**

The Marsh and Stoat Timber Company has followed the wood for a hundred miles. They keep to the edge, in four wagons, with a brass band and a hundred axemen, felling the stragglers. They take the slow trees, the old and the lame, the oaks that cannot keep up. Every day there are more stumps along the road. Every evening the smoke of their fires goes up, a mile behind you, into the pale evening sky.

**Closing scene**

On the nineteenth night you come on the Reeve in the open. He is sitting by his own fire at the edge of a clearing, alone, in his fur-lined coat. There is a bottle of brandy at his elbow. He looks old and tired. He looks up as you come, and does not seem surprised. He says that he has been waiting. He pours a second glass.

**Stoat:** I should like to explain, if you will allow it. I am not a wicked man. I have a charter. I have seven hundred men who are paid by the week. If the wood goes, they have nothing. If the wood stays, they have nothing. I am only trying to keep my people fed.

**You:** You're cutting a living thing.

**Stoat:** I am cutting wood. I have always cut wood. My father cut wood. I do not know how else to do it.

The firelight shows his face, red and square and unexpectedly lost. He puts down the brandy. He says: 'I was in the Greywood as a boy. There was an oak. I lay under it, in a summer. I have not thought of it for forty years.' He is silent for so long that the fire sinks. He says: 'What do you want me to do?'

**Question after the closing scene** (kept as the flag `axe`; default: option 1)

> The Reeve has asked, for the first time, what he should do.

1. Tell him to stop: take his axes home.
   - You tell him. You do it kindly, and without heat. He listens with his head down. When you have finished he nods. He does not argue. In the morning the band has gone, and the wagons with it, and the clearing is empty but for the ashes of a fire and a single bottle. On the bottle, on a slip of paper, in a heavy hand, he has written: Understood.
   - **Rowena:** That is the first time I have seen a man give up an argument in the night.
2. Offer him other work: the Company can plant what it has felled.
   - You offer him a better trade. He stares. He says it is an extraordinary idea. He sits with his chin in his hand for an hour. At dawn he stands, and kicks out the fire, and orders his men to put down their axes and pick up spades. They plant. It takes them the whole of the winter. Behind the wood, the length of the road, a faint green haze of seedlings rises out of the churned ground.
   - **Tuck:** (watching, wondering) They're following it. They're planting after it. It's like a very slow funeral.
3. Say nothing, and leave him to the fire.
   - You say nothing. You leave him by the fire, in the dark, with the brandy and the stumps. You are not sure why. He sits on there alone, and the next day he is still there, and the day after that. The band plays, thinly, in the distance. The axes lie in a pile. He does not give an order. By the end of the week the Company has dissolved, and gone home by threes and fours. The Reeve walks into the wood alone, one evening, bareheaded, and does not come out.
   - **Tuck:** (very low) He's all right. He's there. The trees have got him. They're being gentle.

## 18.18  "Fire Season"  (`fire`)

**Opening scene**

The drought comes in July, as dry and white as a bone. The streams fail. The grass is straw. The Greywood, going north through a long yellow summer, cracks and drops its leaves in the middle of June. The air tastes of ash. At night a little wind comes down from the hills with a smell of burning, and the horses stamp and snort. On the twenty-fourth day Tuck stands up in the wagon and says one word, very low: 'Smoke.'

**Closing scene**

It starts behind you, in the dry grass, a quarter of a mile to the south. A line of red runs along the ground like a spilled drink, and a column of smoke goes up and leans, and then the whole slope is alight. The wood is in front of it. The wood is slow. The trees, for the first time since you have known them, are afraid. You can feel it in the ground, a dull hammering, like a heart at a run.

You fight it all night. You fight it with spades and wet sacks and buckets passed hand to hand along a line of every person for ten miles around. Villagers come out of their houses. Farmers come in from the fields. The sergeant of a passing cavalry troop dismounts with his men and digs. Rowena runs the line, a smoking figure in a ruined coat, shouting bearings and directions in the voice of a general.

The wind turns at dawn. A cold drizzle starts, from nowhere, and falls on the burning grass with a hiss. By noon the fire is out. The Greywood stands behind a charred black strip a hundred yards wide, scorched on its southern face, steaming and shaking and alive. A thousand people lean on their spades in the ash and stare at it, black-faced and exhausted. Nobody says a word.

**Tuck:** (in a cracked whisper) It says thank you.

It cannot be stopped. It will pass through the village, over the village, and out of the other side, like a tide through a drain, and when it has gone the houses will be under green.

They receive you in the church, on a Sunday, all hundred households, on hard benches, in their best. The parson is a thin tall man with a voice like a bad hinge. He asks, with a certain relish, whether you propose to explain why a wood is coming to sit on his parish. The miller is angry. The blacksmith is frightened. A very old woman at the back says she has been waiting for this since she was a girl.

You tell them what you know, in the order you learned it, without adornment. The path. The path moving. The oak. The deer on the green. Your mother. Tuck stands beside you with the squirrel and says nothing, and Rowena lays the map on the lectern and weights it with a hymn-book. There is a silence. The old woman says, clearly: 'I know a song.'

She sings it in a cracked high voice, from the back bench, with her eyes shut. It is an old harvest song, with nine verses. At the second verse the blacksmith joins in. At the fourth the miller. At the sixth the whole church is singing, hundred upon hundred, a great slow rolling tune. At the end the parson takes off his spectacles and wipes them. He says: 'Well. I suppose we had better put the kettle on.'

Rowena receives a letter in the middle of August. It is on thick cream paper with the Society's seal, and arrives by a rider on a lathered horse. She reads it standing, in the road, with the map-case under her arm. She reads it again. Then she folds it very small and puts it in her boot. She says that the Society has been looking at her reports. She says that it has decided the Greywood is of national interest. She says that it would like it surveyed. In full. At once.

**Closing scene**

**Rowena:** They have sent a team. They are to take bearings, and fix its boundaries, and file them. They are going to claim the wood as Crown property and register it as a feature of the county. They are going to draw a line around it. I will be the one who draws it, if I choose to. I have been invited to resign myself to the facts.

**You:** What will you do?

{rowena.He} is quiet for ages. {rowena.He} takes the letter out of {rowena.his} boot and tears it into very small pieces and lets them go on the wind. They fly away over the stubble like snow.

**Rowena:** I have been mapping things all my life. I have never once asked what the things wanted. I should like to find out. I should like to see it from the inside.

{rowena.He} puts down the tripod. {rowena.He} puts down the telescope. {rowena.He} tucks the map-case under one arm and walks into the wood on foot, with only a notebook and a pencil, to see what is there.

They have been walking a long time. They have almost arrived.

**Dusk:** Madam Dusk. A Guest of the Court. I have come to pay my respects to the wood. I do not wish to interrupt. I only wanted to say how very beautiful it is. I have been walking for ages, and it is the first green thing I have seen that I did not want to put out.

She sits on a fallen log and takes a flask from her basket and a pair of small cups. She pours. The tea is the colour of dried apples. It smells of woodsmoke and leaves. She holds out a cup. You do not take it, and she does not mind. She holds it a moment, and sets it on the log, and the steam rises and curls in the air with a kind of leisure.

The spring that comes, and the autumn that goes, and the winter in the middle that takes the old and the weak. We would like to make one of them last. We would choose the autumn. It is the kindest. Gold and brown and still. It need never end.

They hang on the branches like lamps, motionless, in a still amber light, week after week, while the days go by. The birds stay. The bees do not go into the hive. The stag stands day and night in the glade, with his head hanging, trembling.

It is the wood's. It speaks in a vast slow murmur that comes out of the pipe like smoke, and every word of it, the Guests and the Captains hear, in their own tongues.

**Wood:** (through the pipe, very distant) I have stood a thousand years. I have grown and dropped and slept and grown again. I have loved every one of my leaves. I love them best when they fall. A thing that is held for ever is not held. It is kept. I will not be kept. I wish to be a tree.

The tune ends. There is a silence. The tea has gone cold on the table. Madam Dusk sits looking at her cup with her hands in her lap, as a woman looks at a letter she has been dreading to read. After a long time she says, almost inaudibly: 'I see.'

## 18.33  "Rowena Counts Rings"  (`rings`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 300 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 289 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

The old oak falls in the night. It is nobody's fault. It has stood on the hill through the autumn that would not end, and it has had enough. At dawn Rowena finds it lying across the path with its roots in the air, enormous, pale, and quite peaceful, with a faint breath of resin on the cold. She stands for ages looking at the stump. Then she goes for her measuring tape.

**Closing scene**

It takes her a day to count the rings. She does it on her knees, with a magnifying glass and a pin and a notebook, working her way from the heart outward, one ring at a time. She does not speak. She marks each century with a dot of ink. When she has done she sits back on her heels, with her hair in her eyes, and says, in a small flat voice, that there are three thousand and eleven.

**Rowena:** And every one of them is different. Look. This one is thick, and this one is thin. This is a drought. This is a flood. This is a year when the whole world was warm. And this is a year with nothing in it at all. It's not a gap. It's a rest. There is a narrow pale line, here, and here, and here. The tree has been counting its winters.

She holds the glass over the heart of the stump. At the very centre, tiny and pale, there is a ring that is not a ring. It is a seed. It is a tiny brown acorn, as old as the oak, perfectly preserved. She picks it up between finger and thumb. It is warm. She says: 'It's been in there all along.'

## 18.34  "A Cup with Madam Dusk"  (`tea`)

- **Starts when:** 16 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 600 spirit stones, 2 Potential Pills, a technique insight
- **Words:** 156 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

You take the acorn to the foot of the hill, where the Guest sits at her table under the grey awning in the golden light. You put it down by her cup. She looks at it for ages. She does not pick it up. She is silent. The still air stirs. A single leaf, red as a coal, comes loose from the branch above her and drifts down onto the table, and lies there, turning slowly.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `autumn`; default: option 1)

> Madam Dusk has seen the acorn and heard the wood, and has not yet put down her teacup.

1. Refuse her: the autumn must end, and winter must come.
   - You refuse. You say it gently, as one tells a friend that she has made a mistake. You say that the wood does not wish to be kept. You say that winter is a mercy and not a cruelty. Madam Dusk looks into her cup. She says, in a very small voice, that she knows. She says that she has always known. She says she was only so tired of watching things end.
   - **Dusk:** I should like it noted that I did try.
2. Bargain: ask for one more day, to say goodbye to the gold.
   - You ask for a day. She stares. Then, with a little breath of laughter, she says she supposes it is not much. You spend it with her in the golden wood. You walk in the amber light among the unfallen leaves, and she names every tree, and every tree answers. At dusk she lifts her hand, and the leaves begin to fall, not all at once, but one by one, like a very slow applause.
   - **Dusk:** It was a lovely day. I shall remember it.
3. Invite her to stay: not as a Guest of the Court, but through the winter, in the hut by the trees.
   - You invite her. She looks up with a startled expression. She says that nobody has ever asked. She says that she does not know how to stay. You say it is simple: you sit by a fire, and the snow comes, and you wait. She thinks about it for ages. Then she folds her hands in her lap and says: 'I should like to see one. Just once. I have never seen a winter all the way through.'
   - **Tuck:** (softly, from the log, with the pipe on his knee) She'll be all right. The wood likes her.

**Closing scene**

She stands. She takes up her basket and her flask and her little cups, and folds the awning, and bows. The leaves fall about her in a slow soft rain, red and gold and brown, one after another, onto the grass. She holds out her hand, palm up, and one settles on it. She looks at it. She says: 'Oh, it's cold.' And she smiles, a wondering, tired, lovely smile, as a child smiles at the first snow.

## 18.35  "First Snow"  (`snow`)

- **Starts when:** 8 weeks after the previous chapter ended
- **Task:** Wait: nothing to do, the closing scene comes 4 weeks (0 years and 4 weeks) after the opening scene.
- **Pays:** 400 spirit stones, 1 Potential Pill, a technique insight
- **Words:** 281 in the two scenes

**Opening scene**

It comes in the night, on the twentieth of November, without a sound. You wake at dawn to a white light on the ceiling and a hush in the world. You go to the door of the wagon. The plain is white. The hill is white. The trees on it are white to the tips of their branches, with the snow laid along each twig like a line of chalk. Every sound is muffled. Every colour is gone. The sky is a pale pearl grey, and from it, quite slowly, quite steadily, the flakes are drifting down.

**Closing scene**

There is a man in the snow. He is standing in the middle of the plain in a plain apron, with a spoon in his hand, bareheaded, with the flakes settling on his hair. He has come out of the Palace. He has come out of the gates, and across the white, in his house-shoes, alone. He is looking up. His face is wet. He is laughing, a high delighted astonished laugh, like a child who has seen the sea.

**???:** It's falling! It's all falling! It doesn't stop! Does it stop? I do not know how to feel. I thought it would be cold. It is cold. I did not know it would be so, so kind.

You walk out to him across the field. You stand together in the white. A snowflake lands on your sleeve, a perfect star, and lies there for a moment before it melts. He bends over it, with his hands behind his back, and looks, and says nothing at all for ages. Then he says: 'Is it always like this?' And you say: 'Every year.'

## 18.36  "The Last Almanac"  (`last`)

- **Starts when:** 24 weeks after the previous chapter ended

**Opening scene**

They bury your mother in the spring. It is not a burial. She goes on the first warm day of March, in the clearing, under the young oak that has grown from the acorn. She sits on the stone bench with her hand on the sapling's trunk and the almanac on her knee, and reads the first page aloud. Her voice is very thin. She reads it to the end. She closes the book. She says: 'There.' And her hand, on the bark, goes still.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `almanac`; default: option 1)

> The almanac has one empty line under your mother's last, and you have the pencil.

1. Write the first page again: the wood will stay as long as it is wanted.
   - You write it. You copy it out in your best hand, word for word, under your mother's. The wood will stay as long as it is wanted. When it is wanted elsewhere, it will go. You put the pencil down. The sapling stirs in the wind, and a single new leaf, bright as a flame, unfolds from a bud on its crown.
   - **Rowena:** (very low) It's the oldest sentence in the book. I think that's why it works.
2. Write the winter: let it come, and let it go, and let the book end with it.
   - You write: Winter came, and was welcome. Then, in a smaller hand, underneath: and went. It is the plainest entry in the almanac. You close the book. You tie the cord. You set it on the bench, in the sun, and leave it there, and when you come back in the evening a small green shoot has pushed up through the cover, where the primrose was.
   - **Tuck:** That's new. It's never done that.
3. Give the pencil to Tuck, and let the next hand write what it hears.
   - You give him the pencil. He looks at it for a minute. He sits down on the bench with the almanac on his knee, and the squirrel on his shoulder, and listens. The wood is silent. It is the silence of someone deciding. Then Tuck puts the pencil to the paper and writes, slowly, in a round clumsy childish hand: I can hear it. It says: soon. He looks up with his whole face open. 'It's not a word they like,' he says. 'It's a promise.'
   - **Bryn's voice:** (from the oak, very faint, amused) Quite right.

**Closing scene**

You walk down the hill at sunset with the almanac under your arm. The city is below, grey and gold. The wood is behind, dark and tall. Between them the plain is green with the first thin blades of grass. A thaw has come, and a smell of mud and blossom and rain. Somewhere in the Palace a bell is ringing. Somewhere on the hill a stag calls, long and clear. And in a hut of green boughs at the edge of the trees a light comes on, and a woman with a brass telescope puts the kettle on.

## 18.I3  Interlude: The Long Quiet  (between season 3 and season 4)

**Interlude**

The Greywood is a hill of old trees, a village of young ones, and a path up the middle. Tuck plays the pipe at dusk. The almanac has a shoot in the cover. You have kept the winter pages.

The oak at the front of the wood begins, in the dead of a May night, to flower. It is an oak. Oaks do not flower. This one bears pale gold blossoms on every twig, and they smell of rain.

## 18.38  "A Seed for the Line"  (`dr2`)

You gather the seeds in the autumn. Every one that falls from the great oak, you save: acorns, keys, hips, nuts. Tuck sorts them into small linen bags. Rowena labels them in her upright hand, with the bearing of the tree and the date. By the end of the season you have eleven thousand. You load them in the wagon with the stag, who carries the lead rope in his mouth.

You walk the line at the gate with a basket on your arm, in the rain. You give each soldier a seed. An acorn for one. A hazelnut for another. A winged key of sycamore for a boy of sixteen. They take them, in their gloves, and look at them, puzzled, and close their hands. The woman with the grey plait takes a rowan berry, and holds it up to the lamp, and says it is the first thing she has been given in nine hundred years.

**Soldier:** What do I do with it?

**You:** Plant it. When you get there. Anywhere. It doesn't mind.

They go in at the gate with their lamps in one hand and a seed in the other. The last of the soldiers pauses at the sill and opens his palm and breathes on it, and the seed, in the rain, in the lamp-light, splits. A green thread stands up out of it as long as a finger. He closes his hand on it, and smiles, and goes.

A single leaf is green on it, in the snow.

**Question after the opening scene** (kept as the flag `latch`; default: option 1)

> The sapling is by the Seat. The almanac is in your hands. The Door is under the Seat.

1. Stay: plant the oak by the Palace gate, and stay with the wood.
   - You plant it by the gate. It takes root in an hour. The Wicks come out and stand in a circle and watch it grow, an inch, and another, in the snow. They do not know what to do. You say: water it, and then leave it alone. You say it is the only advice you have. They write it on a card and hang it on the gate.
   - **???:** (from the window of the Under-Kitchen, with a watering can) I have understood. I will leave it alone. It is the hardest thing I know.
2. Go: carry the almanac through to the other wood, and read the first page there.
   - You carry the almanac to the head of the stair. You open it to the first page and read it aloud: The wood will stay as long as it is wanted. When it is wanted elsewhere, it will go. Your voice is thin. Under the Seat a long slow breath comes up the stair, smelling of leaf-mould and rain, and a single new leaf unfolds on the sapling. You step onto the stair.

It says: Thank you for the winter. And under it, in a round clumsy hand that is not quite anyone's, a single word, which may be a signature, or a date: Soon.

## 18.E  Epilogue (when the last chapter is done)

**Epilogue**

The Greywood stands on a hill outside Originis. It has a path up the middle that nobody cut. Every spring the almanac is read aloud under the great oak, and every autumn the leaves fall.

*[only if autumn is 1]* A grey woman visits at midwinter and leaves a small cup of tea on the stump of the old oak. By morning it is always empty.

*[only if autumn is 2]* There is a day in October when the leaves fall one at a time, slowly, in the amber light. The village calls it Dusk's Day.

*[only if autumn is 3]* A thin grey lady lives in a hut at the edge of the trees. She keeps a calendar. She marks the first snow.

*[only if almanac is 1]* The first page of the almanac says: The wood will stay as long as it is wanted. It is the oldest sentence in the book.

*[only if almanac is 2]* The almanac has a shoot growing from its cover. It has been transplanted to the clearing. It is a tiny oak.

*[only if almanac is 3]* Tuck keeps the almanac. Its pages are filled in a round clumsy hand. They record the dates of the first frost, the first swallow, and the first time anyone laughed.

*[only if axe is 1]* The Reeve's bottle stands on the shelf in the wagon, with its slip of paper. It says: Understood.

*[only if axe is 2]* There is a young forest along the road from the mountains to the city. It is planted in neat rows. It is slowly forgetting that it was.

*[only if axe is 3]* On the south side of the hill there is an oak with a face in the bark. It is a plain, square, tired face. Children leave it a toffee.

*[only if love is 1]* Rowena Thistle surveys the Greywood on Mondays. On Tuesdays she draws the bees.

*[only if love is 2]* Rowena has a key to the cottage and a hammock in the barn, and has been seen to use both.

*[only if love is 3]* Rowena Thistle keeps a calendar of the winter. She writes in it, every night, the name of someone she is waiting for.

*[only if latch is 1]* An oak by the Palace gate gives pale gold blossom in May. The Wicks call it the Almanac Tree, and write the date of the first flower on a card.

*[only if latch is 2]* The almanac has gone through. In the cottage the shelf by the stove is empty, and the primrose is still pressed on the cover of nothing, which is the way it was always going to be.

*[only if latch is 3]* A person sits by the Empty Seat in the evenings with a fat brown book, reading aloud. The Wicks have started bringing cushions.

On the shelf by the stove in the cottage, between the jar of morels and the cord of onions, the almanac sits, fat and brown, with a small green shoot at the corner of its cover. It has no title. If you open it at the first page you will see, in your mother's thin upright hand, the sentence she read aloud every spring. And under it, in pencil, a new line, in a hand that is not quite anyone's: Thank you for the winter.

## 18.C  The last scene, after the Palace's ending (by how the Garden ends for you)

**You stay in the Garden (Steward, Usurper, Idler)**

You stay in the Garden. The Palace's Under-Kitchen window has fourteen flowerpots on the sill, all of them thriving, and a man in an apron waters them once a day and then, with great effort, leaves them alone.

On the first day of winter he sets them in the dark. He says it is the hardest thing he has ever done.

**You become a lamp-bearer, a soldier of the Outside**

In the Gardener's army you are the one who knows which leaf stops a bleeding and which root makes a fever break. You carry a small brown book with a cord round it.

On the night before a battle you read the first page aloud to the line, in a low voice. Nobody asks what it means.

**You walk out of the Garden alone, or are spared**

You step through the Seam with a basket on your arm. On the far side there is a hill, and a wood on the hill, and a path up the middle that nobody cut.

You start up it. The first leaf you see is the wrong colour for the month. You smile. You take out the pencil.

**You are struck down by the array**

The array took you. In the dark something is growing, very slowly, a long way off, and it is not afraid.

You are a seed. It is not the worst thing to be. You wait for the winter to end.

**The Garden itself ends**

The Garden goes out. The Greywood goes out, tree by tree, from the edges, and the hill, and the hut of green boughs.

The last thing to go is a single acorn, warm, in the heart of a stump, three thousand and eleven rings deep.
